title: UNHCR Afghanistan Situation Regional Update July 2026
content:
Operational Update

Afghanistan’s operating environment in July remained fluid, as large-scale returns from Pakistan and Iran continued alongside heightened regional tensions and insecurity in several parts of the country. Afghanistan–Pakistan tensions escalated during the first half of the month amid reported armed clashes, shelling and airspace violations along the border. Although major cross-border incidents eventually subsided, bilateral relations remained tense. Increased armed opposition activity, including clashes in Badakhshan and elsewhere, also raised concerns over further internal displacement. Administrative and operational constraints affected access and programme delivery, including changes to the delivery of women-focused activities in Herat that resulted in the temporary pause of some programmes.

In Iran, increased deportations and returns of Afghan nationals continued alongside intensified enforcement against undocumented Afghans, documentation renewal challenges and deteriorating socioeconomic conditions. Military strikes and damage to transport and logistics infrastructure also disrupted access, supply chains and commercial activity. In Kerman, Sistan and Baluchestan, reinforced border security measures and risks along irregular routes heightened protection concerns, including for those attempting to cross under dangerous circumstances. Despite the volatile environment, UNHCR maintained its operational presence across Tehran, Mashhad, Shiraz, Kerman and the Dogharoun border, supporting protection monitoring, documentation and assistance.

In Pakistan, enforcement against Afghan nationals without valid visas intensified from 10 July following a Government directive to accelerate implementation of the existing ‘Illegal Foreigners Repatriation Plan’ (IFRP). Arrests, detention, raids and deportations were reported while landlord pressure and evictions added to uncertainty among Afghan communities. Fear of these measures remained a key factor influencing decisions to leave. Afghan students with Proof of Registration cards were also reportedly arrested and deported despite advocacy. Enforcement by authorities was particularly pronounced in Balochistan and Sindh and concerns over possible removal persisted in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Islamabad/Rawalpindi where enforcement was less uniform. Security measures at Torkham and ongoing tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan at the border also impacted cross-border movement and humanitarian access. ¹

title: Indonesia Flores Earthquake Response - DREF Operation (MDRID029)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
15-08-2026

What happened, where and when?

Magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck Flores Island in East Nusa Tenggara Province. According to the Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG), the earthquake was centred offshore at 8.41°S and 121.39°E, approximately 30 kilometres north-east of Mbay, Nagekeo District, at a depth of 15 kilometres. The earthquake was associated with activity along the Flores Back-Arc Thrust.

Following the earthquake, BMKG issued a tsunami warning for several coastal areas. Sea-level changes were observed at several monitoring locations, including approximately 0.94 metres at Maurole in Ende District. The tsunami warning was lifted at approximately 07:30 WIB after BMKG confirmed that the threat had ended. However, frequent aftershocks continued to affect the area. As of 16 August 2026 at 15:00 WIB, BMKG had recorded 995 aftershocks ranging from magnitude 1.9 to 6.2, of which 46 were felt by communities.

The earthquake affected seven districts across Flores Island: West Manggarai, Manggarai, East Manggarai, Ngada, Nagekeo, Ende and Sikka. Earthquake impacts and population evacuations were also reported in Bima, West Nusa Tenggara Province, and the Selayar Islands, South Sulawesi Province.

Landslides, damaged roads and debris continued to restrict access to several affected communities. The Larantuka–Maumere route had reopened, while the Ende–Nagekeo route remained reportedly cut off. Efforts to clear affected roads and establish alternative access routes were ongoing. Electricity and telecommunications services had largely begun to recover, although repairs were still required in several locations. Continued aftershocks were also affecting assessment, evacuation and emergency service delivery.

title: Honduras Drought Assessment 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRHN028)
content:
Description of the Event
Date when the trigger was met
20-07-2026
What happened, where and when?

Since May 2026, Honduras has been facing a progressive deterioration in climatic conditions associated with the delay in the start of the rainy season, the irregular distribution of rainfall, high temperatures, and the influence of the El Niño phenomenon.

According to the Center for Atmospheric, Oceanographic and Seismic Studies (CENAOS), during May precipitation deficits of more than 50% were recorded in sectors of the center and south of the country; In June, the impact extended to municipalities in the center and east, with deficits of more than 40%, conditions that persisted during the first half of July. These developments have increased the risk of meteorological drought, potentially affecting water availability, agricultural production and the livelihoods of the most at-risk communities. (2) Faced with this scenario, on August 18, 2026, the Secretary of State in the Offices of Risk Management and National Contingencies (COPECO), through Alert Bulletin No. 028-2026, declared a Red Alert for 75 municipalities due to drought associated with the El Niño phenomenon, located in the departments of Choluteca, Comayagua, El Paraíso, Francisco Morazán, La Paz and Valle; likewise, it declared a Yellow Alert for 71 municipalities and a Green Alert for 88 municipalities. The alerts were issued indefinitely. COPECO recommended that the population make responsible use of water, stay informed through official channels and heed the recommendations of the authorities. (6)

The CENAOS Seasonal Climate Outlook for the period August-November 2026 indicates the continuity of warm conditions associated with the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon, accompanied by above-normal temperatures and an uneven geographical distribution of rainfall. For August, particularly important rainfall deficits are projected in the south, southwest and some sectors of the center of the country. A partial recovery is expected in September, although negative anomalies could persist in areas of the south, east and center-east. For October, the outlook maintains deficits over large areas of the national territory, while in November there could be a partial and differentiated recovery. (2)

These climatic conditions occur in a context of pre-existing food vulnerability. The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) analysis identifies areas and stocks exposed to potential deterioration in food security, while FEWS NET also identifies unfavourable climatic conditions and risks to livelihoods and food security in areas of the Dry Corridor. (3) (4) The combination of poor rainfall, high temperatures and increased evapotranspiration could progressively reduce soil moisture, affect the establishment and development of crop crops, increase pressure on community water sources and systems, and deteriorate the livelihoods of households that depend on rainfed agriculture and small-scale livestock production. (2) (3) (4)

In this context, and considering that there are still gaps in primary information on the magnitude, location, and characteristics of the humanitarian needs associated with the drought, the Honduran Red Cross will conduct a multisectoral assessment to generate primary evidence on humanitarian needs, complement the secondary information available, and guide decision-making on possible subsequent actions.

According to information from COPECO cited by Proceso Digital on August 4, 2026, around 1 million people are being directly affected by the drought in Honduras. This figure represents a preliminary estimate of the scope of the situation. (5)

Trigger: On August 18, 2026, COPECO, through Alert Bulletin No. 028-2026, declared a Red Alert for 75 municipalities, a Yellow Alert for 71 municipalities, and a Green Alert for 88 municipalities due to drought associated with the El Niño phenomenon. The municipalities on Red Alert are concentrated in the departments of Choluteca, Comayagua, El Paraíso, Francisco Morazán, La Paz and Valle. This update shows an aggravation of drought conditions and constitutes the event that activates this DREF request for Evaluation. (6)

title: VNM: Flood - 08-2026 - Typhoon Narra #3 (2026-08-24)
content:
Description

Typhoon Narra, designated as Storm No.4 in Việt Nam, stalled off the northern coast early Monday, dumping torrential rain that pushed several rivers to their highest flood-alert levels, killed at least one person and damaged more than 4,000 homes in the northern province of Lạng Sơn.

At 4am, the storm's centre sat over the Gulf of Tonkin about 140km east of Quảng Ninh Province, packing sustained winds of 75-88km/h and gusts as strong as 103-117km/h, the National Centre for Hydro-Meteorological Forecasting said.

The system had barely moved in the previous six hours. Forecasters expect it to drift slowly east, then northeast, over the Gulf of Tonkin before making landfall in China's Guangxi region around August 27 and weakening into a tropical depression.

Wind gusts as strong as level 11 (103-117km/h) were recorded on the island of Bạch Long Vĩ while rainfall since August 21 topped 500mm in parts of Quảng Ninh and 520mm in Lạng Sơn, saturating soil across the northeast and raising the risk of flash floods and landslides in mountainous areas, the forecasting centre said.

According to rapid reports from the provinces of Son La, Phu Tho, Thai Nguyen, Cao Bang, Lang Son, Quang Ninh, Hai Phong, Bac Ninh, Hanoi and Thanh Hoa, as well as Vietnam Electricity (EVN), Typhoon No. 4 and heavy rainfall have caused the following damage:

  • Human casualties: 01 person died (Mr. Duong Phuc Hinh, born in 1999, from Thai Binh Commune, Lang Son Province) after a landslide struck his house.
  • Housing: 457 houses were damaged or had their roofs blown off (Son La: 1; Cao Bang: 37; Lang Son: 362; Thai Nguyen: 36; Phu Tho: 6; Bac Ninh: 5; Hai Phong: 10); 3,678 houses were flooded (Cao Bang: 16; Lang Son: 3,623; Bac Ninh: 39).
  • Agriculture and forestry: 10,585 ha of rice crops were damaged (Son La: 12 ha; Cao Bang: 93 ha; Bac Ninh: 4,259 ha; Hanoi: 2,216 ha; Quang Ninh: 519 ha; Hai Phong: 3,300 ha; Thanh Hoa: 186 ha). A further 9,206 ha of other crops were flooded or damaged (Cao Bang: 63 ha; Lang Son: 2,283 ha; Thai Nguyen: 15 ha; Bac Ninh: 4,428 ha; Quang Ninh: 38 ha; Hai Phong: 2,200 ha; Hanoi: 20 ha; Thanh Hoa: 159 ha).
  • Livestock: 106 livestock animals died (Son La: 2; Lang Son: 100; Thanh Hoa: 4), along with 6,000 poultry in Lang Son.
  • Aquaculture: 119 ha of aquaculture areas were damaged (Cao Bang: 3 ha; Bac Ninh: 25 ha; Hai Phong: 45 ha; Hanoi: 17 ha; Thanh Hoa: 29 ha).
  • Irrigation: 545 metres of embankments and irrigation canals were damaged (Bac Ninh: 300 m; Thanh Hoa: 245 m).
  • Transport: 1,023 locations were affected by landslides and flooding, causing traffic disruption (Cao Bang: 21; Lang Son: 903; Phu Tho: 3; Bac Ninh: 72; Hai Phong: 3; Thanh Hoa: 21).
  • Power supply: 56,744 customers are currently without electricity (Lang Son: 25,538; Hai Phong: 488; Bac Ninh: 30,568; Thai Nguyen: 150).

The affected localities are continuing to assess and consolidate damage reports.

Working through the night, using boats to reach flooded areas and provide food and essential supplies, the Lang Son Red Cross Society also coordinated emergency relief assistance for people affected by the heavy rains and Typhoon No. 4 in the communes of That Khe, Trang Dinh, Mau Son, Tan Doan, Quan Son and Van Linh. More than 650 relief packages, with a total value of VND 180 million, were distributed to affected households. Among them, one household whose house was completely destroyed received VND 5 million in assistance. These timely interventions have helped affected communities overcome immediate difficulties and gradually restore their lives following the disaster. At headquarters level, VNRC continued to monitor the evolving situation, coordinate with affected provincial Red Cross Societies, and consolidate damage and response updates to inform further response planning.

Actions taken by others

The Prime Minister issued Official Telegram No. 57/CĐ-TTg on 21 August 2026 and Official Telegram No. 54/CĐ-TTg on 17 August 2026, requesting the Chairpersons of the People’s Committees of northern provinces and cities, as well as those from Thanh Hoa to Quang Tri, and relevant ministries and sectors to proactively respond to disasters, heavy rainfall, flash floods and landslides, and focus on recovery efforts following the floods. On 22 August 2026, the National Civil Defence Steering Committee issued Official Telegram No. 46/BCĐ-BNNMT on proactive response to floods. On 21 August 2026, two official telegrams, No. 44/BCĐ-BNNMT and No. 45/CĐ-BNNMT-ĐĐ, were issued directing response efforts to the tropical depression over the East Sea, Typhoon No. 4, and proactively responding to heavy rainfall and flooding. On 23 August 2026, the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment issued Document No. 9713/BNNMT-ĐĐ on ensuring the safety of the dyke system and responding to rising water levels on the Cau, Thuong, Luc Nam and Thai Binh rivers. The Ministries of National Defence, Public Security, Construction, Education and Training, Science and Technology, and Industry and Trade issued official telegrams requesting relevant units to remain on standby and be prepared to respond to Typhoon No. 4, the tropical depression, heavy rainfall, flooding, flash floods and landslides in the northern region and from Thanh Hoa to Ha Tinh. On 24 August 2026, a Ministry of Agriculture and Environment mission, led by Deputy Minister Nguyen Hoang Hiep, travelled to Lang Son Province to direct response and recovery efforts following the heavy rains and flooding. On 22 August 2026, the Department of Dyke Management and Disaster Prevention and Control issued Document No. 1588/ĐĐ-QLĐĐ to the Departments of Agriculture and Environment of Bac Ninh, Thai Nguyen and Thanh Hoa provinces, requesting urgent implementation of measures to ensure dyke safety and respond to rising water levels on the Thuong, Luc Nam, Cau and Buoi rivers. The Department also deployed two missions to support the response to Typhoon No. 4 in Quang Ninh and inspect the Thuong and Luc Nam river dyke systems in Bac Ninh. Authorities maintained 24/7 duty, closely monitored weather, disaster and dyke conditions, and disseminated forecasts and early warnings to local authorities to support timely decision-making and disaster response. Local authorities issued official telegrams and directives on response to Typhoon No. 4 and heavy rainfall; deployed field missions to inspect preparedness and response measures; mobilised local resources to provide timely assistance to households affected by flooding; maintained emergency duty arrangements; and closely monitored weather conditions, forecasts and warnings. Local authorities evacuated 4,303 households, including 2,625 in Lang Son, 16 in Cao Bang, 22 in Thai Nguyen, 57 in Phu Tho, 31 in Quang Ninh, 1,423 in Bac Ninh, and 129 in Thanh Hoa. Authorities also deployed personnel to monitor and control people and vehicles in areas at risk of deep flooding and landslides.

title: IDN: Earthquake - 08-2026 - Field Report Update 3: M7.7 East Nusa Tenggara Earthquake #4 (2026-08-24)
content:
Description

On 15 August 2026 at 04:58 WIB, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck Flores Island, East Nusa Tenggara Province. The epicentre was located offshore, approximately 30 kilometres northeast of Mbay, Nagekeo District, at a depth of 15 kilometres. The earthquake affected seven districts: Manggarai Barat, Manggarai, Manggarai Timur, Ngada, Nagekeo, Ende and Sikka. Thousands of aftershocks have continued, increasing anxiety among communities and discouraging many families from returning to damaged homes.

As of 24 August 2026 at 09:00 WIB, the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) reported 100 deaths, 1,603 people injured or ill, and 180,327 people displaced. A total of 73,818 houses were damaged, together with 1,378 educational facilities, 118 health facilities, 504 government offices, and 396 places of worship. The figures remain preliminary and may change as assessment and verification continue.

Displaced people are staying in communal sites, temporary shelters, open areas, with relatives or in small self-established sites near their homes. Many independently displaced families remain difficult to identify and reach, particularly in remote, mountainous and island communities. Priority concerns include emergency shelter, safe water and sanitation, healthcare, essential household items, protection and psychosocial support. Children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, older people, persons with disabilities, people with chronic health conditions and families whose homes were severely damaged face increased risks. Although access along major routes has improved, several remote villages and island communities continue to experience logistical constraints. Existing water shortages linked to the dry season and El Niño, together with ongoing volcanic activity in parts of Flores, are further increasing humanitarian needs.

title: IDN: Fire - 07-2026 - Indonesia: Forest Fires and Haze in Sumatra and Kalimantan (2026-08-24)
content:
Description

Since mid-July 2026, forest and land fires have increased across parts of Sumatra and Kalimantan amid prolonged dry conditions and the peak of the dry season. The Government of Indonesia has prioritized response operations in six provinces: Riau, Jambi, South Sumatra, West Kalimantan, Central Kalimantan and South Kalimantan. Fires have also been reported in East and North Kalimantan. Fire suppression remains challenging, particularly in peatland areas and remote locations with limited access to water.

As of 9 August 2026, the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) reported approximately 48,889.69 hectares burned across the six priority provinces. More recent information compiled by PMI West Kalimantan from the Ministry of Forestry’s SIPONGI monitoring platform indicated approximately 38,301.86 hectares burned in West Kalimantan alone. The figures remain subject to verification and may change as assessments continue.

Smoke from the fires has significantly reduced air quality across several locations. On 24 August, the Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) recorded hazardous PM2.5 levels in parts of Palembang, South Sumatra, and very unhealthy conditions in Pekanbaru, Riau. Unhealthy air quality was also recorded in parts of Jambi and West Kalimantan. Visibility in Palembang reportedly fell below 50 metres during the morning, while low visibility has caused delays to air transport in parts of Kalimantan.

Based on information collected by PMI provincial branches, fires have affected all 14 districts and cities in West Kalimantan. Outdoor activities have been restricted and schools have temporarily suspended in-person learning in several affected areas. In Central Kalimantan, the provincial disaster management agency reported 858 detected hotspots, 53 recorded fire incidents and approximately 190.96 hectares burned as of 23 August. Some 66,679 acute respiratory infection cases were recorded during the monitoring period; however, the proportion directly attributable to smoke exposure has not yet been verified. Respiratory symptoms have also been reported among personnel involved in fire suppression.

In East Kalimantan, approximately 200 forest and land fire incidents have been reported since 14 July, affecting areas across most of the province’s districts and cities. In South Kalimantan, Banjarbaru City, Banjar District and Tanah Laut District are among the most affected areas, with smoke and fires near the airport affecting flight operations and nearby communities. Fires have also been reported in Bulungan District and Tarakan City, North Kalimantan.

People living in smoke-affected communities, particularly children, older people, pregnant women, people with existing respiratory or cardiovascular conditions, and outdoor workers, face increased health risks. Communities are also affected by disruptions to education, outdoor livelihoods, transport and daily activities. No consolidated and verified figures on the number of people affected, displaced, injured, missing or deceased were available at the time of reporting. Assessments and data verification remain ongoing.

Summary

PMI is coordinating the response through its national, provincial and district/city structures in the affected areas. Activities include monitoring and assessment, health-risk communication, first aid, ambulance standby, smoke-free health spaces, distribution of masks and health supplies, and ground-based fire suppression support alongside government agencies and other responders. In West Kalimantan, PMI has supported fire suppression in several locations and distributed 42,899 masks and 600 units or packages of vitamins, reaching at least 22,224 people. In Central Kalimantan, PMI distributed 12,380 masks, provided first aid to firefighting personnel, supported fire suppression, maintained ambulance readiness and established smoke-free health spaces. PMI branches in East Kalimantan have supported fire suppression operations in Berau and Samboja in coordination with local government, private-sector actors and communities. In North Kalimantan, PMI has provided health support to firefighting personnel in Bulungan and Tarakan and placed two water trucks on standby to address potential water shortages. To strengthen the provincial response capacity, PMI National Headquarters dispatched 70,000 masks to West Kalimantan and 50,000 masks to Central Kalimantan. PMI continues to consolidate operational data, assess priority needs and coordinate with government authorities. Immediate gaps include masks and respiratory protection, medicines, oxygen equipment, firefighting equipment, water-storage and distribution equipment, fuel and operational funding.

Actions taken by others

The Government of Indonesia is leading the response through the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB), provincial and district disaster management agencies (BPBD), the Ministry of Forestry through Manggala Agni, the Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG), the Indonesian Armed Forces (TNI), the National Police (Polri), fire and rescue services, environmental and forestry agencies, health authorities, and local governments. BNPB has prioritized operations in Riau, Jambi, South Sumatra, West Kalimantan, Central Kalimantan and South Kalimantan. The response combines ground-based suppression, aerial patrols, helicopter water bombing and weather modification operations. As of 21 August, BNPB reported that 39 aerial assets had been deployed across the six priority provinces to support fire detection, suppression and weather modification. In West Kalimantan, four water-bombing helicopters conducted eight sorties and 223 water drops on 23 August, releasing approximately 1.05 million litres of water. Weather modification operations were also conducted, while joint ground teams continued suppression and cooling activities. In Central Kalimantan, aerial patrols identified 25 active fire spots and three helicopters conducted 159 water drops. Ground operations were carried out across 11 affected areas. In South Kalimantan, two helicopters conducted 243 water drops on 23 August, releasing approximately 1.03 million litres of water. In Jambi, aerial patrols, water bombing and ground suppression continued in several locations. Government operations have also been supported by private-sector companies and local communities, particularly in areas where fires occurred near plantations, concessions or settlements. Health authorities are monitoring respiratory illnesses and disseminating public-health advice on reducing smoke exposure. Local governments have distributed masks, restricted outdoor activities and temporarily suspended in-person learning in some heavily affected areas. Transport authorities and airport operators continue to monitor visibility and adjust flight operations where necessary. No specific operational involvement by United Nations agencies or international NGOs had been reported at the time of this update.

title: WHO Situation Report No.2: Health emergencies in the Eastern Mediterranean Region (July 2026)
content:
EEXECUTIVE SUMMARY

• Monsoon rains and flash floods affected Afghanistan and Pakistan, causing 184 deaths and 597 injuries. Damage to homes, water and sanitation infrastructure and health facilities increased public health risks and constrained access in parts of Afghanistan. WHO deployed surge and mobile health teams and emergency supplies in Afghanistan and supported preparedness in Pakistan, where supplies for more than 380 000 people had been pre-positioned.

• Lebanon reported 4 335 deaths and 12 281 injuries since 2 March; attacks in the Islamic Republic of Iran (Iran) between 27 June and 24 July caused 59 deaths and more than 666 injuries; and airstrikes in Iraq on 29 July reportedly caused around 20 deaths and 32 injuries. Localized violence, displacement and access constraints continued in southern Syria. Qatar reported three injuries from falling debris, while Kuwait experienced impacts on energy and water infrastructure. WHO strengthened trauma readiness, including training 5 400 hospital staff in Lebanon and providing trauma supplies in Iran, Iraq and Syria. Mental health and psychosocial support interventions reached around 15 000 health workers in Iran.

• Nineteen attacks on health care were documented across four countries in the Region in July, representing more than half of the 36 incidents reported globally. They caused three deaths and 15 injuries and affected health personnel, patients, facilities, transport, supplies and warehouses.

• WHO strengthened Ebola preparedness in high-risk countries. An assessment in Somalia identified existing preparedness and some laboratory and cross-border capacity, alongside gaps in operational readiness, coordination and testing. Laboratory supplies were delivered for Somalia, Sudan and Djibouti. In Iraq, Arbaeen preparedness included Ebola control guidance, strengthened points of entry and orientation of 50 focal points.

• In July, WHO's Hub for Global Health Emergencies Logistics delivered nearly US$625 400 of medicines and health supplies to 10 countries. Despite regional conflict, the Hub maintained 60–70% of pre-crisis operational volume using overland corridors through Oman, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Syria and Türkiye.

Disease outbreaks and surveillance

• Sudan faced concurrent cholera, dengue, malaria, measles, diphtheria and polio outbreaks, with cholera a major concern in Kordofan. Somalia reported approximately 15 800 cholera/acute watery diarrhoea cases during Weeks 1–30, with cases increasing from approximately 200 in Week 27 to 817 in Week 30. Approximately 2 200 diphtheria cases were reported, with a case fatality ratio of 3.0%; 67% occurred among unvaccinated people and 18% among incompletely vaccinated people.

• Iraq remained affected by seasonal Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever transmission. In Syria, suspected measles cases declined by 53% from Week 29 to Week 30. Phase I of the measles-rubella vaccination campaign began on 26 July in eight priority districts, reaching approximately 199 000 children (77% coverage); surveillance gaps persisted. The Masyaf acute gastroenteritis/acute watery diarrhoea outbreak also declined following response measures.

Displacement, climate change and water, sanitation and hygiene

• Sudan floods affected 11 837 people across seven states and damaged homes, water and sanitation infrastructure and health facilities. Somalia recorded 146 447 new displacements (latest update by the end of June), mainly linked to conflict (68%) and drought (28%) [missing data 4%].

• Lebanon: As of 29 July, 360 132 people remained internally displaced, including 27 177 in 262 collective sites, while 821 077 had begun returning to their communities. In Iraq, extreme temperatures and population movement during Arbaeen increased heat-related and communicabledisease risks.

Health-system functionality and access

• Sudan faced shortages of medicines, emergency kits, laboratory reagents and medical consumables, alongside electricity, water and communications constraints. Somalia's health-sector appeal was 21% funded (US$17 million of US$80 million), contributing to facility closures, including approximately 33% of facilities in South-West State, and workforce attrition. Syria continued to face gaps in referral transport, workforce and laboratory capacity, sample transport and surveillance data completeness.

WHO response and preparedness actions

• In Sudan, WHO supported coordination and health services through 14 hospitals, four primary health care facilities, 18 mobile clinics and 27 stabilization centres. Temporary mobile clinics across eight states recorded 113 849 consultations in July. Two hospitals and four primary health care facilities provided services to 6 590 people, while quality-of-care activities in 10 hospitals reached 85 467 people. WHO also delivered 20.93 metric tonnes of emergency supplies valued at US$258 161 to 16 states and supported treatment for 2 631 children under 5 years with severe acute malnutrition and medical complications.

• In Lebanon, the coordinated response reached an estimated 1.2 million people by end-July, including more than 485 000 through health interventions and over 1.3 million through water, sanitation and hygiene support. In Iran, WHO procured trauma supplies and hospital power equipment, while mental health and psychosocial support interventions reached approximately 15 000 health workers. In Syria, WHO dispatched 695.2 metric tonnes of medical, laboratory and water, sanitation and hygiene supplies and launched Phase I of the measles-rubella vaccination campaign in eight priority districts.

• In Somalia, WHO sustained primary care through 33 facilities across 18 districts and reinforced 41 stabilization centres with 69 paediatric severe acute malnutrition kits. In Iraq, WHO provided 65 trauma backpacks to strengthen pre-hospital response and supported Arbaeen preparedness. In Jordan, WHO continued emergency readiness and support for continuity of essential health services.

title: UNICEF Nigeria Humanitarian Situation Report No.1 (Mid -Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Armed conflict, banditry, communal violence, food insecurity and persistent malnutrition, disease outbreaks, including earlier than usual cholera outbreaks and floods deepened needs during the first half of 2026, with 5.9 million people facing severe humanitarian needs in the Northeast, 1.4 million displaced in the Northwest, and 464,000 in Benue State.
  • UNICEF and partners treated over 453,500 children with severe acute malnutrition across the Northeast and Northwest, achieving cure rates of 98 per cent in the Northeast and above 95 per cent in the Northwest.
  • UNICEF-supported polio vaccination reached 4.5 million children in the Northwest; emergency primary health care reached 157,201 women, children and adolescents; and improved sanitation benefited over 308,000 people across 103 IDP camps in Borno.
  • By Midyear, UNICEF had received US$58.2 million with a funding gap of 72%. As needs rise and funding declines, flexible, timely resources are required to sustain services for affected children.

title: Taw Oo District Situation Update: Burma Army shelling, arrests, and militarisation; drug issues; and challenges to education, transportation, and livelihood in Daw Hpah Hkoh Township (January to March 2026)
content:
This Situation Update describes events occurring in Daw Hpah Hkoh (Thandaunggyi) Township, Taw Oo (Toungoo) District. During the period from January to March 2026, the Burma Army shelled villages, killing two villagers and injuring four villagers. Then, the Burma Army Belu Column arrested five villagers and released four of them, while keeping one of them in detention. Additionally, the Burma Army arrested two villagers who were returning to Ai--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract. The presence of Burma Army in the village caused fear for villagers to live in the village. The Burma Army not only invaded the villages but also looted villagers’ phones and money which belonged to a church. Daw Hpah Hkoh Township is a mixed-control area of both the Karen National Union (KNU) and the Burma Army. The Burma Army mostly administers towns, and they have army camps near towns, while the KNU administers villages and village tracts. For instance, schools in villages and village tract are administered by the Karen Education and Cultural Department (KECD), while schools in towns are administered by the Burma Army. Lastly, the surge in fuel prices led to high prices in goods when goods were transported to and sold in villages; meanwhile, local goods sold at lower profits, which has caused economic hardship for villagers.[1]

Indiscriminate shelling incidents in Thandaunggyi Section (3)

On 22 January 2026, revolutionary armed groups were not conducting their military operations and there was no fighting [in Thandaunggyi Section (3), Daw Hpah Hkoh (Thandaungyi) Township, Taw Oo (Toungoo) District]. However, at 8:50 pm, the SSPC [State Security and Peace Commission[2] also known as the Burma Army[3]] based in Thandaunggyi Ba Yit Naung Tat Myot area, Daw Hpah Hkoh Township, fired a (60 mm) motor shell. The shell landed and exploded in front of Aa--- church, Thandaunggyi Section (3), damaging Ab--- church hall, glasses [windows], and bricks [walls]. Additionally, Naw[4] A---, 34 years old, the wife of a [church leader, position censored for security], sustained an injury to her leg. Later, she received treatment at a hospital run by the SSPC in the Thandaunggyi Bayint Naung Tat Myo area.

On 3 February 2026, in the morning, SSPC Infantry Battalion (IB)[5] #26, based near Ac--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract,[6] Daw Hpah Hkoh Township, fired two (60 mm) mortar shells. The two shells landed and exploded near Naw B---’s house, Ad--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract. The shrapnel hit her neck, leading to her death shortly afterward.[7]

On 14 March 2026, an unknown armed [resistance] group attacked, firing two shots with a sniper [rifle] at the gate of [the army camp of] Light Infantry Battalion (LIB)[8] #603, which is located on a road between Toungoo Town and Leik Tho Town, killing one Burma Army soldier. Following the attack at 4 pm on the same day, [Burma Army soldiers from] Z’Leh army camp, located near Ae--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract, indiscriminately shelled Ae--- village, killing a 60-year-old villager named Ma[9] C--- and injuring three other villagers: Saw[10] D--- on his head, 15-year-old Saw E--- on his leg, and 15-year-old Saw F---, who also sustained an [unspecified] injury.

Burma Army arrests

On 4 January 2026, 19-year-old Ko[11] G--- and 20-year-old H---, who live in Ai--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract, travelled to Toungoo Town to watch and celebrate the Myanmar Independence Day festival. The next morning, 5 January 2026, the two of them and their cousin I---, who was released from prison on Independence Day, returned together to their village. On the way back to their village, Toungoo No. (3) Police arrested and detained them. They were arrested because the police suspected them of having connection with the PDF [People’s Defence Force].[12] A week later, they were released.

On 9 March 2026, in the morning, the SSPC Belu Column[13] arrested five villagers who were traveling between Af--- village and Ag--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract. [On the same day,] four villagers were released; however, one villager had still not been released [as of 11 August 2026]. The missing villager used to live in Ah--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract. Villagers reported that they do not know where he is; however, there was a rumour in the village that he was forcibly recruited as a [Burma Army] soldier. A village head of the P’Shaw Loh village tract reported that the SSPC Belu Column is extremely terrifying and brutal.

Militarisation operation

In January 2026, SSPC Belu Column, IB #26, IB #19, LIB #603, and LIB #604 entered Aj--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract. Villagers did not feel safe to live in the village due to their [Burma Army] presence. Additionally, villagers were not pleased that they [Burma Army soldiers] were checking identification cards of villagers who were traveling in and out of the village. Thus, [some] villagers were displaced.

On 17 February 2026, KNLA [Karen National Liberation Army][14] Battalion #5, under the control of Brigade #2, attacked the SSPC’s military operations on Ah Shay Nyaung Ku La Htaing Kway Road, located at the upper part of Ac--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract. [Later, on the same day, villagers found the dead body of a KNLA soldier with his throat slit on a road near Ak--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract. They believed the Burma Army arrested and killed the soldier following the KNLA attack.]

On 5 March 2026, the Belu Column entered Al--- village, P’Shaw Loh village. Then, they looted 450,000 kyats (214.29 USD[15]) worth of offerings given to the Am--- church, as well as two phones of villagers. A villager [from Al--- village] informed the village tract leader of the incident. One of the soldiers said: “If you want the phones and money, you’ll get shrapnel.”

On 14 March 2026, at 11:30 pm, some villagers reported that KNLA Battalion #5, under the control of Brigade #2, combined with PDF, launched 18 (107 mm) rockets at the Ketu Mati Air Force, [located in Toungoo Town, Bago Division] and hit fuel tanks. 13 out of 18 (107 mm) rockets exploded. The Bayint Naung Tat Myo army camp conducted shelling in return. [It is unknown to KHRG where the shelling landed or if there were any damages.]

On 27 March 2026, combined forces of the PDF and [KNLA] Battalion #5, under the control of Brigade #2, attacked a military training location in Bayint Naung Tat Myo Town. A KNLA authority said that four out of five rockets exploded. Later, on the same day, SSPC [Light Infantry] Battalion #593, under the control of Military Operations Command (MOC)[16] #20, fired two shells, and Bayint Naung Tat Myo army camp also fired more than four shells into villagers’ plantations in Day Loh Mu Nu Lar village tract. However, no one sustained injury.

Administration in Daw Hpah Hkoh Township

On 5 February 2026, the KNU [Karen National Union][17] elected their relevant departments [members] and township administrator in Daw Hpah Hkoh Township. There are nine departments. Some new members were elected. This congress was completed step by step. KNU members were elected from village, village tract, and township. The new township administrator’s name is Saw J---. However, the SSPC still administered Thandaunggyi Town, Leik Tho Town, and Baw Ka Li Town, with SSPC army camps based in those areas. In addition, drugs like Yaba[18] (WY) were sold and villagers were purchasing drugs from those towns. The SSPC had not taken any action or prohibited the drugs yet [as of March 2026].

Education

In 2026, there were Karen Education and Culture Department (KECD)[19] administered schools in all village tracts in the township; yet, villagers from An--- village, Shan Leh Pyin Kyi village tract, [Daw Hpah Hkoh Township] and [throughout] P’Shaw Loh village tract wanted more KECD schools and wanted to link [existing self-funded schools] with the KECD. Schools administered by the SSPC were in Thandaunggyi Town, Thandaung 13 Miles Town, and Leik Tho Town.

Transportation and economy

The roads and bridges which were damaged from flooding and landslides in 2025 were being repaired in 2026. Some bridges and roads had been repaired, and villagers were using them for traveling. When it rained, some of the roads and bridges became difficult to travel by motorcycle, so villagers walked while crossing some bridges.

In March 2026, the price of petrol was between 15,000 kyats (7.14 USD) and 16,000 kyats (7.62 USD) per litre. Cars and motorcycles without licenses were prohibited from purchasing petrol at petrol stations. Some SSPC checkpoints looted fuel from taxi drivers, who carried fuel in bottles for sale, which led to high prices in goods and high taxi fees. In contrast, [selling] local crops made little profit [for villagers].

Further background reading on the situation on shelling in Southeast Burma/Myanmar can be found in the following KHRG reports:

  • Photo Set: Burma Army human rights violations in Southeast Burma (January to June 2026), July 2026.
  • In Spite of Fear: Women’s experiences navigating the compounding challenges of displacement and insecurity in Southeast Burma, July 2026.
  • “Kler Lwee Htoo Incident Report: Burma Army ground operations, air strikes, and shelling killed at least 31 villagers, including 15 children, injured many others, and caused extensive property destruction and displacement in Ler Doh Township (March 2026)”, July 2026.

Footnotes:

[1] The present document is based on information received in April 2026. It was provided by a community member in Taw Oo District who has been trained by KHRG as a researcher to monitor human rights conditions on the ground. The names of the victims, their photos and the exact locations are censored for security reasons. The parts in square brackets are explanations added by KHRG. This document combines several received reports with the following KHRG internal log numbers: #26-125-S1; #26-27-D1; and #26-27-A1-I1.

[2] The State Security and Peace Commission (SSPC) is the new name of the executive governing body created in the aftermath of the 1 February 2021 military coup. Formerly called the State Administration Council (SAC), it was renamed by Senior General Min Aung Hlaing on 31 July 2025.The chairperson serves as the de facto head of government of Burma/Myanmar and leads the Military Cabinet of Myanmar, the executive branch of the government. Min Aung Hlaing assumed the role of SAC chairperson following the coup and remains the head of the SSPC. The name State Security and Peace Commission (SSPC) is used interchangeably with military junta and Burma military regime.

[3] The terms Burma military, Burma Army, SAC, Tatmadaw, and junta are used interchangeably throughout this report to describe the Burma military regime’s armed forces. Villagers themselves commonly use Burma Army, Burmese soldiers, or alternatively the name adopted by the Burma military regime at the time —from the 2021 coup to July 2025, the State Administration Council (SAC). On 31 July 2025, the military junta changed its name to the State Security and Peace Commission (SSPC).

[4] ‘Naw’ is a S’gaw Karen female honorific title used before a person’s name.

[5] An Infantry Battalion (IB) comprises 500 soldiers. However, most Infantry Battalions in the Tatmadaw are under-strength with less than 200 soldiers. Yet up to date information regarding the size of battalions is hard to come by, particularly following the signing of the NCA. They are primarily used for garrison duty but are sometimes used in offensive operations.

[6] A village tract is an administrative unit of between five and 20 villages in a local area, often centred on a large village.

[7] KHRG, “Taw Oo District Short Update: Burma Army shelling killed one villager, injured a pregnant woman, and caused damage in Daw Hpah Hkoh Township (December 2025 and February 2026)”, April 2026.

[8] A Light Infantry Battalion (LIB) comprises 500 soldiers. Most Light Infantry Battalions in the Tatmadaw are under-strength with less than 200 soldiers, yet up-to-date information regarding the size of battalions is hard to come by, particularly following the signing of the NCA. LIBs are primarily used for offensive operations, but they are sometimes used for garrison duties.

[9] ‘Ma’ is a Burmese female honorific title used before a person’s name.

[10] ‘Saw’ is a S’gaw Karen male honorific title used before a person’s name.

[11] ‘Ko’ is a Burmese title meaning older brother. It can be used for relatives as well as non-relatives.

[12] The People’s Defence Force (PDF) is an armed resistance established independently as local civilian militias operating across the country. Following the 1 February 2021 military coup and the ongoing brutal violence enacted by the junta, the majority of these groups began working with the National Unity Government (NUG), a body claiming to be the legitimate government of Burma/Myanmar, which then formalized the PDF on 5 May 2021 as a precursor to a federal army.

[13] A column is a combination of companies assembled for operations, usually 100-300 soldiers fighting strength.

[14] The Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) is the armed wing of the Karen National Union.

[15] All conversion estimates for the Kyat are based on the official market rate as of 30 July 2026 at 1 USD = 2,100 MMK; conversion rate available at https://wise.com/gb/currency-converter/usd-to-mmk-rate

[16] Military Operations Command (MOC) is comprised of ten battalions for offensive operations. Most MOCs have three Tactical Operations Commands (TOCs) made up of three battalions each.

[17] The Karen National Union (KNU) is the main Karen political organisation. It was established in 1947 and has been in conflict with the government since 1949. The KNU wields power across large areas of Southeast Myanmar and has been calling for the creation of a democratic federal system since 1976. Although it signed the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) in 2015, following the 2021 coup staged by Burma Army leaders, the KNU officially stated that the NCA has become void.

[18] Yaba, which means ‘crazy medicine’ in Thai, is a tablet form of methamphetamine. First developed in East Asia during the Second World War to enhance soldiers' performance, methamphetamine has become increasingly popular in Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Burma/Myanmar where it is typically manufactured.

[19] The Karen Education and Culture Department (KECD) is the education department of the Karen National Union. Its main goals are to provide mother tongue education services to rural Karen populations in Southeast Myanmar, as well as to preserve the Karen language, culture and history. Despite being an important education provider in the region, it is not officially recognised by the Myanmar government.

title: Nigeria: GBV Monthly Dashboard - July 2026
content:
In July 2026, Gender-Based Violence (GBV) risks across Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY) States were driven by conflict, food insecurity, camp closures, and the ongoing cholera outbreak. During the June–August lean season, 6.4 million people BAY States were projected to face severe food insecurity, including more than 1.1 million people facing emergency levels (OCHA). Insecurity, restricted access to farmland and markets, high food prices, and reduced purchasing power further heightened pressure on vulnerable households and exacerbated GBV risks for women and girls.

During the period under review, population movements linked to internally displaced persons (IDPs) camp closures in Bama Local Government Area (LGA) remained an important protection concern, with potential implications for the continuity of GBV services and referral pathways. Announced camp closures in Gwoza and Konduga LGAs require continued planning and advocacy by GBV partners to ensure the protection of IDPs during and after relocation.

The ongoing cholera outbreak also constrained service delivery. During the second week of July, partners responding in cholera-affected LGAs reported that fear of infection among community members and frontline workers reduced participation in GBV activities and home visits. Furthermore, overstretched health facilities due to the outbreak, disrupted referral pathways. GBV partners reported protection concerns linked to the cholera outbreak, including unsafe water and sanitation, stigma and discrimination, sexual exploitation, early/forced marriage, intimate partner violence (IPV) and limited access to referral services.

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #210 - 24 August 2026
content:
Highlight

This week, UNHCR is stepping-up its support to Refugee-led Organizations (RLOs) and Community-Based Organizations (CBOs) through the in-kind donation of 17 computers, enhancing their operational capacity and enabling them to better implement activities that support refugee communities. In 2026, and for a third-year, following a comprehensive evaluation process 9 organizations representing diverse refugee and host communities across 8 counties in Romania received UNHCR grants to support their activities addressing the needs of refugees while fostering social cohesion and inclusion. Partnering with RLOs and CBOs is central to UNHCR's commitment to meaningful refugee participation. These organizations are uniquely positioned to identify community priorities, deliver culturally and linguistically appropriate support, build trust, and develop sustainable, locally led solutions that strengthen protection and promote refugee selfreliance. Overall, over 1,500 refugees directly benefit from empowerment and community integration activities; more than 300 refugee women and girls receive psychosocial support, skills development opportunities, and access to safe spaces that promote wellbeing and social inclusion; over 300 refugee children and youth participate in educational, sports, and recreational activities that foster integration and personal development; around 400 refugees engage in cultural exchange programmes, leadership training and mentorship activities that support self-reliance and integration; and some 200 refugees undertake communication and employability training initiatives.

title: Protection Sector Updated Guidance Note on the Return of IDPs in Syria August 2026
content:
The Syrian conflict has resulted in one of the largest displacement crises in recent history, with currently an estimated 5.5 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) across the country. Over the years, shifting frontlines, ceasefires, and changes in territorial control have influenced patterns of displacement and prospects for return. In late 2024, the collapse of the regime in Syria (December 8, 2024) removed a number of major barriers to return. Since then, over 3.7 million people, including IDP returnees and refugee returnees, have returned to their areas of origin. However, these return movements have been fraught with significant protection risks and challenges, primarily due to the limited availability of services and the fragile security and economic context in many areas. Returnees in Syria face a complex landscape of protection risks. Humanitarian actors must maintain a strong field of presence and vigilance to respond to these risks and prevent further harm. One of the most immediate threats is the danger posed by explosive ordnance contamination, which continues to cause injuries and fatalities in areas of return. Additionally, many returnees face homelessness or inadequate shelter, which not only undermines their dignity but also increases their vulnerability to further protection violations. House, land & property (HLP)-related violations are also common, especially when returnees attempt to reclaim homes that have been occupied by others during their displacement. These disputes often lead to forced evictions, threats, intimidation, or other forms of retaliation, further undermining prospects for safe, voluntary, and dignified return. Safety and security concerns are widespread, with returnees at risk of arbitrary detention, extortion, abduction, and exposure to hostilities. Returnees may also encounter social tensions and discrimination, particularly in communities where resources are scarce or where political and sectarian divisions persist. These tensions can hinder reintegration and fuel further marginalization. Access to essential services, such as food, water, sanitation, healthcare, and education, is often limited. This is frequently due to the lack of civil documentation, which restricts individuals' ability to access public services and legal remedies in a context where the legal system is weak or non-functional. Compounding these challenges is the issue of missing or expired personal and family documents, including the registration of births and deaths, which further limits access to rights and services. Furthermore, climate change, economic instability, and other humanitarian needs barriers have significantly worsened the protection environment. Economic hardship due to limited livelihood opportunities, energy shortages, and inflation may lead to harmful coping mechanisms such as child labor, early marriage, school dropouts, and substance abuse and GBV. Vulnerable families are often forced to deprioritize essential needs, including healthcare and nutrition, to afford basic needs. As displacement and return dynamics evolve and increasing numbers of IDPs consider or commence return, there is a growing need for harmonized, principled, and well-coordinated protection interventions.

This Guidance Note seeks to promote a coordinated response across all protection actors, avoid duplication of efforts, and reinforce the centrality of protection in return and broader recovery initiatives. The guidance draws on sub-national practices developed in specific regions of Syria, as well as international standards and best practices from similar contexts, to ensure consistency and contextual relevance at the whole-of-Syria level. It provides unified, national-level operational guidance for the engagement of protection partners on the IDPs’ return across Syria. It covers different return dynamics in all areas of Syria, and support protection partners operating in both areas of displacement and areas of return to uphold the rights, safety, and dignity of IDPs. This Note also seeks to promote a coordinated response across actors, avoid duplication, and promote the centrality of protection in broader return and recovery efforts. Importantly, this guidance is anchored in global protection frameworks – including the UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement (which affirm that IDPs’ returns must be voluntary, safe and dignified), the IASC Framework on Durable Solutions for IDPs (endorsed by the Inter-Agency Standing Committee, providing key principles and criteria for sustainable solutions), relevant Global Protection Cluster operational guidance on returns, and UNHCR protection standards. All protection actors should ensure that all returns are voluntary, safe, dignified, and informed, and that protection risks are identified, prevented, mitigated, and responded to at every stage of the return process.

title: DRC, Ebola Response - Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster Situation Report (01-15 Aug 2026)
content:
1. Operational Context

• According to WHO reporting as of 12 August 2026, active transmission has now been reported across five provinces in DRC: Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, and South Kivu. WHO continues to characterize the outbreak as being in a phase of intense and expanding transmission.
• Insecurity, displacement, population movements and community resistance continue to complicate response efforts and increase the risk of further spread.
• The response is increasingly transitioning into a protracted emergency, with continued geographical expansion driving higher requirements for logistics, transport, storage and emergency telecommunications services.
• WHO and partners continue to expand treatment and operational capacity in eastern DRC, including additional Ebola Treatment Centres (ETCs) and Forward Logistics Bases (FLBs). The LTC remains ready to support increased requirements for cargo transport, storage, last-mile delivery and telecommunications services.
• Preparedness activities continued in South Sudan, Rwanda, Burundi, and CAR, focusing on cross-border readiness, pre-positioning of response assets, emergency telecommunications, logistics preparedness, and coordination along key mobility corridors.

title: Response to Peru Earthquake, Situational Report | August 21st, 2026
content:
Highlights

• A magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck 35 km north of Coracora, Parinacochas, Ayacucho, at 13:00 hrs on 20 August, at a depth of 108 km. The earthquake was felt across several southern regions of Peru.

• At least 3 people have been reported injured and 116 homes have been reported affected or rendered uninhabitable in Upahuacho alone. Earlier assessments identified additional affected homes in Pullo, Coracora, Chumpi, Puquio and other districts.

• 10 educational facilities in Ayacucho and Apurímac have reported preliminary damage, including cracks in classrooms and walls, damaged perimeter fences, broken windows and impacts to sanitation facilities.

• 6 health facilities have been reported affected in Ayacucho, including three in Puquio and three in Coracora.

• Electricity disruptions affected approximately 6,000 users in Nazca, Ica, while interruptions to telecommunications were also reported closer to the epicentre.

• Rockfalls and localized impacts on roads have been reported in areas around the epicentre.

• The impact assessment remains ongoing. National, regional and local authorities continue conducting EDAN/EDANSE assessments to determine the full extent of damage and humanitarian needs.

• Plan International is currently assessing needs in affected areas, with particular attention to children and adolescents, especially girls, and potential risks to their protection, safety, access to essential services and continuity of education. The situation remains under assessment and figures may continue to change.

title: Malawi: Measles Outbreak Response - DREF Operation (MDRMW027)
content:
Description of the Event
Date when the trigger was met
20-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

Malawi is experiencing an escalating measles outbreak, with the Ministry of Health reporting 73 measles alerts through the Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) system during Epidemiological Week 27 (29 June to 5 July 2026). The outbreak follows months of sustained transmission that began with sporadic cases earlier in 2026 and has since developed into localized outbreaks in several districts.

Cumulatively, Nsanje has reported 211 confirmed and epidemiologically linked cases since February 2026, Dedza has reported 90 confirmed cases since July 2026, and Balaka has reported 82 laboratory-confirmed cases since January 2026. Epidemiological data further indicate that more than 85% of confirmed cases have occurred among children under 15 years of age, while over 70% of cases were either unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status, demonstrating significant immunity gaps within affected communities. Continued reporting of new laboratory-confirmed cases indicates ongoing transmission and an increasing risk of expansion to neighbouring districts.

The outbreak is most pronounced in the catchment areas of Comfort and Khwisa health facilities in Balaka District, Golomoti and Kaundu in Dedza District, and Osiyana, Ndamera, Nsanje, and Trinity health facilities in Nsanje District. These areas are experiencing a combination of factors that continue to fuel transmission, including low routine immunization coverage, high numbers of unvaccinated children, delayed health-seeking behaviour, weak community surveillance systems, inadequate risk communication, and widespread misinformation regarding vaccination. In Nsanje, cross-border population movement along the Malawi-Mozambique border has intensified the risk of disease spread, while shortages of trained health workers, volunteers, and operational resources have constrained surveillance and response efforts. In Balaka and Dedza, persistent immunity gaps and delayed case detection are contributing to continued transmission within communities.

The outbreak has generated significant public health and humanitarian impacts. Increasing numbers of suspected and confirmed cases have placed additional pressure on district health services through heightened demand for surveillance, laboratory testing, case management, contact tracing, and vaccination outreach activities. Children under five years of age remain particularly vulnerable due to low vaccination uptake, malnutrition, and limited access to health services. In some communities, particularly within parts of Nsanje, religious beliefs and vaccine hesitancy have contributed to delayed treatment-seeking and reduced acceptance of vaccination services, increasing the risk of severe illness and preventable deaths. The continued accumulation of susceptible children and ongoing transmission in Balaka, Dedza, and Nsanje indicate a high likelihood of further spread unless urgent interventions are implemented to strengthen outbreak-response vaccination, community engagement, surveillance, and risk communication activities.

Given the epidemiological trends and operational gaps identified, Balaka, Dedza, and Nsanje represent the highest-priority districts for immediate intervention. These districts continue to experience active transmission driven by substantial immunity gaps, weak community-level disease detection and reporting systems, and challenges in reaching at-risk populations with vaccination and health promotion services. Without rapid scale-up of surveillance, community engagement, social mobilization, and immunization activities, there is a significant risk that transmission will intensify within these districts and spread to surrounding areas, resulting in additional morbidity and mortality among vulnerable children and other susceptible populations.

title: Colombia | Earthquake - Emergency Appeal Operational Strategy (MDRCO036)
content:
DESCRIPTION OF THE EVENT

On 10 August 2026 at 07:34 local time, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia, with its epicentre near the municipality of San José del Palmar in Chocó Department, at a depth of 96 km. The earthquake was followed by multiple aftershocks and was felt across much of the country, affecting densely populated urban centres and rural communities alike. The departments most severely impacted include Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Caldas, and Quindío, while significant impacts were also reported in Antioquia, Cundinamarca, Huila, Boyacá, Tolima, Cauca, Putumayo, Sucre, and Santander. As of 18 August, the National Disaster Risk Management Unit (UNGRD) reports indicated impacts across 15 departments and 472 municipalities,2 while the earthquake was felt across much of Colombia and reported in Ecuador, Panama, and Venezuela.

According to the latest official information available, the earthquake has resulted in significant loss of life, injuries, and widespread infrastructure damage.

Preliminary reports by 18 August indicated 304 deaths, 4,548 injured people, 426 missing persons, and 356 people rescued. Authorities have also reported 134,342 damaged homes, 29,554 destroyed homes, 303 affected health facilities, 3,443 affected educational facilities, 3,905 affected community centres, 267 collapsed buildings, 413 damaged roads, and impacts to at least five airports.3

Critical disruptions to electricity, water supply, telecommunications, and health services have been reported in several affected areas. Airport closures, damaged roads, communication outages, and continuing aftershocks are affecting access to communities and delaying comprehensive damage and needs assessments, particularly in Chocó, where connectivity remains intermittent and some municipalities remain difficult to reach. Pre-existing vulnerabilities, poor health outcomes, and limited access to health services already constrained the ability of communities to cope with additional shocks.

On the day of the earthquake, the Government of Colombia declared a national State of Emergency and activated national and departmental emergency management mechanisms. The Colombian Red Cross Society (Cruz Roja Colombiana – CRC) immediately activated its National Crisis Room and emergency response mechanisms.

title: LBR: Flood - 08-2026 - Flood (2026-08-21)
content:
Description

Since August 19, 2026, there has been sustained heavy rainfall consistent with the Liberia rainy season, which has caused widespread flash and riverine flooding across seven counties: Montserrado, Cape Mount, Grand Bassa, Bomi, Bong, Rivergss, and Nimba. Montserrado, home to Monrovia ( Liberia's Capital), has a dense urban corridor and the epicenter, with informal settlements along the St. Paul River, StocktonCreek, Du River, and the Mesurado River. Wetlands especially exposed to slow-draining flooding water. More than 5000 residents across 10 communities in Monrovia ( the Capital) are currently displaced, with an estimated 64,000 people affected nationwide, facing damaged housing, contaminated water sources, disrupted livelihoods, and heightened waterborne disease risk. This escalation follows the NDMA's June 30, 2026 warning of rising flood risk in Monrovia, citing the Meteorological Service Forecast of 218.7- 754.2 mm rainfall and 88-90% humidity, conditions that limit drainage and prolong flooding. The current crisis reflects that the projected risk is materializing, compounded by weak urban drainage, wetland encroachment, and unplanned settlement growth

The flooding situation across the affected counties remains active, with heavy rain continuing to compound an already critical humanitarian emergency. In Montserrado County, floodwater continues to settle in wetlands, sheltering with relatives and host homes across the 10 communities. No fatalities have been reported to date, but transportation routes and livelihoods remain challenged, and contaminated water sources are elevating the risk of waterborne disease outbreaks among the estimated 64,000 people affected nationwide.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: Yes

NS Requests International Assistance: Yes

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by Federation

Summary

The LNRCS Community-Based Action Teams (CBATs), together with Branch and Chapter volunteers, have been deployed to collect information for this SITREP and support the evacuation of vulnerable individuals, including older persons, children, and persons with disabilities. LNRCS is also coordinating closely with the NDMA and relevant county-level structures, reinforcing its auxiliary role to the Government in supporting affected and at-risk communities. The National Society response teams have also begun providing Psychological First Aid (PFA) to affected people, particularly those who have been displaced by the flooding. In addition, LNRCS has pre-positioned and deployed additional first-aid kits to affected counties to strengthen its capacity to provide timely first-aid services to individuals who may sustain injuries during the emergency.

Actions taken by RCRC

Summary

Ahead of the flooding, with funding and technical support from the Swedish Red Cross team in-Country, an Anticipatory Action (AA) was piloted in Montserrado and Cape Mount, training 40 volunteers and establishing CBATs in four communities. The pilot mapped vulnerabilities, assessed local capacities, and cleaned key drainage in high-risk zones, groundwork that reduced flood severity in places and enabled a faster response, with Montserrado worst affected.

Actions taken by others

The Government has alerted all partners to strengthen coordination and collaboration in the flooding situation. The National Flood Preparedness Plan has also been activated, along with the Emergency Operations Centre (EOC), to support coordinated response efforts. In addition, the Liberia National Police has issued a flood warning, urging the public and relevant stakeholders to remain vigilant, follow safety guidance, and avoid using flooded roads and streets to reduce the risk of accidents and loss of life.

Planned International Response

DREF: Planned

title: VNM: Cyclone - 08-2026 - Typhoon Narra (2026-08-22)
content:
Description

Storm Narra, the fourth to hit the East Sea this year, brought strong winds and heavy rains to northern Việt Nam early on August 22, with some areas forecast to receive more than 500mm of rain as the storm moves slowly over the northern waters of the East Sea.

According to the National Centre for Hydrometeorological Forecasting, early on August 22, strong winds of level eight (62-74 km/h), with gusts up to level nine, were recorded at Bạch Long Vĩ special zone in Hải Phòng city, while winds reached level six, with gusts up to level nine, in Cô Tô special zone in Quảng Ninh province.

At 4am, the storm's centre was about 130km northeast of Bạch Long Vĩ. The strongest winds near the centre were at level eight, with gusts up to level ten. The storm was moving slowly northward at about 3km per hour.

Forecasters said that early on August 23, the storm is expected to turn southward and move at around 3km per hour. Its centre is forecast to be about 170km east of Hải Phòng and 70km northeast of Bạch Long Vĩ.

Areas likely to be affected include the Gulf of Tonkin, particularly Bạch Long Vĩ, Vân Đồn, Cô Tô and Cát Hải special zones, as well as Hòn Dấu island.

The storm is predicted to cause widespread rain across the northern region on August 22, especially during the night, with moderate to heavy rain and thunderstorms, locally accompanied by torrential downpours. Quảng Ninh is forecast to experience particularly heavy to torrential rain.

From August 22 through the night of August 23, northeastern provinces, southern Phú Thọ province and Thanh Hoá province are expected to receive 70-150mm of rain, with some areas receiving more than 300mm. Quảng Ninh could see 200-300mm, with some areas receiving more than 500mm. Lạng Sơn, Bắc Ninh and Hải Phòng are forecast to receive 150-250mm, with several areas recording more than 400mm.

Rainfall could be particularly intense, exceeding 120mm in three hours, posing a risk of flash floods, inundation and landslides in vulnerable areas.

The rain is expected to persist through August 24

title: VNM: Cyclone - 08-2026 - Typhoon Narra #2 (2026-08-23)
content:
Description

At 07:00 on 23 August, the centre of Typhoon No. 4 was located at approximately 20.7°N and 107.8°E, over the sea area off Quang Ninh–Hai Phong, approximately 100 km east of Quang Ninh, 120 km east of Hai Phong, and 70 km north of Bach Long Vi Special Zone. The strongest winds near the storm centre were at Force 8, with gusts up to Force 10. The typhoon was moving southwest at approximately 3 km/h.

As of 10:00 on 23 August, the centre of Typhoon No. 4 was located over the sea north of Bach Long Vi Special Zone, approximately 135 km east of Quang Ninh and 140 km east of Hai Phong. The storm had maximum sustained winds of Force 8–9, with gusts reaching Force 10–11, and was moving southward at approximately 3 km/h.

  • Rainfall: From 19:00 on 22 August to 10:00 on 23 August, rainfall of 50–100 mm was recorded across the Northeast region and Thanh Hoa. Notable rainfall totals included 216 mm in Ha Lang (Cao Bang), 134 mm in Mau Son (Lang Son), 256 mm in Long Dinh (Quang Ninh), 179 mm in Cam Pha (Quang Ninh), and 89 mm in Son Dien (Thanh Hoa).
  • Forecast: From 23–24 August, rainfall of 50–100 mm is forecast in the Northeast, southern Phu Tho and Thanh Hoa, with locally over 200 mm. Lang Son, Bac Ninh, Quang Ninh, Hai Phong, Hung Yen and Ninh Binh are expected to receive 90–180 mm, with locally over 300 mm.
  • River levels: As of 10:00 on 23 August, water levels on several rivers had exceeded Alert Level 3, including:
    • Luc Nam River at Chu: 13.67 m, 0.67 m above Alert Level 3.
    • Thuong River at Cau Son: 16.52 m, 0.52 m above Alert Level 3.
    • Thuong River at Huu Lung: 20.34 m, 1.34 m above Alert Level 3.
    • Ky Cung River at Lang Son: 256.23 m, 0.23 m above Alert Level 3.
  • River levels are continuing to rise. From 23–25 August, flood peaks on the Thuong, Luc Nam, Trung, Ky Cung, Bac Giang, Bang Giang and Cau rivers are forecast at Alert Level 2–3, with some rivers potentially exceeding Alert Level 3. The Thai Binh River at Pha Lai is forecast to reach Alert Level 1–2.

Local authorities have proactively implemented response measures for the typhoon, heavy rainfall and flooding, including the evacuation of households in areas at risk of flooding, in line with the directions of the Prime Minister and the National Civil Defence Steering Committee.

Due to the circulation of Typhoon No. 4, heavy rainfall has caused water levels in the Luc Nam, Thuong and Ky Cung rivers to rise. From 23–25 August, flood peaks on the Thuong, Luc Nam, Thai Binh (Hai Phong), Trung, Ky Cung, Bac Giang (Lang Son), Bang Giang (Cao Bang) and Cau (Thai Nguyen) rivers are forecast to reach Alert Level 2–3, with some rivers expected to exceed Alert Level 3.

To proactively respond to Typhoon No. 4 and the associated heavy rain and flooding, authorities at both central and local levels have implemented coordinated measures in line with the “four on-the-spot” principle, ensuring proactive, timely and context-specific action, with a focus on protecting people’s lives and property.

To ensure the safety of people and their property, local authorities have evacuated 2,383 households, including 2,335 households in Lang Son (211 in Huu Lung and 2,124 in Ky Cung, of which 733 flooded households were evacuated), 31 households in Quang Ninh, 17 households in Bac Ninh, and 121 households in Thanh Hoa. Forces have also been deployed to guard and control people and vehicles in areas at risk of deep flooding and landslides, helping to minimise damage caused by the heavy rain, flooding and Typhoon No. 4.

As of 07:00 on 23 August 2026, preliminary damage reported in Lang Son, Quang Ninh and Bac Ninh provinces due to Typhoon No. 4 and heavy rainfall is as follows:

  • Casualties: 1 person died — Mr. Duong Phuc Hinh, born in 1999 and residing in Thai Binh Commune, Lang Son Province — due to a landslide hitting his house.
  • Housing: 200 houses were damaged or had their roofs blown off; 733 houses were flooded in Lang Son.
  • Agriculture and forestry: 2,864 hectares of crops were inundated or damaged, including 1,100 ha in Lang Son, 1,687 ha in Bac Ninh and 78 ha in Quang Ninh.
  • Livestock: 100 livestock and 6,000 poultry died in Lang Son.
  • Transport: 603 locations experienced landslides or flooding causing traffic disruption, including 600 in Lang Son and 3 in Bac Ninh.

Local authorities are continuing to assess, verify and consolidate the damage.
