The Viet Nam Red Cross Society (VNRC) has activated its National Disaster Response Team (NDRT) to monitor the situation and support the response to Typhoon No. 4 and the associated heavy rain and flooding. VNRC is also coordinating with domestic and international partners to share information, facilitate coordination and mobilise support as needed. At the local level, Red Cross branches are supporting local authorities in providing assistance to affected communities and households, particularly those impacted by flooding and the evacuation process. VNRC continues to closely monitor the situation and assess emerging needs to inform further response actions.

Actions taken by others

The Prime Minister issued Official Telegram No. 57/CĐ-TTg on 21 August 2026 and Official Telegram No. 54/CĐ-TTg on 17 August 2026, requesting the Chairpersons of the People’s Committees of provinces and centrally governed cities in the Northern region, from Thanh Hoa to Quang Tri, as well as relevant ministries and sectors, to proactively respond to natural disasters and the risks of heavy rainfall, flash floods and landslides, while focusing on recovery efforts following the floods. On 22 August 2026, the National Civil Defence Steering Committee issued Official Telegram No. 46/BCĐ-BNNMT on proactive response to heavy rain and flooding. On 21 August 2026, it issued Official Telegrams No. 44/BCĐ-BNNMT and No. 45/CĐ-BNNMT-ĐĐ, directing response measures to the tropical depression in the East Sea, Typhoon No. 4, and the associated heavy rain and flooding. The Ministries of National Defence, Public Security, Construction, Education and Training, Science and Technology, and Industry and Trade also issued official telegrams requesting their respective agencies and units to remain on standby and be prepared to respond to the typhoon, tropical depression, heavy rainfall, floods, inundation, flash floods and landslides in the Northern region and from Thanh Hoa to Ha Tinh. On 22 August 2026, the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment issued Official Telegram No. 9680/CĐ-BNNMT ordering the closure of one bottom outlet gate of the Hoa Binh Hydropower Reservoir at 16:00 on 22 August 2026. The Ministry also issued Document No. 9681/BNNMT-ĐĐ to the provinces/cities of Phu Tho, Hanoi, Bac Ninh, Hai Phong, Hung Yen and Ninh Binh regarding downstream safety during the operation of the Hoa Binh Hydropower Reservoir. On the same day, the Department of Dyke Management and Disaster Prevention and Control issued Document No. 1588/ĐĐ-QLĐĐ to the Departments of Agriculture and Environment of Bac Ninh, Thai Nguyen and Thanh Hoa, requesting urgent measures to ensure dyke safety and respond to flooding on the Thuong, Luc Nam, Cau and Buoi rivers. The Department also deployed two response teams for Typhoon No. 4 in Quang Ninh and to inspect the Thuong and Luc Nam river dyke systems in Bac Ninh. In coordination with Zalo Vietnam, the Department sent two rounds of safety messages to 11.6 million mobile subscribers in Son La, Phu Tho, Thai Nguyen, Cao Bang, Lang Son, Quang Ninh, Bac Ninh and Thanh Hoa, as well as coastal communes in the four provinces of Quang Ninh, Hai Phong, Hung Yen and Ninh Binh. The 24/7 disaster monitoring and duty system has been maintained, with authorities closely monitoring weather, disaster and dyke conditions and promptly disseminating forecasts and warnings to local authorities to support decision-making, coordination and response. At the local level, Bac Ninh, Lang Son and Quang Ninh provinces have deployed field teams to inspect preparedness and response measures for Typhoon No. 4 and the associated heavy rain and flooding, while mobilising local resources to provide timely assistance to affected households. Local authorities have issued official telegrams and directives on responding to Typhoon No. 4 and heavy rainfall, maintained duty shifts, and proactively monitored weather developments and forecasts/warnings.

title: PAK: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 06-2026 - Update #3 (2026-08-23)
content:
Description

Situation Overview

Pakistan's 2026 monsoon season began around 26 June, with the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) declaring the formal onset in the first week of July. PMD's seasonal outlook points to below-normal rainfall nationally, but officials have cautioned that below-normal totals do not equate to low risk, as short and intense rain spells continue to trigger flash flooding, urban flooding and landslides, particularly in the north and northeast.

As of the latest NDMA daily situation report (21 August), the cumulative death toll since 26 June has crossed 163, with over 483 people injured nationwide. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has recorded the highest number of fatalities, followed by Punjab, Sindh, Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) and Baluchistan. House and roof collapses account for majority of all deaths, followed by flash floods, drowning and lightning strikes.

Rainfall has arrived in successive spells rather than a single peak. Active flood alerts were held on the Chenab, Jhelum and Ravi through late July, with the Flood Forecasting Division reported high-level flooding on the Chenab at Chiniot and moderate flooding at Marala, Khanki and Qadirabad.

Chitral has sustained the most severe and most structurally damaging impact of the 2026 season. On the night of Monday 3 August a cloudburst over Broz, combined with a glacial lake outburst flood and an abnormal surge in temperature, generated flood torrents through Gumbas Gol and Broz Gol. Destruction extends across the district from Sheshi Koh Valley and Drosh in Lower Chitral to Mastuj in Upper Chitral, where swollen streams and mountain nullahs tore through Reshun, Zait, Kuragh, Charun, Booni, Awi, Parwak, Mastuj Khas and Parkusap. At Prayet Gol, high-level flooding carrying heavy sludge blocked the main flow of the Chitral River for several hours. A second event on 12 August triggered renewed flash flooding in the Broz and Gumbas Gol streams, closing the Chitral–Peshawar Road again and cutting off Baroz Gol and Sheedi village.

Weather Forecast (21–27 August 2026)

Monsoon currents and a westerly wave are expected to continue affecting the northern and upper parts of Pakistan, with rain-wind/thunderstorms and isolated heavy rainfall forecast on 21–22 August across Islamabad, Punjab, Kashmir, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Gilgit-Baltistan. Heavy rainfall is particularly possible in parts of Battagram, Buner, Abbottabad and Haripur on 22 August. From 23 August onward, conditions are expected to become predominantly hot and humid, with isolated thunderstorms possible in parts of Kashmir, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab and northeast Baluchistan on 23 August. Mostly hot and humid weather is expected through 26 August, while rain/thunderstorms may return to Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan on 27 August.

Pakistan Red Crescent Society (PRCS) Actions • PRCS continues to closely monitor the evolving monsoon situation through its National Headquarters and Provincial/State Branches, maintaining regular coordination with the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Provincial Disaster Management Authorities (PDMA), district administrations, and other relevant government departments to assess humanitarian needs and support preparedness and response efforts. • The PRCS Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) remains operational on a 24/7 basis, continuously monitoring weather forecasts, official advisories, and field information to facilitate timely information sharing, situational analysis, and operational coordination. Emergency Operations Centers at national and branch levels remain on standby, while National Disaster Response Teams (NDRTs), District Disaster Response Teams (DDRTs), Community Disaster Response Teams (CDRTs), first aid volunteers, and trained staff are ready for rapid deployment. Pre-positioned emergency relief stocks are available for immediate mobilization based on assessed needs. • Following the cloudburst in District Neelum, Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) on 19 July 2026, the PRCS AJK State and District Neelum Branches promptly coordinated with the district administration, supported rapid needs assessments, and shared initial situation reports. PRCS continues to closely monitor the situation in coordination with NDMA, PDMA and local authorities and remains prepared to provide humanitarian assistance should additional needs arise. • To further strengthen preparedness and Movement-wide coordination ahead of the peak monsoon period, PRCS convened the Movement Coordination Meeting on 22 July 2026. The meeting brought together Movement partners to review the evolving monsoon situation, share preparedness measures, identify potential operational and resource gaps, and reinforce coordinated planning to ensure a timely and effective humanitarian response if required. • Following the GLOF and cloudburst impacts in August at Chitral, PRCS Khyber Pakhtunkhwa received relief assistance from Provincial Disaster Management Authority Sindh, which was subsequently distributed to 400 affected families. The relief assistance comprised 400 ration bags containing approximately 27.8 kg of dry food commodities per family, along with 400 tents, 400 kitchen sets and 2,000 blankets (five per family) to address immediate shelter and household needs. In response to the acute shortage of safe drinking water caused by damage to local water supply systems, PRCS also provided 18 water filtration units and 30 water tanks to support affected communities. The transportation and distribution of relief packages were supported through the ongoing Monsoon EA MDRPK028. This support enabled PRCS to facilitate the timely movement and delivery of essential relief items to the affected communities and complemented the response efforts following the flooding. • PRCS has planned to distribute 50 hygiene kits to flood-affected households in District Ghizer and 45 hygiene kits to affected households in District Astore, Gilgit-Baltistan.

Partners continue to monitor the evolving situation and stand ready to scale up response if needed.

A total of 1,997 households (6,134 people) remain affected. The floods have resulted in three fatalities, all reported in Nan Province, including one in Pua District and two in Tha Wang Pha District. The team also supported the mobile kitchen operations of the Nan Provincial Red Cross Chapter and conducted field assessments in Mueang Nan, Wiang Sa, and Phu Phiang districts to inform timely and targeted humanitarian assistance. Red Cross volunteers, together with the Nan Provincial Red Cross Chapter and partner organizations, supported mobile kitchen operations by preparing and distributing more than 1,000 cooked meal boxes to flood-affected communities in Nan Province. The Royal Thai Government has directed all relevant agencies to intensify response and recovery efforts, prioritizing the safety and well-being of affected populations. To support flood response in Nan Province, the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM) deployed a KA-32 helicopter for evacuation missions and mobilized emergency equipment and personnel from three regional disaster prevention centers. title: Bangladesh: Shelter Cluster Response - Floods and Landslides 2026, 23 August 2026
content:
The 2026 monsoon season in Bangladesh triggered severe flash floods and devastating landslides. The disaster affected seven districts, with the Chattogram Division being the hardest-hit region. Driven by torrential monsoon rainfall, active depressions over the Bay of Bengal, and intense hill torrents, the crisis escalated rapidly from early July through August 2026. A total of 36,550 people sought refuge in 1,722 evacuation shelters. The floods and landslides resulted in 59 fatalities and 293 injuries.

The disaster damaged more than 54,000 houses across the seven affected districts, with an estimated US$37 million required for housing repair and reconstruction. As of 23 August 2026, the Government of Bangladesh had allocated 4,200 bundles of CGI sheets and provided US$105,000 in housing grants. Humanitarian partners have supported 7,750 households with essential household items (EHIs), while 1,371 households have received shelter repair assistance. To date, a total of US$745,017 has been mobilized for shelter support. Despite these efforts, significant shelter needs remain, and additional assistance is required to support affected communities.

Key Proposed Interventions:

  • House Repair Assistance with Plinth Raising and Flood Protection.
  • Shelter Repair Materials (CGI Sheets and Toolkits).
  • Essential Household Items (EHIs) and Kitchen Sets.
  • Integrated Shelter and Sanitation Support.
  • Cash Assistance for Shelter Recovery.

title: UNICEF Afghanistan Humanitarian Flash Update No. 4 (Central and Eastern Region Flash Floods), 20 August 2026
content:
Situation Overview

  • A series of flash flood events between 20 July and 3 August affected central and eastern Afghanistan, resulting in casualties, damage to houses and critical infrastructure, and disruption to essential services and livelihoods.
  • In the Eastern Region (ER), Parun district in central Nuristan Province, was among the most severely affected areas. Preliminary reports¹ indicate 24 fatalities and 125 injuries, with additional individuals reported missing. The floods destroyed or damaged 120 houses and affected one private health facility, local markets, bridges, roads, flood protection walls, agricultural land and water supply networks, disrupting livelihoods and access to safe drinking water.
  • Subsequently, on 3 August, a second flash flood struck Barg-e-Matal district in eastern Nuristan, affecting 191 houses, which were either destroyed or damaged. The floods also damaged bridges, roads, flood protection walls, agricultural land and water supply networks, further disrupting livelihoods and constraining access to safe drinking water and essential services.
  • In the Central Region (CR), flash floods across nine provinces² resulted in two fatalities and six injuries. A total of 316 houses were affected, impacting 2,057 people. Approximately 1.6 million square meters of agricultural land were damaged, around 300 livestock were killed, and 17 schools sustained damage, further affecting livelihoods and access to basic services.
  • A separate flooding incident in Paktia province destroyed 11 houses and damaged agricultural land. On 12 August, humanitarian partners carried out a joint emergency response to affected communities.
  • The recent flash floods may also have displaced explosive ordnance (EO) or exposed previously buried hazards, increasing protection risks for affected communities and humanitarian personnel operating in flood-affect areas.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 308: Week 3 - August 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

Market trends were mixed during the third week of August, with declines in several food and agricultural input prices partly offset by increases in vegetables, rice, and fuel. Commodity availability remained broadly sufficient, and weekly price movements were generally moderate. However, elevated diesel prices, ongoing regional trade disruptions, and supply constraints continued to keep transportation and import costs under pressure. Despite these factors, higher fuel costs have so far translated only moderately into retail food prices.

Food Items:

• National food prices showed mixed movements during the third week of August, with several staples recording small declines while others remained firm. Overall, price movements were limited, and market supplies continued to be adequate, although several commodities remained well above last year's levels.

• Wheat and Wheat Flour: Wheat prices edged down during the week, with wheat grain and low-price wheat flour both declining by 0.5%, while high-price wheat flour increased marginally by 0.1%. Compared to last year, prices remained higher, particularly wheat grain and low-price wheat flour, which were 13% and 12% higher, respectively.

• Rice: Rice prices moved slightly upward, with high-price Palawi and low-price Sholae rice increasing by 0.4% and 0.5%, respectively. Nevertheless, rice prices remained substantially above last year and the three-year average.

• Other Staples: Cooking oil, pulses, sugar, and salt prices registered small weekly declines, while bread prices were unchanged. Year-on-year comparisons remained mixed: cooking oil and sugar prices are still higher than last year, whereas pulses are 13% lower, supported by relatively favourable availability and domestic production.

• Vegetables: Vegetable prices experienced mixed movements during the week. Tomato prices fell by 6.0%, while potato and onion prices increased by 3.7% and 5.2%, respectively. Tomato and potato prices remained notably higher than last year, while onion prices were 4% lower, continuing its comparatively favourable price trend.

Non-Food Items:

• Exchange Rate: The Afghani strengthened slightly to AFN 65.2/USD, appreciating by 0.7% week-on-week. It remained 5% stronger than last year and 13% above the three-year average, continuing to provide some relief against imported cost pressures.

• Fuel: Diesel prices edged up by 0.8% during the third week of August to AFN 77.0 per litre. Prices were 15% higher than last year and 18% above the three-year average, maintaining pressure on transportation and supply-chain expenses amid continued regional supply constraints.

• Fertilizers: Fertilizer prices eased during the week, with DAP declining by 0.5% and urea by 2.2%. Despite these reductions, both remained considerably more expensive than last year, with DAP 14% and urea 32% higher, continuing to increase input costs for farmers.

• Livestock: The price of a 1-year-old live female sheep increased by 0.6% week-on-week to AFN 7,784. Nevertheless, the price remained 5% below last year and 1% below the three-year average, suggesting continued weakness in livestock purchasing power. (Pastoralist ToT showing a 15% decline year-on-year).

• Labour Market: Labour market conditions remained subdued during the week, with unskilled labour availability holding at 2.1 days per week. Availability remained 14% below both last year and the three-year average, while unskilled and skilled daily wages declined marginally during the week.

title: Cameroon Humanitarian Update - August 2026
content:
National Humanitarian Forum seeks strategic alignment as Cameroon’s humanitarian transition advances

The National Humanitarian Forum took place in Yaounde on 26 May 2026, bringing together more than 140 participants from government, national and international NGOs, the United Nations, donors, technical and financial partners, and the media. The forum aimed to foster strategic alignment among humanitarian, development and government actors on the humanitarian situation, the ongoing humanitarian transition, the localization of aid, and financing and accountability issues.

Opening the forum, the UN Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator (RC/HC), Issa Sanogo said collaboration between national and local authorities, humanitarian partners and donors delivered life-saving assistance to one million people in 2025. He noted a persistent gap: only half of the 2.1 million people targeted were reached, leaving 1.1 million people without support. He linked the forum to the Humanitarian Reset, the global reform under which Cameroon is one of eight countries selected by the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) to shift toward a more localized, nationally led coordination model.

The Director of Civil Protection (DPC) at the Ministry of Territorial Administration (MINAT), Angele Ndzie Ntsama, welcomed continued partner support and committed the Government to strengthening coordination, consultation and response mechanism. She called for collective reflection on the role of national and local actors, accountability to affected populations, and stronger links between humanitarian action, development and peacebuilding.

Panel discussions confirmed that Area-Based Coordination (ABC) is now operational in the Far North, North-West and South-West regions at a regional level and in some divisions. Under the Civil Protection Law of 23 December 2024, MINAT/DPC holds legal responsibility for coordinating the humanitarian response. Hundreds of national NGOs are still active in the Far North, North-West and South-West coordination platforms, and the Lake Chad Basin Nexus Facility Fund, which reserves 30 per cent of its financing for local actors, has already supported two consortia in Cameroon and Chad.

Recommendations from the forum called for international financing and government contributions to be presented jointly for a transparent view of resources, for responsibilities to transfer together with corresponding human, logistical and budgetary means, and for a dedicated donor meeting to align financing mechanisms behind the transition.

Closing the forum, the RC/HC reiterated that the transition is not a disengagement but an accompanied, responsible transfer of responsibility, and reaffirmed the commitment of the United Nations and humanitarian partners to mobilize funding so that no vulnerable community is left without support. The Directorate of Civil Protection reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to strengthened national coordination and accountability.

title: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 14 (10-16 August 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Burundi
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

According to the World Health Organization, as of 16 August, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 5,001 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus (BVD), including 2,378 deaths.

With the recent increase in figures, the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak has become the largest and fastest-growing outbreak in DRC. The rapidly escalating outbreak is unfolding against the backdrop of an ongoing triple crisis in eastern DRC, where health risks, largescale displacement and persistent conflict intersect. Given the high case fatality rate of 81% in internally displaced persons (IDP) sites, as per WHO and Africa CDC, a multisectoral response to multidimensional needs of displaced populations is critically required.

The spread of the outbreak into Bas-Uélé Province underscores the continued need to comprehensively address the mobility dimensions of the ongoing public health response. Community deaths account for over 50 per cent of fatalities as per government sources, indicating ongoing gaps in case detection and health-care seeking. Contact tracing is particularly weak in Bas-Uélé (18.9%), highlighting the need for continued disease surveillance and monitoring to ensure a complete epidemiological picture.

The rapid geographic expansion of the outbreak creates additional needs for hygiene supplies, infection prevention and control (IPC) consumables and health infrastructure, such as ambulances, to support timely prevention, detection, referral and response. In parallel, the rising number of cases in Haut-Uélé requires enhanced disease surveillance and cross-border coordination to prevent disease transmission into neighbouring South Sudan and the Central African Republic (CAR).

Cross-border movements, displacement and population mobility continue to shape disease transmission, requiring an urgent and rapid response to save lives and protect people in affected areas, while mitigating regional health risks. Given the rapidly escalating crisis, IOM’s preparedness and response efforts aim to enhance monitoring at points of entry (PoEs) and points of control (PoCs), particularly along the Congo River, to strengthen detection and response capacities.

In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) systemwide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM has scaled up its response, enabling enhanced surge support, operational capacity and coordination across affected countries.

IOM’s response continues to focus on Priority 1a countries, DRC and Uganda, where outbreak response and enhanced preparedness activities remain ongoing, and Priority 1b countries, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, which face an elevated risk of crossborder transmission. Preparedness interventions are also being implemented in other at-risk countries across the region, including Priority 2 countries, Angola, CAR, Ethiopia, Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, the United Republic of Tanzania and Zambia, to strengthen readiness and enhance regional health security, while supporting continent-wide efforts, particularly as co-lead of the PoE technical working group at the continental level.

title: UNFPA Colombia Earthquake Situation Report (13 - 21 August 2026)
content:
The 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck Colombia on 10 August continues to generate significant humanitarian needs. The earthquake has destroyed more than 31,460 homes and affected 4,996 community centres and 348 health facilities, disrupting access to essential services. More than 282,700 people have been affected, including approximately 76,330 women of reproductive age and 3,050 pregnant women.

Loss of housing, displacement, and disruption of family and community support networks have heightened protection risks. Thousands of families are relying on temporary shelters, where overcrowding and inadequate privacy, lighting, water, and sanitation are increasing exposure to gender-based violence. Some women and their families are sleeping outdoors, further increasing protection risks and creating additional barriers to accessing essential services.

Chocó is among the most affected departments, where the earthquake is exacerbating pre-existing inequalities and vulnerabilities. For pregnant women, particularly those living in rural and remote areas, access to antenatal care, safe delivery, and emergency obstetric services was already limited. The earthquake has further deepened these barriers, leaving many women without access to life-saving maternal health services and referral mechanisms.

At the national level, UNFPA is leading coordination mechanisms on gender-based violence and sexual and reproductive health to ensure a coordinated response across all affected areas. UNFPA is currently responding in Quibdó and expanding its response to 11 municipalities across Chocó.

In Quibdó, UNFPA conducted a sexual and reproductive health needs assessment and visited the main hospital, identifying critical gaps in essential supplies, emergency reproductive healthcare, and maternal health services. In coordination with traditional ethnic birth attendants and the health system, UNFPA is strengthening the identification of obstetric risks and referral pathways for pregnant women, particularly those living in rural and remote communities.

UNFPA has also conducted protection assessments in temporary shelters and communities in Quibdó and distributed dignity kits to women and adolescent girls. In addition, UNFPA is supporting the identification and referral of survivors of gender-based and sexual violence, providing case management and psychosocial support, and disseminating information on risk mitigation measures and available support services for survivors.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #24 (18 to 20 August 2026)
content:
Situation Report No. 24 provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 18 to 20 August 2026.

Highlights

  • During the reporting period, IOM distributed 348 collapsible jerrycans, 340 plastic tarpaulins, 271 tool kits, 338 hygiene items and 66 kitchen sets. To date, the Organization has delivered 9,260 plastic tarpaulins, 6,116 collapsible jerrycans, 5,887 kitchen sets, 4,788 shelter tool kits and 3,612 personal hygiene items.
  • IOM provided 201 health consultations in César Nieves and 139 consultations in José María Vargas Sports Complex, ensuring continued care for chronic diseases, respiratory infections and other priority health conditions.
  • In Campo de Golf, IOM coordinated the distribution of 115 cleaning kits covering all shelters and supported the installation of solar lamps to improve safety and living conditions.

IOM Activities

IOM continued managing and coordinating the temporary accommodation sites of José María Vargas Sports Complex, César Nieves, Mare Abajo II and Campo de Golf, which hosted 1,629 accommodated people during the reporting period. In Mare Abajo II, IOM coordinated assessments and repairs to infrastructure affected by heavy rainfall, completing roofing works in 90 per cent of the cubicles in the shelter designated for older persons and restoring internal lighting. In Campo de Golf, IOM coordinated the distribution of 115 cleaning kits, 24 clotheslines and items for families with specific needs, while also coordinating the installation of solar lamps and supporting rainfall mitigation measures, including drainage improvements, shelter relocation and planning for a second WASH service area. In César Nieves, IOM maintained the services hub and supported the initial phase of WFP’s gradual reduction of food rations.

In the WASH sector, IOM conducted assessments in Mare Abajo II to guide drainage and mitigation actions following heavy rainfall. In César Nieves, IOM and CISP monitored WASH activities, including the distribution of 15,000 litres of water, collection of 16 m³ of waste, cleaning and disinfection of sanitation facilities and tank chlorination. IOM and NRC also supported advocacy efforts with authorities to address ongoing water supply challenges. In Campo de Golf, WASH actors completed shower drainage works, while IOM produced 22,000 litres of safe water and allocated space for the construction of laundry facilities by Project Hope. At José María Vargas Sports Complex, IOM supported the removal of 14 portable toilets to adjust sanitation infrastructure to the current population.

In health, IOM provided 201 consultations in César Nieves and 139 consultations in José María Vargas Sports Complex, focusing primarily on hypertension, respiratory infections, non-communicable diseases and gastrointestinal illnesses. IOM also coordinated with authorities to clarify misinformation that had been limiting access to health services in César Nieves.

Under information management and needs assessments, IOM presented its registration and information management system to humanitarian partners in César Nieves to strengthen coordination and reduce duplication of assistance. The Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) team completed a household survey across the four IOM co-managed sites, reaching 168 families and collecting information on accommodation conditions, needs, mobility, intentions and prospects for return or relocation.

Protection activities included IOM’s participation in defining measures to address access control gaps, child protection risks and coexistence issues in César Nieves. In Campo de Golf, the protection technical working group led by IOM consolidated agreements on coordination, safe referral pathways and activities for children and adolescents. Following the 18 August earthquake in La Guaira, IOM and NRC conducted community monitoring in Mare Abajo II to identify potential protection needs. IOM also monitored risks related to relocation processes and reports of possible fraud attempts targeting accommodated populations.

IOM continued participating in the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA), providing inputs for the housing and social inclusion sectors as the process advanced to the preliminary analysis stage and presentation of initial findings. IOM also received high-level visits, including the United Nations Humanitarian Coordinator and the IOM Chief of Mission.

IOM Planned Response

IOM plans to:

  • Continue infrastructure repairs in Mare Abajo II and rainfall mitigation measures in Campo de Golf, including drainage improvements, shelter redistribution and expansion of WASH services.
  • Maintain monitoring of water supply and water quality in César Nieves and continue drainage and sanitation infrastructure improvements.
  • Continue delivering mobile health and mental health services and strengthen coordination among health actors operating across the four IOM co-managed sites.
  • Implement a second phase of the characterization of 110 community settlements through key informants to prioritize settlements based on vulnerability, needs and response gaps, and to guide future household-level assessments.
  • Follow up on agreements reached through protection technical working groups, strengthen access control measures in César Nieves and maintain monitoring of protection risks and community-based prevention and reporting mechanisms.
  • Continue participating in the PDNA process and sectoral coordination mechanisms.

title: Agrometeorological 10 days Bulletin for 21-31 August 2026 across the Northern Tonle Sap Basin of the PEARL project
content:
Flood Early Warning

No flood risk for the next 10 days. Keep a clean watering basin around each tree with a low earthen ring about half a palm high to slow splash; during heavy showers cut a small notch so water drains. Mulch under the canopy 10-15 cm (about a palm to a palm-and-a-half thick) using dry rice straw, chopped prunings, dried grass/leaves, leaving a hand-width gap at the trunk. Maintain diversion furrows one hand wide and one palm deep to guide rainwater away from trunks. Keep tools and bags on shelves about one palm above the floor.

Pest & Disease Early Warning

With pests and diseases forecasted for the next 10 days, tighten hygiene and monitoring. Collect and destroy fallen and damaged nuts and apples daily to reduce pest breeding; bury or solarize away from trees. Keep canoрy open for airflow; avoid leaf wetness late day. Inspect new shoots, panicles, and young nuts daily; remove and dispose away from the orchard any shoots or panicles showing rot or blackened lesions. Clean hands and tools with soapy water between trees. If available through extension services, consider locally approved biological controls rather than synthetic chemicals. Maintain mulch 10-15 cm (about a palm to a palm-and-a-half) with a hand-width gap at the trunk.

Cyclone Early Warning

With the possibility of cyclones forecasted during the next 10 days, expect strong winds, lightning, and heavy rain. Reduce canopy "sail" by lightly tipping back long outer shoots; stake or brace young trees with soft ties; remove or secure loose materials. Open drainage one hand wide and one palm deep to move water away from trunks. Do not work under trees when thunder is heard or lightning is seen; move indoors and wait thirty minutes after the last thunder. If nuts or apples are market-ready, harvest one to two days before peak winds/rain and store above floor level. After the event, cut broken limbs cleanly, remove torn bark, and keep cuts small; sanitize tools with soapy water and sun-dry.

Drought/Dry spells

With drought or dry spells forecasted for the next 10 days, conserve soil moisture and reduce heat stress. Restore mulch 10-15 cm (about a palm to a palm-and-a-half) using dry rice straw, chopped prunings, dried grass/leaves, leaving a hand-width gap at the trunk. Do field work in cooler hours. Keep a clean weed strip two to three paces around trunks. Delay heavy pruning until rains resume; only remove dead or rubbing shoots to keep some shade on fruit and nuts.

title: WFP Central African Republic Country Brief, August 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• The updated March 2026 IPC analysis for AprilAugust 2026 projects that over 2 million people will face acute food insecurity, underscoring the need for sustained assistance throughout the lean season.

• WFP provided food and cash assistance to more than 62,000 vulnerable people, contributing to the stabilization of household food consumption, amid rising prices and deteriorating economic access to food.

• Despite insecurity and access constraints in the north-east, WFP continues to deliver an integrated response combining emergency assistance, nutrition support, school feeding, resiliencebuilding activities and critical supply chain services.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• The Central African Republic faces protracted insecurity, regional spillover from Sudan and sustained displacement. Over 2 million people are projected to face acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3+) between April and August 2026, including 262,000 people in Emergency (IPC Phase 4). Refugees, IDPs, returnees and host communities remain among the most affected populations, while access constraints persist in border areas such as Vakaga.

• Humanitarian needs remain high during the peak of the lean season, while food assistance is constrained by limited funding. Market monitoring indicates increasing pressure on household economic access to food, with elevated food basket costs and localized shortages of staple commodities reported in several hard-to-reach areas.

• Operational capacity and humanitarian access remain constrained by insecurity, logistical challenges and reduced funding for common services. Insecurity in north-eastern areas, particularly around Birao, together with seasonal road access constraints, continued to affect the movement of humanitarian supplies and the delivery of assistance.

• While no Ebola cases have been confirmed incountry, WFP is supporting government-led preparedness efforts to the ongoing outbreak in neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo.

title: Cameroon | Floods in Fako DREF Operation No.: MDRCM045
content:
Date of event 05-08-2026

What happened, where and when?

In the early hours of Wednesday, August 5, 2026, after more than a month of continuous rains, torrential downpours fell on the coastal city of Limbe, in the department of Fako, South-West region of Cameroon. At around 6:30 a.m., the waterlogged hillside overlooking the Mbende and Gardens neighborhoods gave way. The landslide swept away an inhabited house, burying its four sleeping occupants. Three adult women died, including a pregnant woman who lost her unborn child. The fourth occupant, an adult male, was pulled alive from the rubble by Cameroon Red Cross volunteers and community members. He is currently hospitalized in intensive care at the regional hospital of Limbe. The lives of many people are threatened and the search continues.

These same rains saturated the drainage systems of Limbe and Jenguele. Runoff from the Mount Cameroon massif carried mud, rocks, vegetation and solid waste accumulated in the residential plain, flooding Down Beach, Church Street, Motowoh, Mawoh, Mabeta New Layout, Cité SIC, Isokolo, Manga Williams Avenue, Bonjo and the Mile 1, 2 and 4 districts. The fence of the Limbé Wildlife Centre has been breached. Water entered the offices of the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), an unprecedented event in the city's institutional memory. Roads have become impassable for pedestrians and vehicles. Cassava fields and markets have been flooded, with significant losses of goods.

As of August 8, 2026, several neighborhoods remain under water. More than 1,500 households, or about 12,000 people, are affected, and nearly 2,000 people (250 households) whose homes were completely flooded are now homeless and in an emergency situation. The fairly large number of people with special needs remains very worrying, with nearly 700 people concerned.

Stagnant water, contaminated with faeces, accumulates in low-lying and densely populated neighbourhoods, where shallow wells are the main source of drinking water, in a region which has repeatedly been the epicenter of national cholera outbreaks.

The Fako Departmental Committee in Limbe, in collaboration with the prefect of Fako, the mayor and the security forces, continues to assess the situation as it evolves. The departmental committee, which does not have a contingency stock, is almost powerless in the face of the situation, which continues to grow. If nothing is done in the coming days, the humanitarian situation in the city of Limbe could spiral out of control.

content:

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture, South-East

Multi-sector

Food Security

title: Tanzania Emergency Preparedness - Quarterly Report, April - June 2026
content:
Highlights

•A simulation design workshop was convened on 4th -7th May 2026, engaging facilitators in the planning of exercise The workshop established methodology, delivery modes, and draft injects to guide the Emergency Logistics simulation exercise.
•Environmental Sustainability Training and Emergency Preparedness Simulation Exercise (TTX) was conducted from June 2nd –4th June 2026, engaging 40 participants to practice the newly developed standard operating procedures for logistics coordination, validate sustainable practices, and strengthen collaboration — resulting in a nationally led, greener, and better-coordinated emergency response system.
•The transition of logistics pillar coordination to the WFP Country Office Supply Chain reinforced sustainability in coordination and alignment with broader emergency preparedness priorities.

Background

Between April and June 2026, Tanzania experienced variable weather conditions, with rainfall gradually decreasing as the country transitioned from the main rainfall season into the cooler and generally drier June–August period. During the quarter, the Tanzania Meteorological Authority continued to monitor and communicate weather-related risks, including rainfall, thunderstorms, strong winds, and localized flooding. By June, the country had entered the cool season, with generally drier conditions prevailing across much of the country, although localized rainfall remained possible in areas including the Lake Victoria Basin, the northern coastal belt, and parts of the northeastern highlands.
During the quarter, national humanitarian logistics efforts continued to prioritize operational readiness for weather-related emergencies. Stakeholders maintained coordination and monitoring of emerging risks and continued preparedness actions in line with the national Contingency Plan for drought, flood, and related hazards (November 2025–June 2026). These efforts supported coordinated preparedness among partners and contributed to strengthening national capacity to anticipate and respond to emergencies.

title: UNICEF Latin America and Caribbean Region Humanitarian Situation Report No. 1 (Disaster Preparedness), January - June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • During the first half of 2026, Latin America and the Caribbean continued to face overlapping climate-related, socio-economic and public health-related emergencies, including floods, landslides, droughts and disease outbreaks that disrupted access to essential services and disproportionately affected children in vulnerable communities. Particularly significant was the ongoing recovery from Hurricane Melissa, which struck Jamaica, Cuba and the Dominican Republic[1] in October 2025 and continued to shape humanitarian needs across the Caribbean throughout the reporting period.
  • UNICEF and its partners implemented emergency preparedness, anticipatory action and response interventions across the region, reinforcing systems for child protection, health, nutrition, education and WASH in close coordination with national authorities, civil society organisations and United Nations partners. Institutional readiness was also strengthened through early warning systems, emergency simulation exercises, anticipatory action frameworks, shock-responsive social protection mechanisms and capacity building for government counterparts and frontline responders, including the activation of the 2026 CERF Anticipatory Action Framework for drought in Guatemala and El Salvador.
  • El Niño conditions were officially declared in June 2026 and are expected to intensify throughout the second half of the year, alongside an above-normal Eastern Pacific hurricane season, posing heightened risks for Mexico and Central America and underscoring the urgency of sustained humanitarian financing.
  • For 2026, UNICEF has appealed for US$53.8 million for disaster preparedness, anticipatory action and emergency response. As of 30 June 2026, approximately US$24.3 million was available, leaving a funding gap of 55 per cent (US$29.5 million). Sustained, flexible and predictable financing remains critical to ensure UNICEF can respond effectively to future shocks across the region.

title: WFP Sierra Leone Country Brief, August 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP completed 207 school kitchens and stores, improving safe meal preparation and storage, with fuel-efficient stove installation planned across five districts.

• WFP formalized a Technical Service Agreement with Sierra Leone Agricultural Research Institute (SLARI) to support soil testing, technical assistance and improved seed supply for sustainable crop and vegetable production.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Sierra Leone’s humanitarian needs remain driven by chronic poverty, economic fragility, high food insecurity and climate-related shocks. Although inflation has eased from previous peaks, rising fuel costs and food prices continue to strain household purchasing power.

• The July 2025 Food Security Monitoring System survey reported a decline in the proportion of severely food insecure households by more than half—from 28 percent in 2023 to 13 percent in July 2025—representing a 15-percentage point reduction.

• Since late February 2026, there has been a 40 percent increase in diesel and 23 percent increase in petrol, driven by external factors.

• WFP’s new Country Strategic Plan 2026-2030 reflects a sharpened strategic focus on food systems, home-grown school feeding, nutrition, resilient livelihoods, women’s economic empowerment and youth opportunities. WFP’s response is increasingly centered on strengthening nationally led systems, while retaining the capacity to respond to shocks, including climate-related disasters, public health emergencies and seasonal food insecurity.

title: WFP Cuba Country Brief, May 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• Despite operational delays caused by power shortages, limited fuel, and reduced logistical capacity, WFP continued implementing activities.

• WFP sustained emergency food assistance in eastern Cuba under the Hurricane Melissa Response Plan, reaching a cumulative 900,000 people since October 2025, while adapting operations to power outages, fuel shortages, and reduced logistics capacity.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Cuba's long-standing policy of providing free and universal access to basic services has historically reduced poverty and hunger. People's right to food is enshrined in the constitution approved in 2019, which also sets the goal of achieving food security for all people, reinforced by the law on food sovereignty and food and nutrition security of 2022.

• Progress toward the 2030 Agenda has suffered significant setbacks due to the cumulative socioeconomic impacts of COVID‑19, compounded by limited access to international financial institutions and rising inflation. These challenges are further exacerbated by an ongoing energy crisis, declining access to basic services, and recurrent devastating natural hazards. Together, these factors have reduced the availability of – and economic access to – food for the population.

• As a result, household diets are often inadequate in energy intake and insufficiently healthy or diverse, contributing to growing concerns over micronutrient deficiencies, overweight, and obesity, particularly among nutritionally vulnerable groups.

• Present in the country since 1963, WFP has supported the Government of Cuba in developing a new management model to enhance the efficiency and sustainability of food‑based social protection programmes. WFP has also been a key partner in emergency response, assisting the most vulnerable populations and strengthening the capacities of Cuban institutions. In addition, WFP promotes nutrition‑sensitive local food systems and supports efforts to improve resilience and disaster risk management.

title: WFP Guatemala Country Brief, August 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• In July, WFP supported 45,426 people (56 percent women) through a combination of emergency assistance, capacity strengthening, and malnutrition prevention activities.

• In parallel, WFP prepared and prepositioned over 671,000 food rations (January-July) to enable a rapid, Government-led emergency response.

• Guatemala faces a convergence of acute food insecurity and malnutrition, seasonal stress and heightened climate risk, making early action critical to protect livelihoods, safeguard food consumption and prevent further deterioration in nutrition outcomes.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Guatemala is facing intensifying climate-related pressures that are increasing risks to vulnerable households.

• Forecasts of severe rainfall deficits during the 2026 Primera and Postrera agricultural seasons—May to August and September to November, respectively—triggered Guatemala’s Anticipatory Action Framework for Drought twice (in March and July 2026), enabling early measures to protect vulnerable households before the anticipated impacts materialized.

• The expected rainfall deficits are associated with an intensifying El Niño, which is predicted to develop into a very strong event during October-December 2026 (81 percent probability), among the strongest on record since 1950, and persist until early spring 2027 (97 percent probability).

• These risks are unfolding against a fragile food security context. The latest IPC projections indicate that around 3.2 million people — approximately 17 percent of the analysed population — were expected to face Crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between July and September 2026.

• Without sustained humanitarian and resilience support, the combined effects of climate shocks, fragile food systems and constrained household purchasing power could further deepen and prolong food insecurity and malnutrition among Guatemala’s most vulnerable households

title: Cameroon Cholera Outbreak: Situation Report #3 (August 20, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • Eighty-three suspected cholera cases, including 18 confirmed by rapid diagnostic test, were reported in Minawao Refugee Camp on August 16.
  • Minawao Camp hosts some 81,000 refugees and is operating at 324% of intended capacity.
  • The wider national cholera outbreak has reported 1,252 cases and 31 deaths across 11 health districts as of August 12.
  • Multiple transmission chains are suspected within the camp, increasing the risk of rapid spread among vulnerable populations.

OUR RESPONSE

  • International Medical Corps is coordinating with health authorities, UN agencies, camp management and humanitarian partners to support a harmonized response.
  • We are implementing cholera prevention and response activities focused on outbreak containment, case management and community activities, and strengthening treatment capacity through additional staff, essential medicines and cholera supplies.
  • We also are strengthening surveillance, community alert systems and risk communication to support early detection and treatment, while scaling up risk communication, hygiene promotion, infection prevention, disinfection and emergency activities involving water, sanitation and hygiene.
  • Since the beginning of the outbreak, our team has managed 83 patients, resulting in 73 recoveries, nine cases currently under observation and one recorded death, with 509 contacts identified and followed. Rapid field investigations, line listing, contact tracing, active case finding, household disinfection and patient referrals remain ongoing, under the leadership of the Mokolo Health District.

title: Afghanistan: Monthly Market Report Issue 74: July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

Major Economic Developments

Economic Growth: Afghanistan’s economy continues to expand modestly, supported by resilient domestic demand, relatively stable prices, and stronger domestic revenue mobilization. However, economic growth remains too weak to keep pace with rapid population growth, particularly amid the return of millions of Afghans. As a result, per capita income declined by 5.6 percent, increasing pressure on household welfare and limiting improvements in living standards. Persistent employment constraints, weak private investment, declining external assistance, and regional uncertainty continue to weigh on the strength and inclusiveness of the recovery.

Trade & External Vulnerability: Afghanistan’s dependence on imports and alternative trade corridors continues to expose domestic markets to regional and global shocks. While trade flows remained broadly functional during July, higher transportation costs, longer transit routes, and regional supply constraints continued to increase import costs, particularly for food, fuel, agricultural inputs, and other essential commodities. Rising global commodity prices and geopolitical uncertainty, alongside continued disruptions to regional trade routes, remain key risks to domestic price stability.

Exchange Rate: The Afghani depreciated moderately against the US dollar in July, averaging AFN 65.8/USD, 2.5 percent weaker than the previous month. However, the currency remained 4.5 percent stronger than last year and 13 percent above its three-year average. The relatively strong Afghani continued to partially offset imported inflation, although higher transport and global commodity costs limited the full pass-through to domestic prices.

Inflation Rate: Inflationary pressures remained elevated (June 2026 data), with headline inflation at 7.6 percent year-on-year and food inflation at 7.2 percent. Key contributors included health, housing, bread and cereals, oils and fats, and transportation, reflecting continued pressures across food, fuel, and other essential goods and service.

Floods: Heavy rainfall, flash floods and landslides affected several provinces during July, with Parun district of Nuristan among the hardest hit, damaging homes, shops, and sections of the local market and temporarily disrupting economic activity. The rapid humanitarian response in Parun helped stabilize local markets and household food demands.

title: WFP Rwanda Country Brief August 2026
content:
• In July, WFP reached 185,830 people through the provision of 137 MT of food and USD 510,639 in cash-based transfers (CBT).
  • WFP requires USD 17.6 million to sustain planned operations over the next six months, representing 59 percent of total requirements for planned activities. Of this amount, USD 9.9 million is urgently needed to maintain food assistance for refugees, asylum seekers, and returnees.
  • WFP and the Ministry of Agriculture and Animal Resources signed a letter of understanding to endorse the new CSP and to strengthen joint efforts to promote inclusive production and market access, improve resilience and nutrition, and leverage innovation, data and analytics to transform Rwanda’s agrifood systems.

title: WFP Djibouti Country Brief August 2026
content:
• July 2026 IPC analysis projects over 256,000 people, more than a quarter of Djibouti’s population, to face Crisis or worse food insecurity (IPC 3+) between July and December 2026, including 30,000 people in Emergency (IPC 4).
  • The transition of the Humanitarian Logistics Base (HLB) to the Government of Djibouti continues, with decommissioning activities actively underway. Following consultation, humanitarian partners confirmed they were not in a position to sustain the facility, and transfer to national ownership was agreed as the means of retaining it for emergency preparedness. Common storage services to partners continue as required from an alternative warehouse, and WFP’s operational capacity in support of the Djibouti–Ethiopia corridor is unaffected.
  • A strong El Niño, intensifying throgh late 2026, drove below-normal June–September rains across Djibouti and the northern Greater Horn, compounding water scarcity and pasture loss. Together with price shocks linked to disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, these are named drivers of the IPC deterioration.

title: Colombia Emergency Response, Situation Report #1 (10 – 17 August 2026)
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

378 Missing persons 13,077 Homes destroyed Colombia is facing a large-scale humanitarian emergency following the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck San José del Palmar, Chocó, on 10 August. The earthquake and subsequent aftershocks have affected hundreds of municipalities across western Colombia. Damage to infrastructure is extensive, as 2,486 educational facilities, 238 health centres and 16 water systems have been affected.ii

The most severe impacts are concentrated in Valle del Cauca, Chocó, Risaralda and Caldas, although damage extends across a much wider area of the country. Thousands of homes have been damaged or destroyed, leaving affected households in need of shelter and basic assistance. Disruptions to electricity, water supply, healthcare and connectivity are restricting access to essential services, while damage to transport infrastructure is compounding the isolation of remote communities and complicating the delivery of assistance.

The full scale of humanitarian needs is still emerging, particularly in harder-to-reach communities, as significant information gaps persist.iii CESVI’s ongoing rapid needs assessment is providing an increasingly comprehensive picture of the scale and severity of needs across the communities assessed,iv with findings highlighting significant and overlapping impacts on housing, livelihoods, protection and psychosocial wellbeing:

title: Population mobility mapping (PMM) report for Bundibugyo Virus disease (BVD) Preparedness in Arua District, Uganda, 6-8 July 2026
content:
1. Introduction and Context

As part of preparedness and response efforts for the ongoing Ebola (Bundibugyo) virus disease (BVD) outbreak affecting the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda, the International Organization for Migration (IOM), in collaboration with the Uganda Ministry of Health (MOH) and district authorities, conducted a Population Mobility Mapping (PMM) exercise in Arua District from 6 to 8 July 2026. The exercise brought together key stakeholders including community representatives, health workers, transport operators, border officials, local leaders, religious leaders, and traders, among others, to map population movements, identify priority mobility corridors, congregation points, and formal and informal points of entry that may facilitate cross border transmission of Bundibugyo Virus Disease (BVD) and therefore and inform targeted preparedness interventions.

As of mid-July 2026, the DRC had reported more than 2,100 confirmed BVD cases and over 800 deaths, representing a crude case fatality rate (CFR) of approximately 39% while Uganda had reported 20 confirmed cases and 2 deaths (CFR: 10%), with no new cases reported since 21 June 2026. The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern DRC, particularly Ituri and North Kivu provinces, with cross-border transmission linked to Uganda. Given Arua district's strategic location along major trade and migration routes connecting Uganda, DRC, South Sudan and the rest of the region, the PMM exercise was undertaken to strengthen evidence based public health preparedness, support risk informed planning and enhance coordination among different government and partner response actors.
