title: WFP Ecuador Country Brief, August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW
• Ecuador continues to face severe security, socioeconomic, and environmental challenges. Violence driven by drug related crime has escalated sharply, making Ecuador one of the most insecure countries in the region.
• Poverty and extreme poverty remain high, with 21.4 percent and 8.3 percent, respectively. The country is experiencing a complex migration dynamic, marked by a continued influx of migrants and increased emigration due to deteriorating security conditions.
• OCHA’s 2026 Shock Analysis estimates that 1.9 million people in Ecuador require humanitarian assistance due to the convergence of armed violence, recurring disasters, and socioeconomic fragility, with the greatest needs concentrated in 10 priority provinces.
• Food insecurity remains a significant concern. Updated IPC analysis (2026) projected 2.6 million people facing acute food insecurity, especially agricultural households with limited access to water and sanitation.
• Undernourishment is at 12.1 percent, and 17.7 percent of children under five are stunted, with disproportionate impacts on women, Indigenous communities, rural populations, and migrants.
• WFP continues to support the response through assistance to migrants, expansion of the National Home-Grown School Feeding programme, and emergency support for climate affected populations, while strengthening partnerships amid limited funding availability to upper middle income countries like Ecuador.

title: WFP Burundi Country Brief August 2026
content:
• Burundi faces heightened risks from the emerging Super El Niño 2026–2027, and WFP is reinforcing early warning and anticipatory actions to protect lives and livelihoods.
  • WFP’s refugee food assistance remains severely underfunded, with ration cuts and a complete pipeline break from October; USD 35 million is urgently required to sustain support and prevent acute food insecurity through August 2027.
  • Burundi’s home‑grown school meals programme faces a significant funding shortfall for the 2026/2027 school year. An additional USD 18 million is required to ensure every child receives a daily meal across 783 schools.

title: Lebanon: Flash Update #50 - Escalation of hostilities in Lebanon (as of 17 August 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • At least 4,346 deaths and 12,303 injuries recorded due to hostilities since 2 March, with 366 people killed and 302 injured since the 19 June ceasefire announcement, according to the Ministry of Public Health.
  • 351,558 people remain displaced within Lebanon as of 13 August, while 863,172 people have reported returning to their areas of origin. As of 17 August, 22,400 Internally Displaced Persons (>53% women and girls) remain in 221 collective shelters.
  • Attacks affecting healthcare personnel on 11 and 12 August, as well as destruction of civilian infrastructure, continued during the reporting period, undermining access to essential services and heightening protection risks for conflict-affected communities.
  • Some 111,000 people temporarily displaced following intensification of military activity in Deir al-Zahrani and Ansar (Nabatieh Governorate) on 15 August; the majority of whom returned within 48 hours.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Humanitarian needs remain acute amid ongoing military activities, protracted displacement, and extensive destruction and basic service disruptions. While the overall number of displaced persons decreased slightly during the reporting period, significant barriers to return remain. Moreover, renewed displacement was reported from Deir al-Zahrani and Ansar (Nabatieh Governorate) following the intensification of military activities and strikes on the two localities on 15 August. Health and water services continued to face disruptions, including reports of attacks affecting medical teams in Nabatieh city and Zawtar El Charqiyeh (Nabatieh Governorate), and ongoing impacts on water infrastructure and service provision in conflict-affected areas. Populations that remain displaced, have returned, or are hosting displaced families continue to require sustained support to address protection risks, meet basic needs, and restore critical services damaged or disrupted by the conflict.

Intensified military activity was reported in parts of the South and Nabatieh governorates during the reporting period, further constraining return movements and exacerbating humanitarian concerns in affected areas. On 15 August, airstrikes in Deir al-Zahrani and Ansar (Nabatieh Governorate) resulted in 11 fatalities and 19 injuries, including four children and one woman killed and one child and 11 women injured, according to the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH). The strikes triggered temporary displacement from the affected areas, with local authorities reporting that approximately 102,000 people (70 per cent of families) in the Cheqif Union of Municipalities, where Ansar and Deir al-Zahrani are located, were displaced. Approximately 8,800 people (30 percent of families) were also displaced from localities within the Iqlim al-Tuffah Union of Municipalities (areas surrounding the targeted localities). Most families returned within 24 to 48 hours following the intensification of airstrikes, although approximately 85 people remain displaced in collective shelters in Houmin, Nabatieh district (Nabatieh Governorate), and Saida City (South Governorate). In Saida, the Disaster Risk Reduction provided mattresses and blankets to displaced families, from prepositioned DRR supplies available to respond to new displacements.

A total of 168 conflict incidents involving shelling, airstrikes, detonations and demolitions were reported between 11 and 17 August, indicating a continued escalation of military activity in South and Nabatieh governorates. This represents an increase from 133 incidents reported between 4 and 10 August and 97 incidents between 28 July and 3 August. While the frequency of artillery shelling remained broadly consistent with the previous reporting period, the number of airstrike incidents tripled, increasing from 12 to 36. The intensification of military activity continues to drive humanitarian needs and protection risks, contributing to further destruction of homes and civilian infrastructure, disruptions to essential services, barriers to return, heightened exposure to explosive ordnance, and prolonged displacement. Airstrikes, shelling, demolitions and other security incidents were reported across Bint Jbeil, Marjaayoun, Hasbaya and Nabatieh districts in Nabatieh Governorate, as well as in Tyre district in South Governorate.

The Ministry of Public Health reported 4,346 people killed (including 393 women and 257 children) and 12,303 injured (1,465 women and 1,039 children) as of 17 August. Since the latest ceasefire announcement on 19 June, 366 people have been killed and 302 injured.

Attacks affecting on-duty healthcare workers and education infrastructure continued during the reporting period, highlighting ongoing protection concerns and challenges to the delivery of essential services. On 11 August, an ambulance responding to casualties from a drone strike in Nabatieh city (Nabatieh Governorate) was targeted, damaging the vehicle and exposing medical teams to additional risk, according to WHO. On 12 August, local authorities reported the demolition of a health clinic in Zawtar El Charqiyeh (Nabatieh Governorate) as well as a public school, which had a pre-conflict enrolment of 130 children, and a children’s centre serving more than 260 children, according to UNICEF. Since 2 March, WHO has recorded 135 health-care workers killed while on duty and 410 injured in Lebanon.

Displacement levels remained high across Lebanon, with only marginal reductions reported during the reporting period. As of 13 August, 351,558 people remained displaced nationwide, according to DTM report, representing a decrease of just 0.35 per cent compared with the previous week (6 August). The largest reductions were recorded in districts hosting the highest numbers of internally displaced persons (IDPs), including Beirut district (Beirut Governorate), where the caseload declined by 3,718 people, Saida district (South Governorate), which recorded a decrease of 4,935 people, and Chouf district (Mount Lebanon Governorate), where the caseload fell by 3,035 people. At the same time, increases in displacement were reported in Tyre district (South) by 9,917 people and Nabatieh district (Nabatieh Governorate) by 4,143 people, reflecting continued population movements linked to insecurity and barriers to sustainable return. For displaced households living outside collective shelters, ongoing pressures on host communities and municipal systems continue to drive needs for health care, medication, rental assistance, protection services, restoration of essential services, and emergency livelihood support to meet essential needs.

Displaced families continue to reside in collective shelters as damaged housing, disruptions to essential services, access constraints, and diminished coping capacities continue to hinder returns. As of 17 August, 22,400 people were accommodated across 221 collective shelters nationwide, according to the Disaster Risk Management Unit. Shelter populations remained largely stable during the reporting period, with the total number of occupants decreasing by approximately 400 people (1.75 per cent) compared with the previous week. Ensuring access to basic services, including reliable water and electricity supply, remains a key challenge, while overcrowding and limited privacy continue to affect living conditions in some sites. These constraints underscore the continued need for sustained support to collective shelters and the populations who remain displaced within them.

Returns continue, though ongoing insecurity and destruction of homes, infrastructure and services remain barriers. 863,172 people have begun returning to their areas of origin as of 17 August, a 3 per cent increase from 6 August. The number of returned IDPs increased most significantly in Nabatieh district (Nabtieh Governorate), with an additional 24,484 returnees bringing the total to 252,430. This was followed by Marjaayoun district (Nabatieh), which recorded 1,800 additional returnees for a total of 11,718, and Bint Jbeil,district (Nabatieh) where 1,762 additional returnees brought the total to 39,384. Despite continued return movements, conditions in many conflict-affected areas remain challenging. Damage to housing, infrastructure and essential services continues to affect returnees and residents, while ongoing security incidents are contributing to protection concerns. Electricity and water networks remain disrupted in several locations, and health services continue to face significant operational constraints. Local authorities also report continued restrictions on access to agricultural land, limiting livelihood opportunities, while constraints on repair and rehabilitation activities are slowing the emergency restoration of essential services. Sustained support remains critical to address immediate needs and facilitate safe, dignified and sustainable returns.

As the end of the six-month Flash Appeal approaches, funding constraints continue to undermine humanitarian efforts. The 2026 Lebanon Flash Appeal has only received $316.8 million (49.5 per cent) of the 639.9 million required as of 17 August. These funding shortfalls are threatening service continuity, restoration of critical services, and provision of timely humanitarian assistance for conflict-affected communities.

title: WFP Niger Country Brief, August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW
• The food security and nutrition situation remains critical in Niger. According to the December 2025 Cadre Harmonisé, 2.4 million people areprojected to face severe food insecurity in 2026. Malnutrition levels remain high with anestimated 1.6 million children to suffer from acute malnutrition this year (IPC Nutrition Analysis, December 2025), including 400,000 facing severe acute malnutrition (SAM).
• The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and ResponsePlan (HNRP) identified 3 million people in need, requiring USD 675 million to reach 2 million people targeted. This includes 1.9 million people targeted with food security responses.
• The Government will assist 1.5 million extremely vulnerable people with two-months of food assistance from July. Partners, including WFP, have resources to reach an additional 400,000 people, leaving 500,000 vulnerable people without any form of assistance between June -September.
• The security situation continued to deteriorate, particularly in Tillabéri and Diffa regions,significantly affecting populations and humanitarian operations. In addition, population movements and forced displacement continued to rise, with more than 251,000 people newly displaced since the beginning of the year, already approaching the 298,000 displaced during 2025. The continued rise in forced displacement is placing increasing pressure on rapid response mechanisms and emergency assistance capacities.

title: WFP Somalia Country Brief August 2026
content:
• Somalia is entering a critical new phase of hunger, where drought, conflict, displacement, sharply reduced humanitarian assistance, and rising food and fuel prices are converging faster than families can recover.
  • One third of Somalia’s population – six million people – is facing acute hunger or worse, including nearly two million people in emergency levels of hunger. These are not abstract numbers; they are families exhausting every last option to survive.
  • Somalia remains one of the world’s worst malnutrition crises in the world, with an estimated 1.88 million children under five projected to suffer acute malnutrition in 2026, including nearly 493,000 requiring treatment for severe acute malnutrition.
  • WFP’s lifesaving nutrition services are extremely limited. Preventive programmes have been cut across the country, increasing risks for vulnerable women and children.
  • WFP launched its new Somalia Country Strategic Plan (2026-2030), providing a strategic framework to save lives, strengthen self-reliance, enable government-led solutions and support humanitarian partners. Aligned with national priorities, the plan advances food security, resilience and sustainable pathways to reduce hunger.

title: Mozambique Health Cluster Bulletin July 2026
content:
Context Overview
Mozambique continues to face a complex humanitarian situation driven by the combined impacts of
climate-related shocks and protracted conflict, with significant consequences for the health and wellbeing
of vulnerable populations. In 2026, severe flooding in the central and southern provinces caused
widespread displacement, damaged health infrastructure, and heightened the risk of waterborne
disease outbreaks, disrupting access to and continuity of essential health services.
At the same time, insecurity in Cabo Delgado continues to trigger displacement and place additional
pressure on already fragile health systems. Humanitarian needs remain acute, particularly among
displaced populations, returnees, and host communities, requiring sustained support for primary health
care, emergency medical services, mental health and psychosocial support, and outbreak prevention
and response.
In response, Health Cluster partners have maintained a coordinated humanitarian effort to ensure the
delivery of life-saving and essential health services. Interventions have focused on integrated
approaches, including mobile health services, disease surveillance and outbreak response, sexual and
reproductive health care, mental health support, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) activities.
Despite these efforts, considerable challenges remain, particularly related to humanitarian access,
funding constraints, shortages of critical resources, and the need to further strengthen health
information management, monitoring, and reporting systems.
This bulletin presents a summary of the key activities, achievements, and operational updates of Health
Cluster partners during July 2026. It highlights collective efforts to address urgent health needs and
support the recovery and resilience of communities affected by conflict in the north and floods in the
central and southern regions of Mozambique.

title: Islamic Relief Pakistan: Humanitarian Situation Report (Period: 26-June to 19-August 2026)
content:
BACKGROUND

Pakistan continues to face significant and interconnected challenges arising from economic instability and climate-related disasters. The country is recognized as one of the world's most vulnerable nations to disasters, ranking 18th out of 191 countries in the INFORM Risk Index due to its high exposure to hazards, underlying vulnerabilities, and limited capacity to respond and recover. Over the last decade, disasters have caused losses exceeding USD 18 billion, placing considerable pressure on the economy and hindering sustainable development and growth.

Pakistan's 2026 monsoon season commenced on 26 June 2026 and is expected to continue until mid-September 2026. According to the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), seasonal rainfall is projected to be 22–26% higher than last year, with risks further intensified by accelerated melting of the country's more than 7,000 glaciers. While the latest NDMA situation reports indicate a cumulative death toll of 161, considerably lower than at the same stage of the devastating 2022 and 2025 monsoon seasons, the situation has worsened significantly over the past 12 days. In response to rising water levels, NDMA and Provincial Disaster Management Authorities (PDMAs) have upgraded their warnings from advisories to active flood alerts. Evacuation measures have already been initiated in vulnerable riverine and low-lying communities. Current casualty and impact figures should therefore be viewed as preliminary, reflecting an ongoing and increasingly severe monsoon season rather than its final outcome.

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP): Upper and central districts of the province are experiencing persistent rainfall and windstorms, increasing the risk of landslides in mountainous areas. Heavy precipitation has triggered localized flash floods in vulnerable streams and river channels. The province has recorded the highest number of weather-related casualties, highlighting the growing impact of the ongoing monsoon season.

Punjab: Intense monsoon rainfall continues to affect major urban centres, including Lahore and Rawalpindi, causing urban flooding and prompting emergency response efforts by government authorities. Rising river flows and continued heavy precipitation have kept disaster management agencies on heightened alert across the province. In southern Punjab, our team is closely monitoring the evolving situation and remains on high alert to support any required response actions.

Balochistan: Northeastern and eastern districts of Balochistan are experiencing intermittent afternoon and evening thunderstorms, while much of the province remains hot and humid. Localized heavy rainfall may trigger flash flooding in hill torrents and other vulnerable areas. Our trained emergency response teams are on high alert and are maintaining close coordination with the Provincial Disaster Management Authority (PDMA) to provide timely support should the situation deteriorate.

Sindh: Most districts of Sindh are experiencing hot and humid conditions with occasional cloudy periods. Isolated windstorms and thunderstorms may occur in eastern areas and coastal districts, posing localized risks. Our teams remain active and prepared in Karachi, Thatta, Sujawal, Mirpurkhas, Larkana, and Dadu districts, closely monitoring the situation and ready to provide timely support and assistance as needed.

AJK & Gilgit-Baltistan: Mountainous areas of AJK and GB are experiencing cloudy conditions with intermittent rainfall, thunderstorms, and gusty winds at isolated locations. Steep slopes and vulnerable hilly routes remain exposed to localized landslides, mudslides, and rapid surface runoff. Our teams are closely monitoring the situation and maintaining coordination with local authorities to support emergency response efforts if required.

title: UNHCR Peru: Factsheet 2026
content:
Context

Peru remains the second destination country for Venezuelan nationals who have been forced to flee, with over 1.64 million residing in the country by the end of 2025. The capital, Lima, hosts over one million Venezuelans, making it the city with the largest Venezuelan population outside of Venezuela.

As of December 2025, 556,791 people are asylum-seekers and 6,818 have been formally recognised as refugees. Peru hosts the second largest number of Venezuelan asylum-seekers worldwide. According to migration authorities, almost two-thirds of Venezuelans lack a regular stay permit. One in three also struggle to cover their most basic needs.

Forcibly displaced people in Peru face important challenges in accessing documentation, which is essential for the full
enjoyment of rights and State services, including public healthcare and financial inclusion. Given these circumstances,
specialized orientation and support for local integration remain essential.

UNHCR works with authorities to promote access to rights and services, focusing on areas with high numbers of refugees, high levels of poverty, and strong local commitment for inclusion of forcibly displaced people.

title: Locust Watch: Seasonal precipitation predictions in the Desert Locust summer and winter breeding areas (September 2026 - February 2027) (19 August 2026)
content: The rapid intensification of El Niño has continued in the recent weeks, and the episode is already the strongest on record for this time of year, while the positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is expected to persist in the coming months. In September, above-normal rainfall is forecast from northern Africa to the central Middle East, with wetter conditions also expected in eastern Ethiopia and Somalia due to the positive IOD. A dry signal may remain over India and Pakistan toward the close of the monsoon season. During October and November, the El Niño-related wet signal is expected to expand across northern and eastern Africa and the Middle East. Interior eastern Africa, the southern Arabian Peninsula, and Pakistan are likely to become wetter than normal. However, northwestern Africa may turn drier than normal by November. Overall, the forecast is consistent with rainfall patterns observed during previous strong El Niño events, with generally good model agreement. Some uncertainty remains over the northern Sahel and the strength of the IOD.

title: UNFPA Bangladesh Situation Report | Protracted Humanitarian Crisis in Bangladesh, 1 April - 30 June 2026
content:
New refugees fleeing conflict in Myanmar continued to arrive in Bangladesh, with 5,524 new arrivals documented between January and June 2026. Restrictions on camp expansion and limited shelter capacity have further exacerbated overcrowding and protection risks, particularly for women and girls. Between April and June, reported cases of gender-based violence (GBV) increased by 10 per cent compared with the previous quarter, highlighting a concerning deterioration in the protection environment in the Rohingya camps. The data also indicated the continued prevalence of intimate partner violence and abuse.

Maternal deaths declined, with six recorded during the reporting period—a 50 per cent decrease compared with the same period in 2025. The number of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services provided through women-friendly spaces also increased by 10.5 per cent from the previous quarter, indicating a positive trend in the utilization of these spaces and their continued importance. However, reduced community outreach, alongside the prioritization of essential life-saving services, contributed to slightly lower access to SRH services overall.

Between April and June, UNFPA-supported facilities delivered 78,076 SRH services. In addition, UNFPA reached 187,000 people—most of them women and girls—with GBV prevention and response services. It also distributed 1,760 dignity kits to Rohingya women and adolescent girls, the majority of whom had recently arrived from Myanmar, helping to address immediate protection and dignity needs.

Due to the worsening funding outlook and the resulting prioritization of the Joint Response Plan for Bangladesh, UNFPA’s appeal was reduced from US$26.4 million to US$20.4 million, of which US$20.09 million has been secured. Despite strong support for UNFPA’s core life-saving work, funding gaps across the wider response continue to affect the delivery of essential services. The GBV Sub-Sector faces a US$10.7 million funding gap, while the Health Sector faces a US$20 million gap for priority services, including comprehensive SRH services. These shortfalls are placing additional pressure on referral systems and other services on which UNFPA-supported programmes depend, putting essential SRH and GBV services at risk and threatening the progress made in recent years.

title: Yemen Market and Trade Bulletin July 2026 - Issued on 19th August 2026
content:
SHORT-TERM OUTLOOK AND IMPLICATIONS ON FOOD SECURITY:

Yemen remains in the grip of a severe humanitarian crisis, with over 53% of its population projected in IPC Phase 3+ during the June–September 2026 lean season and millions enduring IPC Phase 4 Emergency conditions—the highest global burden. Exacerbated by extreme El Niño climate impacts—where rainfall in key southern, central, and western agricultural zones is expected to drop more than 80% below normal alongside temperatures up to 3°C above average—the crisis directly threatens rainfed crops, pasture, and water resources. Compounding this, food basket and fuel prices have remained stable but high level in a nation heavily reliant on imports for over 80% of its staple foods, leaving households vulnerable to currency depreciation and Red Sea trade bottlenecks. These escalating needs coincide with a critical funding deficit, as the 2026 humanitarian appeal remained about 20% funded by August, forcing WFP and partners to scale back emergency life-saving operations. This stark regional shortfall reflects broader global patterns seen in the SOFI 2026 report, where despite a gradual decline in global hunger to 7.8% in 2025, persistent regional conflicts and energy price shocks continue to disproportionately inflate the cost of nutrient-dense foods across Africa and the Middle East.

KEY HIGHLIGHTS:

  • EXCHANGE RATES: The exchange rate in GoY-controlled areas held steady at about YER 1,555 per USD in July. This level is 82% stronger than in July 2025 and 31% higher than the three year average, which helped ease short term exchange rate pressure on import prices.
  • FOOD PRICES: Staple food prices were broadly stable in July: sunflower oil rose 2%, kidney beans fell 1%, and rice and wheat flour were essentially unchanged. All four commodities remained 24–34% below July 2025 levels and 1–16% below their three year averages.
  • MINIMUM FOOD BASKET (MFB): The Minimum Food Basket held steady at YER 132,678 in July—32% lower than in July 2025 and 12% below the three year average—yet irregular incomes and weak employment continued to constrain household access to food.
  • FOOD AND FUEL IMPORTS: Recorded wheat and wheat flour imports declined 19% from June but were still 95% higher than in July 2025 and 59% above the three year average. Fuel imports increased 15% month on month yet remained 68% below last year and 65% below the three year average; recorded flows may not reflect national stocks or actual availability.
  • FUEL PRICES: Diesel prices fell 4% in July and were flat year on year, yet remained 32% above the three year average. Petrol rose 2% month on month, stood 7% below last year, and was 13% higher than the three year average.
  • TERMS OF TRADE (ToT): Agricultural labor-to-cereal terms of trade (ToT) eased slightly in July, down 3% month on month, but remained 36% above last year and 30% above the three year average. Casual labor-to-cereal ToT fell by about 1% month on month, yet stayed 18% higher than last year and 6% above the three year average.
  • CASUAL LABOR WAGE RATES: Agricultural wages fell 3% in July, leaving them 5% below July 2025 but 8% above the three year average. Unskilled wages were largely unchanged, yet remained 22% below last year and 9% below the three year average, underscoring ongoing pressure on daily workers’ earnings.
  • LIVESTOCK PRICES: Goat and sheep prices fell a further 3% and 4% respectively after June’s declines. Both are roughly 31–32% below July 2025 levels and about 4% under their three year averages, eroding the cash value of livestock assets.

title: Global Weather Hazards Summary, August 20, 2026 – August 26, 2026
content:
Global Overview: El Niño is strengthening. Abnormal heat continues to pose a threat in many parts of western and eastern Africa, Central Asia, Hispaniola, Central America, and northern South America. Dryness is worsening in Central America and Venezuela.

Africa Weather Hazards

Abnormal heat is anticipated across the Sahel region of West Africa and extending into Eastern Africa, while dryness persists in much of Eastern Africa.

1) Inundation in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan persists.
2) Severe rainfall deficits across large parts of East Africa over the past 90 days have led to abnormal dryness. As a result, conditions have been upgraded to "Drought" across southern South Sudan and parts of Ethiopia’s northern, eastern, and central regions.
3) Southeastern Mali and central and eastern Liberia remain under abnormal dryness because of sustained below-average rainfall.
4) Persistent heavy rainfall continues to pose an elevated risk of flooding across southeastern Nigeria and the western part of Cameroon.
5) In the coming week, abnormal heat is expected across parts of eastern Mauritania, northern Mali, southern Algeria, eastern Niger, northeastern Nigeria, northern Cameroon, Chad, Sudan, southeastern South Sudan, southwestern and eastern Ethiopia, and western Eritrea.
6) Moderate to heavy rainfall over the month, along with a forecast of moderate to heavy rainfall, maintains a high alert for flash flooding in western Ethiopia. Flooding has been reported in Tawila town in western Sudan, which displaced hundreds of people and destroyed several homes.

title: UNHCR Ukraine Operational Update - 14 August 2026
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT & HIGHLIGHTS:

• The Russian Federation has continued to carry out massive attacks across Ukraine, including repeated large-scale attacks on Kyiv. The increasing use of ballistic missiles and other long-range weapons in populated areas is contributing to rising civilian casualties and widespread damage to civilian homes and infrastructure. According to the UN HRMMU , at least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July 2026, a 30% increase compared to June 2026, and a 70% increase compared to July 2025. The number of those killed and injured is the highest recorded since March 2022, while the number of those killed is the highest since May 2022. August 2026 has already started with more Russian attacks which have killed and injured civilians.

• Overnight on 31 July-1 August, a Russian attack destroyed the warehouse and office of UNHCR’s local NGO partner Proliska in Pavlohrad, Dnipropetrovska oblast, impacting stocks of humanitarian supplies and emergency shelter materials. Fortunately, no staff members were injured.

• The humanitarian community launched the inter-agency 2026-2027 Winter Response Plan in July. As part of the inter-agency response, and as millions of people in Ukraine brace themselves for the fifth winter since the Russian fullscale invasion, UNHCR plans to deliver critical assistance to help war-affected people stay safe and warm in their homes. UNHCR’s winter assistance will complement the response by the Government of Ukraine and will be delivered in close coordination with partners, prioritizing war-affected people with specific vulnerabilities. See UNHCR’s winter response plan here .

• In the fifth year since the start of the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and more than 12 years since the war began, UNHCR’s programme in Ukraine increasingly aims to help war-affected people and communities to recover, and displaced people to find durable solutions, particularly through housing and strategic protection advocacy.

title: WFP Mauritania Country Brief, August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Mauritania hosts the largest number of Malian refugees in West Africa, Mauritania provides protection to almost 309,000 refugees, including 14,402 newly arrivals in Hodh Chargui (HEC) between October 2025 and May 2026. Of these new arrivals, 20 percent are women and 68 percent are children. WFP continues to provide life-saving food and nutrition assistance to refugees and host communities in HEC, adapting its response to increasing humanitarian needs.

• Mauritania’s heavy reliance on food and fuel imports has heightened its exposure to the crisis in the Middle East and Gulf region, prompting a fourth fuel price increase since March, most recently in June. This increases transportation costs and contributes to higher prices for food and other essential commodities, especially in remote and inland regions. WFP continues to monitor the potential implications for operational costs, market dynamics, and food security.

• In response to forecasts of below-average rainfall and a heightened risk of drought associated with the El Niño phenomenon in several regions, the Government triggered anticipatory actions for the first time. Assistance was officially launched with humanitarian partners, including WFP, on 26 July.

title: Ebola Outbreak, DRC and Region, Situation Report #12 (August 19, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • On May 15, the DRC declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease (EVD), later confirmed to be caused by the Bundibugyo strain.
  • As of August 18, 5,021 confirmed cases and 2,378 confirmed deaths had been reported in the DRC, with 20 confirmed cases and two confirmed deaths in Uganda.
  • In the DRC, the outbreak remains centered in Ituri province, but cases have also been confirmed in Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, North Kivu, South Kivu and Tshopo provinces.
  • In Uganda, the last confirmed case was discharged on July 16.
  • No EVD cases have been confirmed in South Sudan, but risk of an outbreak remains high due to transient populations and porous borders with the DRC.

OUR RESPONSE

  • Across the region, our teams are providing case management, infection prevention and control (IPC), screening and triage, risk communication and community engagement, training and preparedness planning.
  • We are supporting 162 facilities in the screening, identification and treatment of EVD.
  • Our supported sites have conducted 376,857 screenings and provided treatment to 1,374 patients, including 377 confirmed cases.
  • We have so far trained 2,820 people in the DRC on EVD case management, response and transmission prevention.

With the support of the US Department of State, DG ECHO and other donors, International Medical Corps teams are actively responding to the outbreak across the region while collaborating closely with ministries of health, key actors and response partners. International Medical Corps has used a hub-and-spoke model since the outbreak was declared, providing case-management support at designated treatment and transit facilities, strengthening IPC in referring health facilities, conducting screening and triage, supporting risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) in surrounding communities and training health workers on EVD response protocols.

In the DRC, International Medical Corps is running three Ebola Treatment Centers (including one that is the country's largest) and seven Ebola transit centers. We continue to closely coordinate with the MoH and relevant partners to support case management, screening-and-referral units, facility-based surveillance, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), IPC, logistics, just-in-time training, continuity of essential health services, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services. International Medical Corps also is part of broader efforts to expand contact tracing, helping to strengthen mapping, daily monitoring and follow-up activities to address the risk of undetected transmission across operational areas and beyond.

In Uganda, we are working through a partner to to strengthen Ebola preparedness, surveillance, IPC, WASH, and RCCE activities across Ntoroko and Bundibugyo districts. We continue to support EVD national preparedness in South Sudan, where no cases have yet been confirmed, by upgrading and expanding infectious-disease units, training health staff and managing suspected cases.

title: WHO Weekly Situation Update on Ongoing Health Emergency Events in South Sudan - Week #33, Date: 10 - 16 Aug 2026
content:

title: DTM Pakistan Flow Monitoring of Afghan Returnees — Bi-Weekly Report (16–31 July 2026)
content:
About Flow Monitoring

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) Pakistan’s FM provides key insights into cross-border migration trends, returning Afghan nationals to Afghanistan, including their profiles, mobility patterns, routes, vulnerabilities, demographics and other social characteristics. Between 16 and 31 July 2026, DTM border monitors (BMs) interviewed 3,585 heads of households through a Flow Monitoring Registry (FMR) form, while a total of 52,975 Afghan returnees were identified through the five border crossing points (BCPs). For more information on FM methodology, see page 5.

Highlights

• Cumulatively, from 15 September 2023 to 31 July 2026, 2,652,720 individuals have returned.

• During the reporting period, the number of returns and deportations did not change significantly compared to the previous reporting period (1–15 July 2026). Returns decreased by 1 per cent and deportations increased by 16 per cent. • Since 1 April 2025, 1,798,687 Afghan nationals returned, of which 224,335 (12%) were deported.

• Fear of arrest (96%) remained the most important reason among respondents to return to Afghanistan.

title: Operational Update - Central African Republic - April - June 2026
content: UNHCR's operations in the Central African Republic (CAR) are based on protection through presence, a central pillar of the humanitarian response. In a context marked by security volatility and the repercussions of the Sudanese crisis, particular attention is also being paid to emergency response. At the same time, the search for durable solutions is a major priority, by supporting the voluntary, safe and dignified return of Central African refugees, while ensuring their sustainable reintegration and their contribution to national development. The Central African Government, UNHCR and partners are providing protection and multi-sectoral assistance to internally displaced persons (IDPs) and refugees, including Chadians and Sudanese, while promoting durable solutions for Central African returnees. UNHCR aligns its interventions with national priorities, including the National Development Programme, the National Strategy for Durable Solutions and the Platform to Support Solutions from the 2022 Yaoundé Declaration.

title: Flash Update: No. 1 – Flooding in Ayeyarwady and Kayin, Myanmar – 19 August 2026
content:
OVERVIEW: Heavy and continuous rainfall since 30 July 2026 triggered flooding in several areas in Myanmar. According to the Department of Disaster Management (DDM) Myanmar, severe weather resulted to flooding and riverbank erosion that caused a breach in the Ngawun River embankment in Laymyethna Township, Ayeyarwady Region, which resulted in flooding of five urban wards, major roads, and 150 surrounding villages. In Kayin State, DDM reported displaced households and a casualty due to overflowing of the Thanlwin River. Forecasts indicate that heavy rainfall may persist in the coming week (DMH).

IMPACTS: The following impacts have been reported by DDM Myanmar:

  • Ayeyarwady Region (as of 18 August 2026 at 1630 HRS UTC+7)
    • Affected townships: Laymyethna, Hinthada, Yekyi, and Kyangin
    • 63K affected population
    • 15K displaced households
    • 1 dead
    • 45 evacuation centres
    • 47 affected schools
    • 66 affected roads
    • 97 religious buildings
  • Kayin State (as of 14 August 2026)
    • 1 dead
    • 2.4K affected population (538 households)
      • 212 households, (485 males and 520 females) were displaced to the Leytha School Temporary Flood Relief Camp and the Moe Leylon Temporary Flood Relief Camp.
      • 248 households, (523 males and 598 females) were relocated to Mya Kyi Hmun Temporary Flood Relief Camp, Shwe Yai Myaw Temporary Flood Relief Camp and Temporary Flood Relief Camp.
  • Data collection and assessments are ongoing.

HAZARDS & ANTIPICATED RISKS:

  • Heavy Rain Warning: According to DMH Myanmar, as of 07000H UTC+7, due to the strong monsoon winds in the Andaman Sea and the southern Bay of Bengal and the strong development of clusters of rain clouds, strong winds, flash floods and landslides may occur along with heavy rains. There may be scattered showers and thunderstorms in Nay Pyi Taw, Yangon Region, Mandalay Region, Bago Region, Magway Region, Sagaing Region, Ayeyarwady Region, Tanintharyi Region, Kachin State, Kayin State, Chin State, Mon State, Rakhine State and Shan State from this morning to 23 August 2026, while scattered heavy rains may occur in Nay Pyi Taw, Yangon Region, Mandalay Region, Bago Region, Upper Sagaing Region, Ayeyarwady Region, Tanintharyi Region, Kachin State, Kayin State, Mon State, Rakhine State and Shan State for this forecast period.

PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE:

  • DDM Myanmar, together with relevant ministries, technical experts, military personnel, firefighters, civil society organisations (CSOs), and charitable organisations, is working around the clock to repair the breached sections of the embankment and control the flooding.
  • Search and rescue operations are also underway, alongside the provision of food, drinking water, and essential healthcare services to affected communities.
  • The Government of Myanmar has provided approximately USD 85.2K in assistance to affected communities.
  • DMH continues to monitor the prevailing weather systems and provides regular updates and advisories.

The AHA Centre will continue to monitor for further developments and issue necessary updates. The AHA Centre stands ready to support DDM Myanmar should the need arises.

title: UNHCR Iraq Monthly Update July 2026
content:
CONTEXT

As of the end of July 2026, Iraq generously hosts over 343,000 refugees and asylumseekers, the majority (88%) of whom are Syrians. Close to 80% of this population resides in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. While most refugees and asylum-seekers live in urban and peri-urban settings, 30% remain in nine refugee camps across the country. title: Humanitarian Feedback Bulletin: Accountability to Affected Populations - Malakal, South Sudan I July 2026 Issue #4
content:
The Concern Worldwide Accountability to Affected Populations project, supported by WFP, aims at creating a bottom-up feedback and communication mechanism between responders and people we serve, that is community-based, easily accessible, and built on mutual understanding and genuine information-sharing.

Through local responders and community correspondents, Concern Worldwide, Community Engagement Network (hereafter: CEN), and the Radio Community (hereafter: TRC) work together to set up a complete community feedback mechanism that is accessible to all participants regardless of their literacy levels and access to assets and internet. Using TRCs and CEN’s longstanding experience in radio broadcasting, the project ensures a wide outreach beyond people with access to written updates.

Together, and alongside WFP, the project partners respond to information and feedback gaps. This way, and by consolidating and sharing the feedback received, the project increases accountability to affected populations in the targetedareas.

title: UNICEF Lebanon Humanitarian Situation Report No. 4 (Mid - Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Children and caregivers continue to bear the brunt of conflict and instability. Despite successive ceasefires, 4,278 people have been killed and 12,196 injured since 2 March, including 253 children killed and 1,036 injured.﻿

title: UNICEF Democratic Republic of the Congo Humanitarian Situation Report No. 2 – Ebola Outbreak (Bundibugyo Virus), 31 July 2026
content:
Highlights

  • UNICEF is scaling up its response from 21 to over 50 affected and high-risk health zones, supporting Government-led efforts across community-based surveillance, RCCE, IPC/WASH, nutrition, MHPSS, clinical care, PSEA and continuity of essential services.
  • UNICEF-supported community surveillance networks generated 15,927 alerts in July, following the deployment and support of 6,009 community mobilizers since the start of the response, strengthening early detection, alert reporting, contact tracing, and community-level surveillance capacities across affected areas.
  • UNICEF and partners reached over 1.4 million people with Ebola prevention and response messages through direct interpersonal communication approaches including door-to-door outreach, focused discussions, and community dialogues during this reporting period, while community feedback and social listening mechanisms continued to inform adaptive response strategies and address rumours and misinformation.
  • UNICEF and partners continued to deliver integrated support for children and families, including MHPSS services for 12,780 children, adolescents and caregivers, case management for 407 Ebola-affected children, and treatment for 6,587 children with severe or moderate acute malnutrition.
  • UNICEF supported the procurement of US$6.3 million worth of essential Ebola response supplies, including PPE, IPC materials and medical commodities, to sustain life-saving response operations across affected and high-risk health zones.
  • UNICEF requires US$113.5 million for its revised six-month response plan. As of 31 July 2026, US$32.7 million had been mobilized, leaving a US$80.8 million funding gap, equivalent to 71 per cent of the requirement.

content: South Sudan is currently facing a severe humanitarian crisis characterised by extensive internal displacement. title: Sierra Leone: Freetown Flash Floods 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRSL022)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event 08-03-2026

What happened, where and when?

On the night of 3 August 2026, Freetown experienced approximately six consecutive hours of exceptionally heavy rainfall, triggering widespread flash flooding, severe soil erosion, and multiple slope and structural failures across several densely populated urban and peri-urban communities. The most severely affected areas included Portor Community (Juba Hills), Metchem Community, 44 Femi Turner Drive (Goderich), Regent Road-Lumley, Bonga Town, and settlements along the Cain Water Stream, where floodwaters rapidly inundated homes, businesses, and critical community infrastructure.

The intensity and duration of the rainfall overwhelmed drainage systems and exceeded the absorption capacity of flood-prone low-lying areas and hillside settlements. The resulting flash floods caused extensive destruction of homes, public infrastructure, and community assets, while saturated soils triggered erosion, retaining wall failures, and structural collapses in several locations. As the event occurred overnight, many residents had little time to evacuate or protect their belongings, contributing to fatalities, injuries, displacement, and significant losses of household assets and livelihoods.

While flooding is a recurrent seasonal hazard in Sierra Leone, the August 2026 floods were exceptional in both scale and impact and exceeded the level of localized flooding typically experienced during the rainy season. Freetown has not experienced a flood emergency of this magnitude since 2022, largely due to sustained investments in drainage improvements, environmental management initiatives, and other flood mitigation measures implemented by the Government and its partners. However, the intensity of the rainfall on 3 August 2026 exceeded the capacity of existing mitigation measures and generated humanitarian impacts far beyond normal seasonal flooding patterns.

The severity of the event was amplified by its impact on densely populated urban and hillside communities, where high population concentrations, vulnerable housing conditions, and proximity to waterways significantly increased exposure to flood hazards. Unlike the localized flooding commonly experienced during the rainy season, this event affected 1,763 families (8,915 people), damaged or flooded more than 700 houses, including over 300 houses in Portor Community alone, caused four fatalities, displaced thousands of people, contaminated 18 community boreholes, damaged a community school, and disrupted livelihoods and access to essential services. The scale and concentration of impacts demonstrate that this event exceeded normal seasonal flooding patterns and overwhelmed the coping capacities of affected households and communities.

Rapid assessments conducted by the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA), the Sierra Leone Red Cross Society (SLRCS), and partners confirmed extensive humanitarian impacts across the affected communities, including loss of life, displacement, damage to critical infrastructure, livelihood disruption, and heightened public health risks arising from contaminated water sources and deteriorating environmental conditions.

The crisis has been further compounded by continuous rainfall across Freetown and other parts of Sierra Leone from 4 to 7 August 2026, which has caused additional flooding in other communities and continues to increase pressure on drainage systems, waterways, and unstable slopes. Persistent rainfall has maintained high levels of soil saturation, increasing the risk of further flash flooding, erosion, and localized landslides. As a result, communities already affected remain highly vulnerable, while additional communities across Freetown and other districts face an elevated likelihood of flooding as the rainy season continues.

As of the time of the DREF request, affected households continue to face urgent humanitarian needs, including safe water, sanitation services, shelter support, essential household items, health services, protection assistance, and livelihood recovery. With 8,915 people affected, more than 700 homes damaged or flooded, four confirmed fatalities, contamination of critical water sources, and continued heavy rainfall across the country, the scale of humanitarian needs exceeds the coping capacities of affected communities and available local response resources. Immediate humanitarian assistance is required to save lives, alleviate suffering, prevent further deterioration of living conditions, and reduce the risk of additional losses during the remainder of the rainy season.

title: UNRWA Situation Report #232 on the Humanitarian Crisis in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem [EN/AR]
content:
All information updated for 29 July - 11 August 2026 [1]
Days 1025 - 1038 since the start of the war in the Gaza Strip

Highlights

The Gaza Strip

  • UNRWA and other humanitarian actors continue to face mounting operational challenges that are affecting the delivery of essential services across Gaza. The prolonged shortage of lubricant oil and other critical supplies required to maintain generators, vehicles, and operational equipment is placing additional strain on already overstretched service delivery systems. These constraints are affecting humanitarian movements and operational capacity, increasing the risk of disruptions to health, WASH, education, and other life-saving interventions amid persistently high levels of need. Several UNRWA operations have already been suspended, including services in more than half of the 11 UNRWA health centres currently active. The provision of water and electricity in seven emergency shelters has also been affected as generators have been forced to shut down. In addition, shortages of lubricant oil and spare parts have hindered critical WASH operations, leaving garbage trucks, water tankers, and other essential equipment out of service. Following wartime impacts on their structural integrity and three years of continuous use, 95 per cent of UNRWA’s WASH fleet is deteriorating and malfunctioning.
  • A new UNRWA Temporary Learning Space opened in Jabalia, northern Gaza, on 10 August, expanding access to learning for up to 1,200 children. UNRWA summer learning activities also continued, reaching 41,849 children (22,956 girls, 18,893 boys, including 878 children with disabilities) between 3 and 9 August. Participation has increased by more than 2,300 children since the programme commenced on 18 July.
  • A new assessment by the UN Satellite Centre (UNOSAT), shared by the UN Secretary-General's spokesperson estimates that the number of destroyed structures across Gaza has increased by 9 per cent since the declaration of a ceasefire in October 2025. Overall, about 82 per cent of the structures in Gaza are damaged. This means that more than 200,000 structures are damaged to some degree, and two thirds of them are assessed to have been destroyed. Since the start of the ceasefire, UNRWA has received reports of demolitions affecting schools and other UN facilities in areas under Israeli military control. However, these reports could not be independently verified due to ongoing access restrictions.

The occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem

  • During the course of a two-day operation in and around Kalandiya Camp, Israeli forces accompanying Jerusalem Municipality officials forcibly entered UNRWA’s Kalandia Training Centre in East Jerusalem on 6 August. UNRWA subsequently released a statement on the Kalandia Training Centre.

title: NGA: Flood - 08-2026 - Flood and landslide – rainfall-induced, Anambra State, Nigeria #2 (2026-08-18)
content:
Description

On Thursday, 13th August 2026, Anambra State experienced prolonged and heavy rainfall that commenced at approximately 3:30am and continued through the evening. The sustained intensity and duration of the rainfall caused severe flooding across several parts of the state, with Obosi Community among the most significantly affected locations.

The accumulated floodwater in Obosi Community eventually triggered a major landslide, cutting off an affected road and severely disrupting movement within the area. Houses in close proximity to the landslide and flooded zones sustained partial damage, and road access was completely severed at the point of the landslide. The Nigerian Red Cross Society Anambra State Branch deployed its Disaster Management team to conduct a rapid assessment of the affected community immediately following the incident.

Although no deaths or injuries were recorded at the time of assessment, the situation poses a significant ongoing safety risk to residents, road users and surrounding structures, particularly in the event of further rainfall. The landslide area remains unstable, with continued risk of further ground movement, possible damage to additional structures and restricted access threatening the safety of the affected population. Approximately 350 persons are affected and approximately 15 houses have been partially damaged.

Anambra State is identified in the NIHSA 2026 Annual Flood Outlook among the high-risk states for the current rainy season, with communities along river corridors and low-lying areas at particular risk. The combination of flash flooding and landslide activity in Obosi reflects the compounded hazard profile of communities in the state during the July to September peak flood period.

title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #06 (Reporting period: 01 – 14 August 2026)
content:
This Situation Report provides an overview of the twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026 (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5), and their impact on telecommunications. It outlines the activities of the WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 Telecoms Area in supporting emergency communications for the humanitarian response. The Cluster is currently not formally activated for this emergency.

Summary Points

  • LTC Telecoms continues to support the earthquake response through coordinated internet connectivity and renewable power solutions, working with government authorities, telecommunications providers and humanitarian partners to sustain critical services for affected communities and responders.

title: Indonesian Humanitarian Coordination Platform: Situation Report No. 2 - Earthquake and Tsunami in Flores and Surrounding Areas (18 August 2026)
content:
Situation Report

• BMKG noted that on Monday (August 17) there had been 1,576 aftershocks. BMKG appeals to people on Flores Island and its surroundings to remain calm, evacuate independently away from the beach area to the gathering point.

• Damage occurred to 264 educational facilities, 83 health facilities, 1 warehouse of the Logictics Affairs Agency (BULOG), 116 public facilities, 1 market, 157 houses of worship, 171 office units, 7 irrigation facilities, 34 road points, and 5 bridges.

• The Ministry of Health reported on August 17 at 07:30 WIB of the impact on 21 hospitals and 190 health centers. Most hospitals and health centers are still operating even though many services are carried out outside the building.

• The Coordination Meeting of the Reproductive Health Subcluster (Kespro) on August 17, 2026 in Flores, NTT, discussed the implementation of the Minimum Initial Service Package (PPAM) of Kespro as part of the earthquake emergency response. This package includes nine main components, ranging from the appointment of coordinators, prevention of sexual violence, handling HIV and STIs, to efforts to reduce maternal and neonatal mortality rates. In addition, PPAM also highlights the prevention of unwanted pregnancies, adolescent health, minimum services for toddlers and the elderly, and the integration of reproductive health services into basic services.

title: WFP Côte d’Ivoire Country Brief, June 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Despite strong economic growth, with GDP projected to grow by around 6 percent in 2026, Côte d’Ivoire continues to face food security and nutrition challenges, with over 1.3 million acutely food insecure people and an additional 3.9 million at risk. Among children under five, 21.4 percent are stunted, while anaemia affects 68 percent of children. Despite a relatively low national global acute malnutrition (GAM) rate of 3.7 percent, significant regional disparities persist, with higher rates recorded in the Savanes (6.7 percent), Abidjan (6.3 percent) and Vallée du Bandama (4 percent) districts. The country hosts nearly 83,000 refugees and asylum seekers who have fled insecurity in Burkina Faso and Mali.

• WFP supports national efforts to address food insecurity, malnutrition and humanitarian needs, particularly in northern regions hosting refugees and vulnerable communities.

• Beyond direct implementation, WFP strengthens national systems and capacities to advance sustainable, government-led solutions.

title: WFP Côte d’Ivoire Country Brief, July 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Despite strong economic growth (GDP projected to grow by around 6 percent in 2026), Côte d’Ivoire continues to face food security and nutrition challenges.

• According to the October 2025 Cadre Harmonisé projections, over 1.3 million people face acute food insecurity (Phases 3-4) between June and August 2026, with an additional 3.9 million at risk (Phase 2), representing a 43 percent increase compared to 2025. In Tchologo and Bounkani regions, over 150,000 people (13 percent of the population) are acutely food insecure, a 36 percent increase from 2025.

• Among children under five, 21.4 percent are stunted and 68 percent suffer from anaemia. Despite a low national Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) rate of 3.7 percent, significant regional disparities persist, particularly in the Savanes (6.7 percent), Abidjan (6.3 percent) and Vallée du Bandama (4 percent) districts.

• According to UNHCR’s June 2026 statistics, the country hosts 93,266 forcibly displaced people, primarily from Burkina Faso, Mali and other neighbouring countries with 82 percent of refugees living in host communities and 18 percent residing in two transit sites. This includes 80,162 refugees, 3,443 asylum seekers and 9,661 people not yet registered. Women and children represent 79 percent of this population.

title: WFP Chad Country Brief, August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Between June and September 2026, crisis levels of acute food insecurity (IPC 3) are expected in Chad’s eastern provinces that host Sudanese refugees, as well as in the western Lake Province, which has a large internally displaced population due to persistent attacks by armed groups, according to FEWS NET’s latest analysis. The analysis highlights that refugees – more than 940,610 people who have arrived since the outbreak of the Sudan crisis in April 2023 (UNHCR) – have lost access to their livelihoods, have very limited sources of income, and must compete with host communities for scarce agricultural and nonagricultural employment opportunities. As a result, refugees rely heavily on food assistance to meet their basic food needs. In Lake Province, worsening insecurity has led to the abandonment of arable land, population displacement, and a decline in fishing activities. As a consequence, an estimated 75,000 people have been displaced since May 2026, adding to an already severe humanitarian situation affecting nearly 220,000 IDPs, as well as returnees and refugees.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #23 (14 to 17 August 2026)
content:
Situation Report No. 23 provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June 2026 earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 14 to 17 August 2026.

Highlights

  • Heavy rainfall affected infrastructure and services in the César Nieves, Mare Abajo, Campo de Golf and José María Vargas temporary accommodation sites, generating additional needs related to drainage, site rehabilitation and flood mitigation.
  • IOM strengthened camp coordination and camp management across the four temporary accommodation sites under its management, including beneficiary registration updates, needs assessments and planning for household-level surveys to strengthen evidence-based response activities.
  • Humanitarian operations continued adapting to changes in camp management and service delivery, including adjustments in food assistance, protection, health and community support activities to maintain operational continuity.

IOM Activities

IOM continued camp coordination and camp management activities in Mare Abajo, Campo de Golf, José María Vargas and César Nieves, including beneficiary registration updates, infrastructure assessments and coordination of mitigation measures following heavy rainfall. IOM also maintained information management activities and population verification exercises to support operational planning and service delivery.

Through its shelter and essential item response, IOM has delivered 5,887 kitchen sets, 8,907 plastic tarpaulins, 4,500 collapsible jerrycans, 3,612 hygiene items, 5,000 buckets, 2,802 mosquito nets and 4,217 emergency shelter kits, reaching more than 15,500 people affected by the earthquakes.

In WASH, IOM continued ensuring access to safe drinking water in Campo de Golf through the site's water treatment plant and coordinated with sector partners on water supply, sanitation improvements, water-quality monitoring and hygiene promotion activities. Following rainfall impacts, assessments and mitigation measures were undertaken to address drainage and sanitation challenges in affected sites.

In health, IOM and implementing partner Ven Da Tu Mano continued providing primary health care and mental health services through mobile teams in temporary accommodation sites. Activities included medical consultations, referrals for specialized care, follow-up of chronic conditions and monitoring of communicable diseases.

IOM also continued protection activities through case management, referrals and coordination with specialized actors, while maintaining community information activities and follow-up of protection concerns in temporary accommodation sites.

IOM Planned Response

  • Continue monitoring rainfall-related impacts and support rehabilitation, site improvement and risk mitigation measures in temporary accommodation sites.
  • Maintain beneficiary registration updates, household-level assessments and information management activities to support evidence-based response planning.
  • Continue coordinating water supply, sanitation, hygiene promotion and infrastructure improvements in collaboration with WASH partners.
  • Maintain mobile health and mental health services and strengthen referral pathways for specialized care, diagnostic services and chronic disease management.
  • Strengthen protection case management, referral mechanisms and technical coordination platforms in temporary accommodation sites.
  • Continue integrating Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) measures into humanitarian activities and coordination mechanisms while promoting safe reporting channels.

title: IOM Colombia Earthquake Response - Situation Report #3 (17 August 2026)
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

On 10 August 2026, at 7:34 a.m., a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck with its epicenter in San José del Palmar, Chocó Department. In response, the National Government declared a national disaster situation through Presidential Decree No. 1171 of 2026. In the days following the event, response operations have concentrated on the departments most severely affected: Valle del Cauca, Chocó, Risaralda, Caldas, and Quindío.

4,400 people injured

title: Protection and Solutions - UNHCR in Colombia progress update (January - June 2026)
content:
Highlights

  • UNHCR's response in Colombia focuses on refugees, asylum-seekers and internally displaced people. Colombia hosts the world's largest refugee population (2.8 million, mostly from Venezuela) and 7.1 million internally displaced people, the second-largest internally displaced population after Sudan. Forced displacement and confinement remain the main protection challenges driving this response.
  • By 30 June 2026, according to UNHCR’s monitoring, some 17.797 people were affected by large displacement events and 59.989 by confinement due to violence, particuraly in Antioquia, Bolívar, Cauca, Chocó, Norte de Santander and Magdalena. UNHCR responded with emergency protection, shelter and cash assistance in the most affected areas.
  • With the national Ombudsperson's Office and the European Union, UNHCR opened Confined Paradises in Bogotá, a photographic exhibition showing how armed groups trap entire communities in remote territories, restricting their access to food, health, education and livelihoods, and making one of Colombia's fastest-growing protection risks visible.
  • As part of the Humanitarian Fund for Colombia (RhPF), UNHCR scaled up a life-saving response in municipalities at heightened severity. The six-month intervention is reaching over 59,000 people with community shelter and habitat kits, legal orientation and protection services, Information and Orientation Centres (PAOs) and cashbased interventions (CBI).

title: WFP Bangladesh Country Brief, August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW
• Bangladesh continues to face significant food security and nutrition challenges. According to the latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) analysis, approximately 15.3 million people (15 percent of the analysed population) are experiencing acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between May and August 2026. The situation is projected to deteriorate further, with the estimated number of people facing acute food insecurity expected to increase to 18.1 million between September and December 2026.
• Nutrition outcomes remain a major concern. According to the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World (SOFI) 2026, 26 percent of children under five are stunted and 11 percent are wasted, reflecting persistent chronic and acute undernutrition. In addition, the National Micronutrient and Micronutrient Intervention (MIMI) study found that around 40 percent of households suffer from significant micronutrient deficiencies, which continue to undermine health, cognitive development, and productivity. Addressing these challenges requires prudent and evidence-based policies, including the promotion of food fortification, improved dietary diversity, strengthened nutrition-sensitive social protection programmes, and enhanced access to nutritious foods for populations at risk of food insecurity and malnutrition.

title: IDN: Earthquake - 08-2026 - Field Report Update 2: M7.7 East Nusa Tenggara Earthquake #3 (2026-08-18)
content:
Sources for data marked as Other

PMI Assessment Team, BNPB

Description

A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck offshore Nagekeo Regency, East Nusa Tenggara Province, on 15 August 2026 at 04:58 WIB. The epicentre was located approximately 30 kilometres northeast of Mbay at a depth of 15 kilometres. The earthquake triggered a tsunami warning, which was lifted at 07:31 WIB after sea-level changes were detected in several coastal areas.

The earthquake affected seven regencies in East Nusa Tenggara: Manggarai, East Manggarai, West Manggarai, Sikka, Ende, Nagekeo and Ngada. Impacts and displacement were also reported in West Nusa Tenggara and South Sulawesi.

As of 18 August 2026, 69 people were reported dead and 1,199 injured, including 115 people with serious injuries and 1,084 with minor injuries. A total of 46,252 people remain displaced, including 46,181 people across the seven affected regencies in East Nusa Tenggara and 71 people in Bima Regency, West Nusa Tenggara. Assessment and verification remain ongoing.

Preliminary damage includes 5,713 houses severely damaged, 2,098 moderately damaged and 3,402 slightly damaged. A further 283 educational facilities, 211 health facilities, 97 government buildings, 96 places of worship and 106 business premises or offices were affected.

As of 18 August 2026 at 05:00 WIB, BMKG had recorded 2,119 aftershocks ranging from magnitude 1.3 to 6.2. The Larantuka-Maumere road is accessible, while the Ende-Nagekeo road remains cut off by landslides and rock debris. Damaged roads, electricity outages and communication disruptions continue to affect assessments and humanitarian operations.

title: Middle East Situation Lebanon - Flash Update #15 (1 – 31 July 2026)
content:
Overview

Humanitarian needs remain high. Displacement is becoming protracted, with more than 821,000 IDPs have been reported as returned. However, returns are often not sustainable, as homes are damaged, destroyed, or located in areas where insecurity remains prevalent. There is widespread destruction of infrastructure, limited services, and livelihood opportunities. Protection concerns, include psychosocial distress, unexploded ordnance (UXO), child labour, and vulnerabilities affecting women and children remain elevated, while funding gaps continue to constrain the humanitarian response.

Security remains fragile. Ongoing military activity continues, mainly in southern Lebanon, and unresolved issues related to withdrawal, security arrangements, and disarmament has kept the situation tense and the ceasefire fragile. Diplomatic engagement continues through talks in Rome and high-level international discussions.

title: IOM Yemen Dispatch July 2026: Updates on the humanitarian crisis, people on the move and IOM's response in Yemen
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

Frontlines in Yemen witnessed an uptick in reinforcements as government forces raised combat readiness and received ammunition and arms support from Saudi Arabia amidst heightened tensions with Ansar Allah (AA). During this period, AA announced a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, threatening to interdict vessels bound for Saudi ports and potentially close the Bab al Mandeb under their ‘eye for an eye’ policy. This escalation followed airstrikes on Sana’a Airport, designed to prevent AA from establishing a direct air route between Tehran and Sana’a. AA missile and drone strikes targeting Saudi oil tankers and Saudilinked vessels continued throughout the final weeks of July, while also hitting Saudi Aramco oil facilities along the Red Sea coast. The deterioration of maritime security led to an increase in global oil prices and reduced commercial traffic through the Bab alMandeb strait. The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2826, extending reporting requirements on AA maritime attacks in the Red Sea through January 2027. Concurrently, UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg maintained continuous diplomatic travel between Muscat and Riyadh, briefing regional leadership and UN Security Council members on preserving the political framework of the 2022 UN-brokered truce.

On July 1, Saudi Arabia delivered a first batch of emergency generators to Hadramawt under the Saudi Development and Reconstruction Program for Yemen (SDRPY). However, electricity shortages persisted, with power outages in Aden reaching six hours of blackout for every two hours of electricity. The General Union of Southern Workers’ Syndicates organized a protest outside UN headquarters in Khormaksar on July 20 to demand improved public services. Meanwhile, local media reported that food prices rose in Sana’a and other AA-controlled areas as a result of an estimated 400 per cent rise in customs duties on flour and an additional levy of YR 5,000 imposed on each carton or sack of imported goods. Torrential downpours further exacerbated humanitarian conditions, especially for populations in Sana’a, Ibb, Amran, Al Hodeidah, Taiz and other areas. Heavy rainfall and windstorms also caused widespread damage to shelters across IOM-managed IDP sites, increasing humanitarian needs beyond available response capacity.

On July 20, the National Defense Council approved military, security, economic, and administrative measures to strengthen state institutions and boost state revenue, including a decision to resume oil exports. Oil production had been halted since October 2022, and years of conflict have damaged critical infrastructure including wells, pipelines and refineries, posing significant challenges to a speedy recovery. Regardless, anticipated proceeds from oil sales are to be deposited into the government-run Central Bank of Yemen in Aden to stabilize the currency and support essential government spending.

title: WFP scales up emergency food support for Colombian earthquake survivors
content:
BOGOTA, Colombia – The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) is scaling up emergency operations in Colombia, reaching survivors in some of the country’s most affected and vulnerable regions with critical food assistance following the 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck on 10 August.

WFP teams have been supporting government-led relief and recovery efforts with more than 2,000 people receiving food assistance in Pereira and Quibdó on Sunday alone. Operations will expand throughout the week with WFP deploying food stocks and leveraging its network of field offices and logistics hubs in Cali, Quibdó and Medellín to reach affected communities.

"The solidarity shown in the immediate aftermath of the earthquake has been extraordinary,” said Nils Grede, WFP Country Director in Colombia. “Communities, businesses and individuals have stepped forward to help those affected, but we know from experience that recovery does not end when the first wave of support subsides. Sustained humanitarian assistance will be essential in the weeks and months to come, and WFP is committed to standing alongside affected communities for as long as they need support.”

As the scale of humanitarian needs becomes clearer, WFP is appealing for an initial USD 23 million to deliver emergency food assistance to 100,000 people over three months and continues to adapt its response to conditions on the ground. In remote communities where markets are not functioning and access remains difficult, WFP is prioritizing in-kind food assistance. In urban centres such as Valle del Cauca and Risaralda, where markets and basic services are beginning to recover, cash-based assistance can be rapidly scaled up, allowing families to buy the food they need while supporting local businesses and economic recovery.

In close coordination with government authorities and humanitarian partners, WFP is also supporting the broader response through logistics expertise and common services. Four mobile storage units are on standby and additional relief items are available for deployment from the WFP-managed Humanitarian Response Depot in Panama.

Even before the earthquake, close to seven million people in Colombia faced moderate or severe food insecurity, with the worst-hit regions also impacted by conflict and displacement. In Chocó and Valle del Cauca, close to one third of the population is food insecure. These vulnerabilities are now deepening as families grapple with the loss of their homes, livelihoods, and access to essential services.
