title: Somalia Monthly Humanitarian Update July 2026
content:
• Severe drought and dwindling assistance have taken a heavy toll on livelihoods, particularly in northern and central regions; 1.9 million people in Sool, Sanaag, Bari, Nugaal and Mudug regions are acutely food insecure.
  • Humanitarian response in drought-affected areas is critically low. An analysis in 12 districts found that only four achieved 25 to 50 per cent reach, seven were below 25 per cent, and one recorded no response at all.
  • Humanitarian partners in close collaboration with authorities have stepped up flood preparedness measures including risk analysis, contingency planning, mapping of resources, early warning messages in identified hotspots.
  • More than 216,900 people were displaced across the country during the second quarter of 2026 (April to June), nearly three times the number recorded during the same period in 2025.
  • Access constraints remain significant in several regions, disrupting humanitarian operations, restricting population movement, and delaying the delivery of life-saving assistance.

title: WFP Benin Country Brief, August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW
• The resurgence of armed incidents linked to the Sahel crisis continues to exacerbate the humanitarian situation in Benin, particularly in the departments of Atacora, Alibori and Borgou. These areas host refugees and asylum seekers from Burkina Faso, Niger, Togo and Nigeria, as well as internally displaced persons (IDPs) fleeing violence.
• The ongoing displacement in the northern and now central regions of the country heightens risks for vulnerable populations. Women, children, and pregnant women are particularly affected by displacement and limited access to basic services, while insecurity disrupts education, livelihoods, and community protection systems.
• Humanitarian access also remains challenging during the rainy season due to deteriorating roads, impassable routes and damaged infrastructure, including collapsed bridges. These constraints, combined with security risks, require new and enhanced security measures.
• Food insecurity is worsening under multiple shocks. Approximately 201,226 people are projected to be in IPC Phase 3–5 during the upcoming three months, with many more at risk due to insecurity, climate shocks, and constrained livelihoods.
• Economic pressures are deepening vulnerability despite growth. Price increases and rising fuel costs are eroding purchasing power, disproportionately affecting poor households and increasing food security risks, particularly in rural and underserved areas.

title: Reporting Sexual Violence and Abuse in Conflict - July 2026
content:
This News Brief bears testimony to the brave survivors who speak about sexual violence by state bodies or conflict actors. Most events of violence are never reported. This compilation is neither complete nor representative of the extent or nature of sexual violence in general. It brings together dispersed accounts about survivors from around the world who broke the silence.

Developments in July 2026
Central African Republic: In July 2026, reported incidents in Ouham-Fafa and Vakaga highlight the exposure of women and girls to sexual violence amid insecurity and armed-group activity, particularly in remote and rural communities. The incidents, involving unidentified armed men and LRA fighters, reflect recurring trends of sexual violence by multiple armed actors, heightened risks for women and girls while carrying out everyday livelihood activities, and limited access to protection and essential services in isolated, conflict-affected areas. See the Central African Republic section for more details.

Democratic Republic of the Congo: In July 2026, reported incidents in Kwilu and South Kivu provinces highlight the continued risk of sexual violence faced by women amid insecurity and armed activity, including attacks by both state forces and unidentified armed men. The incidents reflect recurring trends of sexual violence occurring in the context of everyday activities, armed attacks and insecurity along key transport routes. title: NGA: Flood - 08-2026 - Flood – Ondo State, Nigeria (2026-08-18)
content:
Description

Sustained and heavy rainfall across Ondo State beginning in early August 2026 has triggered widespread riverine and urban flooding across at least seven Local Government Areas in the state, inundating homes, submerging roads and bridges, destroying property and displacing large numbers of residents. The flooding is ongoing and worsening, with multiple communities in the riverine south of the state particularly severely affected as water levels continue to rise.

The situation in Ilaje Local Government Area is the most critical. Igbokoda community in Ilaje LGA, including the Naval Base in Igbokoda and the council headquarters, has been submerged. Displaced residents have been observed sleeping under improvised shelters by the roadside, while others have sought refuge with friends and relatives in other LGAs. The Nigerian Red Cross Society Ondo State Branch has formally recommended to the Ondo State Government that an urgent IDP camp be established in a safe LGA to accommodate the displaced population. In Okitipupa LGA, communities including Ayeka, Ikoya, Igbodigo, Igbotako, Erinje, Kuneyin and Apata have been severely affected, with homes and commercial premises submerged, bridges destroyed and movement restricted. Properties worth millions of naira have been lost.

The NRCS Ondo State Branch conducted a rapid assessment of three of the seven affected LGAs; Ondo West, Ilaje and Okitipupa through the branch volunteers. Assessment of the remaining four LGAs (Irele, Ese-odo, Ile-oluji/Okeigbo and Odigbo) is ongoing in coordination with the Ondo State Emergency Management Agency (ODSEMA) and NEMA. From the three assessed LGAs alone, 2,527 households have been confirmed as affected. The true scale of impact across all seven LGAs is significantly higher and will be confirmed upon completion of the full assessment.

The Ondo State Government has deployed amphibious machines to clear waterways and drainage channels in Ilaje LGA under the direction of Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa, targeting the removal of obstructions from canals and river channels to reduce the risk of further flooding. NEMA has also conducted an assessment in the affected LGAs, attributing the severity of the flooding to blocked waterways, indiscriminate refuse disposal and illegal structures erected along river channels. Ondo State is explicitly listed among 21 states identified by the Federal Government on critical flood alert for 2 to 15 August 2026, which covers 944 communities at highest risk nationally.

title: Indonesian Humanitarian Coordination Platform: Situation Report No. 1 - Earthquake and Tsunami in Flores and Surrounding Areas (17 August 2026)
content:
Situation Report

• Telecommunications services have been restored to 86.02 per cent. According to monitoring by the Ministry of Communications and Digital Affairs as of 16 August at 18:00 WIB, 683 of 794 base transceiver station (BTS) sites across 11 regencies/cities were operational; 111 sites remained out of service. Disruptions included power outages affecting 701 sites and transmission problems affecting 93 sites. Services in Alor, Lembata, and North Central Timor have been fully restored.

• Manggarai Regional Hospital sustained damage that affected clinical and administrative services. Patients are being treated temporarily in the hospital grounds. BNPB and the Ministry of Health will establish a field hospital at Golo Dukal Stadium in Ruteng. The facility is still being prepared and has not yet been declared operational.

• MDMC reported that many residents have chosen to remain outside their homes or in open areas because of trauma and concern about continuing aftershocks. Some displaced people are staying in public facilities, including sports halls and open fields, while others have erected emergency tents in the yards around their homes.

• The Larantuka–Maumere road is open and passable by logistics vehicles. The Ende– Nagekeo road remains completely cut off by landslide debris, and work to clear alternative routes is ongoing. Sections of the Ruteng–Km 210 and Aegela–Ende City roads have been affected by severe landslides. The Government is prioritising the deployment of heavy equipment to these areas.

title: Myanmar Flood 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRMM024)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
05-08-2026

What happened, where and when?

Heavy and continuous monsoon rainfall caused rising water levels and flooding across low-lying and flood-prone areas of Ayeyarwady Region. The situation escalated on 30 July 2026, when an embankment near Myit Kyo Village in Laymyatna Township breached, and floodwaters rapidly entered Laymyatna town and surrounding communities. The flooding has affected residential areas, agricultural land, roads, and public infrastructure, with communities along the Ngawun River being particularly affected. Water levels in the Ngawun River have exceeded the danger level and remain elevated, with further rainfall potentially worsening the situation.

The Myanmar Red Cross Society (MRCS) Regional Branch started the response with its own resources on 1 August 2026, and the information indicates impacts across 5 wards, 23 village tracts, and 122 villages in Laymyatna Township; 2 wards, 16 village tracts, and 14 villages in Yegyi Township; and 10 village tracts and 33 villages in Hinthada Township. The most significant impacts are in Laymyethna, Yegyi, and Hinthada Townships, among other townships in Ayeyarwady, particularly communities located along the Ngawun River and other low-lying areas. In August 2026, the request was submitted to IFRC by MRCS Headquarters, following six days after the trigger date, as the situation had escalated and required more support from the Headquarters level.

The same preliminary information estimated that approximately 8,907 households, representing 28,455 people, had been affected and displaced to 28 evacuation camps, including community centres, schools, temporary shelters, and monasteries. The situation remains ongoing, with water levels continuing to pose a risk to additional communities. Rescue and evacuation operations are underway, but access to affected areas is severely constrained by inundated roads, making motorboats the primary means of rescue and emergency transportation. The number of affected people and the overall extent of damage remain provisional and subject to further assessment, particularly as additional rainfall during the monsoon may further expand the impact.

title: Attacks on Health Care Bi-Monthly News Brief, 22 July - 04 August 2026
content:
Attacks on health care were relentless in 2025. Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) recorded 2,546 incidents in 33 countries in which damage to or the destruction of health care facilities was reported on at least 790 occasions, 455 health workers were killed, 218 kidnapped and 263 arrested.

In 2025, violence by state actors was reported in 26 countries and territories, an increase of nine compared to 2024. Over 80% of these incidents involved state actors attacking health care outside their own territory, including through cross-border operations or attacks in contested areas. The vast majority of such incidents were attributed to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) in Iran, Lebanon, the oPt, Syria, and Yemen and to Russian forces in Ukraine. Other state actors linked to attacks on health care outside their own territories included the Bolivarian National Intelligence Service (in Venezuela), the Burundi National Defence Force (in the DRC), the Indian Armed Forces (in Pakistan), Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (in Israel), the Turkish Armed Forces (in Syria), the US Armed Forces (in Yemen), and the Ukrainian Armed Forces (in Russia).

The report includes detailed profiles of 21 countries and territories where many acts of violence against health care by state parties and non-state armed groups, including organized criminal groups, took place. These include:

  • Africa: Burkina Faso, Cameroon, the CAR, the DRC, Ethiopia, Mali, Nigeria, Somalia, South Sudan and Sudan
  • Asia: Myanmar and Pakistan
  • Middle East and Europe: Lebanon, Iran, the occupied Palestinian territory; Syria, Ukraine and Yemen
  • The Americas: Colombia, Haiti and Mexico
  • Year in Review: 2025; 2024; 2023

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #209 - 17 August 2026
content:
Key figures

215,532 refugees obtained temporary protection and refugee status in Romania (as of end June 2026).

1,949 refugees supported with community-based protection activities in 2026.

5,775 refugees provided with protection counselling services and legal support in 2026.

1,872 refugees supported with livelihood and employment services in 2026.

Highlight

The UNHCR Inter-Agency Coordination Unit finalised its assessment of the funding situation of the 2026 Refugee Response Plan (RRP). Of the $48.6 million appealed for by the 43 RRP partners, only $6.4 million (13 per cent) had been received, leaving a funding gap of $42.2 million. Funding remained particularly limited for Basic Needs, which had received no funding against the appeal, Child Protection (1 per cent funded), Education (4 per cent), Gender-Based Violence (5 per cent), and Health (11 per cent). 32 partners reported receiving no new funding. The funding shortfall is constraining operational capacity: 13 partners reported no ongoing activities, while another 10 maintained only limited or occasional activities, often through voluntary efforts or alternative funding sources. These constraints come at a time when needs persist among refugees from Ukraine and progress towards inclusion remains uneven. The 2025 SocioEconomic Insights Survey (SEIS) found that 34 per cent of surveyed refugee households experienced severe material and social deprivation, twice Romania's national rate of 17 per cent, while 40 per cent reported a decrease in household income over the previous 12 months. Financial pressure is translating into difficult trade-offs: among households resorting to crisis coping mechanisms, 33 per cent reported reducing essential health expenditure and 13 per cent reducing education expenditure. At the same time, limited RRP funding is constraining partners' capacity to respond. By June 2026, partners had reached only 650 people with Basic Needs assistance against a target of over 23,000, 1,524 children with Child Protection services against a target of 4,957, and 4,442 people with support to access health services against a target of nearly 24,000. These gaps illustrate the growing mismatch between persistent refugee needs and resources available to address them, risking further constraints on refugees' access to essential services and longer-term socio-economic inclusion in Romania. Detailed findings are illustrated in the Inter-Agency accompanying infographic. The results will help inform fundraising efforts to ensure continued provision of essential support to refugees.

title: Afghanistan WASH Cluster Bulletin, Issue 1, January –June 2026
content:
Performance Overview

During the first half of 2026, Afghanistan’s WASH response continued to operate in a complex humanitarian environment characterized by prolonged drought and water scarcity, localized flooding, earthquakes, Acute Watery Diarrhoea (AWD), displacement, and increasing return movements from Iran and Pakistan. These overlapping shocks placed additional pressure on already limited water resources and essential WASH infrastructure, particularly in underserved and high-risk communities. Against an estimated 15.9M PiN and an annual WASH Cluster target of 7.84M people, 25 operational partners reached 908,176 beneficiaries between January and June 2026, without double counting across WASH interventions. Partners delivered an integrated package of lifesaving and resilience-building assistance, including safe drinking water, gender and disability sensitive sanitation, hygiene promotion, critical WASH supplies, and basic WASH services in schools, health facilities and nutrition centers. At intervention level, partners reported reaching over 1.01 million people with safe water, 1.48 million through hygiene promotion, 987,447 with critical WASH supplies, and 118,633 with sanitation services. In addition, 608,954 people benefited from WASH services in institutions. These intervention level achievements may overlap and should therefore be distinguished from the Cluster’s unduplicated overall reach of 908,176 people. Emergency WASH assistance remained particularly important at key border reception and transit locations in response to continued return movements from Iran and Pakistan. Partners sustained water supply, sanitation, hygiene promotion and essential WASH supplies while the Cluster supported preparedness, operational coordination and continuity of services. AWD preparedness and response also remained a priority as rising temperatures, deteriorating water availability and water-quality risks increased the threat of waterborne diseases. Partners strengthened water-quality monitoring, chlorination, hygiene promotion and coordination with health actors, complemented by continued engagement through AWD coordination mechanisms. Alongside emergency interventions, partners continued rehabilitating and constructing climate-resilient water systems to improve sustainable access to safe water and strengthen the resilience of communities exposed to recurrent drought and climate-related shocks. However, response coverage remained geographically uneven, with substantial differences in achievement and operational partner presence across provinces. The Cluster continued using response monitoring and partner-presence analysis to identify underserved areas, support geographic prioritization and promote more effective use of available operational capacity. The WASH Cluster maintained national and sub-national coordination throughout the reporting period, bringing together partners, government counterparts and inter-sector actors to review response progress, identify gaps and address implementation bottlenecks. Engagement focused on preparedness for population movements and AWD, border response coordination, administrative and MoU-related challenges, continuity of essential services, and strengthening partner capacity in priority locations. The Cluster also maintained donor engagement and advocacy while contributing to efforts to strengthen localization and the participation of national organizations in humanitarian coordination. Despite these efforts, the response remained critically underfunded. By mid-year, only US$43.06M of the US$163.3M required had been received approximately 26% of requirements, leaving a funding gap of around US$120.2M. Funding shortfalls, rising operational costs, administrative delays, limited emergency supplies and uneven partner capacity continued to restrict response scale and coverage. With return movements, drought and water scarcity, seasonal AWD risks and potential climate-related shocks expected to continue during the second half of 2026, additional donor support and strengthened operational partnerships will be critical to sustain life-saving WASH services, close geographic and sectoral gaps, and strengthen preparedness and resilience.

title: Colombia Earthquake: Situation Report #3 (August 13, 2026)
content:
Project HOPE's Emergency Response Team is on the ground in the Valle del Cauca and Risaralda departments of Colombia, distributing hygiene supplies and rapidly assessing needs after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck 150 miles west of Bogotá causing widespread damage, landslides, and impacted critical infrastructure across a large geographic area.

Situational Context

The full scale of the impact continues to be assessed since a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck near San Jose del Palmar, Colombia, on Monday August 10, continued to be assessed. Damage extends across a wide geographic area, including urban and rural areas across a range of socio-economic levels. More than 395 municipalities across western Colombia were affected and connectivity and access issues continue to limit a full assessment.

As of this morning, August 13, Colombia’s national disaster management agency (UNGRD) reports 273 dead, 3,824 injured, and 377 missing nationwide. Other sources state the number of missing at nearly 500. Approximately 75% of fatalities are concentrated in Quibdó, Pereira, and Valle del Cauca.

Over 12,500 homes have been destroyed and nearly 75,000 homes have been damaged, and 172 structures collapsed. Search and rescue operations, led by the National Risk and Disaster Management System, are transitioning from active rescue to recovery in the hardest hit areas. Chocó’s SAR phase was formally closed yesterday after a family of four was located alive. In Pereira and Cali, teams report shifting to recovery of bodies as the window for finding and rescuing survivors narrows, though efforts continue.

With 216 health centers sustaining damage, the need for hygiene, water, and medical support is significant. Access to more rural areas, especially Chocó, continues to be difficult. Chocó also sustained a 4.2 magnitude aftershock this morning, and officials stated the aftershock hindered utility restoration efforts.

title: Yemen: A Sharp Escalation in Houthi Strike Lethality, and a Widening Cross-Border Campaign (3–9 August 2026)
content:
119 incidents and 102 confirmed fatalities. Two Houthi mass-casualty strikes on 6 August, against Nation's Shield camps in Hadramawt and against Marib, killed some 45 and drove the week's toll, as ballistic missiles and drones concentrated on the Marib and Hadramawt fronts.

Data Analysis

119 operational incidents and 102 fatalities were recorded across Yemen from 3 to 9 August 2026, in a week marked by a sharp escalation in the lethality of the conflict. Ansar Allah, the Houthi movement, initiated 36 incidents causing 61 fatalities, and Yemeni Government forces of the Presidential Leadership Council initiated 32 incidents. The single deadliest event was a Houthi strike on camps of the Nation's Shield Forces in Hadramawt on 6 August, which killed approximately 30, while a Houthi ballistic missile and drone strike on Marib the same day killed a further 15, making 6 August the deadliest day of the week with 49 fatalities. 8 August recorded the highest incident volume at 24. Ballistic missiles, drones and artillery were the dominant conflict modalities, concentrated on the Marib and Hadramawt fronts, and Houthi forces also conducted cross-border attacks against Saudi and maritime targets. Hazards, principally flooding and a declared public health emergency in Marib, caused a further 20 fatalities.

title: Syria: The Assad Death Sentence, Israeli Entrenchment in the South, and Consolidation Rather Than Stabilisation (3–9 August 2026)
content:
178 incidents and 20 confirmed fatalities, a low toll for the volume. An in-absentia death sentence against Bashar al-Assad drove a nationwide wave of at least 17 peaceful demonstrations, as Israeli forces sustained 17 operations in the south and rejected any withdrawal.

Data Analysis

178 operational incidents and 20 fatalities were recorded across Syria from 7 to 13 August 2026, a low toll relative to the incident volume that reflects a week dominated by political mobilisation, policing and localised violence rather than large-scale armed conflict. The defining development was the issuance of an in-absentia death sentence against former President Bashar al-Assad and other senior former officials, which triggered a nationwide wave of at least 17 public demonstrations marking a major milestone in the postAssad transitional justice process. Israeli military activity in the south continued at a steady tempo, with 17 recorded incidents concentrated in Quneitra and Dar'a and comprising incursions, checkpoints and searches with zero Syrian fatalities, coinciding with an Israeli statement rejecting withdrawal from Syrian territory. Syrian security forces sustained a high tempo of law-enforcement and counter-narcotics operations and dismantled an ISIS-linked cell in Khan Arnabeh, Quneitra. Dar'a recorded the highest incident volume at 25, and 11 August was the peak day with 40 incidents.

title: Situation report #1 - Nagekeo earthquake, East Nusa Tenggara (NTT) - Update: Saturday, 15 August 2026
content:
EARTHQUAKE INFORMATION

Time of Incident: Saturday, 15 August 2026, at 04:58:24 WIB (05:58:24 WITA).

Magnitude: M 7.7 (BMKG / USGS). The earthquake was triggered by an upthrust fault mechanism (Flores Back Arc Thrust) at a shallow depth of 10–15 km. USGS estimates that up to 1.5 million people experienced strong shaking at intensity IV–V MMI across Flores Island to Sumbawa.

Tsunami Potential & Detection: A tsunami early warning was temporarily activated by BMKG after sea-level rises were detected at 10 observation stations. The highest rise was recorded in Maurole, Ende, at 0.94 metres at 05:27 WIB. The tsunami early warning was officially lifted by BMKG at 07:30 WIB.

Aftershocks: BMKG recorded at least 54 aftershocks up to 07:30 WIB, with the strongest reaching M 6.1.

Earthquake Epicentre: Offshore at coordinates 8.41° S – 121.39° E, approximately 30 km northeast of Mbay, Nagekeo Regency, East Nusa Tenggara.

title: Situation report #2 - Nagekeo earthquake, East Nusa Tenggara (NTT) - Update: Sunday, 16 August 2026
content:
SITUATION REPORT #2 NAGEKEO EARTHQUAKE, EAST NUSA TENGGARA

Update: Sunday, 16 August 2026, 07:30 WIB / 08:30 WITA

  • Time of Main Earthquake: Saturday, 15 August 2026, at 04:58:24 WIB (05:58:24 WITA).
  • Magnitude & Depth: Magnitude (M) 7.7 | Depth: 15 km. The earthquake was caused by a thrust-fault mechanism along the Flores Back-Arc Thrust.
  • Tsunami Potential & Aftershocks: The tsunami early warning has been officially lifted. Aftershock activity has begun to subside, although monitoring for secondary hazards remains ongoing.
  • Epicentre: Located offshore at coordinates 8.42° S – 121.39° E, approximately 30 km northeast of Mbay, Nagekeo Regency, East Nusa Tenggara.
  • Geographical Extent of Impact: 10 regencies and 1 city in East Nusa Tenggara (NTT), 2 areas in West Nusa Tenggara (NTB), and 2 regencies in South Sulawesi.

UPDATE ON EMERGENCY STATUS AND RESPONSE (AS OF SUNDAY MORNING)

Based on the latest multi-stakeholder disaster-response coordination as of Sunday morning, 16 August 2026:

• Provincial Level: The decree establishing a 14-day Provincial Disaster Emergency Response Status for East Nusa Tenggara has been officially finalised to accelerate the delivery of ground and air logistics assistance to the 10 affected regencies.

• Manggarai Regency: A Regent’s Decree establishes a Disaster Emergency Response Status, effective from 15 August to 13 November 2026.

• East Manggarai Regency: A Regent’s Decree establishes a Disaster Emergency Preparedness Status, effective from 15 August to 4 September 2026.

• Ngada Regency: A Regent’s Decree establishes a 30-day Earthquake Disaster Emergency Response Status, effective from 15 August to 15 September 2026.

title: Comoros | Volcanic Ash: Simplified Early Action Protocol - Final Report (EAP №: sEAP2023KM01, Operation N°: MDRKM012 / PKM514), June 2026
content:
SUMMARY OF THE SIMPLIFIED EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL

The IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) allocated CHF 210,958 for the implementation of anticipatory actions to reduce and mitigate the impact of volcanic ash in Comoros. This simplified Early Action Protocol (sEAP) includes an allocation of CHF 136,906 to preposition stock and undertake annual readiness activities in order to implement early actions, if and when the trigger is reached. The early actions to be conducted have been pre-agreed with the National Society and are described in the simplified Early Action Protocol [Link to the EAP summary on IFRC’s appeals website].

This Final report summarizes the achievements, results, challenges, and lessons learned from the implementation of the sEAP for Volcanic Ash in Comoros, implemented from April 2024 to April 2026. The operation aimed to strengthen anticipatory action capacities and preparedness for volcanic ash hazards associated with Mount Karthala through institutional capacity building, community engagement, institutional coordination, and the prepositioning of critical response supplies. During the reporting period, the activation trigger threshold for the volcanic ash sEAP was not reached and, therefore, no early actions were activated.

Nevertheless, the operation achieved its primary preparedness objectives by establishing the systems, capacities, partnerships, and prepositioned resources required for rapid activation should volcanic activity escalate in the future. Through the implementation of readiness activities, the Comoros Red Crescent (CoRC) directly reached 4,121 community members with preparedness and risk awareness interventions, trained 160 volunteers across Health, WASH, PGI and DRR/CCA sectors, strengthened community feedback and engagement mechanisms, and prepositioned essential protective, WASH, and dignity supplies in Ngazidja. The operating context continued to be shaped by the persistent threat posed by Mount Karthala, while implementation built on lessons learned from previous disruptions caused by the cholera outbreak and Tropical Cyclone Chido. CoRC further strengthened its institutional preparedness and operational capacity through enhanced coordination with key government partners, particularly the Directorate General for Civil Security (DGSC) and the Karthala Volcanological Observatory (OVK), ensuring alignment with the latest risk assessments and preparedness planning.

Collaboration with IFRC, the French Red Cross PIROI, and other technical and Movement partners also contributed to timely progress against planned objectives, strengthening logistics, stock management, anticipatory action systems, and overall readiness for a potential volcanic emergency.

title: Colombia | Earthquake - DREF Operation (MDRCO036)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
10-08-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 10 August 2026, at 07:34 a.m. local time, a magnitude 7.4 (Mw) earthquake struck western Colombia. According to the Colombian Geological Service (SGC), the epicentre was located in the municipality of San José del Palmar, department of Chocó, at a depth of 103 km.

The SGC identified it as the highest-magnitude earthquake recorded in Colombia during the twenty-first century. The main event was followed by at least 103 aftershocks, including a magnitude 4.8 event recorded near San José del Palmar 44 minutes later. Further aftershocks may continue to occur.

The earthquake was felt across much of Colombia and was also reported in parts of Panama and Venezuela. Initial reports indicated possible impacts in as many as 16 departments. As information was subsequently verified and consolidated, the latest available humanitarian update, issued on 12 August 2026, reported impacts across 14 departments and 395 municipalities. The most severe impacts are concentrated in Chocó and Valle del Cauca, in western Colombia, and in Risaralda, Caldas and Quindío, which comprise the Coffee Region (Eje Cafetero). Major affected urban areas include the departmental capitals of Quibdó, Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Armenia.

Preliminary information indicates significant loss of life and injuries, as well as damage to housing, public buildings and essential infrastructure. Access and communications constraints, particularly in remote and rural areas of Chocó, continue to complicate the consolidation of information and the identification of affected communities and priority humanitarian needs.

Following the earthquake, the coordination mechanisms of the National Disaster Risk Management System (SNGRD) were activated at national and territorial levels. The National Government convened the National Committee for Disaster Management and established a Unified Command Post at the headquarters of the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) to coordinate search and rescue
operations, emergency assistance, initial damage and needs assessments, and the deployment of response capacities.

Given the magnitude of the earthquake, its geographical reach and the severity of the reported impacts, the National Government declared a national disaster situation on the same day. This declaration enables the administrative, budgetary and coordination mechanisms required to mobilise resources, support affected territorial authorities and facilitate the immediate response and subsequent recovery.

The situation remains fluid. Assessments by the Colombian Red Cross Society and the competent government authorities are ongoing, including in remote and hard-to-reach areas. Consequently, the situation overview, geographical scope, identified needs and reported figures are expected to evolve as further information is verified and consolidated.

title: NGA: Flood - 08-2026 - Nigeria: Flood – Lafia, Nasarawa State (2026-08-15)
content:
Description

In the early hours of Wednesday, 13 August 2026, between approximately 4:42am and 8:39am, a heavy downpour struck Lafia, the capital of Nasarawa State, triggering severe urban flooding across four communities in Lafia Local Government Area: Bukansidi, Millionaires Quarters, Sadaji Junction/Police B Division and the Makurdi Road/Local Government Secretariat area. The intense and sustained rainfall overwhelmed the area’s inadequate drainage infrastructure, causing floodwaters to inundate residential buildings, damage essential public facilities and disrupt livelihoods.

In total, 37 houses were destroyed across the four affected communities, with further damage reported to household property, non-food items and furniture workshops in the affected areas. Many furniture workshops and businesses along the flooded streets sustained significant losses. Floodwaters also caused heavy traffic disruption across Lafia metropolis. A total of 307 persons were displaced by the flooding and are currently sheltering in host communities within Lafia LGA.

No deaths or injuries were recorded. The displaced population now faces pressing needs for shelter support, food, non-food items and psychosocial assistance, with particular attention required for the most vulnerable among them including women, children and older persons. The Nigerian Red Cross Society Nasarawa Branch conducted a rapid assessment of the affected communities, and the figures in this report reflect confirmed assessment findings.

Nasarawa State and Lafia LGA sit within a wider flood-risk context: the NiMet 2026 Seasonal Climate Prediction specifically identifies Lafia and Doma LGAs among the areas in Nasarawa most likely to experience severe flooding, and the NIHSA 2026 Annual Flood Outlook lists Nasarawa among 23 high-risk states, with the state’s vulnerability closely linked to proximity to the River Benue, rapid urban expansion and inadequate drainage infrastructure. The flooding on 13 August 2026 is consistent with this forecast pattern, and further flooding is anticipated as the rainy season peaks through September.

The Nigerian Red Cross Society Nasarawa Branch conducted a rapid assessment of the flood-affected communities across Lafia LGA, establishing the figures presented in this report. The National Society is monitoring the situation and stands ready to support the affected population in line with its auxiliary role and humanitarian mandate.

The Nasarawa State Commissioner for Environment and Natural Resources, Princess Dr Margaret Elayo, inspected flood-affected areas in Lafia. She cautioned residents against constructing buildings on water channels, urged those in flood-prone areas to temporarily relocate to safer locations, and attributed the flooding to depleted underground water sources, obstructed drainage channels and poor urban infrastructure. The government ordered the temporary closure of Sandaji Hotel for non-compliance with environmental standards. Residents are appealing for urgent government intervention.

title: IDN: Earthquake - 08-2026 - Impact Assessment Report: East Nusa Tenggara Earthquake (2026-08-15)
content:
Description

An earthquake with a magnitude of 7.7 struck the Nagekeo Regency, East Nusa Tenggara (NTT) Province, on Saturday (15/08) at 04:58 WIB. The earthquake occurred at a depth of 15 km, with coordinates located at 8.41 S – 121.39 E, approximately 30 km Northeast of Mbay, Nagekeo Regency.

The earthquake triggered a tsunami warning. According to BMKG (Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency) monitoring, tsunami waves were detected in several areas with sea level heights reaching 0.94 meters in Maurole–Ende, 0.36 meters in Labuan Bajo, 0.38 meters at Kewapante Port–Sikka, and 0.25 meters in East Flores. The tsunami warning was officially lifted at 07:30 WIB.

Casualties and Damages by Region:

  • East Manggarai Regency: 14 fatalities and 2 people seriously injured. Data on building and public facility damage is currently being processed.
  • Manggarai Regency: 14 fatalities, 7 people seriously injured, 5 slightly injured, and 15 people displaced. Recorded damage includes 28 heavily damaged houses, 9 moderately damaged houses, and 9 slightly damaged houses.
  • Ende Regency: 2 fatalities and 1 person seriously injured. Impacted infrastructure includes 15 slightly damaged houses, 1 community health center (Puskesmas), and 1 house of worship.
  • Sikka Regency: 3 fatalities, 1 person seriously injured, 3 slightly injured, and 4 people reported missing.
  • Nagekeo, West Manggarai, and Ngada Regencies: These areas were affected; however, casualty and damage assessments are still ongoing.
  • Bima City: 1 person slightly injured, 2 moderately damaged houses, and 1 house of worship affected.

Total Impact Summary:
A total of 33 people have died, 11 are seriously injured, 11 have minor injuries, and 4 people remain missing. Furthermore, 15 individuals have been displaced. Infrastructure damage consists of 28 heavily damaged houses, 11 moderately damaged, 24 slightly damaged, 12 community health center, and 2 houses of worship.

Based on preliminary information from BNPB (National Disaster Management Authority), reports of casualties and damage to homes, government facilities, and infrastructure continue to come in from several affected areas. In Nagekeo Regency, approximately 2,000 residents conducted self-evacuations as a precaution following the quake and tsunami warning. Field verification and data collection are ongoing.

As of Saturday, August 15, 2026, at 02:55 pm, 172 aftershocks have been recorded with magnitudes ranging from 2.5 to 6.2. BMKG urges the public to remain vigilant regarding potential aftershocks. According to current reports, community activities in the affected areas have returned to normal. Meanwhile, rescue teams are still searching for 4 victims who reportedly fell from a boat during the event.

title: IDN: Earthquake - 08-2026 - Field Report Update 1: M7.7 East Nusa Tenggara Earthquake #2 (2026-08-16)
content:
Description

A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck offshore Nagekeo Regency, East Nusa Tenggara Province, on 15 August 2026 at 04:58 WIB. The earthquake occurred at a depth of 15 km, approximately 38 km northeast of Mbay. The tsunami warning issued for several coastal areas was officially lifted by BMKG at 07:31 WIB.

As of 16 August 2026 at 00:00 WIB, BNPB reported 47 fatalities and 101 injuries. More than 5,000 people remain displaced, including 3,356 people in Sikka, 2,078 in Manggarai, and 500 in Nagekeo. Additional displacement was reported in Bima and the Selayar Islands.

Preliminary assessments recorded 914 houses severely damaged, 126 moderately damaged, and 317 slightly damaged. At least 93 educational facilities, 36 health facilities, and 38 government offices were also affected.

BMKG recorded 341 aftershocks with magnitudes ranging from 2.5 to 6.2. Continuing aftershocks, damaged roads, electricity outages, and communication disruptions are affecting assessments and humanitarian operations. The Larantuka–Maumere road is accessible, while the Ende–Nagekeo road remains cut off. Data collection and verification are ongoing.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 14 August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Humanitarian response efforts continue across the Occupied Palestinian Territory despite persistent restrictions and funding shortfalls.
  • In Gaza, most people remain internally displaced, in harsh living conditions, and exposed to ongoing military strikes; in early July, 90 per cent was experiencing moderate-to-high water insecurity, an increase from 84 per cent in June, a survey finds.
  • Every fourth Palestinian injured in Gaza since October 2023 is estimated to live with spinal cord or brain injuries among other potentially life-changing conditions, while the entry of rehabilitation supplies and assistive products remains restricted.
  • In the West Bank, a large-scale operation by Israeli forces in Qalandiya Camp injured 51 Palestinians and disrupted health services. Nine structures were also demolished in nearby Kafr Aqab and near Qalandiya checkpoint, affecting 71 people.
  • In just one week, 38 settler attacks were reported, resulting in casualties, property damage or both. In Tuba, Masafer Yatta, settlers injured five Palestinians and destroyed three homes, displacing 23 people, including 14 children.
  • Israeli authorities demolished 25 Palestinian-owned structures in eight incidents, displacing 29 people, including 17 children. The demolitions included part of a school in Masafer Yatta, affecting 54 students.

Overview

In a statement issued on 12 August for International Youth Day, Deputy Special Coordinator, Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov said that for Palestinian youth, hopes for dignity, opportunity and a peaceful future remain constrained “by occupation, conflict, displacement, violence and profound uncertainty.”

In Gaza, young people have borne “the devastating consequences of the ongoing conflict, including persistent violence, the loss of loved ones, repeated displacement and the widespread destruction of homes, schools and universities.” Dr. Alakbarov warned that the future of an entire generation in Gaza is threatened by “the collapse of essential services, disruption of education and loss of livelihoods.” In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, “youth continue to face escalating violence, expanding settler presence, severe restrictions on movement and access, and shrinking economic opportunities.”

Dr. Alakbarov, who is also the Acting United Nations Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, reaffirmed UN’s commitment to work alongside young people in Palestine, advocating for their rights and supporting access to education, health, decent work, meaningful participation and pathways to economic and social recovery.

Gaza Strip

The reporting period for this section is 3-9 August unless otherwise specified.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza remained critical, with military activities continuing across the Strip, causing more casualties and displacement.

According to the Ministry of Health (MoH) in Gaza, which operates under the de facto authorities, seven Palestinians were reported killed, including those who died of wounds and had their bodies retrieved from under the rubble, and 28 people were injured between 5 and 12 August. This brings the overall reported casualty toll since the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 to a total of 1,259 fatalities and 4,148 injuries, according to MoH.

So far in 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recorded 45 attacks affecting health care in the Gaza Strip, nearly half of them in Rafah. In most cases, health transport was affected and the delivery of health care obstructed. The majority of reported incidents occurred during medical evacuation operations in the vicinity of Rafah crossing, convoys were obstructed, delayed or searched, and, in some cases, patients or their companions were detained.

Access to safe drinking water remains a challenge for the people of Gaza. The Light Touch Monitoring Survey completed by the Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Cluster in early July shows that 90 per cent of the population are experiencing frequent, unpredictable disruptions in access to safe, clean, and reliable water for daily drinking, cooking, and hygiene, an increase from 84 per cent in the previous month. At the governorate level, Gaza city scored the lowest, with 92 per cent of surveyed households moderately-to-highly water insecure, followed by Khan Younis at 90 per cent and Deir al Balah at 87 per cent.

Despite ongoing efforts to increase water trucking operations to address the overwhelming needs (see cluster section below), challenges persist. Since early July, for instance, WASH partners have been unable to access approximately 5,000 people sheltering in six displacement sites in northern Rafah due to ongoing insecurity and stray bullets.

When it comes to hygiene and sanitation conditions, the proportion of households reporting sewage or sludge within 10 metres of their shelter decreased to 43 per cent, from 52 per cent in June, while those reporting nearby solid waste piles declined from 43 to 26 per cent. Regular domestic waste collection at household level also improved slightly, increasing from 65 to 68 per cent. Consistent funding, more approvals to bring in spare parts, and renewed access to Gaza’s landfills, which are in the access-restricted areas, remain essential.

According to the Health Cluster’s Rehabilitation Task Force, a quarter of those injured in Gaza since the escalation of hostilities in October 2023, are estimated to live with potentially life-changing injuries such as amputations, spinal cord injuries and traumatic brain injuries. According to the task force’s latest report, MoH data suggests that children account for 18 per cent of amputations and 31 per cent of spinal cord and traumatic brain injuries. The report notes that there are no specialized paediatric rehabilitation services available in Gaza.

Overall, the task force estimates that approximately 2 per cent of Gaza’s population – as it was before the October 2023 escalation – is now living with severe conflict-related injuries.

The importation of rehabilitation equipment, supplies and assistive products continues to face significant constraints, including engine oil and spares for generators. No rehabilitation equipment for rehabilitation facilities entered Gaza between May 2024 and 14 April 2026, the task force notes, adding that the average waiting time for pending shipments containing assistive products is 136 days (as of 14 April 2026). According to the report, overstretched rehabilitation services, combined with shortages of essential equipment, assistive products and consumables, are contributing to preventable secondary complications and further increasing pressure on already limited rehabilitation capacity; presently, about 30 per cent of inpatient beds in remaining specialist rehabilitation services are reportedly occupied by patients with advanced pressure sores. Limited beds are also driving early discharge, increasing risks of deterioration, loss of function and avoidable readmission, the report says.

On 4 August, in North Gaza, a 13-year-old child was injured by the detonation of an abandoned explosive ordnance at his displacement site, as reported by Mine Action partners. Since October 2023, partners have reported a total of 589 explosive ordnance incidents across Gaza, resulting in the killing of 274 people and the injury of 1,142. For background, see last week’s report. For mine action response during the reporting period, see below.

Incoming Supplies

According to data collected by the Logistics Cluster, the UN and partners’ aid offloading rate, representing the proportion of truckloads that were successfully offloaded at Kerem Shalom against those authorized to be manifested each day, increased from 77 per cent in the previous reporting period to 87 per cent in the current one. The Egyptian corridor continues to face the highest levels of truck returns and rejections with a 72 per cent offloading rate. The Jordanian route was the most utilized route for UN and partners’ humanitarian cargo entering Gaza during the week, with 170 truckloads offloaded. Kerem Shalom remained the only operational crossing point for cargo.

On the commercial front, data from the Gaza Chamber of Commerce, shared with the Cash Working Group, indicates that the private sector collected 878 truckloads into Gaza between 3 and 9 August. Overall, the number of commercial truckloads reported as entering Gaza has remained stable in recent weeks, with only minor variations. This remains insufficient to sustain the demand. Moreover, of all private sector trucks, 264 (30 per cent) still carried non-essential items, at the expense of more critical supplies as shelter and WASH materials. Only eight trucks reportedly carried animal feed and two medical equipment.

According to the Chamber of Commerce, prices of basic commodities on the local market remained relatively stable, with only minor variations compared to the previous week. According to the Gaza Consumer Index, the inflation rate has increased to 209 per cent more than the time before October 2023. Cash-out fees equally remain stable at 7-8 per cent, according to Cash Working Group, but they are again closely monitored in light of the announced development of the banking system.

The UN is only able to confirm the entry of supplies tracked by UN 2720. For breakdowns of those, see the online UN 2720 Mechanism Dashboard.

For a detailed account of the latest humanitarian operations in Gaza, see Annex 1 below.

West Bank

The reporting period for this section is 4 to 10 August unless otherwise specified.

Humanitarian needs across the West Bank continued to be driven by operations by Israeli forces, settler violence, demolitions and movement restrictions, which disrupted access to essential services and constrained humanitarian operations. In Qalandiya Camp, a large-scale two-day operation by Israeli forces resulted in dozens of injuries, temporary displacement, damage to residential property and disruption of health services.

Despite these constraints, Health Cluster partners continued to support life-saving and essential health services through a network of 870 service points, including 59 hospitals, 477 primary health-care centres, 230 mobile clinic locations and 16 emergency centres. Mobile clinics remain particularly critical for communities in Area C, the “Seam Zone” and H2 area of Hebron, where they are often the main or only source of essential primary health care. Many facilities run by the Ministry of Health have reduced operating hours and service days amid the ongoing fiscal crisis. In addition, shortages of medicines, medical supplies and consumables, which the Ministry has attributed to the prolonged withholding of Palestinian clearance revenues, have persisted since at least early June and continue to affect the availability and continuity of care. Checkpoints, road closures and operations by Israeli forces also continued to delay or prevent the movement of ambulances, mobile health teams, patients and health workers.

Against this backdrop, according to the latest WHO data, which cover incidents through the end of July, 37 attacks on health care were recorded in July, compared with eight in June and a monthly average of about 10 incidents during the first six months of 2026, bringing the total recorded between January and July to 98. Overall, these attacks affected 83 health transport vehicles and 11 health facilities and resulted in 33 injuries and four fatalities. Obstruction of health-care delivery was documented in 92 incidents, while 66 involved the use of force against health care, 25 involved the arrest or detention of health personnel or patients, and 13 involved militarized searches of health personnel, facilities or transport. WHO identifies obstruction and detention at checkpoints, full closures during operations and requirements for “prior coordination” of ambulance movements among the factors impeding access to health care across the West Bank.

In July, WASH partners delivered more than 9,000 cubic metres of water across the West Bank (66 per cent of which supported internally displaced people) and distributed more than 400 household water tanks. Partners rehabilitated nearly 15 kilometres of water networks benefiting more than 65,000 people, installed or rehabilitated 127 household latrines, provided sewage desludging services to displaced populations in the northern West Bank and collected 200 metric tonnes of solid waste from displacement sites. Nearly 1,200 household hygiene kits were distributed, about half to internally displaced people.

In the northern West Bank, where the humanitarian situation remains particularly severe following prolonged operations by Israeli forces and large-scale displacement, child protection partners have provided psychosocial support, awareness-raising, in-kind assistance, services for children with disabilities and case management to more than 29,600 children and 14,300 adults since the beginning of 2026. In July, mine action partners conducted 761 sessions to educate people on explosive ordnance risks, awareness and conflict preparedness and protection, reaching over 11,600 people across Tulkarm, Hebron, Tubas, Jenin, Nablus and Bethlehem governorates. According to the Palestinian Mine Action Centre and Palestinian Explosive Ordnance Disposal Police, nine explosive ordnance-related casualties were recorded across the West Bank between January and July 2026.

Operations by Israeli Forces

During the reporting period, no Palestinian fatalities were reported in the West Bank. At least 89 Palestinians were injured by Israeli forces or Israeli settlers, most during a large-scale operation in Qalandiya refugee camp, in northern East Jerusalem, and six during two separate raids in Burqa, in Nablus governorate.

The operation in Qalandiya Camp, with an estimated 16,900 residents, took place on 5 and 6 August, involving extensive deployments of Israeli forces, military bulldozers and other heavy vehicles. Israeli forces sealed the camp’s entrances for about 48 hours and restricted movement within the camp. The majority of residential buildings in the camp were searched, with some residents reporting that family members were confined to single rooms for prolonged hours. Israeli forces took over three houses, as well as the offices of the camp’s Popular Committee and the Jerusalem Governorate, for use as temporary interrogation centres. At least six households were temporarily displaced from their homes and sought shelter with relatives and neighbours; all have since returned. Local sources reported that approximately 150 Palestinians were detained and interrogated inside the camp, most of whom were subsequently released. On 6 August, Israeli forces entered the UNRWA Kalandia Training Centre and inspected the premises before leaving after approximately an hour.

According to the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS), 51 Palestinians were injured during the operation: 44 (including a 9-year-old) were physically assaulted; one was hit by a rubber-coated metal bullet; and six were treated for tear gas inhalation. According to the Health Cluster, the operation and associated movement restrictions prevented the UNRWA Health Centre in Qalandiya Camp from operating on 5 and 6 August. Medical teams also faced restrictions entering the camp, but were able to evacuate at least 11 patients following coordination with the Israeli authorities through the Palestinian District Coordination Liaison Office. Following the end of the operation, Israeli forces eased access constraints, and UNRWA extended the operating hours of its health centre and waste collection services through 8 August to address health and sanitation needs following the two-day disruption. On 7 August, humanitarian partners conducted a joint assessment and documented damage to doors, windows, furniture and other household property in approximately 30 homes. Affected families reported significant financial losses associated with damage to their homes and belongings. No significant structural damage to residential properties or displacement resulting from the damage was identified.

During the same two-day operation, Israeli forces also carried out demolitions in Kafr Aqab and the vicinity of Qalandiya checkpoint, citing the lack of Israeli-issued building permits. A post-operation humanitarian assessment documented the demolition of nine structures, affecting 13 Palestinian households comprising 71 people, including 31 children. These included four livelihood structures hosting six commercial facilities as well as five agricultural and storage structures attached to residential buildings near the Barrier. Israeli forces also dug a trench alongside the Barrier, destroying the backyards of private properties and leaving some residential buildings immediately adjacent to the excavation. Humanitarian partners are mobilizing assistance to address needs identified through the assessment.

Late on 10 August, during a raid in Burqa (Nablus), five Palestinians, including two children, were physically assaulted while their homes were searched and subsequently taken to hospital. Earlier, on 4 August, an elderly Palestinian woman was treated for tear gas inhalation during another raid in the village. Elsewhere, Israeli forces injured two Palestinians with live ammunition or shrapnel during raids in Balata Camp (Nablus) and Jenin city, including a 14-year-old child in Jenin.

Settler Attacks

During the reporting period, a total of 38 incidents involving Israeli settlers resulted in Palestinian casualties, property damage or both. Attacks affected Palestinians and their property across the West Bank, including homes, vehicles, agricultural land, water and electricity infrastructure and other livelihood assets.

On 5 August, about 30 Israeli settlers attacked the Tuba community in Masafer Yatta (Hebron), throwing stones and flammable materials at homes and physically assaulting residents. Five Palestinians, including two girls, were injured. Three residential structures were destroyed by fire, displacing three families comprising 23 people, including 14 children, who subsequently sheltered with relatives and neighbours. A kitchen, storage tent, about 10 tonnes of animal fodder, a mobile latrine and the community's solar power system were also destroyed, leaving about 100 residents without electricity. Elsewhere in Masafer Yatta, on 9 August, settlers threw flammable material into a Palestinian home in Shi'b al Butum while its residents were sleeping, destroying furniture before the family and neighbours extinguished the fire.

Palestinian access to agricultural land and livelihoods was also affected, particularly in Nablus and Ramallah governorates. Between 6 and 8 August, four attacks in Beit Furik and neighbouring Beit Dajan (Nablus) resulted in seven Palestinian injuries, primarily while Palestinians were accessing agricultural land or working in the area. In three incidents, settlers were reportedly wearing military or military-style uniforms. On 7 August, more than 200 olive trees were found vandalized in Deir Sharaf (Nablus), after landowners had reportedly been threatened by settlers and told not to return to their land two days earlier. In Beitillu (Ramallah), settlers expelled Palestinian farmers from agricultural land in Area B and set fire to a vehicle.

Access to essential services, including health care, was also impeded. On 7 August, Israeli settlers attacked a PRCS team responding to reports of injuries near Abu Njeim (Bethlehem), injuring four Palestinians, including two paramedics who were sprayed with pepper spray, and damaging three PRCS vehicles and a mobile water tanker. In Qusra (Nablus), settlers installed a road gate on 9 August that isolated at least three Palestinian households comprising about 13 people and restricted their access to food, water and other essential supplies. Late on 10 August, settlers reportedly stopped an ambulance that had coordinated access to evacuate a sick child; it was subsequently able to leave after Israeli forces arrived.

Demolitions

During the reporting period, eight demolition incidents were documented (including in Kufr Aqab as reported above) in which 25 Palestinian-owned structures were demolished across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. The demolitions displaced six households comprising 29 people, including 17 children, and otherwise affected more than 160 people, including nearly 100 children. Of the 25 structures demolished, 24 were demolished for lacking Israeli-issued building permits and one on punitive grounds.

On 10 August, the owners of two apartments in Jabal al Mukabbir, East Jerusalem, were forced to demolish their properties that lacked Israeli-issued building permits. As a result, two households comprising 10 people, including six children, were displaced. According to the family, attempts to obtain building permits had been rejected and they had accumulated more than NIS 800,000 (US$270,000) in fines for unlicensed construction. In July, the family received a final demolition order giving them 21 days to carry out the demolition themselves or face additional costs if the demolition was carried out by the Israeli authorities.

Lack-of-permit demolitions in Area C also displaced three families comprising 13 people in Nahhalin and Al Maniya (Bethlehem) and Khallet al Farah (Hebron). The demolitions included residential, commercial and agricultural structures.

Demolitions also affected education and agricultural livelihoods. On 4 August, Israeli authorities demolished two administrative rooms and a storage room at a mixed basic school in Shi'b al Butum in Masafer Yatta (Hebron), citing the lack of an Israeli-issued building permit. The main school building remains intact but is also subject to a demolition order. The demolition affected 54 school and kindergarten students and 14 educational personnel, including 11 teachers. According to the Education Cluster, the resulting rubble has created safety and access concerns ahead of the new academic year. Reconstruction remains on hold due to the risk of further demolition and ongoing legal proceedings, while efforts are under way to clear the rubble and mobilize mental health and psychosocial support for affected students. On 9 August, Israeli authorities also demolished three agricultural structures in Mirka (Jenin), following a seizure order affecting about 3.5 dunums of land for stated military purposes, affecting the livelihood of a family of five.

Separately, late on 10 August, Israeli forces used explosives to demolish, on punitive grounds, the family home of a Palestinian accused by the Israeli authorities of killing a member of Israeli forces in Tell (Nablus) on 24 July. The demolition displaced a woman and her five daughters. Residents of about 25 neighbouring homes were evacuated during the operation and could subsequently return; several homes sustained damage to doors, windows and water tanks.

For key figures and additional breakdowns of casualties, displacement, and settler violence between January 2005 and June 2026, please refer to the OCHA West Bank June 2026 Snapshot. For key figures on the impact of settler attacks, please refer to the West Bank – The Impact of Settler Attacks, January 2023 – April 2026.

title: UNHCR Tanzania Operational Update - July 2026
content:
As of 31 July 2026, Tanzania hosts 130,924 refugees and asylum seekers, mainly from the DRC and Burundi. Of these, 89,574 live in Nyarugusu Camp, while 41,350 (mostly Burundian) refugees live in urban areas, villages, and old settlements in Dar es Salaam, Kigoma, Katavi, and Tabora regions.

In collaboration with the Government, UNHCR, and partners, have been receiving asylum seekers fleeing violent clashes in the DRC. In July 2026, a total of 175 new arrivals were received in Tanzania, bringing the total number of arrivals to 4,566 since renewed violence in eastern DRC in January 2025.

UNHCR continues to provide protection and assistance to the people we serve. Some services, including primary health care and education, are also extended to the host community. In addition, UNHCR seeks durable solutions for refugees.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 307: Week 2 – August 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

Market conditions remained generally stable at the national level during the second week of August, with moderate price movements across most monitored commodities. Several food prices eased during the week, although key staples remained elevated compared to last year and the three-year average. Persistent trade disruptions, regional supply constraints, and high transportation costs continued to influence market prices. Diesel prices increased during the week and remained significantly above historical levels, adding to supply-chain and delivery costs. However, the pass-through of elevated fuel costs to retail food prices remained moderate.

Food Items:

• National average food prices showed a modest easing during the second week of August, with several commodities recording week-on-week declines. Despite this moderation, prices for several key staples remained elevated compared to historical levels, while market availability remained generally adequate.

• Wheat and Wheat Flour: Wheat grain and wheat flour prices remained broadly stable week-on-week, with only marginal increases recorded across the three commodities. However, prices remained significantly higher than last year, particularly wheat grain and low-price wheat flour, which were 14% and 13% higher, respectively.

• Rice: Rice prices declined during the week, with high-price Palawi and low-price Sholae rice falling by 1.5% and 0.7%, respectively. Nevertheless, rice prices remained substantially above last year and the three-year average.

• Other Staples: Prices of cooking oil, pulses, sugar, and salt showed negligible movements during the week. Meanwhile, compared to last year, cooking oil and sugar remained elevated, while pulse prices were 14% lower, reflecting relatively favourable availability and domestic production.

• Vegetables: Vegetable prices eased during the second week of August, led by a 7.1% decline in tomato prices. Potato and onion prices also decreased by 2.1% and 2.0%, respectively. Compared to last year, tomato and potato prices remained significantly higher, while onion prices continued to remain below last year's level.

Non-Food Items:

• Exchange Rate: The Afghani remained broadly stable at AFN 65.6/USD, appreciating by 0.6% week-on-week. The currency remained 4% stronger than last year and 12% stronger than the three-year average, helping to partially offset imported inflationary pressures.

• Fuel: Diesel prices increased by 1.2% during the second week of August and remained significantly elevated, at 15% above last year and 17% above the three-year average. Continued regional supply constraints and elevated international fuel prices are sustaining pressure on transportation and supply-chain costs.

• Fertilizers: Fertilizer prices declined during the week, with DAP falling by 1.4% and urea by 4.7%. Despite the weekly declines, prices remained substantially above last year's levels, with DAP 15% and urea 35% higher.

• Livestock: The price of a 1-year-old live female sheep remained broadly stable, with negligible week-on-week fluctuations. However, it remained 5% below last year and 2% below the three-year average, indicating a slight decline in pastoralists' terms of trade.

• Labour Market: Labour market conditions remained subdued, with labour availability unchanged at an average of 2.1 days per week. Availability remained 14% below both last year and the three-year average, while unskilled and skilled daily wages remained unchanged during the week.

title: UNICEF Guinea-Bissau Flash Update No. 2 (Mpox Outbreak Response), 21 July – 13 August 2026
content:
