title: Colombia: Flash Update 004 - Update on the Impact of the Earthquake in Colombia - August 12, 2026
content:
This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia in collaboration with humanitarian partners, based on official reports (as of 12 August, 18:30 local time)

The emergency continues to escalate and has exceeded the local response capacity, with at least 49,214 people affected, 30,324 families impacted, 3,771 injured people, and 241 fatalities across 13 departments of the country. The damage to housing, social infrastructure, and essential services highlights a large-scale humanitarian crisis that requires a sustained and coordinated response.

Humanitarian needs are multisectoral, and significant response gaps remain, particularly in Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó, and Caldas. Damage to more than 54,900 homes (destroyed and damaged), educational institutions, health facilities, water supply systems, and roads is limiting access for thousands of people to basic services, protection, healthcare, safe water, and livelihoods.

The national and international response is underway and continues to expand to save lives and complement institutional capacity. While search and rescue operations, humanitarian assistance, and rapid needs assessments continue, the USD 5 million CERF allocation represents a critical boost to scale up the emergency response and support the populations most affected by the earthquake in Colombia.

title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #6 (August 12, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • On June 24, two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 hit northern Venezuela in rapid succession, impacting at least seven states—including the capital city of Caracas and the neighboring city of La Guaira.
  • Official figures have so far confirmed 6,125 fatalities, 16,740 injuries and 24,477 people currently displaced.
  • Priority needs include healthcare services, clean water, food, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services, adequate sanitation and hygiene facilities, protection support and shelter.

Our Response

  • International Medical Corps has deployed three mobile medical units, which have provided 3,819 consultations since July 1.
  • On July 11, International Medical Corps opened an Emergency Medical Team (EMT) Type 1 Fixed facility to provide free medical services to impacted communities. To date, we have provided 3,263 consultations through the EMT.
  • Our teams have delivered 390,000 liters of safe water across displacement sites, benefitting an estimated 4,000 people.
  • Our teams have provided 759 MHPSS consultations.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 13, Data as of 09 August 2026
content:
Event description

The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains in a phase of intense and expanding transmission, with cumulative deaths crossing the grim milestone of 2,000 only 86 days after the outbreak was officially declared on 15 May 2026. Since External Situation Report #12, an additional 579 confirmed cases and 304 confirmed deaths have been reported, bringing the cumulative total to 4,381 confirmed cases and 2,011 confirmed deaths as of 9 August 2026, corresponding to a case fatality ratio of 45.9%. Ituri remains the epicentre, accounting for 85.8% of cumulative cases and 80.6% of cumulative deaths.

title: WFP Colombia: Earthquake Emergency Situation Report #1, 12 August 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• A 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia on 10 August, prompting the Government to declare a National Disaster Situation and activate a national response through the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) and the Unified Command Post (PMU).

• OCHA reports impacts across 16 departments and 357 municipalities, including areas already affected by conflict, displacement and recurrent climaterelated shocks, raising concerns over increased humanitarian needs and access constraints.

• The USGS estimates that approximately 2 million people experienced strong shaking and indicates a one-in-three probability that fatalities could exceed 1,000 people, highlighting the potential severity of the event.

• WFP currently operates emergency response activities in Chocó, Valle del Cauca and Risaralda, reaching approximately 100,000 people, and maintains field offices in Quibdó and Cali, providing an operational platform for assessments and response planning.

• All WFP personnel have been accounted for. WFP offices in Quibdó and Cali reported infrastructure damage and business continuity measures have been activated.

Situation Update

• At 07:34 local time on 10 August 2026, a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, with its epicenter near San José del Palmar, Chocó Department, at a depth of approximately 96 km. The earthquake was felt across the country, triggering evacuations and emergency response activations in multiple departments and major urban centers. Several aftershocks have been reported following the main event.

• The departments of Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Caldas and Quindío are among the most affected. Following an emergency meeting convened at UNGRD, the President declared a National Disaster Situation and established a centralized PMU to coordinate response efforts and consolidate official information.

• According to the latest official government balance, as of 7:00am COT - 11 August 2026, the earthquake has resulted in 176 confirmed fatalities and 2,503 injured people. Authorities also reported 7,436 damaged houses, 1,136 destroyed houses, and 48 collapsed buildings. Damage to essential infrastructure includes 377 health facilities, 791 educational facilities and 377 community centers, while 69 roads have been affected.

• According to Colombia´s Civil Aviation Authority six airports remain affected and suspended for commercial operations, pending safety and infrastructure assessments, and one additional airport has reported damage to its runway.

• Search and rescue operations remain ongoing in the most severely affected areas and casualty figures are expected to evolve as assessments continue.

• According to the USGS modelling, approximately 2 million people experienced strong shaking across western and central Colombia. USGS impact modelling also estimates a 33 percent probability that fatalities could eventually exceed 1,000 people, reflecting the severity of ground shaking and the concentration of exposed populations in affected urban areas. These figures are predictive estimates and remain subject to confirmation through ongoing government-led assessments.

• National and local authorities have mobilized Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams, emergency services, and technical assessment teams to support affected communities and restore critical services. The Government has indicated that updated information will be released regularly through the PMU as new reports are received from departmental and municipal authorities.

• The earthquake has affected several areas already facing humanitarian challenges linked to conflict, displacement, poverty and food insecurity. Damage to transport infrastructure, public services and local markets may further increase humanitarian needs and constrain access to food and basic services for vulnerable populations. WFP is monitoring the evolving situation and coordinating with government authorities, UN agencies and humanitarian partners to assess food security implications and potential response requirements.

• According to the National Route Institute (INVÍAS), the earthquake affected at least 13 locations across the national road network. The most significant access constraints include the total closure of the Cali-Loboguerrero corridor in Dagua (Valle del Cauca), the Cartago-Alcalá corridor, the Manizales-Fresno corridor in Caldas, and the Santa Cecilia-Asia corridor in Pueblo Rico (Risaralda). Multiple landslides have also affected strategic transport routes in Quindío, including the Calarcá-Cajamarca and Armenia-Montenegro-Alcalá corridors.

• Access assessments remain ongoing, particularly in earthquake-affected areas of Chocó, where access limitations continue to constrain damage assessments and the identification of humanitarian needs. Official estimates of the total number of affected people are not yet available.

title: Situation Report No.9: Earthquakes in Venezuela 2026 (M7.2 and M7.5), 12 August 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Seven weeks after the two earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026, the response continues to sustain emergency operations while transitioning toward early recovery. Current efforts are focused on maintaining essential health services, rehabilitating affected facilities, supporting transitional camps, and delivering health services through a comprehensive approach, while mitigating public health risks and ensuring a continuous, needs-based supply of medicines and essential equipment.

• Health service recovery and critical care capacity are advancing, with rehabilitation planning progressing in priority facilities and intensive care and maternity capacity being restored at Hospital Dr. José Gregorio Hernández, while assessments in Caracas and Miranda continue to identify critical gaps in equipment and human resources.

• Public health surveillance and immunization systems are being reinforced, with expanded epidemiological analysis and digital reporting, enhanced laboratory diagnostic capacity, and more than 31,000 vaccine doses administered; national vaccine supply security was further supported through a USD 18 million Revolving Fund credit line.

• Efforts advanced toward the provision of comprehensive care, focusing on mental health, sexual and reproductive health, noncommunicable diseases, and rehabilitation. This included dissemination of the national mental health protocol, training of transitional camp focal points, continuity of oncology care through three designated centers, and attention to emerging needs such as assessing rehabilitation center capacities and training on amputee management and wound care.

• PAHO/WHO continued supporting the response with critical medicines and equipment, most recently delivering targeted emergency medical supplies – including specialized kits, medicines, and high-complexity surgical instruments – to the Maternal and Child Hospital Leopoldo Aguerrevere in Petare, Sucre.

• PAHO/WHO continues to support the health response through its Regional Response Team, covering key areas such as emergency coordination, logistics, information management, epidemiology, laboratory services, WASH, immunization, risk communication, and Emergency Medical Teams (EMT) coordination. Additional experts in entomology and infection prevention and control are being deployed.

title: CORE Libya: Sudanese Refugees and Asylum-Seekers - Apr 2026
content:
Overview

It is estimated that over 559,920 Sudanese refugees have arrived in Libya since April 2023. This includes 76,904 individuals who were registered post-conflict, bringing the total number of Sudanese registered by UNHCR at its registration centre in Tripoli to 93,159. Increased border monitoring by Libyan authorities has led refugees to take longer routes, and arrivals via Chad have decreased to an average of 70 per day. Due to the irregular nature of entry, the ad hoc data shared by authorities, and the vast remote land border with Chad, Egypt, and Sudan, combined with movements towards cities along the coast, it remains challenging to provide an accurate number of Sudanese refugees.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 25 – 31 July 2026
content:
Ukraine Conflict Monitor Update

Ukraine continued its campaign on energy infrastructure in occupied territories, while its strikes on oil tankers briefly suspended work at the CPC terminal.

Number of events and change compared to last week (per target):

  • In July, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (SBS) launched a middle-strike drone campaign on energy infrastructure in the occupied territories, and particularly in Crimea. Over 170 energy infrastructure sites were struck, leading to water shortages in the occupied territories and a sharp decrease in both electricity consumption and production in the Crimean peninsula in July. The SBS’ Operation Crimean Switch Off — alongside the Ukrainian Security Service’s (SBU) campaign targeting military logistics on and around the R-280 road — aims to undermine the economic basis of the Russian occupation in Crimea and southern occupied territories. These continuous strikes are worsening living conditions for the Ukrainian civilians remaining in these territories, prompting Kyiv to issue instructions on how to deal with potential power outages, food shortages, and military actions. As Russia has shown little ability to contain the strikes, the SBS can be expected to continue the campaign well into August.
  • In Russia, the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) suspended its supplies of Kazakh oil for the third time in a month, after Ukrainian drones reportedly attacked two oil tankers near its mooring facilities used for loading. Although Chevron reported resuming oil flows and tanker loading through the CPC on 31 July, anxieties remain about Kazakhstan’s main route for 80-90% of its oil exports, and Chevron has resumed diplomatic efforts in Washington to persuade Kyiv to stop its CPC targeting. Meanwhile, the Kazakh president publicly asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to freeze the war, and the Astana government denounced the strikes without naming Kyiv. Kazakhstan also told the International Maritime Organization that it may seek compensation for damages inflicted by the strikes. Meanwhile, the United States recently issued another objection to the Ukrainian strikes on the CPC. Other staunch Ukraine allies may follow suit, albeit likely behind closed doors, as they suffer from high oil prices amid the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Nevertheless, the strikes on a terminal that provides 1-2% of global oil supplies are likely to continue in August.

title: CORE Libya: Sudanese Refugees and Asylum-Seekers - May 2026
content:
Overview

It is estimated that over 564,358 Sudanese refugees have arrived in Libya since April 2023. This includes 78,067 individuals who were registered post-conflict, bringing the total number of Sudanese registered by UNHCR at its registration centre in Tripoli to 93,919. Increased border monitoring by Libyan authorities has led refugees to take longer routes, and arrivals via Chad have decreased to an average of 70 per day. Due to the irregular nature of entry, the ad hoc data shared by authorities, and the vast remote land border with Chad, Egypt, and Sudan, combined with movements towards cities along the coast, it remains challenging to provide an accurate number of Sudanese refugees.

title: Nigeria: Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe (BAY) states - Quarter 2 Situation Report, April - June 2026
content:
This report is produced by OCHA Nigeria in collaboration with humanitarian partners. It covers the April-June 2026 period. The next report will be issued in October 2026.

Highlights

  • Lean season takes hold with 6.4 million people food insecure across Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states
  • Record Nigeria Humanitarian Fund (NHF) allocation gets underway in northeast, northwest and northcentral Nigeria.
  • As cholera cases rise across Borno, humanitarian partners scale-up life-saving responses
  • Borno State progresses with plans to close IDP camps
  • Escalating insecurity disrupts lives and humanitarian operations across the northeast
  • Nigeria on its way to locally- led and financed humanitarian coordination

Situation overview

Lean season hits northeast communities, driving rising food insecurity.

More than 6.4 million people in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY) states are projected to face crisis-level hunger or worse during the June–August 2026 lean season, marking the worst acute food insecurity peak recorded in northeast Nigeria in more than a decade.

According to the latest Cadre Harmonisé (CH) food security analysis, conducted jointly by the Government and humanitarian partners, nearly 4 in every 10 people in the BAY states - about 36 per cent of the population - are expected to experience acute food insecurity during the season. The latest projection represents a 10 per cent increase from previously estimates made in October 2025, highlighting the rapid deterioration of food security conditions across the region.

The situation is particularly alarming for the most vulnerable households. More than 1.1 million people are projected to face Emergency (Phase 4) levels of food insecurity, characterized by severe food consumption gaps and heightened risks of acute malnutrition. At the same time, about 10,300 people could fall into Catastrophe (Phase 5), the most extreme level of food insecurity, by August 2026 if urgent action is not taken.

The CH warns that a combination of conflict, economic hardship and climate-related shocks is driving the crisis. Persistent insecurity continues to limit access to farmland and markets, undermining livelihoods and reducing food production. Renewed attacks in parts of Borno State, including Askira/Uba, Chibok, Gwoza and Kaga local government areas, have further restricted agricultural activities and access to essential services.

At the same time, families are grappling with soaring food prices, elevated fuel costs and expensive agricultural inputs as a result of the conflict in the Middle East. Inflation, currency depreciation and rising transportation costs have reduced household purchasing power, making it increasingly difficult for vulnerable communities to meet their basic food needs.

Climate risks are complicating the food security landscape. Early warning information points to the likelihood of localized El Niño-related impacts, including both dry spells and flooding during the current agricultural season. Such shocks could destroy crops, disrupt farming activities and further erode household food stocks and incomes, particularly among already vulnerable rural communities.

Humanitarian agencies say assistance remains a critical lifeline, but current resources are insufficient to match rising needs. As of May 2026, approximately 700,000 people targeted for food assistance under the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan had not received support, while 830,000 people missed out on planned emergency agricultural assistance because of funding shortfalls.

The Food Security Sector needs US$224.4 million in 2026 to provide food assistance to 1.5 million people and emergency agricultural support to 900,000 people. However, funding remains critically low. As of mid-year, the sector had received only US$76 million, representing only a third of requirements, leaving a funding gap of approximately 66 per cent (US$148.4 million). The shortfall is particularly concerning for agricultural interventions which are critical to helping vulnerable households produce food, protect livelihoods, and reduce dependence on humanitarian assistance.

Without urgent action during the lean season, aid agencies warn that worsening food insecurity could lead to increased displacement, deeper poverty, heightened malnutrition and greater instability across north-east Nigeria. Every day of delay increases the risk of irreversible harm for families already struggling to survive. Additional and rapid funding is urgently needed to expand lifesaving food assistance, support food production and reach the most vulnerable people before hunger escalates further across Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 80, as of 11 August 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Living conditions of internally displaced persons deteriorate in Gbazara, Ouham-Fafa Prefecture.
  • More than 1,000 medical consultations provided for displaced people in Am-Dafock.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Ouham-Fafa Prefecture – North-West

  • In Gbazara, living conditions for some 4,480 internally displaced persons (IDPs) continue to deteriorate. Since their arrival at the site on 22 April 2026, they have not received any food assistance, limiting their ability to meet essential needs. Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) needs remain high due to the lack of adequate latrines and shower facilities. Open defecation is increasing the risk of waterborne diseases. The rainy season could further exacerbate health risks at the site. Humanitarian partners continue to mobilize resources to address priority needs. The displaced families fled Béhilié in April 2026 following an armed attack that resulted in the village being burned down.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Multi-sector

Ouham-Fafa Prefecture – North-West

  • The Association des Femmes pour la Promotion et l’Entrepreneuriat (AFPE), with support from the Central African Republic Humanitarian Fund (CAR HF), provided cash assistance to 30 households caring for unaccompanied or separated children at the Batangafo displacement site. The assistance benefited 19 girls and 11 boys. Emergency food and clothing kits were also distributed to help meet the households’ immediate needs. Six gender-based violence (GBV) survivors were referred to the Gbazara health facility for appropriate care and support.

Health

Vakaga Prefecture – North-East

  • From 3 to 8 August, International Medical Corps (IMC) provided health services through a mobile clinic at the Am-Dafock gathering site. A total of 1,046 consultations were conducted, including 303 malaria cases, 195 acute respiratory infection cases and 89 diarrhoea cases. IMC continues to provide health services through a fixed clinic at the IDP site.

title: UNHCR Egypt - Monthly Operational Update (July 2026)
content:
LATEST DEVELOPMENTS – HIGHLIGHTS

• On 15 July, UNHCR engaged with Egypt's Permanent Committee for Refugee Affairs to advance preparations for the implementation of the country's new asylum system. Discussions focused on a proposed capacity-development package, including technical training, institutional strengthening, a strategic retreat, a learning management system, and a study visit to support the Committee's operational readiness. UNHCR and the Permanent Committee agreed to co-design the programme ahead of its planned implementation in September 2026, while UNHCR reiterated its appeal for sustained donor support to facilitate the transition towards a fully State-owned asylum system in Egypt.

• On 22 July, UNHCR briefed a visiting European Parliament Subcommittee on Human Rights (DROI) delegation on Egypt’s evolving displacement context, including the continued arrivals of refugees fleeing the conflict in Sudan, developments related to Egypt’s Asylum Law and Executive Regulations, registration and documentation challenges, and the impact of severe funding shortfalls. Discussions also covered refugees’ and asylum-seekers’ access to asylum, healthcare and education, as well as their livelihoods and self-reliance. The engagement helped raise awareness among European policymakers of the protection needs of refugees and the operational pressures facing Egypt and UNHCR.

title: WFP Tajikistan Country Brief, August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Tajikistan is a landlocked, mountainous country with a population of 10.27 million, growing at 2 percent yearly, the highest rate in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Half of the population is under 25 years, and a quarter resides in cities (TAJSTAT, 2020).

• Nutrition outcomes have improved substantially since 2023: stunting among children under five declined from 26 percent in 2012 to 14 percent in 2023, while wasting dropped from 10 percent in 2012 to 6 percent by 2017 and remained at 6 percent in 2023 (TDHS, 2023).

• Tajikistan’s economy remains strong, with Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growing above 8 percent in 2024 and early 2025, supported by remittances, services, and industrial activity, while inflation remains low. However, the economy remains highly exposed to external shocks, as remittances account for nearly half of GDP and export performance continues to be weak.

• Poverty declined from 20.4 percent in 2023 to 19.8 percent in 2024, driven by economic growth and remittances. However, rural households remain vulnerable due to limited employment opportunities and exposure to climate and economic shocks.

title: Syrian Arab Republic — Emergency Mobility Tracking and Cross Border Monitoring Situation Update — Round 19 (10 August 2026)
content:
OVERVIEW

Cross-border movements from Lebanon into the Syrian Arab Republic (hereafter referred to as Syria) have declined following the ceasefire in Lebanon announced on 17 April 2026. After reaching a peak of 153,087 arrivals on 27 April, DTM estimates that around 29,467 Syrian and Lebanese nationals have since returned to Lebanon. This trend suggests cross-border mobility is increasingly characterised by more gradual and stabilised patterns.

From 2 March to 10 August, DTM identified 123,620 arrivals across 1,163 locations in all 14 governorates. Syrian nationals continued to account for the overwhelming majority of arrivals, with Lebanese nationals representing less than 1 per cent. Flow monitoring at four assessed Syrian-Lebanese border crossings recorded 655,720 movements into Syria over the same period, of which approximately 98 per cent were Syrian nationals and 2 per cent Lebanese nationals. In addition, 3,375 Lebanese nationals were recorded transiting through Syria towards Jordan, highlighting the continued use of Syria as a route for onward regional movement.

The Arida border crossing was temporarily closed from 6 August, with closure expected to continue until 22 August due to technical works on the Lebanese side. Consequently, Arida movement figures are available only through 5 August and are substantially lower than in previous reporting periods. The closure has also created additional access constraints for travellers, with key informants (KIs) reporting that those previously using Arida have had to rely on alternative crossings located further from Tartous Governorate, increasing both travel times and associated costs.

title: Attacks on Health Care Bi-Monthly News Brief, 22 July - 04 August 2026
content:
Attacks on Health Care
in the occupied Palestinian territory

Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified 190 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care across the West Bank and East Jerusalem in 2025. Health workers were arrested, threatened, or injured; health facilities were damaged, violently raided, or surrounded; and ambulances and emergency medical teams were repeatedly delayed, blocked, or searched amid Israeli military incursions and increasingly restrictive movement and access constraints imposed across the West Bank.

Most incidents were attributed to IDF troops armed with guns. Some incidents also involved the use of explosive weapons, including drone-fired missiles and controlled demolitions, which in several cases killed health workers and damaged nearby health facilities, including a hospital in Jenin.

Attacks on health care linked to Israeli settlers, typically armed with guns or rocks, more than doubled in 2025, compared to 2024, rising from around 2% to 9% of total reported attacks. Most Israeli settler attacks targeted ambulances and first responders, including blocking their access to those needing care. In one case, paramedics in Tubas governorate were reported assaulted by Israeli settlers under the protection of the IDF. Settler violence also impacted a health facility when around 17 Israeli settlers attacked and destroyed a clinic in Hebron governorate.

title: Lebanon: Flash Update #49 - Escalation of hostilities in Lebanon (as of 10 August 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • At least 4,335 deaths and 12,277 injuries recorded due to hostilities since 2 March, with 355 people killed and 276 injured since the 19 June ceasefire announcement, according to the Ministry of Public Health.
  • 352,793 people remain displaced within Lebanon as of 6 August, while 834,651 people have reported returning to their areas of origin. As of 10 August, 22,800 Internally Displaced Persons (>53% women and girls) remain in 232 collective shelters.
  • On 5 August, a new displacement order was issued for Mansouri in Tyre District (South Governorate), the first displacement order since 11 July. At least 130 families were newly displaced from Mansouri to Tyre following the displacement order.
  • 5 August demolition of a well and 7 August fires at Chaqra and Wadi Saluki water stations in Nabatieh Governorate, underscoring the continued destruction of infrastructure that limits civilian access to basic services.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

The humanitarian situation in Lebanon remains critical, as ongoing military activities, unstable returns, and prolonged displacement continue to drive humanitarian needs and exacerbate protection concerns. Displacement remains significant across the country, with access to adequate shelter, essential services, and livelihood opportunities posing persistent challenges for displaced populations. Returnees, particularly in conflict-affected areas of South and Nabatieh governorates, continue to face insecurity, recurring military activity, and widespread destruction of infrastructure and basic services. These conditions are hindering safe returns while amplifying protection risks and humanitarian needs among affected communities.

An increase in military activities was reported during the period covered across South and Nabatieh Governorates, with the first new displacement order in nearly a month issued on 5 August, for Mansouri, a village in Tyre District (South Governorate). Prior to the displacement order, approximately 130 families were present in Mansouri – all families were displaced to Tyre after the order, with 50 families now hosted in existing collective shelters, and the remaining 80 hosted by family members in Tyre city. Humanitarian partners supported the Tyre Union of Municipalities in providing emergency assistance, including non-food item kits, to the newly displaced families. Both ahead of and following the displacement order, artillery shelling on Mansouri village occurred daily from 3 August through 10 August, with airstrikes occurring on 5-7 and 9-10 August.

A total of 133 conflict incidents involving shelling, airstrikes, detonations and demolitions were reported between 4 and 10 August, compared with 97 incidents reported during 28 July-3 August and 130 incidents during 21-27 July. This increase was driven primarily by a surge in reports of artillery shelling (some 83 incidents), of which half were reported as targeting Mansouri as well as Ali el Taher and Haddatha (both Nabatieh Governorate). Airstrikes, shelling, demolitions and other security incidents were also reported in locations across Bint Jbeil, Marjaayoun, Hasbaya and Nabatieh districts in Nabatieh Governorate, as well as Tyre district in South Governorate.

The 5 August displacement order for Mansouri was only the second such order issued since the latest ceasefire announcement on 19 June. The first, on 11 July, involved leaflets dropped over the same municipality declaring it a "threatened area" and urging civilians to evacuate. Continued insecurity, destruction of civilian infrastructure, and recurring displacement are further exacerbating humanitarian and protection concerns by prolonging and triggering displacement, hindering safe returns, and increasing risks to civilian safety.

Ongoing destruction of critical infrastructure, agricultural land, and residential buildings continues to reduce access to services and exacerbate protection concerns. New incidents affecting water infrastructure were reported, including a fire at the Chaqra water station in Bint Jbeil District on 7 August and demolition activities affecting a water well at Wadi Saluki in Marjaayoun District on 5 August, followed by fires affecting the Wadi Saluki water station on 7 August. The incidents affecting the two water facilities further impacted access to water for the villages of Bint Jbeil and Chaqra in Bint Jbeil district and Mais al-Jabal in Marjaayoun district (Nabatieh Governorate). With water access already severely constrained by widespread damage to water infrastructure, continued attacks on civilian assets are further disrupting access to safe water for affected communities. In addition, reported incendiary strikes caused extensive fires in forested and mountainous areas of western Bekaa Governorate, resulting in further damage to agricultural land and environmental resources.

Conflict-related damage continues to pose threats to civilians. On 5 August, a building previously damaged by an airstrike collapsed in Haret Hreik, Baabda district (Mount Lebanon). While no casualties were reported, the incident underscores the ongoing dangers associated with conflict-damaged structures and highlights the need for timely debris removal, structural assessments, and rehabilitation of damaged infrastructure to reduce risks to affected populations.

The Ministry of Public Health reported 4,335 people killed (including 392 women and 253 children) and 12,250 injured (1,452 women and 1,037 children) as of 10 August. Since the latest ceasefire announcement on 19 June, 355 people have been killed and 276 injured. Since 2 March, 135 health care professionals have been killed while on duty and 410 injured, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Displacement levels remain significant nationwide. As of 6 August, 352,793 people remain displaced across Lebanon, according to the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), representing a 2 per cent decrease compared with 30 July. 61 per cent of the displaced are from three districts in Nabatieh Governorate – Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil, and Marjaayoun, and 20 per cent are from Tyre, South Governorate. While overall displacement continued to decline across most districts, increases in the number of displaced people were recorded in several districts, including Tyre (increase of 1,551), Nabatieh (increase of 1,217) and Bint Jbeil (increase of 60). Beirut (Beirut Governorate), Saida (South), Chouf (Mount Lebanon) and Tyre (South) host the largest caseload of IDPs, with 106,800 in Beirut and 63,800 in Saida. For displaced households outside collective shelters, where there is continued strain on local households and municipal systems, access to health care and medication, rental support, restoration of services, access to protection services, and emergency livelihoods interventions remain critical to support households' basic needs and safety.

Collective shelters continue to host displaced people from communities facing barriers to return. 22,800 remain hosted across 232 collective shelters in Lebanon as of 10 August (DRM). Most remaining shelters are in Mount Lebanon Governorate (96) and Beirut Governorate (50), with 7,600 and 7,000 people respectively hosted in each. In South Governorate, 42 shelters remain, hosting 6,100 people. IDPs in collective shelters continue to face challenges in accessing basic services. Limited fuel availability is affecting the continuity of electricity and water services, heightening health, hygiene and safety risks. Displaced households continue to identify cash assistance as a critical need to help cover essential living costs.

Persistent barriers to return contribute to slower return rates and ongoing humanitarian and protection needs. 834,651 people had begun the return to their areas of origin as of 6 August, representing a 2 per cent increase from the previous week (30 July). Notably, an additional 12,240 people returned to Nabatieh district (Nabatieh Governorate), 1,210 to Tyre district (South) and 929 to Bint Jbeil (Nabatieh). Returnees continue to face significant humanitarian needs and protection concerns, particularly for those returning to areas of South and Nabatieh governorates where continued military activities continue to pose risks to civilians, trigger new displacement, and impact service access. Returnees have expressed key priorities for housing, restoration of basic services, cash assistance, and livelihoods support to enable safe and sustainable returns. Protection needs also remain high as access to healthcare, mental health and psychosocial support, GBV and child protection services, Housing Land and Property (HLP) assistance, and mine clearance remain critical gaps.

Funding shortfalls continue to pose barriers to sustained humanitarian assistance as the end of the six-month Flash Appeal approaches. The 2026 Lebanon Flash Appeal has received less than half of the $639.9 million required as of 3 August, or $307.6 million (48.1 per cent).

title: Attacks on Health Care in Sudan, 22 July - 04 August 2026
content:
Using data collected by Insecurity Insight, the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition (SHCC) identified 134 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care in Sudan in 2025.

Drone strikes impacting health care surged in 2025, increasing from three incidents in 2024 to 24 in 2025. Over 75% of armed drone strikes that impacted health care were linked to the RSF, with high incident numbers reported in North Darfur and North Kordofan states.

Several other incidents were recorded of air strikes and shelling near or in the vicinity of hospitals, killing and injuring civilians in the area, and often forcing health care providers to suspend medical services. In turn, this impeded patients’ access to health care. Explosive weapons were most often used indiscriminately, with their wide-area effects causing widespread deaths, injuries or damage in populated areas.

title: Colombia: Flash Update 003- Actualización afectaciones por terremoto en 13 departamentos de Colombia - 11 agosto de 2026 [ES/EN]
content:
SP

Este Flash update es producido por OCHA Colombia en colaboración con los socios humanitarios y reportes oficiales. Corte a 11 agosto (17:30 horas)

La magnitud e impacto de la emergencia supera lo esperado. El terremoto de magnitud 7,4 registrado el 10 de agosto en San José del Palmar (Chocó), junto con 29 réplicas significativas, ha generado una emergencia humanitaria de gran escala en Colombia. Hasta el momento, 13 departamentos y 357 municipios reportan afectaciones, con un saldo preliminar de 224 personas fallecidas, 2.595 heridas y severos daños en viviendas e infraestructura esencial, siendo Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó y Caldas los departamentos más impactados.

La respuesta se implementa y coordinada a pesar de desafíos operacionales. El Gobierno Nacional, a través del Sistema Nacional de Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres (SNGRD), lidera las operaciones de respuesta, rescate y asistencia inicial, con el apoyo complementario de Naciones Unidas y socios humanitarios nacionales e internacionales. No obstante, la continuidad de las afectaciones a servicios esenciales, incluyendo electricidad, agua, salud y conectividad, así como las restricciones de acceso derivadas de daños en al menos 73 vías, representan desafíos críticos para la asistencia y recuperación temprana de las comunidades afectadas.

Persisten necesidades humanitarias y brechas de información. Las necesidades prioritarias identificadas incluyen búsqueda y rescate, alojamiento temporal, atención en salud, seguridad alimentaria, educación y protección. Sin embargo, persisten importantes vacíos de información sobre el número total de personas damnificadas, la ubicación y condiciones de los albergues, así como sobre las necesidades específicas a nivel municipal, limitando una respuesta plenamente focalizada y basada en evidencias.

ENG

This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia in collaboration with humanitarian partners and based on official reports. Reporting cut-off: 11 August (5:30 p.m.).

The scale and impact of the emergency exceed initial expectations. The 7.4-magnitude earthquake recorded on 10 August in San José del Palmar, Chocó Department, together with 29 significant aftershocks, has triggered a large-scale humanitarian emergency in Colombia. To date, 13 departments and 357 municipalities have reported impacts, with a preliminary toll of 224 fatalities and 2,595 injuries, as well as extensive damage to housing and critical infrastructure. Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó and Caldas are the most affected departments.

Response efforts are being implemented and coordinated despite operational challenges. The National Government, through the National System for Disaster Risk Management (SNGRD), is leading response operations, including search and rescue efforts and the provision of initial assistance, with complementary support from the United Nations and national and international humanitarian partners. However, continued disruptions to essential services, including electricity, water, health care and telecommunications, together with access constraints resulting from damage to at least 73 roads, pose critical challenges to humanitarian assistance and early recovery efforts in affected communities.

Humanitarian needs and information gaps persist. Priority needs identified to date include search and rescue, temporary shelter, health care, food security, education and protection. However, significant information gaps remain regarding the total number of affected people, the location and conditions of shelters, and specific needs at the municipal level, limiting a fully targeted and evidence-based response.

title: Afghanistan Flash Floods - Flash Update (20-30 July 2026)
content:
Since 20 July 2026, heavy rainfall and flash floods have affected Laghman, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Logar, Kapisa, Parwan, Ghazni, Paktia, and Paktika provinces, resulting in deaths and injuries, displacement, and widespread damage to homes, livelihoods, and public infrastructure.

Flooding has severely constrained access to essential health and protection services, affecting an estimated 1,994 women and girls of reproductive age. Pregnant women, adolescent girls, older women, and women-headed households face heightened protection and reproductive health risks as a result of disrupted services and limited access to care.

UNFPA continues to scale up its response by providing emergency sexual and reproductive health services and psychosocial support. As of 30 July, UNFPA’s mobile sexual and reproductive health and psychosocial support team had reached more than 1,400 people, providing antenatal and postnatal care, reproductive health and family planning services, general health consultations, and psychosocial support. In addition, 227 dignity kits and 50 mama and baby kits have been distributed to flood-affected women.

UNFPA is conducting joint needs assessments to identify emerging priority needs in sexual and reproductive health, gender-based violence, and psychosocial support among affected populations, alongside dedicated community feedback mechanisms. The findings continue to inform the scale, targeting, and prioritization of UNFPA’s response, in close coordination with humanitarian partners.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Earthquakes in Venezuela (24 June – 7 August 2026)
content:
Venezuela continues to face significant humanitarian needs following the earthquakes of 24 June 2026. The most urgent needs among affected populations include healthcare, including sexual and reproductive health (SRH); food and safe water; mental health and psychosocial support; shelter; sanitation and hygiene; and specialized protection services, particularly for gender-based violence (GBV).

The loss of livelihoods, disruptions to health and protection services, and precarious living conditions—particularly for people residing in temporary shelters—are increasing the risk of GBV and harmful coping strategies. Currently, 24,477 people are residing in 107 transitional shelters, where overcrowding, limited privacy in sleeping and bathroom facilities, and inadequate lighting are heightening protection risks, particularly for women, girls, and adolescents.

Numerous health facilities in affected areas have sustained structural damage, while others are facing shortages of medicines, equipment, and health personnel, placing additional strain on an already overstretched health system. UNFPA is supporting the continuity of life-saving maternal, newborn, and obstetric care through its support to maternity wards in 16 hospitals across La Guaira, Caracas, and Miranda. UNFPA is also providing on-the-job training for health personnel and delivering critical medical equipment and supplies, including 62 Inter-Agency Reproductive Health Kits, which will support the needs of approximately 2,250 people.

UNFPA and its implementing partners are also delivering SRH and GBV services across four transitional shelters. To date, 4,327 people have received prenatal care, family planning services, psychosocial support, GBV case management, and dignity kits. In addition, 4,186 people have been reached through SRH and GBV awareness-raising and information sessions.

UNFPA is appealing for US$10 million to support the emergency response to the earthquakes in Venezuela. To date, US$4 million has been mobilized, leaving a 60 per cent funding gap. Additional support is urgently needed to sustain the delivery of life-saving SRH and GBV services to affected populations.

title: UNICEF Haiti Humanitarian Situation Report No. 2 (Mid - Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights:

  • A total of 1.5 million people, including 751,000 children are displaced. Some 5.8 million people, or about half of the Haitian population, faced high levels of acute food insecurity. 442 suspected cholera cases were reported, and 9 confirmed cases, including two deaths. Additionally, 11,550 children were forcibly returned to Haiti during the reporting period.
  • UNICEF and its partners continued to provide critical life-saving assistance, treating 21,500 children for severe wasting, enabling healthcare access to 198,800 people and providing safe water to 336,400 people. Protection Cluster partners supported the reintegration of 118 children formerly associated with armed groups. UNICEF's IDP response in sites, including Health/Nutrition, WASH and Protection interventions, covered the needs of about 103,000 IDPs.
  • With the 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children appeal only 21 per cent funded, urgent support is needed to sustain critical life-saving support.

title: DRC Eastern DR Congo Ebola Situational Report #4 (5 August 2026)
content:
Contextual updates

The Ebola outbreak continues to evolve in a highly complex operational environment, with more than 3,000 confirmed cases to date. Community transmission remains a major concern, with approximately 63% of reported deaths from 14-20 July occurring in the community, indicating that many patients continue to die at home rather than accessing timely treatment. This highlights persistent challenges related to risk communication, community engagement, trust in the response, and timely care-seeking. In addition, the Cash Working Group has monitored an increase of 35% in the minimum expenditure basket value between May and June 2026 in Bunia, showing the impact of Ebola outbreak on local markets and inflation.

The geographical scope of the outbreak also remains under close monitoring. Two additional provinces recently reported affected cases, including Tshopo and Haut-Uele Provinces (bordering the Central African Republic). Crossborder transmission continues to pose a significant regional concern.

title: WFP Ghana Country Brief, June 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Ghana continues to face widening regional and socioeconomic disparities, with northern and rural communities bearing the greatest vulnerability. In the north, where most households rely on climate‑sensitive agriculture, families remain highly exposed to erratic rainfall, rising temperatures, low farm‑gate prices and limited infrastructure. As a food‑deficit country, Ghana is also vulnerable to global price shocks, which continue to drive up the cost of staple foods.

• According to recent Cadre Harmonisé analysis, an estimated 1.5 million people (IPC Phase 3–5) are projected to face crisis‑level food insecurity between June and August 2026. Although severe food insecurity declined slightly, data from the Ghana Statistical Service and WFP’s Mobile Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping (mVAM) show that the number of people facing overlapping risks, food insecurity, multidimensional poverty and unemployment, continues to rise. Rural women are disproportionately affected, with severe food insecurity among female‑headed rural households reaching 8.1 percent.

• These trends risk undermining progress toward national development and the SDGs, particularly Zero Hunger. Through its 2024–2028 Country Strategic Plan, WFP Ghana supports the Government in building resilient, scalable systems and strengthening national capacity for effective emergency preparedness, response and recovery.

title: WFP Liberia Country Brief, August 2026
content:
SITUATIONAL OVERVIEW

• Liberia continues to face overlapping economic, climate and public health shocks. The country is responding to ongoing Mpox, Lassa fever and measles outbreaks, while declining external assistance and funding constraints continue to affect national response capacities.

• According to the 2025 Comprehensive Food Security and Nutrition Survey (CFSNS), 22.2 percent of households are food insecure, while 26.3 percent of children under five are stunted and 7.4 percent suffer from acute malnutrition. Food insecurity and poor nutrition remain significant challenges, particularly in rural areas.

• The Government of Liberia's ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (2025–2029)— Agriculture, Roads, Rule of Law, Education, Sanitation and Tourism, provides the national framework for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.

• WFP’s Liberia new Country Strategic Plan (CSP) 2026-20230 was approved during WFP’s Executive Board June session. The Government of Liberia expressed strong support for the new CSP and reaffirmed its commitment to continued collaboration with WFP to advance national development priorities, strengthen human capital, and address food security and nutrition challenges. WFP has operated in Liberia since 1968.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #21 (7 to 10 August 2026)
content:
Situation Report No. 21 provides an update on IOM's response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 7 to 10 August 2026.

Highlights

  • On 10 August, IOM launched the distribution of non-food items in Mare II and Algarín following household registration and verification activities in Mare Abajo II and surrounding communities.
  • IOM and its partner Ven Da Tu Mano maintained mobile health and mental health services in temporary accommodation sites. Cumulative services reached 3,267 consultations at the José María Vargas Sports Complex and 2,864 consultations in César Nieves, while surveillance of diarrhoeal diseases was reinforced.
  • From 17 July to 7 August, NFI distributions supported by IOM and Fundación Vivienda Popular reached a cumulative total of 2,244 kits in La Guaira, Miranda, Capital District and Carabobo. The Playa Grande temporary accommodation site closed on 10 August.

IOM activities

IOM maintained the management of five temporary accommodation sites during the reporting period, including three sites co-managed with the Norwegian Refugee Council. Activities included service coordination, population registration, household verification and needs monitoring. At the José María Vargas Sports Complex, essential services were maintained for 751 people from 202 households, while population movements in Campo de Golf were monitored.

Household verification in Mare Abajo II supported the launch of NFI distributions in Mare II and Algarín on 10 August. IOM and Fundación Vivienda Popular also supported the provision of NFIs in sites and communities managed by the authorities. On 7 August, 70 kits were distributed at the Colegio Olivia Andrade temporary accommodation site in La Guaira.

IOM and Ven Da Tu Mano continued providing mobile health and mental health services, including care for chronic conditions and mental health needs associated with the emergency. In César Nieves, health teams responded to an incident affecting approximately 20 adults and 12 children, providing medical care, monitoring hydration status and strengthening surveillance of diarrhoeal diseases.

IOM expanded household verification in Mare Abajo II and surrounding communities and continued updating population records in César Nieves and José María Vargas. Needs assessments in community settlements and formal accommodation sites also continued in La Guaira, Miranda and Carabobo.

Protection activities included coordination of access to case management, health, legal assistance and specialized services. At José María Vargas, 40 women participated in information sessions on violence against women and girls and safeguarding. IOM also facilitated inter-agency coordination to update service coverage and schedules, strengthen referral mechanisms and monitor population movements.

IOM planned response

IOM will:

  • Complete NFI distributions in prioritized communities surrounding Mare Abajo II.
  • Address identified infrastructure gaps in Mare Abajo II, particularly drainage for newly installed showers and adjustments to tent anchoring systems.
  • Continue health surveillance and medical follow-up for diarrhoeal diseases and support continuity of treatment for hypertension, diabetes and other chronic conditions.
  • Strengthen referral pathways for mental health, legal assistance and specialized protection services.
  • Complete household verification in prioritized communities and expand needs assessments and population movement monitoring in Carabobo and other affected locations.
  • Maintain updated information on available services, operating schedules and referral mechanisms in temporary accommodation sites.
  • Strengthen accessible community information and feedback mechanisms.

title: WFP DRC Country Brief July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • In June 2026, WFP reached 1,433,057 people in the DRC, the highest monthly reach so far this year. In the four conflict-affected eastern provinces, life-saving assistance was delivered to some 898,608 people.
  • WFP also rolled out a verification system for in-kind distributions through its SCOPE platform to improve the efficiency of its operations, specifically using digital tools for supply chain optimization and predictive analysis, which help reduce response times and reach vulnerable populations more quickly.
  • UNHAS transported 3,570 passengers and 57 mt of cargo for 100 organizations across through 463 flights. Following the DRC Government’s reopening of Bunia airport under strict hygiene protocols, UNHAS resumed operations to facilitate critical humanitarian access for the response. As a result, UNHAS deployed two additional aircraft to support humanitarian and Ebola response operations in Bunia.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• The security and humanitarian situation in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo remains worrying. The provinces of North Kivu, South Kivu, and Ituri continue to grapple with armed conflicts and repeated violence, leading to massive population displacements.

• According to OCHA, more than 74,000 people have newly been displaced in the DRC, bringing the total to about 6.47 million internally displaced people (IDPs). Insecurity persisted with escalated fighting advancing frontlines into the Fizi highlands in South Kivu forcing thousands of people to move further south to Tanganyika.

• The 17th outbreak in the DRC declared in May continues to spread in DRC worsening an already fragile humanitarian situation. As of 31 July, there were 3,674 confirmed cases, 1, 621 deaths, and 666 recoveries across 48 health zones in three provinces. Uganda officially declared the end of the outbreak on July 28, after 42 days without a new confirmed case. However, the Ugandan authorities maintain high alert at the borders, as the disease is still active in the DRC.

• The affected areas overlap with regions facing food crises (2.6 million people in phase 3 or worse levels of food insecurity). Movement restrictions and the impact of the outbreak threaten access to food and risk worsening the food security situation and humanitarian situations further.

title: Colombia: Flash Update 002- Afectaciones por terremoto en 12 departamentos de Colombia - 10 agosto de 2026 [ES/EN]
content:

title: Colombia Earthquake: Situation Report #1 (August 10, 2026)
content:
Key Updates

• Project HOPE is assessing health facilities and deploying an additional team to identify needs in Pereira, Cali, and other affected communities in Colombia following today’s 7.4-magnitude earthquake.

• Early reporting indicates over 60 buildings collapsed, 1,500 homes damaged, 111 people killed, and 87 injured, with those numbers expected to rise in the coming days.

• Just hours after the earthquake, Project HOPE staff began assessments at Hospital Universitario del Valle Evaristo García in Cali, Colombia, which has partially collapsed.

• Public officials declared a “red alert” for hospitals in Cali and health facilities are setting up tents outside to treat injured survivors. • Displaced families are setting up temporary shelters outside homes that have been damaged and destroyed.

title: Occupied Palestinian Territory (oPt) Situation Analysis: [27/7/2026--2/8/2026]
content:
Executive Summary

The Occupied Palestinian Territories face a catastrophic humanitarian crisis marked by severe food insecurity, mass displacement, and the near-collapse of essential services. In Gaza, the majority of the population relies entirely on humanitarian assistance, with widespread destruction of housing, health facilities, water infrastructure, and educational institutions compounding the challenges faced by displaced families. Harsh winter conditions, repeated evacuation orders, and constrained humanitarian access continue to threaten the safety and well-being of civilians, with children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups bearing a disproportionate burden.

In the West Bank, escalating military operations, settler violence, and movement restrictions have driven significant displacement and disrupted access to livelihoods, healthcare, and education. Economic contraction and rising unemployment have eroded household resilience, while demolitions and settlement expansion threaten further territorial fragmentation. Across both territories, humanitarian organizations are working to scale up food assistance, shelter support, health services, and protection programming, yet persistent access barriers, funding shortfalls, and ongoing hostilities continue to outpace the response, leaving Palestinians in urgent need of sustained international support and durable solutions.

title: Quarterly Complaint and Feedback Mechanism Snapshot | Q3 & Q4 | July–December 2025
content: This snapshot provides an overview of how UNHCR listens and responds to Rohingya refugees’ questions, concerns, and feedback in Bangladesh between July and December 2025. It focuses on the Complaints and Feedback Mechanism (CFM), which allows refugees to share issues, seek information, and report problems through multiple safe and accessible channels, including helpdesks and a toll-free helpline. In Bangladesh, the CFM operates through the Centralized Automated, Information Processing Platform (CAIPP), which helps ensure automated referral of the issues, the provision of information provided by the service provider, supported by a FAQs messages library for reliable information, and access to needed services supporting UNHCR’s commitment to transparency, accountability to affected populations (AAP) and responsive humanitarian action.

title: Quarterly Complaint and Feedback Mechanism Snapshot | Q1 | January–March 2026
content:
KeyHighlights

• UNHCR strengthened remote engagement channels and reinforced the Helpline with additional staff during the four-day public holiday for Bangladesh national elections (11-14 February), mitigating impact of reduced in-person humanitarian presence. On 11 February, 11 staff (responded to over 500 calls, including election-related inquiries,

• UNHCR, the Protection Sector and AAP Technical Working Group delivered election-related safety messages through broadcast calls and the helpline IVR system, reaching approximately 7,000 refugee households and supporting access to critical information during the election period.

• Staff of partner CODEC were onboarded and trained to support 14 CFM desks across 11 camps.

• UNHCR helped facilitate a CAIPP orientation session for WFP–UNHCR Coordinated Help Desk (CHD) focal covering case intake, ticket submission and dashboard use.

title: WFP India Country Brief, August 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• To promote climate resilience approaches and strengthen community capacities, in collaboration with the Assam Agriculture University, over 60 plant clinics have been organised at the Climate Adaptation Information Centre. Under the ENACT-Assam project, the clinics connect smallholder farmers with experts to help protect diversified livelihoods.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Despite decades of gains in food production and nutrition, India continues to face significant food and nutrition insecurity. It ranks 102nd out of 123 countries on the 2025 Global Hunger Index, with malnutrition indicators remaining above acceptable thresholds: 35 percent of children under five are stunted, 19 percent are underweight, and anaemia affects 57 percent of women of reproductive age and 67 percent of children aged 6–59 months. The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World, released in July 2026, demonstrated India’s significant improvements in the prevalence of undernourishment and the affordability of a healthy diet.

• India operates some of the world’s largest food-based safety nets, reaching nearly 800 million people every month. WFP has partnered with the Government of India for over 60 years, providing technical assistance and capacity strengthening to enhance efficiency, nutrition quality, digital innovation, and climate resilience across the food system.

title: UNHCR India Factsheet, March - April 2026
content:
Operational Context

India continues to be a generous host to refugees and asylum-seekers from across the region and beyond. UNHCR works in close coordination with the Government of India and other UN agencies in fulfilling its mandate of ensuring access to protection, solutions, and humanitarian assistance to persons forced to flee.

Civil society organizations, working in partnership with UNHCR, are at the forefront of the refugee response ensuring that assistance reaches the most vulnerable within the overall objective of “leaving no one behind”.
Partnership agreements are in place with five national NGOs.

UNHCR works closely with the Government of India and the UN Country Team to ensure that refugees and asylum‑seekers are included in national efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, in line with the principle of leaving no one behind

title: WFP Ebola Response Situation Report, Democratic Republic of Congo, 31 July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• The Ebola outbreak is spreading rapidly and geographically across eastern DRC with compounding effects across food security and nutrition to worsen an already dire humanitarian crisis. WFP requires USD 75.5 million for the Ebola response in DRC.

• Good governance & Efficient Delivery: In coordination with the Government, WHO and other partners, WFP is providing key support to the response through delivery of food and nutrition assistance, logistics and UNHAS support ensuring that assistance is provided where it is most needed.

• Humanitarian Solutions: WFP is implementing simultaneous delivery of hot meals in Ebola treatment facilities and food assistance to affected communities as a response strategy to protect ongoing assistance while responding to Ebola-specific needs.

Situation Overview

• The 17th Ebola outbreak (Bundibugyo strain) declared on 14 May 2026 continued to spread in eastern DRC. The outbreak has spread rapidly with 3,674 confirmed cases, 1,621 deaths and 666 recovered cases across 48 health zones in five provinces in eastern DRC as of 31 July.

• Transmission has been recorded in the Tshopo and Haut-Uele health zones, indicating continued geographic expansion of the outbreak. WHO has described it as the thirdlargest Ebola outbreak on record and the fastest-spreading to date.

• The outbreak has deepened humanitarian needs in DRC, increasing the number of people in need from 14.9 million to 18.6 million (including 8 million directly affected by EVD), according to the amended Humanitarian Needs Response Plan. Food security remains one of the most critical needs for affected people.

• Acting Executive Director for WFP Mr. Carl Skau and Emergency Coordinator for Ebola response Ms. Hsiao-Wei Lee visited DRC between 28 and 30 July, meeting with Authorities and key partners and staff in Kinshasa, followed by field visit to Bunia to witness WFP operations at the frontlines of the Ebola response in Ituri.

title: UNICEF State of Palestine Humanitarian Situation Report No. 48 (Mid - Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • The ceasefire has not brought safety for Gaza’s children. Since 10 October 2025, 277 children have been reported killed, while nearly nine in ten children consulted said they need psychosocial support.
  • Despite severe access restrictions and critical supply shortages, UNICEF provided safe water to 1 million people in Gaza, including 470,000 children, while sustaining essential health, nutrition, education and protection services.
  • UNICEF reached over 265,000 children through 173 Learning Centres across Gaza, supporting learning, psychosocial wellbeing and referrals to specialized services for children with disabilities.
  • In the West Bank, escalating violence, demolitions and movement restrictions continued to displace families and strain essential public services. UNICEF’s Rapid Response Mechanism reached 1,620 people, including 844 children. UNICEF and partners admitted 19,425 children (6-59 months) for treatment of acute malnutrition, including severe and moderate wasting.

title: WFP Venezuela Earthquakes Response Situation Report #08, 10 August 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

One month after the earthquakes in Venezuela, access to food remains one of the top concerns for families across the affected areas.

WFP has reached more than 120,000 people with food assistance through four modalities, since no two families are living through this period the same way. Assistance include hot meals in shelters, ready-to-eat rations for those still on the move, food baskets for households that can still cook and in communities who lost their sources of income, and prepaid electronic vouchers in areas where markets are functioning, giving families the power to prioritize their own needs.

The agency is also serving as the logistics backbone of the humanitarian response, moving relief supplies into hard-to-reach communities. WFP's logistics services have supported NGOs and UN agencies with the transport and storage of supplies spanning shelter, health, protection, and WASH.

To date, WFP has secured one third of the USD 80 million required to sustain and scale the response. Efforts continue to close the gap and safeguard the support for 500,000 people in 3 months.

Situation Update

  • A month after two powerful earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela, the World Food Programme (WFP) continues to provide food assistance to communities impacted by the devastation. This unprecedented response, tailored to different needs in each affected area, has already reached more than 120,000 people and, with proper funding, hopes to reach a total of half a million over the next two months.
  • Following needs assessments, WFP has expanded the scope of its assistance from assistance in temporary shelters, community kitchens and communities in the most populated cities, to remote communities in La Guaira, where residents have retained cooking capacities, but whose livelihoods have been severely affected.
  • WFP's response extends well beyond La Guaira. The operation plan spans seven states, considering both families directly displaced or affected in their homes, and those whose livelihoods were disrupted by the earthquake — people whose sources of income collapsed overnight.

title: TKM: Heat Wave - 07-2026 - Heat Wave (2026-08-10)
content:
Description

Turkmenistan is experiencing a severe heatwave combined with hydrological drought conditions, affecting vulnerable communities across several regions of the country. The situation is part of a wider regional climate crisis impacting Central Asia, characterized by exceptionally high temperatures, prolonged dry conditions, and increasing pressure on water resources.

According to national hydrometeorological observations and regional climate monitoring data:

  • Daytime temperatures have consistently reached 40-45°C, with localized temperatures exceeding 48°C in desert and remote communities.
  • Night-time temperatures have remained between 32-36°C, limiting physiological recovery from prolonged heat exposure.
  • Rainfall deficits during the spring recharge season, combined with exceptionally high summer evaporation, have resulted in reduced groundwater recharge and declining water availability.
  • Water levels in boreholes have fallen significantly, irrigation channel flows have decreased, and water availability for domestic and agricultural use has become increasingly limited.
  • The combined impacts of extreme heat and water scarcity are placing significant pressure on public health services, water supply systems, energy infrastructure, and agricultural livelihoods.

The most affected areas are located in:

  • Mary Velayat: Uchajy and Serhetabat districts
  • Lebap Velayat: Repetek and Koytendag districts
  • Balkan Velayat: Etrek and Esenguly districts

These areas are characterized by arid climatic conditions, remote settlements, limited access to treated drinking water, and increased vulnerability to drought and heat-related health risks.

Severity and Duration

The heatwave has persisted for several consecutive weeks, with sustained temperatures above seasonal norms and little overnight cooling. The prolonged exposure to extreme temperatures, combined with deteriorating water availability, has significantly increased humanitarian risks.

Key indicators include:

  • Sustained daytime temperatures of 40-45°C;
  • Night-time temperatures above 32°C;
  • Reduced access to safe drinking water due to declining groundwater and surface water availability;
  • Significant crop losses resulting from reduced irrigation water;
  • Reduced pasture productivity leading to decreased livestock production and household income;
  • Increased risk of dehydration, heat exhaustion, heat stroke, and exacerbation of chronic illnesses among vulnerable populations.

The situation continues to worsen as water resources become increasingly strained and vulnerable households exhaust their coping mechanisms.

Trigger for DREF Request

The proposed trigger date is the onset of sustained extreme heat conditions starting from April 2026 and associated drought impacts in the targeted districts, marked by:

  • Consecutive days of temperatures exceeding nationally recognized heatwave thresholds;
  • Reports of significant water shortages in affected communities;
  • Evidence of heat-related health risks among vulnerable populations;
  • Documented reductions in water availability from boreholes and irrigation systems.

The Turkmen Red Crescent Society will ensure that the DREF submission complies with the IFRC requirement that drought-related DREF requests are submitted within 21 days of the agreed trigger date.

title: COL: Earthquake - 08-2026 - 2026 Colombia Earthquake (2026-08-10)
content:
Description

According to information from the Colombian Geological Service (SGC), an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.4 was recorded on Monday, August 10, 2026, in the morning, with its epicenter in the town of San José del Palmar, in the department of Chocó, located on the Colombian Pacific coast, at a depth of 82 kilometers.

Although the epicenter was in the department of Chocó, direct impacts were also felt in the departments of Caldas, Risaralda, and Valle del Cauca. Preliminary reports from media outlets and municipal governments indicate damage in the capitals and other municipalities of these departments: in Valle de Cauca, 3 people were injured in El Cairo and 2 died in El Zarzal, in addition to the collapse of 20 buildings and minor structural damage to 2 hospitals; in Risaralda, 18 people died; and in Chocó, 10 people were injured and 3 are missing. The number of people affected in the area continues to rise, and the President of the Republic has established a Unified Command Post.
