title: Eastern Chad: Sudan Situation - Flash Updates #56
content:
UPDATE ON SITUATION IN SUDAN

Context

The security situation in Chad remains generally stable, although some border areas with Sudan, particularly in the Wadi Fira and Sila provinces, continue to be closely monitored. Security incidents reported between 3 and 4 August 2026 in Birséliba and surrounding localities near the Sudanese border reportedly had a severe impact on civilian populations, causing loss of life, injuries, and new population displacements. As a result, several families were forced to flee to the Chadian localities of Korabo and Birak in search of protection and safety.

A joint mission by UNHCR, the National Commission for the Reception and Reintegration of Refugees and Returnees (CNARR), and the Chadian Red Cross (CRT) was deployed to the border area to better understand the evolving situation and assess humanitarian needs. The mission observed the arrival of new households from Sudan and initiated preregistration activities while maintaining regular monitoring of population movements. Authorities and humanitarian partners continue to monitor the area closely to guide any necessary assistance based on identified needs.

In eastern Chad, the security situation in refugee-hosting areas remains relatively calm. The ongoing disarmament operation in Sila Province continues to contribute to a secure environment, although the partial withdrawal of security forces from Goz Beïda calls for continued vigilance. Protection concerns nevertheless persist in Wadi Fira, where a refugee family relocated for security reasons continues to face threats.

In addition, several incidents of crime and delinquency, including burglaries and assaults involving minors, were reported in some refugee sites. Tensions were also observed in Métché between refugees and host communities, as well as in Adré and Goudrane, where demonstrations by local youth linked to access to land and economic opportunities were reported.

The rainy season currently represents one of the main threats to both affected populations and humanitarian actors. Flooding and rising seasonal rivers (wadis) have caused several deaths, material damage, and disruptions along major road networks, complicating access to refugee sites and the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

title: UNHCR Weekly Relocation Update - Eastern Chad (31 July 2026)
content:
Weekly Highlights

• From 27 - 31 July, 2,387 refugees (679 households) were relocated from border areas to the inland sites of Arkoum (Ouaddaï Province) under the accelerated relocation programme.

• Since 15 April 2026, a cumulative 31,059 individuals (8,519 households) have been relocated under the accelerated relocation programme, bringing the total number relocated since January 2026 to 47,902 refugees (15,910 households).

• Since April 2023, UNHCR and its partners have relocated 648,797 individuals (173,847 households) from border areas to safer sites, representing 69% of the 940,612 Sudanese refugees who have arrived in Chad since April 2023.

• Relocations have taken place to Ennedi Est (79,516 individuals), Sila (81,304), Wadi Fira (198,479), and Ouaddaï (289,498). • Since 15 April 2026, a total of 50,508 refugees has been biometrically registered and 11,293 others have been preregistered, making a total of 61,801 individuals under OCHA-US funding.

• Since 15 April, a total of 23,605 refugee documentation (households and individuals) has been delivered to refugees in Eastern Chad. • Since April 2026, a total of 10,542 emergency shelters constructed across selected sites in the Ouaddai, Sila and Wadi Fira, improving living conditions for newly relocated refugee families.

title: Yemen - Rapid Displacement Tracking Update (2 - 8 August 2026)
content:
IOM Yemen DTM’s Rapid Displacement Tracking (RDT) tool collects data on estimated numbers of households forced to flee on a daily basis from their locations of origin or displacement, allowing for regular reporting of new displacements in terms of estimated numbers, geography, and needs. It also tracks returnees who returned to their location of origin.

From 1 January to 8 August 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 1,742 households (HH) (10,452 Individuals) who experienced displacement at least once.

Between 2 and 8 August 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 50 households (300 individuals) displaced at least once. The majority of people moved into/within the following governorates and districts:

  • Ma’rib (20 HHs) – Ma’rib City (14 HHs), Harib (3 HHs), Ma’rib (3 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate originated from Ibb and Sanaa.
  • Tai’z (14 HHs) – Maqbanah (6 HHs), Jabal Habashi (6 HHs), Al Makha (2 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate were internal.
  • Lahj (8 HHs) – Al Musaymir (6 HHs), Al Hawtah (2 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate originated from Lahj and Tai’z.

The majority of people moved from the following governorates and districts:

  • Ta’iz (16 HHs) – Jabal Habashi (7 HHs), Maqbanah (6 HHs), Dimnat Khadir (3 HHs) districts.
  • Al Hodeidah (8 HHs) – Alluhayah (3 HHs), Al Jarrahi (3 HHs), Al Marawiah (1 HH) districts.
  • Shabwah (7 HHs) – Ayn (7 HHs) district.

IOM identified 28 additional households displaced in the previous reporting period, which covered 26 July - 01 August 2026, in the governorates of Ta’iz (16 HHs), M’arib (7 HHs), and Lahj (5 HHs). These figures have been added to the cumulative displacement total recorded since the beginning of the year.

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #208 - 10 August 2026
content:
Key figures

215,532 refugees obtained temporary protection and refugee status in Romania (as of end June 2026).
1,949 refugees supported with community-based protection activities in 2026.
5,492 refugees provided with protection counselling services and legal support in 2026.
1,628 refugees supported with livelihood and employment services in 2026.

Highlight

On 30 July 2026, the EU Council adopted Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/1912, extending temporary protection for people displaced from Ukraine until 4 March 2028. The Decision, published in the Official Journal of the European Union, applies from 5 March 2027. It also introduces a requirement for people newly seeking temporary protection to provide, where applicable, proof of having fulfilled their military obligations in Ukraine, with this provision applying from 31 July 2026. The requirement does not apply to people who held temporary protection in a Member State on or before 30 July 2026 and continuously retained that status. UNHCR and its partner, the Romanian National Council for Refugees (CNRR), monitored the situation at UNHCR’s Community Centre for refugees at RomExpo, in Bucharest, and other locations. UNHCR is consulting with the General Inspectorate for Immigration (GII) to clarify the eligibility criteria and documentation they require to demonstrate compliance. UNHCR and CNRR noted an increase in the number of enquiries from Ukrainian men and procedural changes related to the renewal or updating of temporary protection permits.

title: Situation Report 6 - Extreme Weather Events in India - Assam, Odisha and Kerala (Date: 8th August 2026)
content:
A. Situation Overview : ( 2-8th Aug 2026)

Assam, Odisha and Kerala continue to face significant monsoon-related flooding with widespread humanitarian impacts. Assam reports 1.55 lakh people affected across 13 districts; Odisha faces one of its largest flood emergencies in recent years with 8.64 lakh people affected across 22 districts; Kerala’s situation remains dynamic with multiple districts reporting camp evacuations, road cuts, and rising river levels, as per media and SEOC updates.

1. Assam Flood - Severe Flooding Across 13 Districts

Impact on Humans

Floods continue to affect large parts of Assam, with 13 districts and 33 revenue circles impacted. A total of 464 villages remain inundated, affecting 1,55,849 people across multiple districts. While human casualties remain low, one confirmed death was reported from Charaideo. Relief camp populations have risen, with 10,326 people currently sheltered and 6,881 non-camp beneficiaries receiving assistance through distribution centres.

Animal Husbandry Loss

The floods have severely impacted livestock, with 47,879 animals affected, including 22,846 big animals, 18,083 small animals, and 6,950 poultry. No major incidents of animals washed away were reported, but widespread distress is evident across Golaghat, Lakhimpur, Darrang, and Nagaon. Livestock feed distribution has begun in several districts.

Structural and Property Damages

Structural damages are concentrated in Sivasagar, Dhemaji, and Darrang. A total of 126 houses have been fully/severely damaged and 344 houses partially damaged. Additional damages include 213 cattle sheds, multiple government buildings, schools, and water supply pipelines. Embankment breaches were reported in Biswanath and Karbi Anglong, posing continued risk.

Irrigation and Water Supply

Flooding has disrupted water supply systems in multiple districts. Two PWSS systems—Sonajuli (Biswanath) and Uriagaon (Nagaon)—have suffered pipeline damage and inundation, affecting household water access. Irrigation channels and agricultural bunds have been submerged or eroded in several locations.

Road and Transport Infrastructure

Floodwaters have damaged 32 roads across districts, with major impacts in Golaghat, Sivasagar, Darrang, and Kamrup. Several PWD roads have been overtopped, eroded, or suffered slope failures. One bamboo footbridge was washed away in Darrang. Culvert approach roads have also been damaged in Udalguri.

Electricity and Power Supply

Power infrastructure has sustained moderate damage, with 7 transformers and 6 poles affected across Sivasagar and Sribhumi. Conductors spanning 1.03 km were damaged in Nilambazar due to heavy rainfall. Restoration work is ongoing by APDCL teams.

title: Vanuatu Dengue Outbreak Situation Report #9 (South-West Efate, Shefa Province)
content:
Key highlights:

  • Nine new laboratory-confirmed dengue cases were reported in EW32, bringing the cumulative total to 76 confirmed cases.
  • Weekly case counts have remained above the outbreak threshold since EW24, indicating ongoing community transmission.
  • A total of 12 dengue-related hospitalisations (16%) have been reported; all patients have recovered and been discharged.
  • No severe dengue cases or dengue-related deaths have been reported to date.
  • DENV-1 remains the confirmed circulating serotype.
  • Cases continue to be reported across multiple Area Councils on Efate, with the highest proportions in Erakor, Pango, Eratap, and Port Vila.
  • Response activities, including enhanced surveillance, case investigations, vector control, risk communication, and community engagement, are ongoing

title: Ethiopia Monthly Protection Overview - January 2026
content:
Attacks on Civilians

Amhara: Debark-Gondar road remains unsafe for travel.

Benishangul: Due to ongoing armed conflict, 1,112 individuals displaced from Kura Woreda to Almahal Kebele in Guba Woreda. 4,000+ individuals displaced from Jawi Woreda to Mandura Woreda in Metekel Zone.

Somali: Inter-ethnic clashes on 21–22 December along the Dekasuftu–Negele Borena border and in Dungoye village reportedly caused fatalities, injuries, displacement, and temporary road closure, later reopened. Reported clashes between clans and renewed fighting on 23 January in Fafan Zone caused further casualties, heightening tensions and worsening security.

Southern Ethiopia: Armed groups seized civilian crops and livestock and extorted merchants while local authorities remain inactive.

New Displacements

Amhara: New arrivals reported in North Shewa, Debre Birhane IDP sites, numbers not yet confirmed by IDP committee.

Returns, Relocations and Durable Solutions

Somali: Final relocation from Qoloji camp to Gorywil site in Awbare woreda planned for completion by mid-year for 376 households, with durable housing, WASH, and livelihood support underway, alongside construction of communal latrines. Fayda national ID registration now reaching 31,405 people - distribution of 9,927 IDs.

Southern Ethiopia: Previously displaced continue to live with host communities and require humanitarian support, including 47 households (458 individuals, 76 children) from Kurbo Kebele in Konso Zone after local conflicts. In Melegadugaya, 501 households (78 female-headed), totaling 2,934 people (1,403 females), remain in makeshift plastic shelters with restricted movement and no rehabilitation programs have started.

title: Ethiopia Monthly Protection Overview - March 2026
content:
Attacks on Civilians

Somali: Inter-clan violence in Gololcha and Welgo kebeles resulted in a reported two fatalities. Inter-ethnic clashes in Babile district reportedly caused seven deaths, driven by resource competition, boundary disputes, and weak conflict resolution mechanisms.

Southern Ethiopia: Reported attacks in West Guji Zone, including in Killenso Mokonisa (Bule Hora), with civilians targeted, daily activities disrupted, and several families temporarily displaced. In Birbirsa Kojowa District, violence by armed actors led to the displacement of approx. 367 HHs.Increased armed group presence and movement restrictions, including a motorcycle ban, further limit civilians’ mobility, access to services, and humanitarian assistance.

Socio-economic Developments

Tigray: Reported further decline in the fuel supply, and a shortage of physical cash in the banks resulting in long queues daily at the banks. It is reported that the banks only provide a maximum of 1,000 ETB or less daily and often no cash at all, impacting overall humanitarian interventions.

Southern Ethiopia: Deepening socioeconomic crisis driven by inflation, fuel shortages, and ongoing insecurity. Rising prices of essential goods sharply reduce household purchasing power, leaving vulnerable families unable to meet basic needs. Fuel scarcity and high fuel costs disrupt transportation, markets, and public services, limiting farmers’ and traders’ ability to move goods. .

Drought, Floods and Other Hazards

Somali: Heavy rains and strong winds on 19 March caused flooding and widespread damage in Afder Zone’s Hargele District, especially in Dirindir Kebele, affecting shelters, infrastructure, salt mining areas, and livestock. Similar flooding in Siti Zone led to reported fatalities, livestock losses, and damaged farmland and shelters, with ongoing rainfall increasing risks and requiring continued monitoring.

Southern Ethiopia: Flooding and landslides displaced households and destroyed shelters, farmland, and livelihoods, with significant impacts reported in Galana, Kercha, and Bule Hora woredas, with 1,452 HHs displaced.

title: Ethiopia Monthly Protection Overview - May 2026
content:
Attacks on Civilians

Amhara: On 27–28 May, two humanitarian vehicles reportedly taken by UAGs in Waghimira Zone.

Amhara: Displacements from Abargele zone to Sekota Town due to continued conflict; estimated total of 13,206 individuals so far displaced, comprising 6,845 males and 6,361 females.

Sidama: Recent violent clashes along the border of Eastern Sidama (Chire woreda) and neighboring Oromia triggered by an incident at a local market, escalating into conflict reportedly involving armed groups, resulting in civilian deaths, including women and children, and significant destruction of property, including burned homes.

Somali: Inter-ethnic and communal conflict in Muli district, Dobo Kebelle over the use and ownership of agricultural land caused reported two deaths and one sustained injury.

Southern Ethiopia: Gedeo Zone facing a worsening security crisis in its border areas, marked by reported kidnappings, UAGs and restricted civilian movement, which is disrupting livelihoods and limiting humanitarian access. In contrast, while no recent attacks were reported in Konso Zone, persistent insecurity concerns, especially in remote border areas, and damaged infrastructure continue to hinder safe movement and access to basic services.

New Displacements (specify the reason for displacement)

Southern Ethiopia: Gedeo Zone experienced new displacements during the reporting period, particularly in Kochore and Yirgachefe districts, due to insecurity caused by UAGs, which has created fear, restricted movement, and forced residents to flee, thereby increasing humanitarian needs and limiting access to services and farmlands.

Sidama: Localized displacement has occurred in border areas of Sidama and Oromia due to recent violence and destruction of homes.

Oromia: During the reporting period, significant new displacement recorded across West Guji Zone, including in Bule Hora, Kercha, and Dugda Dawa woredas. The main drivers were internal conflict and climate-related factors, particularly affecting communities in Dugda Dawa.

Returns, Relocations & Durable Solutions

Somali: DRMB/DSWG confirmed final relocation of 376 HHs from Qoloji to Goroyawil to be carried out in two phases.

Southern Ethiopia: In Konso Zone, some returnees have gone back to their areas of origin, while others remain with host communities. Many still face challenges such as inadequate shelter, limited livelihoods, poor water access, and food insecurity, with recovery efforts constrained by limited resources and damaged infrastructure.

title: Ethiopia Monthly Protection Overview - July 2026
content:
Attacks on Civilians

Amhara: Security situation remained tense and volatile across the region, significantly impacting humanitarian access. A total of 55 security incidents were reported, including abductions, shootings, and illegal taxation affecting commuters and humanitarian workers. Armed crimes outnumbered other incidents in Gondar AoR, indicating heightened risks for humanitarian movement.

Oromia: Continued security challenges in western Oromia, reportedly including incidents of armed violence, reported civilian casualties, and protection concerns involving different conflict actors.

Somali: A road traffic accident in Jigjiga on 23 July killed 8 people and injured 6 others. Multiple violent incidents across Fafan, Sitti, and Dollo Zones reportedly resulted in deaths, injuries, and temporary displacement. At least 10 individuals reportedly killed in major incidents in Fafan and Dollo Zones. An attack in Sitti Zone left one person dead and two others injured.

Tigray: Allegations of forced conscription reported.

New Displacements

Amhara: A total of 60 HHs displaced from Abergele to Sekota during the reporting period.

Somali: At least 30 HHs displaced from Chinaksen district due to conflict-related violence and insecurity.

Returns, Relocations and Durable Solutions

Amhara: Spontaneous returns from Sekota Town to Abergele reported; however, number of returnees remains unknown.

Somali: Consultations were conducted with victims and survivors in Jigjiga to contribute recommendations for Ethiopia's national reparations and transitional justice framework.

Socio-economic Developments

Oromia: Prolonged drought and declining agricultural production continue to affect livelihoods.

Tigray: Continued fuel and cash shortages affecting humanitarian operations. Non-payment of salaries, including teachers, continues to disrupt service delivery.

Drought, Floods and Other Hazards

Amhara: North Gondar Zone reported highly uneven rainfall distribution across 181 kebeles. 54 kebeles experienced complete rainfall failure. 43 kebeles received only 40-50% of expected rainfall. Kinfaz-Begela and East Belessa woredas severely affected by drought conditions. Beyeda, Janamora, and Telemit experienced lowest rainfall levels since the onset of the rainy season. Households in Telemit and Debark began migrating to urban areas due to worsening drought conditions.

Oromia: Three consecutive below-average rainfall seasons have resulted in prolonged drought conditions. Reduced agricultural production, livestock losses, and worsening food insecurity reported across Hararge zones. Continued risk of drought in coming seasons.

title: WFP Palestine Emergency Response External Situation Report #94, 10 August 2026 (Reporting period: 1-31 July 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Gaza’s humanitarian situation remains critical and fragile. While the latest IPC analysis shows modest improvement, 1.4 million people – two thirds of the population, remain acutely food insecure. Improvements since the last IPC are driven by sustained humanitarian assistance rather than durable recovery of livelihoods, markets or food systems, and could quickly reverse if aid declines.
  • Access and funding constraints put these gains at risk. Kerem Shalom remains the sole entry point for humanitarian and commercial cargo, limiting the scale and efficiency of operations. At the same time, WFP faces a USD 565 million funding gap over the next sixth months. Cash transfers have already been reduced, and further cuts to in-kind assistance will be unavoidable as of October without urgent funding.
  • Humanitarian assistance remains a critical lifeline. WFP has reached 1.5 – 2 million people each month since the October 2025 ceasefire with food, cash and nutrition assistance, while supporting recovery and market-based approaches where feasible.

title: WFP Burkina Faso Country Brief, July 2026
content:
278,190 people assisted in June 2026 (61% female)

1,384.48 mt food distributed in May 2026

USD 61 M required in the next six months (July – December 2026)

KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• In June, WFP assisted 278,190 people and distributed 1,384.48 mt of food assistance, reaching 44 percent of the planned target.

• School feeding, malnutrition treatment and asset creation activities recorded strong results, while emergency assistance and malnutrition prevention remained below target mostly due to access challenges.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 7 August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • In the West Bank, demolitions displaced 22 people and affected over 100 others in one week. Since 2024, the monthly average of structures demolished in Area C and East Jerusalem has been at least twice the average recorded over the preceding 15 years.
  • Demolition proceedings affecting four schools in Area C, including the demolition of three school structures in Masafer Yatta, highlight broader risks to education. Overall, 84 schools serving nearly 13,000 students are subject to demolition orders.
  • The Israeli military issued orders extending movement restrictions in Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams refugee camps until 20 August and 30 September, while more than 33,000 displaced Palestine refugees remain unable to return to their homes.
  • In Gaza, the humanitarian situation remains critical, amid intense military activity causing civilian casualties and hitting health and education infrastructure; overall structural damage continues to rise, a new assessment shows.
  • Since October 2023, partners have conducted 3,199 assessment missions across Gaza to identify and mark explosive hazards, while constantly informing civilians about the risks. Yet, they still lack authorization to move or safely dispose of these hazardous items.
  • A new nutrition survey finds maternal malnutrition, persistent stunting, and poor-quality diets among children.

Overview

Humanitarian needs across the Occupied Palestinian Territory remained severe. In Gaza, military activities, displacement, and damage to civilian infrastructure continued to deepen humanitarian needs. In the West Bank, operations by Israeli forces, settler attacks, demolitions and movement restrictions continued to drive displacement, undermine livelihoods and restrict access to essential services.

Across the Occupied Palestinian Territory, civilians continued to face heightened protection risks, repeated displacement, damage to civilian infrastructure, and disruptions to essential services, including health care, education and water supply. Humanitarian partners continued to deliver life-saving assistance despite insecurity, movement restrictions and funding constraints, responding to growing needs through food, health, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), shelter, protection, education and other essential services.

West Bank

The reporting period for this section is 28 July to 3 August unless otherwise specified.

Humanitarian needs across the West Bank continued to be driven by operations by Israeli forces, settler attacks, demolitions and damage to civilian infrastructure, while insecurity and movement restrictions continued to constrain humanitarian operations. These challenges have been compounded by recent legal developments affecting schools in Area C and water supply disruptions affecting multiple communities in the northern West Bank.

A breakdown of the pumping system at the Beit Iba well on 24 July disrupted water supply to 11 communities across Nablus, Qalqiliya and Jenin governorates. Although the outage was initially expected to be resolved within a few days, it became clear over the past week that repairs would require approximately 45 days. WASH Cluster partners have since initiated an emergency response through rapid assessments, in close coordination with the Palestinian Water Authority (PWA) and local service providers, to identify priority needs and response options, including emergency water trucking.

Across the West Bank, shelter partners reached 478 people through shelter repairs, non-food items and cash assistance. With schools closed for the summer, child protection partners carried out mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) and recreational activities despite fuel shortages affecting service delivery across the West Bank. Education partners continued to support 303 summer learning camps, which had to temporarily suspend activities as a precaution following the escalation in the Nablus area and the anticipated intensification of operations by Israeli forces. By 27 July, 298 of the 303 camps had resumed activities after partners assessed that conditions were safe for children and teachers. Partners specializing in addressing gender-based violence (GBV) maintained life-saving services through safe spaces for women and girls (WGSSs) and mobile outreach teams despite movement restrictions and funding constraints that recently forced the closure of two WGSSs.

Operations by Israeli Forces and Settler Attacks

During the reporting period, no Palestinian fatalities were reported in the West Bank. At least 37 Palestinians were injured by Israeli forces or Israeli settlers, and 35 settler attacks that resulted in casualties, property damage, or both were documented. On 29 July, the Israeli military issued new orders extending movement restrictions in Jenin refugee camp until 20 August and in Tulkarm and Nur Shams refugee camps until 30 September. The orders designate "closure areas", where entry and exit are prohibited without a permit issued by the Israeli military commander or an authorized official. Since January 2025, more than 33,000 Palestine refugees have been displaced from Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams refugee camps and surrounding areas, according to UNRWA.

On 30 July, during an operation in Beita village (Nablus governorate), Israeli forces shot and seriously injured a 59-year-old Palestinian man while he was driving. Israeli forces also temporarily overtook Palestinian homes in Tell and Jalud (Nablus governorate), displacing the families while using the properties for military purposes before departing the following day. Elsewhere, search-and-arrest operations and other raids resulted in additional injuries and disruption to daily life in several communities.

Settler attacks continued to affect Palestinian communities across the West Bank, particularly in Ramallah, Nablus and Jerusalem governorates, resulting in injuries and damage to homes, vehicles, agricultural land and other civilian property. Al Mughayyir (Ramallah governorate) experienced repeated settler attacks over three consecutive days. On 31 July alone, settlers carried out three attacks that injured a nine-year-old Palestinian child with live ammunition, injured two adults with pepper spray, and damaged two Palestinian-owned vehicles. Further attacks on 1 and 2 August injured two additional Palestinians and caused damage to a Palestinian-owned vehicle. Elsewhere, settlers physically assaulted two elderly Palestinian farmers in Beitillu (Ramallah governorate), while a 59-year-old Palestinian bus driver was seriously injured after being assaulted by a group of Israelis in East Jerusalem. Settlers also damaged water tanks in Turmus'ayya and East Tayba Bedouin community (Ramallah governorate) and Beit Furik (Nablus governorate), as well as two greenhouses in Beit Furik, further undermining access to water and agricultural livelihoods.

Demolitions and Forced Evictions

During the reporting period, Israeli authorities demolished or forced Palestinian owners to demolish 39 Palestinian-owned structures in Area C and East Jerusalem for lacking Israeli-issued building permits, which are nearly impossible for Palestinians to obtain. The demolished structures included 15 residential structures and 24 livelihood-related, agricultural, and water and sanitation structures. As a result, five households comprising 22 people, including five children, were displaced in Ras al Amud and Sur Bahir (East Jerusalem), Khirbet Jamrura (Hebron governorate), and Ein al Hilwe (Tubas governorate) in the northern Jordan Valley. An additional 19 households comprising more than 100 people were otherwise affected by the demolitions. Of the 33 structures demolished in Area C, 11 were in the Bedouin community of An Nuwei'meh Al Fauqa (Jericho governorate), affecting more than 30 people.

Since the beginning of 2026, approximately 700 Palestinian-owned structures have been demolished in Area C and about 170 in East Jerusalem for lacking Israeli-issued building permits. Since 2024, the monthly average of demolished structures in Area C and East Jerusalem has been at least twice the average recorded during the preceding 15 years. Across demolition incidents documented in 2026, many affected families had pursued legal avenues over several years in an effort to obtain building permits or challenge demolition orders, but their efforts were ultimately unsuccessful. In East Jerusalem, a substantial proportion of residential structures were demolished by their owners to avoid paying additional fines and fees. In Area C, some demolitions were carried out despite pending legal proceedings.

During the previous reporting period, on 26 July, Israeli forces forcibly evicted five Palestinian households comprising eight people from a three-storey residential building comprising six residential apartments in the Old City of East Jerusalem. The family had lived in the building since the 1930s. The eviction followed a lawsuit filed in 2018 by the Israeli General Custodian after Israeli courts upheld ownership claims to the property. Following the eviction, the building was taken over by settlers affiliated with the settler organization Ateret Cohanim. After Israeli courts rejected successive petitions submitted by the family, a final eviction order required the households to vacate the property by 5 July 2026.

Since the beginning of 2026, 22 Palestinian households comprising 85 people, including 30 children, have been forcibly evicted from their homes following Israeli court decisions. Most of these evictions have taken place in the Silwan area of East Jerusalem. Approximately 200 Palestinian households across East Jerusalem are at risk of forced displacement due to ongoing eviction cases before Israeli courts, the majority of which have been initiated by Israeli settler organizations.

Demolition orders raise concerns over access to education in Area C

The restrictive planning regime in Area C and East Jerusalem, where it is nearly impossible for Palestinians to obtain Israeli-issued building permits, continues to place homes, schools and other essential infrastructure at risk of demolition. This undermines access to education and other basic services and exacerbates displacement pressures on Palestinian communities.

According to the Education Cluster, 84 schools in Area C and East Jerusalem serving nearly 13,000 students are subject to demolition orders. Of these, 54 face the threat of full demolition, while 30 are subject to demolition orders targeting parts of the facilities. Recent legal developments involving four of these schools – three in Hebron and one in Bethlehem – have heightened concerns over access to education for more than 700 students and nearly 60 teachers.

In Hebron governorate, Ar Rifa'iyya Mixed Basic School, which serves 175 students, faced imminent demolition in early July following the rejection of the community's appeal. However, on 21 July, the community secured a temporary injunction suspending the execution of the demolition order pending court proceedings. In Masafer Yatta area of Hebron, an interim injunction is also being pursued following the dismissal of an appeal against the demolition of Zeef Girls Secondary School, which serves 253 students. In Sha'ab Al Butum, although no interim injunction against the demolition of the school had been granted, pending legal proceedings, including a court hearing scheduled for 15 September, were generally expected to delay enforcement of the demolition order. However, on 4 August, Israeli authorities demolished three of the school’s structures – two administrative rooms and one storage room. The original school building remains intact but continues to be subject to a demolition order. The school served 47 students during the 2025-2026 academic year.

Separately, on 3 August, the Jerusalem District Court issued an interim injunction suspending demolition measures in the neighbouring communities of Isfey and Khirbet al Majaz in Masafer Yatta, pending legal proceedings concerning their master plans. According to the Protection Cluster, the order provides temporary protection for approximately 160 structures, including two schools, homes, a mosque, health clinics, water infrastructure and livestock shelters, benefiting approximately 400 Palestinian residents.

The two schools in Masafer Yatta are in an area designated by Israeli authorities as "Firing Zone 918", encompassing 13 Palestinian communities, home to approximately 1,200 Palestinians, including more than 500 children. Since 2009, OCHA has documented more than 100 demolition incidents in these communities, involving over 300 structures, more than 60 per cent of which had been provided as humanitarian assistance. Humanitarian partners have expressed concern that recent legal developments, including the Israeli High Court ruling concerning residential structures in Umm Fagarah, could increase the risk of demolitions affecting homes, schools and other essential infrastructure across Masafer Yatta.

In Al Walaja (Bethlehem governorate), on 8 July, the Israeli Civil Administration issued a notice allowing objections to a demolition case dating back to 2006 against Al Walaja Basic Co-educational School, an UNRWA-operated school located in Area C of the village and serving 235 students from grades one to nine. The village, which has a population of about 3,000 residents, extends across Area C and East Jerusalem, with only about seven per cent of its built-up area estimated to be located in Area B, where the Israeli planning regime does not apply. With the support of a legal aid organization, an objection has been filed and a court hearing is scheduled for 24 August. If implemented, the demolition order would leave the community without a local primary school, requiring children to travel to neighbouring communities to access education.

Since 2014, OCHA has documented the demolition of 141 Palestinian-owned structures in the village for lacking Israeli-issued building permits. Nearly half of these demolitions (68 structures) have taken place since the beginning of 2023, including a record 37 structures demolished in 2024 alone (see graph). Residents have pursued planning initiatives over many years in an effort to obtain building permits and regularize existing construction, but these efforts have faced repeated obstacles.

The developments in Al Walaja also coincide with broader efforts to intensify the enforcement of planning and building regulations in the village. The Israeli settler organization Regavim recently petitioned the Israeli High Court of Justice seeking the enforcement of demolition orders against Palestinian construction in Al Walaja. According to the Al Walaja Village Council, the Israeli Civil Administration has issued about 70 demolition notices in the Area C part of the village since the beginning of 2026, most of them stop-work orders targeting inhabited residential buildings and other structures.

For key figures and additional breakdowns of casualties, displacement, and settler violence between January 2005 and June 2026, please refer to the OCHA West Bank June 2026 Snapshot. For key figures on the impact of settler attacks, please refer to the West Bank – The Impact of Settler Attacks, January 2023 – April 2026.

Gaza Strip

The reporting period for this section is 27 July to 2 August unless otherwise specified.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza remained critical, military activities continued across the Strip throughout the reporting period, with daily air strikes, shelling, gunfire and naval fire reported mainly west of the agreed deployment line known as the “Yellow Line" where nearly the entire population of 2.1 million people remains concentrated in less than half of the Strip amid extremely overcrowded conditions. The United Nations Deputy Special Coordinator, Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov, has expressed concern over the recent Israeli airstrikes in Gaza, which reportedly resulted in civilian casualties and damage to critical medical supplies and civilian infrastructure.

On 2 August, a strike hit the vicinity of Al Aqsa Hospital in Deir al Balah, damaging a medical storage facility and destroying essential medical supplies, including items recently delivered by the World Health Organization (WHO). Due to the proximity of the attack, the hospital building also sustained minor damage, WHO reported.

On 3 August (after the reporting period) in North Gaza’s Beit Lahia area, Israeli forces reportedly demolished homes, as well as the last remaining school in what was previously a four-school compound. A week earlier, Israeli forces had already reportedly advanced towards the area, destroying the tents of nearly a dozen families sheltering in the schoolyard and placing new cement blocks nearby, marking a further expansion of areas where Israeli authorities have imposed access restrictions.

One 4 August (after the reporting period) in Gaza city, partners report that a sixth-grade student was taken to the hospital after being hit by a bullet and injured in a tented classroom.

According to the Gaza Ministry of Health, more than 150 fatalities, including dozens of civilians, were documented in July, marking the highest reported monthly death toll since the beginning of the year. Since the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 and as of 5 August 2026, 1,254 Palestinians were killed, 4,121 were injured, and 804 were retrieved from under the rubble, MoH reports. On 1 August, the Palestinian Civil Defense (PCD) announced the completion of a two-week recovery operation during which it recovered 112 Palestinian bodies from the rubble of a residential block struck in November 2023 in As Sabra, southern Gaza city. The recovered bodies include 40 children, 38 women, and 7 persons with disabilities, PCD reported, adding that the bodies of 157 other Palestinians reportedly killed in the same incident remain unrecovered, with no trace of them found. On 4 August, the recovered bodies were buried in a collective funeral.

Nutrition and Child Feeding

Between 2 and 16 June, Nutrition Cluster partners carried out a survey in Gaza to better understand malnutrition levels across the Strip. The survey was undertaken following the Standardized Monitoring and Assessment of Relief and Transitions (SMART) methodology, an internationally recognized standard for conducting population-based nutrition surveys in humanitarian settings. The survey looked at accessible areas of all five governorates, covering approximately 83 per cent of the population. A total of 1,335 children aged 0-59 months and 3,071 women of reproductive age, including 598 pregnant and breastfeeding women, participated in the survey.

Following are some of the findings:

  • 1.3 per cent of the children are acutely malnourished as detected through the three diagnostic criteria of mid-upper arm circumference screening, weight-for-height Z-score, or bilateral pitting oedema.
  • 12.2 per cent of children suffer from stunting.
  • 9.4 per cent of non-pregnant or non-lactating women and 7.2 per cent of pregnant and lactating women had maternal malnutrition.
  • 37.1 per cent of children had diarrhea and 31.9 per cent had fevers in the two weeks preceding the survey.
  • 20.4 per cent of infants under six months are exclusively breastfed, well below the 100 per cent recommended levels.
  • Only 30.3 per cent of children aged 6-23 months achieve minimum dietary diversity, and 22.4 per cent receive a minimum acceptable diet.
  • 75.9 per cent of children received measles vaccination and 69.8 per cent received vitamin A supplementation, both below optimal levels of over 90 per cent and 95 per cent respectively.

According to the Nutrition Cluster, although the low prevalence of acute malnutrition is encouraging, it should not be interpreted as an indication that the nutrition crisis has ended. Rather, the findings suggest that humanitarian assistance has likely prevented a more severe nutrition outcome, while persistent stunting, poor diet quality, maternal malnutrition, and high levels of childhood illness demonstrate that nutritional vulnerability remains widespread. They also underscore the continued need for sustained food assistance, community-based management of acute malnutrition services, maternal nutrition support, improved complementary feeding, WASH interventions, and routine nutrition surveillance.

Mine Action

After years of intense hostilities during which explosive weapons have been used throughout the Gaza Strip, explosive ordnance contamination is widespread and significant. Presently, mine action partners do not have permission to move or dispose of these hazards or to conduct the full spectrum of explosive ordnance disposal activities. Specialized equipment required for such operations remains subject to authorization and cannot be imported at this stage. Still, mine action continues to play a critical role in reducing risks to affected populations, enabling humanitarian access, and supporting life-saving operations.

The following provides an overview of three ongoing mine action activities.

1. Explosive hazard assessments (EHAs)

EHAs contribute to reducing risks for communities and support humanitarian actors in operating more safely by identifying and marking EO threats. Since October 2023, mine action partners have identified and marked 1,052 explosive ordnance items through EHAs. Thanks to the identification of EO through EHAs, shelters could be established, damaged WASH facilities restored, debris removed, access to critical infrastructure enabled.

These activities have also played a vital role in supporting early recovery and livelihoods. Sheikh Ajleen in southern Gaza city has historically been one of the Gaza Strip's most fertile agricultural areas, producing high-quality grapes, figs, citrus fruits, and a wide range of vegetables, including cauliflower, courgettes, aubergines, green beans, cabbage, herbs, and mint. For generations, families in the area have relied on this land for their livelihoods and food security.

To facilitate the safe return of internally displaced farmers following the declaration of a ceasefire in October 2025, UN Mine Action Service (UNMAS) EO disposal teams conducted assessments across nine large agricultural zones in Sheikh Ajleen. They identified and marked numerous EO items, established safety cordons around hazardous locations, and confirmed that surrounding areas could be used safely. Subsequently, farmers could safely resume agricultural activities, restoring livelihoods and contributing to local food production.

Since October 2023, mine action partners have conducted 3,199 EHAs, assessing nine square kilometres of land cumulatively. Of the assessed area, 48.2 per cent has been classified as “low risk”, enabling humanitarian partners to continue and expand essential humanitarian and early recovery activities, and communities to safely access these areas.

2. Explosive ordnance risk education (EORE)

EORE raises people’s awareness of the risks and promotes their safe behaviour. Through sessions with communities that are potentially affected by explosive ordnance, humanitarians inform of ways to recognize hazards and respond appropriately if they come across suspicious items. In July 2026, over 63,000 people participated in such sessions.

During one of the sessions, a participant shared the details of a serious incident where his son, Kinan, was injured by EO. "It looked like a toy, so he picked it up. Now my son needs more surgeries than I can count. Every family here needs to know what these objects look like before it is their child."

During a EORE session for women, Walaa, a 30-year-old mother of five, also shared her painful experience. She explained that her family was forced to flee from Beit Hanoun in North Gaza to Gaza city in search of safety. While sheltering near the Islamic University, a quadcopter drone dropped an explosive object that did not detonate immediately. Believing the area was safe, the family remained there until the object suddenly exploded.

The explosion killed her husband, her children, and six other relatives. She was the only survivor. Walaa spent nearly five months receiving treatment at Al-Quds Hospital under severe shortages of medical resources and suffered serious injuries and permanent physical disfigurements.

Walaa said: “After what happened, I was afraid of everything on the ground. Any piece of metal, any strange object I did not know what could kill me and what could not. That not knowing was the hardest part. Now I know what to look at, what to stay away from, and who to call. The fear is still there, but it is quieter.”

On 7 July, a 13-year-old child who had previously attended an EORE session delivered by a Child Protection partner identified an unfamiliar object that appeared to be abandoned ammunition while walking on the seashore near his displacement site in southern Al Mawasi, Khan Younis. The child moved to a safe distance and informed his father, who reported the object, allowing teams to address the hazard and prevent injury – a concrete example of how EORE can save lives.

3. Victim Assistance

Since October 2023, 274 people have been killed and 1,134 injured in 580 EO-related accidents recorded across the Gaza Strip, according to UNMAS data. All identified survivors have been referred for medical care, rehabilitation, psychosocial support and other specialized assistance, helping to address both their immediate and long-term needs.

In June 2025, Mohammad from Jabalya Camp was seriously injured by an explosive device that detonated while he was trying to move his family's belongings to a safer place. He lost his left eye and suffered multiple shrapnel injuries, leaving him unable to work and struggling to support himself. Through the Danish Refugee Council Victim Assistance programme, he was referred for medical care and received cash assistance, which helped him meet urgent needs and establish a small street vendor business. The support enabled Mohammad to regain a source of income and begin rebuilding his independence despite his injuries.

“My injury changed my life, but it did not take away my determination to live with dignity and rely on myself again.”

Damage to Structures

Damage to structures across Gaza continues to increase, according to the latest satellite-based assessment by the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT). As of 16 June 2026, 201,290 structures – or an estimated 82 per cent of all structures in the Gaza Strip -- had sustained damage. Of these, 134,422 are assessed as destroyed, 13,848 as severely damaged, 28,096 as moderately damaged, and 24,924 as possibly damaged. Compared with UNOSAT’s previous assessment of 11 October 2025, the total number of affected structures increased by 1.5 per cent, while the number of destroyed structures rose by 9 per cent, indicating continued deterioration of the built environment.

The assessment further estimates that 328,627 housing units have been damaged, representing a 2.5 per cent increase since October 2025. The largest increases in newly affected structures were recorded in Gaza and North Gaza governorates, with approximately 381 and 258 additional damaged structures, respectively.

For the complete assessment and interactive damage map, see the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT) Gaza Strip Comprehensive Damage Assessment of 16 June 2026.

Incoming Supplies

According to UN 2720 mechanism data, UN agencies and NGO partners offloaded over 55,800 pallets of aid at the Kerem Shalom Crossing for collection within Gaza in July. This marked a substantial increase from the approximately 41,800 pallets recorded in June and the 47,800 pallets recorded on average each month between March and May, appearing more in line with the volumes recorded before the onset of the regional escalation, in February (54,600) and January (58,600). Kerem Shalom remains the only operational crossing for cargo entering Gaza.

According to data collected by the Logistics Cluster, the UN and partners’ aid offloading rate, representing the proportion of trucks that were successfully offloaded at Kerem Shalom against those authorized to be manifested each day, declined from 90 per cent over the previous three weeks to 77 per cent during the reporting period. This decrease was primarily driven by a 30 per cent offloading rate through Egypt. Of the trucks that did not offload, 94 per cent were returned by the Israeli authorities with no reason provided, while the remainder were rejected due to pallet conditions or were unable to offload because of operational constraints.

Ashdod remained the primary route for UN and partners’ humanitarian cargo entering Gaza, with 260 aid trucks successfully offloaded, followed by Jordan with 100 trucks offloaded. Kerem Shalom remained the only operational crossing point for cargo.

On the commercial front, data from the Gaza Chamber of Commerce, shared with the Cash Working Group, indicates that the private sector collected 824 truckloads into Gaza between 27 July and 2 August. Overall, the number of commercial truckloads reported as entering Gaza has remained stable in recent weeks, with only minor variations. This remains insufficient to sustain the demand. Moreover, of all private sector trucks, 234 (28 per cent) still carried non-essential items, at the expense of more critical supplies as shelter and WASH materials.

The UN is only able to confirm the entry of supplies tracked by UN 2720. For breakdowns of those, see the online UN 2720 Mechanism Dashboard.

title: Venezuela: Floods DREF Final Report (MDRVE012)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

25-06-2025

What happened, where and when?

The passage of Tropical Wave number 9 through western Venezuela caused heavy rains that led to flooding and landslides in the states of Barinas, Mérida, Trujillo, and Táchira. Local and national authorities agreed that this was the strongest rain episode of the season in the Andean region. In response to this situation, on 25 June, the government activated the "Andes 2025" Emergency Plan, which included the mobilization of the Bolivarian National Armed Forces, Civil Protection, and regional authorities to carry out evacuations, clear blocked roads, assist isolated communities, and mitigate the effects of flooding and landslides.

Since late April 2025, Venezuela experienced an exceptionally active rainy season characterized by frequent rainfall, thunderstorms, and landslides that impacted several vulnerable regions across the country. The National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (INAMEH) attributed the situation to various meteorological factors, including the early onset of the rainy season with the arrival of the first tropical wave on 24 May, followed by a second on 30 May. Additionally, persistent troughs and atmospheric disturbances contributed to climatic instability, particularly in the central, western, and southern regions.

INAMEH estimated that between 45 and 50 tropical waves were expected during the extended rainy season, projected to last until November, 2025. The effects were severe, particularly in the Andean, plains, and Amazonian regions, where communities and infrastructure experienced significant damage.

As of Friday, 20 June, the passage of the first eight tropical waves caused persistent and intense rainfall, resulting in river overflows and widespread flooding. The most affected states included Zulia, Barinas, Mérida, Apure, and Trujillo, with additional flooding reported in Bolívar and Sucre. Assessments conducted by Civil Protection and Red Cross teams indicated that more than 24,095 people, grouped into 4,819 families, were affected across eight states: Amazonas, Apure, Barinas, Mérida, Monagas, Táchira, Trujillo, and Zulia.

As of July 2025, weather conditions intensified dramatically due to the interaction of tropical waves with the La Niña phenomenon, according to reports from INAMEH; in some regions, rainfall exceeded historical averages for the year by as much as 300%. Weather disturbances and troughs continued to batter the country one after another, extending structural damage and soil saturation beyond the limits initially estimated in the west, the center, and Guayana Esequiba, which required constant monitoring due to the imminent risk of further flooding and landslides. Faced with this situation, volunteers and technical teams from the Venezuelan Red Cross intensified their frontline deployment for the duration of the operation, working side by side with communities.

Toward the end of December 2025, the rainy season in Venezuela came to a close, having established itself as one of the most severe and prolonged in recent years following the passage of nearly fifty tropical waves. The "Andes 2025" Emergency Plan, implemented by the national government and the National Risk Management System, continued its efforts to clear roads and reconnect isolated communities in Mérida, Trujillo, and Táchira. Although the weather pattern began to give way to a drier, more neutral transition as 2026 approached, local authorities continued with plans to rebuild road and housing infrastructure in the states hardest hit by the floods. Meanwhile, the Venezuelan Red Cross focused on addressing the most urgent needs.

This emergency unfolded against the backdrop of an already difficult humanitarian context in Venezuela. Floods and landslides have endangered lives, destroyed homes and crops, and severely damaged drinking water systems, road infrastructure, and essential services, which left many communities without access to basic needs.

Among those affected, particularly vulnerable groups included older adults, people with disabilities, and children, all of whom faced significant challenges in evacuating or accessing humanitarian assistance. The situation was further complicated by the presence of people in migratory contexts—such as returnees, those in transit, and internally displaced persons—many of whom returned without resources or support networks, leaving them especially exposed.

Venezuela faced increasingly severe rainy seasons over the past five years, which revealed the country's limited preparedness and the vulnerability of many communities to extreme weather events. This crisis underscored the urgent need for sustained efforts to build resilience and safeguard the most at-risk populations.

title: Lesotho | Drought induced food insecurity - Final Report (MDRLS008)
content:
SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

Overview of the 2022/2023–2024/2025 Rainy Season Conditions and Impacts

The 2021/2022 and 2022/2023 rainy seasons in Lesotho were marked by excessive rainfall that disrupted farming, damaged crops, and reduced agricultural productivity, resulting in poor harvests, lower food production, and increased food insecurity nationwide. Beyond damaging crops, the heavy rains also destroyed stored food supplies and damaged critical infrastructure, including roads, bridges, and irrigation systems, particularly in the rural districts of Maseru and Quthing. These impacts disrupted livelihoods, limited access to essential services, and further deepened food insecurity among vulnerable communities. While communities were still recovering from the previous years (2021 to 2023) heavy rainfall events, the country was hit by El Niño-induced drought in 2023/2024 and this period was characterized by late onset of rains and recurrent heatwaves from October 2023 to early 2024/2025, further worsening the already fragile livelihoods and living conditions.

For the past three years, the country has continued to experience persistent and compounding climatic shocks, including periods of excessive rainfall (2022–2024) followed by severe drought (2024/2025) conditions, which disrupted agriculture, weakened livelihoods, and worsened rural livelihoods, increasing food insecurity and slowing recovery efforts. In July 2024, over 22% of the Lesotho population (approximately 335,000 people) were estimated to be food insecure (LVAC Report 2024) and required urgent humanitarian assistance. Alongside drought related food insecurity, increase in staple food prices and declining livestock production have reduced household purchasing power and weakened livelihoods, further increasing vulnerability and worsening food insecurity. Livestock farmers in the southern side of the country were also affected by livestock disease outbreak “ Blue Tongue,” which resulted in losses of around 200 sheep and goats. The situation further undermined household incomes that depend on wool and mohair production. As a result, many vulnerable households resorted to negative coping strategies, including selling productive assets to either meet their basic needs or restore their damaged houses. The worsening conditions in Lesotho led to a crisis that prompted the government to declare a state of emergency in July 2024, to address widespread food insecurity, livelihood disruptions, and to mobilize urgent humanitarian response.

title: Djibouti Storm Surge 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRDJ010)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

27-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

In the locality of Mouloud, Dhikil region was struck by a severe windstorm accompanied by heavy rainfall on 27 July 2026, between 5:00 and 6:00 p.m. This was the second storm to affect the locality within a few days, following an earlier event on 24 July 2026, which caused no major damage. Preliminary reports indicate that more than 4160 people (693HH) were affected with approximately 290 households (1740 people) that have seen their houses partially of fully demolished. The disaster has resulted in two fatalities (an elderly man and an infant) and 10 injuries, including three children and 168 HH fully displaced. The injured were evacuated to the Ali Sabieh Regional Hospital and Dikhil Hospital for medical treatment.

Concurrently, extra ordinary temperature rise has been observed with temperatures going for beyond 42 degrees in recent days, with the weekly forecast ranging between 42 to 45 degrees of centigrade. https://weather.metoffice.gov.uk/forecast/sfn9tysge#?date=2026-07-30. This situation is exacerbated by heavy storms posing more risk to the displaced and other weak shelters. Several isolated domestic fires are also reported in the rise due the heavy winds, and the extra ordinary temperature rises. The communities living in Djibouti-Ville, especially Balbala and Boulaos communes, which are densely populated areas, characterized by informal settlements, with limited resources to cope with extreme heat, poor housing, reduced access to cooling, these population are highly impacted by intense heat stress and extreme mugginess during long hot spells from May through September, exposing them to negative coping strategies and more secondary impacts.

The storm affected communities in areas like Dikhil are the most exposed to storms likely to continue concurrently with the high temperatures. The effect of the heatwave on life and wellbeing is higher now where families have been displaced or have severe damages to their houses when these are first layer of protection in heatwaves context.

As much as this IFRC-DREF is for now essentially triggered by the effects of the storm, the response strategy will have a multi hazard approach to both the rising heat wave, storms in Dhikil. Noting that heatwaves impact is already witnessed and projected to get worse especially in Djibouti densely populated suburbs of Balbala and Boulaos , extending to regions already facing storms specifically Mouloud, in Dikhil, the key messages for early warning and early actions will be disseminated to inform the preventive measures.

title: Afghanistan | Northern - Earthquake - DREF Operational Update #4 (MDRAF019), 7 August 2026
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

03-11-2025

What happened, where and when?

On 3 November 2025, a magnitude 6.3 earthquake struck northern Afghanistan near the Balkh-Samangan border at a depth of 28 km. The tremor was felt widely across northern and central Afghanistan and as far as Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The earthquake caused 26 deaths and 1,172 injuries in communities that were already highly vulnerable. Verified assessments recorded 3,027 families with damaged homes across the affected districts, of which 874 homes were destroyed and 2,153 damaged. Broader United Nations assessments estimate that nearly 4,000 families were affected overall, alongside 91 schools and 18 water sources rendered unusable (OCHA, Humanitarian Update, January 2026). The earthquake also disrupted essential services, including health facilities, and temporarily blocked the Balkh-Kabul highway, exposing the fragility of access routes and the risk of secondary hazards such as landslides and rockfall.

The earthquake triggered a mountain collapse in the Tangi Ashburnham Valley, which temporarily obstructed the Balkh-Kabul highway with falling rocks. Clearance operations have since been completed, and the route has reopened to traffic.

Prior to the earthquake, the affected provinces already hosted significant numbers of vulnerable people, including an estimated 9,129 internally displaced persons (IDPs), 12,032 IDP returnees, and more than 16,404 people returning from abroad. In total, approximately 220,311 people; 52 per cent male and 48 per cent female were living in highly vulnerable conditions. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) estimates that around 1.53 million people experienced strong ground shaking in areas surrounding the epicenter.

The event caused widespread fear among affected communities and damaged residential buildings and community infrastructure across multiple districts. In response, Provincial Disaster Management Committees (PDMCs) in Balkh and Samangan convened emergency coordination meetings on 3 November and mobilized joint inter-agency assessment teams to determine the scale of the impact and identify urgent humanitarian needs. Winter conditions have since compounded the crisis: between 21 and 23 January 2026, heavy snowfall, storms, and avalanches affected 15 provinces—including Balkh and Samangan—further isolating communities and constraining access to essential supplies and services (OCHA, Humanitarian Update, January 2026).

In response to the earthquake, the IFRC immediately released CHF 100,000 Emergency Advance Payment under DREF procedures to enable ARCS's initial response. The subsequent DREF grant allocation brought the total DREF allocation to CHF 1,000,000. The earthquake response falls within the scope of the Afghanistan Earthquake Emergency Appeal (MDRAF019), launched on 3 September 2025 at CHF 25 million and revised upward to CHF 30 million following the northern earthquake, which supports ARCS's wider relief and early recovery efforts. This Operational Update reports on the first six months of the DREF grant implementation; further details on the DREF and Emergency Appeal is provided under the IFRC Network Actions section below.

title: UNHCR Bangladesh: Quarterly Protection & Solutions Report - Q1 2026 | January–March
content:
1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

PROTECTION ENVIRONMENT SNAPSHOT

As of March 2026, some 1.19 million Rohingya refugees lived in highly congested camps in Cox’s Bazar and on the island of Bhasan Char. The population remained extremely vulnerable: women and children comprised 78%, and more than 136,800 people had specific needs, including nearly 100,000 persons with disabilities. Restrictions on movement, livelihoods, skills development, and education kept refugees highly dependent on humanitarian assistance.

Rohingya continued fleeing violence in Rakhine State. Following government approval of biometric identification of the new arrivals, 146,989 newly arrived Rohingya were identified between January 2025 and March 2026. The Government maintained a closed border policy, and UNHCR recorded 778 refoulement incidents in Q1. Despite ongoing border monitoring and engagement with authorities, interventions succeeded in only 9% of cases.

Serious security incidents rose by 14% from the previous quarter, including abductions, kidnapping for ransom, and forced recruitment. Gender-based violence, especially intimate partner violence, and child protection incidents remained high. Armed groups and organized criminal gangs continued to undermine security and the civilian and humanitarian character of the camps.

Access to justice remained limited by weak accountability mechanisms, adherence to rule-of-law, lengthy procedures, documentation gaps, and delays in biometric identification. Fear of retaliation also deterred reporting, with 64% of gender-based violence survivors declining legal services.

Human trafficking incidents increased sharply, reflecting worsening protection risks and greater exposure to exploitation. Land and ownership disputes, perceived service disparities, and limited shared spaces continued to strain social cohesion with host communities.

Funding cuts reduced staffing capacity across UNHCR and partners by about 30%, increasing pressure on remaining teams to manage expanded responsibilities while maintaining time and quality standards. Despite this, the operation maintained controls to safeguard integrity and uphold case-processing standards.

title: Gaza Rehabilitation Task Force Sitrep (January - June 2026)
content:
Summary

As of 27 June 2026, 173 480 people have been injured in Gaza since 7 October 2023. 43 370 (25%) of these people are estimated to have potentially life-changing injuries including amputations, spinal cord, and brain injuries. Approximately 2% of the Gaza Strip’s pre-conflict population is now living with severe conflict-related injury. Around 3400 people have been injured since the ceasefire. The importation of rehabilitation equipment, supplies and assistive products continues to face significant constraints. No rehabilitation equipment for rehabilitation facilities entered Gaza from May 2024 to 14 April 2026. The average waiting time for pending shipments containing assistive products is 136 days (as of 14 April 2026). Available services remain insufficient to meet ongoing needs. Critical gaps remain in specialized rehabilitation services, including inpatient rehabilitation, prosthetics and orthotics provision, and long-term follow-up for people with permanent disability. Overstretched rehabilitation services, combined with shortages of essential equipment, assistive products and consumables, are contributing to preventable secondary complications and further increasing pressure on already limited rehabilitation capacity. This is particularly evident in Gaza’s remaining specialist rehabilitation services, where around 30% of inpatient beds are reportedly occupied by patients with advanced pressure sores. Limited bed availability is also contributing to early discharge, increasing the risk of further deterioration, loss of function, and avoidable readmission.

title: UNHCR Middle East Situation: Emergency Update #22 as of 6 August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

REGIONAL CONTEXT

Since late February 2026, hostilities in Iran and Lebanon have caused significant harm for civilians directly affected, while generating humanitarian consequences and elevated protection risks across the region, including refugee returns in adverse circumstances to Afghanistan and Syria. While diplomatic efforts have contributed to an overall reduction in large-scale military activity, uncertainty remains high and the situation continues to unfold against an already fragile regional baseline. Prior to the escalation, there were more than 31 million forcibly displaced people and recent returnees across the region, alongside host communities facing significant economic and social pressures.

Inter-agency emergency response efforts are underway in directly affected countries. In Iran, the Refugee Response Plan supports refugees and others in need of international protection alongside affected host communities. In Lebanon, a Flash Appeal extended through August 2026 complements the Lebanon Response Plan, while in Afghanistan, support for returnees is reflected under the Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan.

UNHCR and partners continue to focus on the wider consequences of the situation, including returns under adverse circumstances, economic deterioration and pressure on national systems affecting growing protection risks facing refugees and vulnerable populations across the region. Preparedness arrangements remain in place, including border monitoring, reception and protection readiness, but continue to depend on flexible and predictable funding in an increasingly constrained resource environment.

title: UNICEF Ukraine Humanitarian Situation Report 61, January - June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • In the first half of 2026, civilian casualties were 37 per cent higher than in the same period in 2025 and 114 per cent higher than 2024. The impact of the war on civilians is escalating month by month: at least seven children were killed and 116 injured in June, the highest monthly number of verified child casualties since 2022.
  • Since January 2026, UNICEF has ensured safe water and sanitation for 3.6 million people; supported 228,000 children, adolescents and caregivers to access mental health and psychosocial support services as well as 23,000 to access primary health care services; provided opportunity for formal and informal learning to 107,000 children; and delivered cash assistance to 94,350 people, including 53,435 children.
  • Additionally, 2,670,044 people benefitted from restored municipal heating systems over the recent harsh winter. Across the eight frontline regions as well as Kyiv city, UNICEF repaired damaged heating networks, installed boiler houses and delivered generators to allow heating systems to function during lengthy blackouts.
  • As air strikes increasingly impact families with children, UNICEF continues to ensure a package of responses including mobile teams deployed to strike sites to deliver psychological first aid and critical supplies; cash assistance for 4,647 affected families; repairs to water, sanitation and heating networks and 22 kindergartens and schools, as well as two health facilities damaged in attacks.

title: UNICEF Burundi Humanitarian Situation Report No. 22, 31 July 2026
content:
Situation Overview & Humanitarian Needs

In July 2026, Burundi continued to face overlapping humanitarian challenges driven by the conflict in Eastern DRC, large-scale population movements, disease outbreak risks, climate shocks and chronic vulnerabilities. In coordination with the Government, UN agencies and partners, humanitarian actors scaled up response and preparedness efforts to address growing needs.

Busuma refugee site, which hosted over 66,000 refugees at its peak, continued to accommodate large numbers of Congolese refugees. Since the launch of voluntary repatriation in April 2026, more than 10,000 refugees have voluntarily returned to eastern DRC; however, over 54,000 refugees remained in Busuma and approximately 21,000 in Musenyi by the end of July. Meanwhile, nearly 100,000 Burundian refugees had returned from Tanzania since January 2026, with the repatriation operation expected to conclude in August 2026.

These concurrent population movements continue to place significant pressure on already fragile basic services and limited local capacities, particularly in education, health, WASH and child protection, while increasing vulnerabilities among refugees, returnees and host communities.

title: Epidemiological Alert: Measles in the Americas Region - 7 August 2026
content:
Given the increase in reported measles cases during 2026 in the Americas Region and in other regions of the world, as well as the holding of mass gatherings with broad international participation, the Pan American Health Organization / World Health Organization (PAHO/WHO) urges Member States to prioritize strengthening epidemiological surveillance and vaccination activities, and to ensure a rapid and effective response to suspected measles cases. PAHO/WHO also recommends intensifying active community, institutional, and laboratory-based case-finding efforts for the early identification of cases, as well as implementing supplementary vaccination activities aimed at closing existing immunity gaps.

Global Summary

According to monthly data on measles and rubella surveillance published by the World Health Organization (WHO), between 1 January and as of July 2026, 186,168 measles cases were reported in 165 Member States across the six WHO Regions, of which 83,201 (44.69%) were laboratory-confirmed (1). Of the confirmed1 cases, 32% were reported in the WHO Southeast Asia Region, followed by the WHO Americas Region with 27%, the Eastern Mediterranean Region with 14% of cases, the European Region with 13%, the African Region with 9%, and the Western Pacific Region with 4% (Figure 1) (1).

title: UNHCR-IOM Pakistan Flash update # 105 on Arrest and Detention/Flow Monitoring, 15 Sep 2023 to 1 Aug 2026
content:
INTRODUCTION

In response to the Ministry of Interior's (MoI) decision of 26 September 2023 to enact an “Illegal Foreigners' Repatriation Plan”, UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency and IOM, the UN Migration Agency, have collated their data on the arrest, detention, and deportation of Proof of Registration (PoR) holders, Afghan Citizen Card (ACC) holders, and undocumented Afghan nationals as well as on the outflows of Afghan nationals at the Torkham, Ghulam Khan, Chaman, Badini and Bahramcha border crossing points, to better understand the protection environment and movements of Afghan nationals returning to Afghanistan from Pakistan.

In 2025, the Government of Pakistan (GoP) issued several directives impacting Afghan nationals. In January, the GoP announced that Afghan nationals should relocate from Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) and Rawalpindi, or else face deportation. In April, further announcements indicated the implementation of the second phase of the “IFRP”, targeting ACC holders, in addition to undocumented Afghans. In July, the GoP issued a Statutory Regulation Order (SRO) directing the repatriation/deportation of PoR card holders following the expiry of PoR card validity on 30 June. The GoP later indicated a deadline of 1 September for PoR holders to leave Pakistan, before the start of the repatriation/deportation process. UNHCR issued a press briefing expressing concern regarding the decision and urging the GoP to exempt Afghans with international protection needs, as well as those with particular circumstances or vulnerabilities, from involuntary return.

title: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 12 (27 July - 2 August 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Central African Republic
content:
According to the World Health Organization, as of 29 July, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 3,532 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus (BVD), including 1,556 deaths.

With the recent increase in figures, the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak has become the largest and fastest-growing outbreak in DRC. The rapidly escalating outbreak is unfolding against the backdrop of an ongoing triple crisis in eastern DRC, where health risks, large-scale displacement and persistent conflict intersect. Displaced populations in camps require multisectoral interventions in response to multidimensional needs. Across affected areas, most deaths continue to occur within communities, underscoring the urgent need to strengthen contact tracing and community event-based surveillance.

The spread of the outbreak into Tshopo and Haut-Uélé introduce new risks within these provinces, across the country and for the wider region. In Tshopo, patient movement in search of health care is contributing to further transmission, while the rising number of cases in Haut-Uélé requires enhanced disease surveillance and cross-border coordination to prevent disease transmission into neighbouring South Sudan and the Central African Republic (CAR).

Key Highlights:

  • The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reported 3,532 confirmed Ebola Bundibugyo cases and 1,556 deaths, making this the largest and fastest-growing BVD outbreak recorded in the country.
  • IOM has supported over 12.2 million health screenings at 223 points of entry and points of control across affected and at-risk countries.
  • More than 10.7 million people have been reached through risk communication and community engagement activities.
  • During the reporting period, IOM supported 1.4 million health screenings in DRC, activating additional screening locations in response to the outbreak's geographic expansion.
  • Uganda officially declared the end of its BVD outbreak on 28 July 2026, but preparedness and post-outbreak monitoring activities continue given the persistent regional risk.
  • IOM is rapidly expanding surveillance and response efforts in Kinshasa, including support following an alert involving a vessel carrying approximately 200 passengers and a probable Ebola case.

The outbreak continues to unfold in a complex operational environment marked by insecurity, displacement, and population mobility. As transmission persists in eastern DRC, sustained investment in surveillance, border health measures, community engagement, and support to displaced and mobile populations remains critical to containing the outbreak and preventing cross-border spread.
