title: Kler Lwee Htoo District Situation Update: Burma Army offensive operations, armed conflict, and drugs resulted in challenges to local villagers in Hsaw Htee Township (May to November 2025)
content:
This Situation Update describes events occurring in Hsaw Htee (Shwegyin) Township, Kler Lwee Htoo (Nyaunglebin) District during the period between May 2025 and November 2025. This report documents local villagers’ testimonies and experiences of the human rights situation in Hsaw Htee Township during the reporting period. It covers a range of human rights violations, including armed conflict; security concerns; forced recruitment by the Burma Army; arbitrary arrest, including for portering; the forced use of villagers as navigators and human shields; house burnings; shelling; air strikes; killings; injuries; destruction of civilian property; displacement; and the resulting impacts on livelihoods, healthcare, and education. The report also examines villagers’ perspectives on the Burma military regime’s planned 2025-2026 general election and the increasing availability and use of drugs in local communities. Since the Burma military regime seized power in the 2021 coup, armed conflict between the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) and the Burma Army has intensified across the township. As a result of the Burma Army’s ongoing military operations, including shelling and air strikes, villagers continued to face serious threats to their safety and security. Many were forcibly displaced and lived in constant fear and uncertainty, while others were injured or killed during attacks. The escalation of the conflict also severely disrupted civilians’ access to essential services. Students and teachers faced increasing insecurity due to repeated military attacks, making it unsafe to attend or conduct classes and negatively affecting children's access to education and interest in learning. In addition, ongoing displacement and insecurity limited access to healthcare and undermined villagers’ livelihoods. Alongside the impacts of armed conflict, villagers in Hsaw Htee Township also faced significant livelihood challenges resulting from climate change. The combined effects of insecurity, displacement, and environmental pressures further reduced their ability to sustain their livelihoods and meet their basic needs.[1]

1. Armed conflict caused injuries and healthcare challenges to local villagers

Healthcare remained a major challenge for local villagers in Hsaw Htee (Shwegyin) Township, Kler Lwee Htoo (Nyaunglebin) District, an area under the control of the Karen National Union (KNU),[2] in Southeast Burma.[3] Only five Karen Department of Health and Welfare (KDHW)[4] clinics and three community clinics supported by local community-based organisations were available across the entire township. These village tract[5]-level clinics provided only basic healthcare services. Compared to areas where hospitals are available, access to healthcare in Hsaw Htee Township was limited and insufficient to meet the needs of the local population.

During the 2024 and 2025 rainy seasons, local villagers faced additional health challenges caused by flooding and an increase in seasonal illnesses, including influenza. The shortage of medicines and medical supplies at local clinics made it difficult for healthcare workers to provide adequate treatment. In August 2025, several children in Hsaw Htee Township were also diagnosed with dengue fever, placing further pressure on the already limited healthcare services.

Political insecurity has also affected villagers' access to healthcare. Due to the ongoing armed conflict, villagers and family members of individuals affiliated with the resistance movement, including those participating in the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM),[6] often feared travelling to hospitals in towns controlled by the Burma military junta.[7] As a result, many delayed or avoided seeking medical treatment, further limiting their access to healthcare services and affecting their right to health.

In addition to illness, local villagers faced serious health risks as a result of the ongoing armed conflict. Civilians were injured during fighting and required medical treatment. However, shortages of medicines, medical supplies, and equipment made it difficult for healthcare workers to provide adequate care. Many villagers also did not dare to seek treatment at hospitals in towns because they feared being questioned or harassed by the Burma military junta authorities, including the State Security and Peace Commission (SSPC)[8] [Burma Army]. As a result, some delayed or avoided seeking medical care despite their injuries or illnesses. Financial barriers also limited villagers' access to healthcare. Many local villagers could not afford the cost of transportation or medical treatment, making it difficult for them to receive appropriate care. Some villagers instead relied on the KNU, which arranged transportation to rural clinics and hospitals administered by the KDHW. However, access to these healthcare facilities was also challenging due to flooding and damaged roads, particularly during the rainy season.

To improve healthcare services in local communities, the KNU organised medical training for local youths in 2025 [exact date unknown] so that they could provide basic healthcare support in their villages. Approximately 600 participants attended the training, including staff from local organisations and village representatives. Villagers reported that the training was beneficial because it helped strengthen community-based healthcare capacity. However, despite these efforts, shortages of medicines and medical supplies continued to limit the provision of healthcare services.

Medics from the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA)[9] and the People's Defence Force (PDF)[10] also provided medical assistance to local villagers whenever they were operating in nearby areas and were able to offer support. They treated villagers who were sick or injured whenever possible, and some villagers relied on them for healthcare when other services were inaccessible. However, access to medicines remained a major challenge. Villagers often struggled to obtain the medicines they needed, and purchasing medicine was also difficult due to limited availability. Even when villagers had sufficient money to buy medicine, it was often unavailable. Although the KNU, through the KDHW, provided some medical supplies and healthcare support, these efforts were insufficient to meet the healthcare needs of the local population.

Overall, local villagers were unable to fully realise their right to healthcare. Compared to the period before the 2021 military coup,[11] access to healthcare significantly deteriorated. The combined impacts of armed conflict, insecurity, shortages of medicines and medical supplies, transportation challenges, and limited healthcare facilities made it increasingly difficult for villagers to access timely and adequate medical treatment.

2. Impacts of local armed conflict and Burma military junta military operations: injuries, difficulties, fear, and anxiety

a) Challenges to education

Education is essential to the development of a nation. However, local villagers faced significant challenges in accessing education following the Burma military junta's seizure of power. Armed conflict between the Burma military junta and revolutionary armed groups frequently occurred in Hsaw Htee Township, disrupting education and creating an insecure learning environment. As a result, teachers were unable to teach regularly, and many students experienced interruptions to their education. On 10 February 2024, the Burma military junta imposed a conscription law, requiring eligible civilians aged 18 and above to serve in the military. At the time, the junta referred to itself as the State Administration Council (SAC).[12] On 31 July 2025, it was reconstituted as the State Security and Peace Commission (SSPC). The implementation of the conscription law caused many young people to feel fearful and anxious about their future. As a result, some lost interest in continuing their education. Nevertheless, some parents continued to encourage their children to remain in school and pursue their studies despite the ongoing insecurity.

Many local villagers opposed the Burma military junta's conscription law and did not want to join the military. As a result, villagers reported fearing that the Burma military junta would enter their villages and forcibly recruit young people into military service. This fear affected access to education, particularly for families living in remote areas. Some parents were reluctant to send their children to schools in towns because they feared their children might be forcibly arrested and recruited by the Burma military junta. Despite these challenges, the Karen Education and Culture Department (KECD)[13] continued its efforts to improve access to education by establishing schools in local areas so that children and young people could continue their studies closer to their communities. Compared to previous years, access to education in the area improved. However, the ongoing armed conflict meant that students were still unable to study in a safe and secure environment, as schools remained at risk from insecurity related to the conflict.

The Burma military junta also targeted areas where local villagers were perceived to oppose its rule or support resistance groups, placing civilians at increased risk. One of the greatest concerns for local communities was the use of air attacks, including drone strikes and aircraft carrying out air strikes with machine-gun fire and bombings. These attacks created a constant threat to civilians, including students and teachers. In response to the deteriorating security situation, education stakeholders, including school committee members, responsible community leaders, and parents, worked together to establish schools in forested and concealed locations to reduce the risk of attack and enable children to continue their education. However, these arrangements also created additional challenges. During the rainy season, students faced difficulties travelling to and from school through forested areas and were frequently bitten by mosquitoes and other insects while attending classes. These were among the challenges experienced by students in Hsaw Htee Township.

During the reporting period, schools in the lower part of Hsaw Htee Township were temporarily closed for approximately two weeks following flooding on 26 July 2025. Later, on 26 September 2025, fighting broke out between combined Burma Army forces and combined local resistance forces, including the KNLA, Karen National Defence Organisation (KNDO),[14] and PDF. Due to the deteriorating security situation, ten schools in four village tracts including Pyay Yay, Aye Waing, and Pazon Myaung village tracts were forced to close. Some schools closed on 3 October 2025, while others closed on 5 or 6 October 2025. As of November 2025, the ongoing armed conflict and insecurity had prevented these schools from reopening, leaving many students unable to resume their education.

On 29 October 2025, at approximately 10 am, two Burma Army paramotors dropped five bombs on Kk--- village, Pyay Yay village tract, Hsaw Htee Township. Four of the bombs landed on farmland near the village, while one bomb struck the compound of the Kk--- school. The school had been closed since the Burma military junta seized power in the February 2021 coup because of the deteriorating security situation. As a result, there were no casualties when the bombs struck the school compound. However, bomb fragments damaged the school buildings. Following the attack, village authorities, including the village administrator and village leaders, arranged alternative learning spaces so that students could continue their education. Some students attended classes in villagers' houses, while others studied at a monastery. The KECD provided the curriculum, textbooks, and other teaching materials, and continued to administer the schools.

There were two types of schools operating in Hsaw Htee Township during the reporting period. Some schools were administered by the KECD, while others were community-established and self-funded. These self-funded schools used the Burma national curriculum; however, they were not permitted by the KNU to teach history from the Burma national curriculum. This situation arose because KECD had insufficient curriculum materials to distribute to all schools, and some schools also faced shortages of qualified teachers. As a result, many parents living in the Plaw (Per Htee) area chose to send their children to schools in nearby towns. Similarly, families living close to urban areas often preferred town-based schools. According to local villagers, some parents perceived that qualifications obtained through the Kaw Thoo Lei[15] (KECD) education system were not widely recognised and that graduates might face difficulties accessing higher education or securing employment. Consequently, some parents lacked confidence in the KECD education system and preferred to enrol their children in schools using the Burma national curriculum. The information above describes the educational system and the situation of high school students in Hsaw Htee Township during the reporting period.

b) Livelihoods and livelihood challenges

Most local villagers in Hsaw Htee Township relied on agriculture as their primary source of income during the reporting period. In addition to farming, villagers depended on natural resources, including timber, bamboo, fruits, and forest products, as well as rubber plantations, hill farming, and, for some households, small-scale gold mining. Communities living near rivers also relied on fishing and other aquatic resources to support their livelihoods.

  • Difficulties with transportation and increased taxation

Many villagers cultivated perennial crops, including jengkol bean (dog fruit), betel nut, citron, lime, betel vine, and durian. Although durian prices were relatively high in 2025, the benefits were limited to households that owned durian plantations. Prices for many other agricultural products remained low. According to local villagers, transporting agricultural products to markets became increasingly difficult because of insecurity and the presence of Burma Army checkpoints. Traders and farmers reported being required to pay taxes or other unofficial payments while transporting goods. These additional costs reduced farmers' incomes and increased the prices of essential goods sold in villages.

Local traders also faced difficulties purchasing goods from towns because of transportation costs, checkpoint restrictions, and multiple taxes and fees. As a result, consumer goods became more expensive in rural communities. In the Plaw (Per Htee) area, most villagers relied on farming, fishing, and river-based livelihoods. Many households had limited cash income and depended primarily on subsistence agriculture.

Some villagers earned a living by harvesting timber and bamboo. However, these activities were regulated by the KNU, which established seasonal restrictions and permit requirements. When harvesting was temporarily prohibited, villagers who depended on these activities were required to seek alternative legal sources of income.

Gold mining also provided income for some households in Hsaw Htee Township, although this work generally required significant financial investment and was carried out mainly by wealthier individuals. According to local sources, those engaged in gold mining were required to pay taxes and other fees to authorities operating in areas under mixed control of the KNU and the Burma military junta.

  • The Burma Army arrested villagers [affecting livelihoods]

Some local villagers who did not own farmland or plantations relied on trade to support their families’ livelihoods. However, travelling to buy or sell goods exposed them to security risks. According to local villagers, traders were frequently stopped at Burma Army checkpoints, where they were required to pay money before being allowed to continue their journeys. Others were reportedly arrested under the conscription law and transferred to military training centres instead of being released.

Many households also depended on river resources, including fish, prawns, crabs, frogs, and other aquatic products. Because these products are highly perishable, villagers needed to transport them quickly to markets. However, insecurity, travel restrictions, and checkpoints frequently delayed transportation. Local villagers also reported that some people transporting fish, prawns, crabs, and frogs were arrested by the Burma Army, further affecting their livelihoods.

  • Weather-related challenges

This year [2025], flooding that began on 21 July 2025 continued for approximately one month, damaging paddy fields [across Hsaw Htee Township]. Although floodwaters receded, many fields did not recover. According to local farmers, rice plants turned yellow and dried before harvest, reducing agricultural production. Moreover, in October 2025, flooding along the Kaw Lo River continued to affect farmland. Farmers whose fields were located near the Kaw Lo River were forced to harvest rice while their fields remained flooded because the paddies on their farms were ready to be reaped. After harvesting, they also experienced difficulties selling their rice because market prices remained low, ranging from approximately 130,000 to 150,000 kyats (61.90 to 71.43 USD[16]) per large basket (32 kg). According to local farmers, production costs often exceeded their earnings, leaving many households without profit and, in some cases, in debt.

Heavy rainfall in October 2025 also disrupted the planting of green beans. Some farmers were unable to plant on time, while others lost crops that had already been planted because of excessive rainfall. Despite these challenges, local villagers continued to work hard to sustain their livelihoods.

Agriculture remained the main source of income for most households, including the cultivation of both perennial and seasonal crops. However, agricultural production depended heavily on weather conditions, market demand, and traders' ability to access local communities. According to local villagers, prices for agricultural products remained low, while the prices of essential consumer goods continued to rise, placing additional financial pressure on rural households.

c) Security concerns affecting travel and daily life

During the reporting period, the security situation in Hsaw Htee Township continued to affect the daily lives of local villagers. According to local villagers, they lived and worked under constant fear and uncertainty because of the ongoing armed conflict and military operations in the area. Many described feeling that even routine activities involved significant risks to their safety and livelihoods. The continuing political and armed conflict disrupted many aspects of civilian life. Local villagers faced difficulties travelling between villages, accessing farmland and workplaces, pursuing their livelihoods, and ensuring that children could continue their education. The insecurity also had significant psychological impacts. Villagers reported experiencing fear, anxiety, stress, and trauma, and many felt that neither their lives nor their property were secure. In addition to the risks posed by armed conflict, villagers encountered numerous challenges while travelling. According to local sources, they frequently passed through Burma Army checkpoints, where they faced questioning, demands for money, the risk of arbitrary arrest under the conscription law, and being forced to serve as porters. These security concerns restricted freedom of movement and made it increasingly difficult for local villagers to carry out their daily activities and sustain their livelihoods. Despite these ongoing hardships, local villagers continued to adapt to the conflict and sought ways to maintain their livelihoods and support their families, even as they remained exposed to persistent insecurity and human rights abuses.

d) Displacement, armed conflict, and house burnings

Ongoing armed conflict and military operations by the Burma Army continued to cause widespread displacement in Hsaw Htee Township [during the reporting period]. Local villagers reported living in constant fear that Burma Army troops would enter their villages and conduct military operations. As a result, some families temporarily relocated to stay with relatives, while others fled to forests or other safer locations. The continuing armed conflict also exposed civilians to the risk of death and injury.

In May 2025, fighting between Burma Army soldiers and combined local resistance forces affected Pyay Yay, Aye Waing, and Pazon Myaung village tracts. As a result, villagers from eight villages fled to nearby forests, while others sought safety in other areas.

Beginning on 26 September 2025, fighting resumed in the area between Kler Lwee Htoo (Nyaunglaybin) Town and Way Htoo (Shwegyin) Town. The renewed clashes forced many local villagers to abandon their homes and seek refuge elsewhere. According to local sources, approximately 10,000 villagers from 11 villages were displaced. Some sought shelter in nearby towns, while others fled to neighbouring villages. On 16 October 2025, Burma Army soldiers entered Kq--- village, Pazon Myaung village tract, and burned down approximately 70 houses, causing extensive destruction and further displacement of local residents.

e) Force recruitment and extortion by the Burma Army

According to local villagers, forced recruitment by the Burma Army remained a serious concern in Hsaw Htee Township during the reporting period. Following the enforcement of the conscription law after 10 February 2024, villagers reported frequent arbitrary arrests for military recruitment. These incidents continued throughout 2025 and created widespread fear among local communities. Local villagers reported that individuals selected for military service could avoid recruitment only by paying a conscription exemption fee. The amount demanded reportedly varied depending on local authorities and administrative practices, ranging from 20,000 kyats to 150,000 kyats (9.52 to 71.43 USD) per household in some areas. In villages where no one volunteered to join the military, local authorities reportedly used a lottery system to select individuals for conscription. Those selected who did not wish to serve were reportedly required to pay more than 500,000 kyats (238.10 USD) to avoid recruitment. According to local sources, these payments were reportedly used to provide financial support to individuals who agreed to join the military. Villagers also reported that people who were arbitrarily arrested for recruitment were often required to pay large sums of money to secure their release. In some documented cases, families paid between 10 million (4,761.90 USD) and more than 20 million kyats (9,523.81 USD) to obtain the release of detained relatives.

According to local villagers, these practices created opportunities for corruption and extortion by members of the Burma Army. Local sources reported that recruitment quotas were assigned to townships and that pressure to meet these quotas contributed to arbitrary arrests. Because many villagers were unwilling to join the military, families often paid whatever they could afford to prevent or end the forced recruitment of their relatives.

In August, September, and November 2025, local sources reported that more than 100 villagers were arrested for recruitment in Hsaw Htee Township, with more than 30 people arrested in each of those months. Those detained were reportedly transferred to military training centres, including Aung Twin and Taik Gyi. According to local villagers, in November 2025, some Burma Army units were reportedly instructed to recruit 13 people but arrested around 30 villagers instead. Local sources alleged that the additional arrests were carried out to obtain money from families seeking the release of their relatives. Local villagers further alleged that some Burma Army units transferred detained villagers to units in other townships that had failed to meet their recruitment quotas in exchange for money. According to local sources, payments of approximately 15 million kyats (7,142.86 USD) were made for each transferred detainee. Local villagers viewed these practices as amounting to human trafficking because individuals were treated as commodities and transferred for financial gain. These allegations could not be independently verified by KHRG but were consistently reported by local sources during the reporting period.

f) Fighting, house burning, air strikes, death, injuries, and destruction of local villagers’ property

During the reporting period, ongoing fighting between the Burma Army and combined local resistance forces had severe consequences for civilians in Hsaw Htee Township. In May 2025, combined local resistance forces captured two Burma Army military camps belonging to Light Infantry Battalion (LIB)[17] #598 at Hpa Bawh and Kwin Seik [villages, Kwin Seik (Section 1), Hsaw Htee Township]. Following the loss of these camps, the Burma Army launched military operations to retake them. According to local sources, these operations included indiscriminate mortar shelling, drone strikes, and air strikes. Local villagers reported that the attacks were not limited to military targets but also struck villages, religious buildings, and civilian property. As a result of air strikes carried out by drones and aircraft, more than 35 villagers' houses were destroyed. Additional homes were damaged or destroyed by indiscriminate mortar shelling. During ground operations, Burma Army soldiers also burned down more than 70 villagers' houses.

On 26 September 2025, fighting broke out between Burma Army soldiers and combined KNLA forces near Kg--- village, Pyay Yay village tract. According to local sources, after the Burma Army sustained casualties during the fighting, a Burma Army Y-12 aircraft carried out an air strike at approximately 12 pm, dropping six bombs on Pyay Yay village tract. Two of the bombs landed within the compound of a monastery in Kk--- village, damaging the monastery's roof, walls, and other property.

On 8 October 2025, at 3:32 pm, a Burma Army fighter jet dropped a 500-pound bomb on the garden of U K---'s house in Ke--- village, Thet Kel Kone village tract, Hsaw Htee Township. The explosion killed 18-year-old Ma G--- after bomb shrapnel struck her in the face. The blast also damaged two houses belonging to U K--- and U Q---.

Furthermore, the Burma Army continued to conduct air strikes on villages using drones and fighter jets [throughout the reporting period]. Additionally, beginning on 26 October 2025, the Burma Army also reportedly used paramotors to drop bombs on villages in Hsaw Htee Township, further increasing the risk to local villagers.

g) The Burma Army forced villagers to serve as porters, navigators, and human shields

During the reporting period, one Burma Army Military Operations Command (MOC)[18] and five battalions were based in Hsaw Htee Township. The Burma Army maintained more than 12 military camps and operated numerous checkpoints throughout the township. According to local villagers, the Burma Army carried out various military operations that adversely affected civilians. These included forced recruitment, compelling villagers to transport military supplies as porters, and forcing civilians to act as navigators and human shields during military operations. In October 2025, following an ambush by combined KNLA, KNDO, and PDF troops on a Burma Army supply convoy transporting rations to frontline troops, the Burma Army reportedly faced difficulties resupplying its forces. On 21 and 22 October 2025, Burma Army personnel held meetings with local traders and forced them to transport food supplies to soldiers stationed on the frontlines.

On 6 November 2025, at approximately 9 am, soldiers from Burma Army Infantry Battalion (IB)[19] #57 arrested six villagers at a rubber plantation in Aa--- village, Aye Ka Ni village tract, Hsaw Htee Township. According to local sources, the soldiers forced the six villagers to carry military equipment as porters and required them to accompany the troops as navigators and human shields during their movement. When the Burma Army column reached Ik--- village, Aye Ka Ni village tract, fighting broke out between Burma Army soldiers and combined KNLA forces. During the fighting, some of the villagers who had been forced to accompany the troops as porters were injured.

h) 2025-2026 sham election caused difficulties and dangers for local villagers

Following the 2020 general election, the Burma military alleged that electoral fraud had occurred and called for the election results to be reviewed. After the National League for Democracy (NLD),[20] which had won the election, rejected these allegations, the Burma military was not satisfied. Therefore, the Burma military seized power [in the February 2021 coup] and detained senior government and NLD leaders.

Under the 2008 Constitution, the Burma military was permitted to assume power during a declared state of emergency for an initial period of six months, with the possibility of extending the emergency under certain conditions. The constitution also requires that a general election be held following the end of the state of emergency. However, as of the reporting period, the Burma military had remained in power for more than four years since the February 2021 coup. In 2025, after reconstituting itself as the SSPC, the Burma military regime announced that it planned to hold [the first of three phrases of] an election in December 2025.[21]

According to local villagers in Hsaw Htee Township, many people did not believe that the planned election would be free or fair. Villagers reported that the ongoing presence of the Burma Army, together with threats, violence, and other forms of pressure, limited their ability to express their political views freely. Some villagers stated that they felt they had little choice but to comply with the authorities' instructions. Three political parties, the People Life for Development Party (PLDP), the Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP), and the People's Pioneer Party (PPP), conducted political activities in Hsaw Htee Township ahead of the planned election. On 9 October 2025, these parties opened offices in Shwegyin Town and began organising local residents to participate in the election. They also collected household registration information from local villagers for election-related purposes. According to local sources, these political activities were mainly conducted in towns and villages under the control of the Burma Army or in areas where local resistance forces had not carried out public awareness activities. Many villagers reported that they believed the planned election would not be free or fair and stated that if they had not faced pressure from the authorities, they would not have chosen to participate.

i) Drug situation

According to local information, the drug situation in Hsaw Htee Township worsened following the Burma military junta's seizure of power in the February 2021 coup. Compared to previous years, a wider variety of drugs became available, and drug use reportedly increased in many villages. Alcohol has long been available in Hsaw Htee Township. However, local villagers reported that the production and consumption of chemically produced alcohol increased in recent years. In 2024, methamphetamine and other illegal drugs became increasingly available in the township. However, local authorities [KNU] reported facing challenges in investigating drug trafficking and taking effective action against those involved.

In 2025, checkpoints operated by the KNLA intercepted several drug shipments. According to local authorities, most of the seized drugs were WY methamphetamine tablets [yaba[22]]. Those arrested for transporting or using drugs reportedly included people from the Per Htee (Plaw) area and nearby towns. The Karen National Police Force (KNPF)[23] also conducted operations against suspected drug dealers and users, including the arrest of both men and women involved in drug-related activities. According to local authorities, individuals arrested for drug-related offences were dealt with in accordance with the drug control policies established by the KNU. In Hsaw Htee Township, drug-related offences are addressed under six provisions of the KNU's drug control regulations. In addition to law enforcement, the KNU and KNPF organised awareness-raising activities to educate local communities about drug-related laws and the harmful effects of drug use, with the aim of reducing drug use and trafficking in the area.

Conclusion

This report describes the experiences of local villagers and the human rights violations in Hsaw Htee Township documented by KHRG between May and November 2025. As described throughout this report, the human rights situation did not improve during the reporting period. Instead, violations continued and, in many cases, intensified. Local villagers were affected by ongoing armed conflict and the operations of the Burma military junta. Reported violations included arbitrary arrest, forced portering, the use of local villagers as human shields, the burning of villagers' houses, shelling, and air attacks involving drones and aircraft. These attacks caused civilian casualties and damaged or destroyed homes, religious buildings, plantations, and other local villagers’ property. In addition to conflict-related abuses, local communities also faced hardships caused by flooding and other adverse weather conditions. The combined effects of armed conflict and insecurity further worsened access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, transportation, and freedom of movement compared with previous years. Despite these challenges, local villagers continued to demonstrate resilience by working together to protect their communities and finding ways to address the difficulties they faced. At the same time, many villagers continued to experience forced labour, torture, arbitrary arrest, extortion, threats, and other forms of abuse. Many also saw their livelihoods repeatedly disrupted or destroyed by armed conflict and military operations, causing the benefits of their hard work to be lost. Nevertheless, local communities continued to adapt to the changing security situation and sought to maintain their daily lives despite the ongoing risks and hardships.

Further background reading on the human rights situation in Kler Lwee Htoo (Nyaunglebin) District in Southeast Burma/Myanmar can be found in the following KHRG reports:

  • Stolen Childhoods: Violations of children’s rights, urgent needs, and local agency in rural Southeast Burma during the conflict, October 2025.
  • “Kler Lwee Htoo District Situation Update: Burma Army attacks caused death, injuries, property damage, displacement, and challenges to villagers’ daily routine in Moo Township (February to May 2025)”, June 2026.
  • “Photo Set: Burma Army air strikes on local communities, resulting in casualties, destruction, and displacement (January to December 2025)”, March 2026.

title: Yemen: Conflict - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms Area) #116, Reporting period: June - July 2026
content:
The WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) was activated as the Emergency Telecommunications Cluster (ETC) in Yemen in April 2015 in response to the conflict. This Situation Report provides a monthly update on LTC telecommunications activities. All references to the LTC in this report relate specifically to the telecommunications component of the cluster.

Summary Points

• LTC Telecoms connectivity services supported 231 humanitarian staff in Al Mukalla and Al Makha, while services in northern Al Hodeidah, Ibb, and Sana’a remained suspended since September 2025. Connectivity and conferencing support across Humanitarian hubs enabled operational continuity, partner coordination, and day-to-day humanitarian activities.

• LTC Telecoms strengthened network resilience and service reliability through infrastructure maintenance, network configuration updates, router troubleshooting, and expanded the Wi-Fi coverage in Al Turba, reducing the risk of service disruption across key operational locations.

• Security communications services supported 845 humanitarian responders through five UNDSS-managed Security Operations Centres (SOC) in Aden, Al Makha, Al Mukalla, Al Turba, and Ma’rib. LTC Telecoms restored VHF radio services after a power-related outage and reinforced secure field communications through radio reconfiguration and distribution.

title: Desert Locust Bulletin 574 (5 August 2026)
content:
LOCUST POPULATIONS DECLINED IN MOROCCO

In July, the gregarious, transiens and solitarious locust populations declined in Morocco while continued to appear at some sites until about mid-July and were not seen after mid-month. In Mauritania, increasing populations of solitarious adults were observed, while isolated adults were seen at some locations in Algeria. Localized small scale breeding was detected in southwest Libya, where scattered hoppers and adults were seen. In the Central Region, isolated hoppers and adults were seen in Egypt, while isolated and scattered adults were observed in Sudan. No locusts were seen in the Eastern Region. During the forecast period, solitarious hoppers and adults may still be present in Morocco, Algeria, and southwest Libya where breeding occurred last month. Increasing populations may appear in Mauritania, where summer breeding is expected to increase and in other Sahelian countries after the recent rains. Surveys should increase in all summer breeding areas of Sahelian countries as well as southern Algeria, Libya and Morocco. Preventive control operations are likely to become necessary in Mauritania and eventually in other Sahelian countries. In the Central and Eastern Regions, small-scale summer breeding is expected to continue in Sudan, western Eritrea, the interior of Yemen and along the Indo-Pakistan border; however, no significant developments are expected.

KEY POINTS

  • Overview: The Desert Locust populations declined in Morocco, and no locusts were seen after mid-month.
  • Current situation: Groups and scattered adult populations were seen until mid-July in Morocco; increasing numbers of solitarious adults in Mauritania; isolated adults at some locations in Algeria; localized small scale breeding in southwest Libya. isolated hoppers and adults in Egypt, while isolated and scattered adults in Sudan. No locusts were reported elsewhere.
  • Control operations: Declined in July (2 435 ha treated) compared to June (88 537 ha).
  • Forecast: Solitarious hoppers and adults may still be present in Morocco, Algeria, southwest Libya, and summer breeding in Mauritania and other Sahelian countries. Small-scale summer breeding is expected to continue in Sudan, western Eritrea, the interior of Yemen and along the Indo-Pakistan border; however, no significant developments are expected.

title: Plataforma Subregional Cono Sur: #5 Special Sitrep on Bolivia (Update - June 2026)
content:
CONTEXT

• Road blockades across the country continue to limit mobility, restrict access to food and livelihoods, and drive an increase in protection risks and humanitarian needs. The situation is particularly deteriorating in El Alto/La Paz and Cochabamba due to the intensification of these blockades.

•Blockades are forcing the use of high-risk alternative routes, increasing travel times from around 3 hours to up to 24 hours, with some journeys lasting between 12 and 14 days. Families have been stranded along routes, with rising reports of accidents and a significant increase in transportation costs. Harsh weather conditions, including temperatures as low as -10°C, are further aggravating the vulnerability of people on the move.

•In Desaguadero, closures of the border with Peru have been reported, including the suspension of crossings via both the international bridge and boats. Access is still partial and irregular, with limited night-time crossings via the lake under strict controls, restricting both movement and access to food and essential goods.

•Push factors from Chile are also influencing current movements, including restrictions on access to employment, tighter documentation controls, and measures involving the detention and transfer of individuals.

•Oruro has become a key convergence point for flows from Pisiga and alternative routes, with a steady arrival of people who are either stranded or forced to reorganize their onward movement.

•Protection risks are increasing, including gender-based violence, exploitation—particularly in blockade contexts—and violence between groups over access to resources and space.

• Response capacity is still severely constrained due to limited availability of goods and food in local markets, in the context of supply chain disruptions, rising prices, and restrictions imposed by suppliers

title: Plataforma Subregional Cono Sur: #6 Special Sitrep on Bolivia (Update - 15 June 2026)
content:
CONTEXT

•Road blockages continue to disrupt mobility nationwide, limiting access to food and services and increasing protection risks. The use of high-risk alternative routes persists, alongside a shift toward more fragmented and unsafe mobility patterns, with people travelling in segments on foot or relying on informal transport. This results in longer travel times, higher costs, and, in many cases, no guarantee of reaching their destination, further compounded by extreme low temperatures.

• In Desaguadero, intermittent restrictions at the border crossing with Peru continue, with reduced movement of people and goods, shortages of basic items, and reliance on costly lake routes as alternatives. In Pisiga, movement remains low and concentrated at night. Oruro continues to serve as a key convergence point, with ongoing arrivals and a mixed population of new arrivals and people experiencing prolonged stays.

• As resources become increasingly scarce and travel times lengthen, more people are moving toward La Paz under precarious conditions. In La Paz and El Alto, daily arrivals remain steady, placing pressure on services, with reports of people stranded in bus terminals for extended periods. Patacamaya is emerging as a secondary transit hub, where people remain stranded or move intermittently between Oruro and La Paz, in a context of limited local response capacity and a lack of sustainable shelter solutions.

• Protection risks are increasing, including gender-based violence, exploitation, and cases of individuals being left without support following medical discharge. Low temperatures are further increasing exposure during transit and prolonged stays. At the same time, reduced operational presence of humanitarian staff in some locations—particularly in Desaguadero—is limiting direct response capacity, amid ongoing logistical constraints and supply challenges.

title: Plataforma Subregional Cono Sur: #7 Special Sitrep on Bolivia (Update - 23 June 2026)
content:
CONTEXT

• The blockade situation is beginning to gradually ease after more than 50 days, with partial reactivation of transit and supply along several routes across the country.

•In Desaguadero, population flows have been significantly reduced, with no current reports of stranded populations and with progressive normalization of transport, though constraints persist due to fuel shortages.

•In Oruro and La Paz, the number of people in transit has declined, with individuals gradually continuing toward their destinations.

•Mobility continues among people with limited resources, who remain dependent on different movement strategies and transport support.

•Operational challenges remain, particularly associated with fuel availability, which continues to drive fluctuations in transport costs and restrict regular mobility.

•At the regional level, reinforced restrictions are identified at the border with Chile, including increased control and security measures that may affect cross-border flows.

• While the overall situation is stabilizing, needs persist due to accumulated impacts, especially in health, protection and livelihoods.

title: Mozambique Conflict Monitor Update: 5 August 2026
content:
Overview

State forces made a concerted push to contest ISM’s control of Catupa forest on two fronts in July. Since mid-June, there have been repeated clashes around the Defense Armed Forces of Mozambique (FADM) outposts at Catupa and Namabo, and an RDF operation close to Cogolo (see map below). These account for approximately half of all engagements between the forces since mid-2025. ISM claims that on 5 July they successfully countered a FADM attempt to recapture the Catupa outpost, which FADM had abandoned in January, and that they pushed FADM from Namabo the same day. Namabo, located less than 4 kilometers east of the N380, was most recently taken by ISM on 22 June, then recaptured by FADM and the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) on 28 June. Since mid-June, there have been at least 64 fatalities in these operations. Fighting between 5 and 12 July alone led to conservative estimates of at least 20 fatalities, though some local sources have given estimates of up to 60 fatalities among state forces.

To the east, on 23 July, the RDF attacked an ISM position close to Cogolo village, approximately 10 km from the coast. The RDF shelled and raided the position, killing at least five ISM militants. ISM claims to have attacked an RDF position in the area the following day, and to have killed six RDF soldiers and one informant, damaged a vehicle, and taken weapons. Such positions, known as ribats, are often temporary, and established to protect the main base.

FADM and RDF operations prompted some ISM militants to move north in smaller groups. They clashed with a FADM patrol in southern Mocímboa da Praia district on 4 July, and on 23 July with an RDF patrol at Miangelewa in Muidumbe district on the N380.

Since international intervention in 2021, all attempts to dislodge ISM from its Catupa stronghold have been unsuccessful. These latest efforts, particularly those by the RDF at Cogolo, however, demonstrate state forces’ renewed focus on limiting ISM’s influence on the Macomia coast, which has grown in recent years. While the operations have created short-term disruption to ISM, previous operations in Catupa have been short-lived, so we expect ISM to maintain its stronghold in Catupa.

ISM pushes south and west, exposing roadways and mining sites to predatory activity

In response to state forces’ pressure in Catupa, some ISM fighters have moved southward. Initially moving through Quissanga, Mecufi, and Meluco districts they subsequently moved south to Ancuabe and Chiúre districts and west to Montepuez. One group proceeded further south to cross to Eráti district in Nampula province. The group in Montepuez is moving toward Niassa province.

The southward movement had begun by 8 July, when over 30 fighters arrived in Cagembe village in Quissanga. Despite subsequent sightings in the area, they were not disturbed by FADM until 29 July, when the two forces clashed at Ntessa village, about 15 km south of Cagembe.

Informal gold mining sites were targeted in Ancuabe district. At a mining site on 13 July and at Muaja gold mines on 20 July, miners and others were kidnapped. At Muaja, some were held for ransom of up to 60,000 meticais (900 USD), while others were forcibly recruited into ISM, according to a local source.

After the move west into Montepuez, on 26 July they held three vehicles and their passengers for ransom on the R698 linking Montepuez to Mueda. The incident occurred near Nicocue village. According to victims, 389,000 meticais ($6,000) was transferred to the insurgents for at least 10 people, along with three vehicles including a logging truck. The group, numbering as many as 150, moved north after the Nicocue incident toward Niassa province, passing through the Shamba Kubwa mining area on 31 July.

Past behavior suggests that ISM will maintain a presence in the south through August. In that time, ISM will continue to threaten road traffic and mining sites with a view to raising money. FADM will be under pressure to increase escorts on the N1 and the R698 routes in order to keep them open to commercial and humanitarian traffic.

title: Middle East Conflict: Lebanon Response Situation Report #9 | August 5, 2026
content:
FAST FACTS

  • The number of registered displaced people In Lebanon has fallen to 360,132, with 27,200 residing in collective shelters.

OUR FOOTPRINT

  • International Medical Corps maintains a wide operational presence across the Middle East, delivering lifesaving assistance in active conflict zones and high-risk environments.

OUR RESPONSE

  • Across the region, International Medical Corps sustains integrated health, nutrition, mental health, protection, and water, sanitation and hygiene programming through mobile teams, field hospitals and fixed facilities, with established systems in place to expand rapidly as needs intensify.
  • In Lebanon, 41 mobile medical teams have operated across 187 shelters and community sites, delivering 26,893 consultations, treating 14,446 acute cases and managing 2,870 chronic conditions. Teams have also conducted health awareness sessions for 3,647 people, referred 1,550 patients to specialized care and vaccinated 480 children.
  • Nutrition teams have screened 1,327 children and pregnant or breastfeeding women for malnutrition, while mental health teams have reached 1,864 people with psychosocial and psychological support services. In addition, teams have distributed 2,639 hygiene kits to displaced and vulnerable households and individuals.

Across the Middle East region, humanitarian needs remain severe and increasingly complex. In Gaza, the ongoing crisis, repeated displacement and the widespread destruction of critical infrastructure continue to leave millions in urgent need of support across multiple sectors. In Syria, fragile institutions and political uncertainty have weakened the delivery of essential services while increasing protection concerns for vulnerable communities. Yemen faces persistently high levels of acute food insecurity, compounded by reduced access to basic care.

International Medical Corps continues to adapt our operations across the region, drawing on decades of experience, trusted local partnerships and well-established emergency response systems. This enables us to deliver timely, effective and lifesaving assistance to communities affected by crisis, while remaining responsive to evolving humanitarian needs.

title: Global Weather Hazards Summary, August 6, 2026 – August 12, 2026
content:
Global Overview: El Niño is present. Abnormal heat continues to pose a threat across central Africa, northern and southern Central Asia, Hispaniola, as well as several areas of Central America and northern South America.

Africa Weather Hazards

Above-average rainfall has caused persistent flooding along the Gulf of Guinea’s coastal areas, while dryness continues in East Africa due to months of rainfall deficits.
1) Inundation continues in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan.
2) Severe rainfall deficits across large parts of East Africa over the past 90 days have resulted in abnormal dryness. Due to this persistent dryness, conditions have been upgraded to "Drought" across the equatorial provinces of South Sudan and the eastern, central, and north-central regions of Ethiopia.
3) The southern part of Mali and central and eastern Liberia remain under abnormal dryness conditions due to sustained below-average rainfall.
4) Persistent and forecasted localized heavy rainfall maintains an elevated risk of flooding across coastal areas of Guinea and Sierra Leone, southern Nigeria, and western Cameroon.
5) In the coming week, abnormal heat is expected across eastern Niger, Chad, Sudan, southwestern and eastern Ethiopia, and parts of southeastern Eritrea.
6) As heavy rainfall migrates slightly northward, the high alert for flash flooding is shifting north across western Ethiopia.
7) Heavy rainfall (up to 100 mm) on July 27–28 triggered coastal flooding, road disruptions, and damage near KuGompo along South Africa's southeastern coast. Forecasted above-average rainfall maintains an elevated risk of continued flooding in this area.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 18 – 24 July 2026
content:
Ukraine continued its campaign on energy infrastructure in occupied territories, while its strikes on oil tankers briefly suspended work at the CPC terminal.

Key trends

  • Ukraine has been attacking warehouses of Russia’s largest online retailer across at least nine regions in Russia and in occupied Crimea since 17 July. While primarily a civilian store, the retailer sells dual-use products, including unarmed drones, drone payload-release components, and military clothing. Ukraine is targeting these warehouses in an attempt to affect Russia’s military logistics, but also to generally further worsen Russia’s economy. It is also likely in retaliation against Russia's long history of strikes on the Ukrainian postal service and shopping centers.
  • Russia launched a massive wave of missile strikes targeting Kyiv city on 19 July. It deployed 41 ballistic and Zircon hypersonic missiles in the attack, the largest number deployed in a single wave of attacks to date. Russia has been increasingly using ballistic and Zircon missiles to attack Ukraine’s population centers, mainly Kyiv city and the eponymous region, exploiting Ukraine’s shortage of Patriot missiles required for their interception. Between 1 and 19 July, Russia reportedly used more ballistic missiles than it produces in a month, as well as two-thirds of its planned annual Zircon missile production.

title: Plataforma Subregional Cono Sur: #3 Special Sitrep on Bolivia (Update May 25 - 2026)
content:
CONTEXT

• Since the beginning of May Bolivia has been facing sustained road blockades associated with multi-sector protests, with direct impact on regular transit routes for the refugee and migrant population.

• This has increased the number of stranded persons at various points across the country, in a context of increased complexity in mobility dynamics, including the use of alternative routes, travel on foot, and returns to border crossing points.Access is limited or nonexistent to temporary shelter, food, water, health care, warm clothing, and protection measures. Requests for assistance frompersons living in Santa Cruz de la Sierra and Cochabamba has started to arise.The ongoing roadblocks are worsening the supply of food and other essential goods to the general population in various cities, mainly along the Andean corridor.

• Children and adolescents, pregnant women, and persons with disabilities who are part of the stranded population groups are in situations of particular vulnerability.

• The rapid deterioration of humanitarian conditions continues, along with growing pressure on response capacity, with operational limitations for humanitarian actors and the absence of an adequate structured response.

• Sustained coordination with the Ombudsman’s Office and humanitarian actors continues to be key in preserving the protection space for persons in transit.

• Several countries have expressed support for democratic institutions, and neighboring countries have sent humanitarian aid.

title: Plataforma Subregional Cono Sur: #4 Special Sitrep on Bolivia (Update - 1 June 2026)
content:
CONTEXT

• The second month of blockades affecting the main transit routes for refugee and migrant populations begins, leading to an increase in stranded persons, the extended use of alternative routes —including on-foot stretches and informal transport—, as well as limited availability and higher travel costs, with no guarantees of arrival.

• The reopening of the Pisiga-Oruro route has increased arrivals to this city; however, the Oruro–La Paz route remains blocked limiting displacement options and contributing to the prolonged stay of populations at intermediate points.

• In Oruro, access to shelter remains severely restricted. Available capacity is saturated or subject to documentation requirements, significantly reducing shelter options, even for those with themeans to pay. Evictions from temporary shelter spaces, including bus terminals and other collective sites, have been reported, leaving at least 50 people without shelter in temperatures reaching as low as -8°C.

• Critical health cases and increasing needs among vulnerable populations have been reported, including children, pregnant women, and persons with medical conditions. Additionally, the death of a refugee/migrant in Pisiga has been reported, presumably associated with adverse conditions during transit.

• Humanitarian conditions continue to deteriorate, with significant increases in the prices of basic goods (estimated at between 50% and 70%) and signs of shortages in affected cities, further limiting access to essential goods and services.

• Although humanitarian corridors have beenmentioned in the media, no concrete information is available regarding their implementation.

title: UNICEF Bangladesh Humanitarian Situation Report No. 75 (Mid-Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • UNICEF continues delivering life-saving assistance amid multiple humanitarian challenges, including the protracted Rohingya refugee crisis affecting 1.2 million refugees and a nationwide measles outbreak.
  • Bangladesh had reported more than 100,000 suspected measles cases and 625 suspected deaths across all 64 districts, with children under five accounting for 81 per cent of cases. UNICEF supported the Government's Emergency Measles-Rubella Campaign, reaching 18.5 million children to help interrupt transmission.
  • In Cox's Bazar and Bhasan Char, UNICEF sustained essential services for Rohingya children, reaching 341,300 people with safe water, 229,850 children with education, 169,700 children with nutrition screening, and 157,100 children and women with primary healthcare.
  • Across all humanitarian responses, UNICEF reached 433,330 people (34 per cent of the HAC target), including 234,100 children, with integrated life-saving assistance.
  • The overall 2026 HAC appeal of US$108 million nonetheless remains 24 per cent underfunded, with the most critical sector gaps in Child Protection (44 per cent) and WASH (33 per cent). Despite these constraints, prioritization efforts have protected the most critical services, with 90 per cent of life-saving interventions funded.

title: UNICEF East Asia and the Pacific Region Humanitarian Situation Report No. 1 (Mid-Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Humanitarian context: Approximately 290 million children in East Asia and the Pacific are exposed to multiple extreme climate hazards, increasing their risk of climate-related disasters and emergencies. Between January and June, Tropical Cyclone Maila affected nearly 300,000 people in the Solomon Islands and Papua New Guinea and a major earthquake in the Philippines affected around 1.9 million people. Disease outbreaks strained essential services, while 3.75 million people remained displaced in Myanmar.
  • Coordinated response: Across the region, UNICEF supported governments and partners to deliver life-saving, child-focused, inclusive and accountable humanitarian action across health, nutrition, WASH, child protection, education and shock-responsive social protection in Cambodia, China, Fiji, Federated States of Micronesia, Kiribati, Lao PDR, Marshall Islands, Mongolia, Myanmar, Papua New Guinea, Philippines, Solomon Islands, Thailand, Vanuatu and Viet Nam.
  • Results for children: With UNICEF support, 3.4 million children were vaccinated against polio and 1.3 million against measles, and 20,231 children aged 6–59 months were treated for severe wasting. Critical WASH supplies reached more than 113,000 people and over 96,000 children received individual learning materials. Mental health and psychosocial support reached over 171,000 children, adolescents and caregivers. 7,610 households received humanitarian cash assistance to support their immediate response and recovery needs; and over 35 million people received life-saving information.
  • Funding: US$9.8 million in new funding has been received so far in 2026. In addition to addressing gaps in funding for ongoing emergency responses, further investment in preparedness and anticipatory action ahead of the strong El Niño impact anticipated across the region is urgently needed.

title: UNICEF Venezuela Humanitarian Situation Report No.7 (Earthquake Response), 25 July - 3 August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • UNICEF continued to scale up its humanitarian response across earthquake-affected areas, supporting the continuity of essential health, nutrition, WASH, child protection, and education services for children and families in temporary camps and affected communities.
  • To date, UNICEF has reached 25,483 people with primary health care, 22,424 children, adults, and pregnant women with routine and catch-up vaccinations, 9,412 people with critical WASH supplies, 5,804 children and caregivers with nutrition services, and 6,134 children, adolescents, and caregivers with child protection services, including MHPSS.
  • UNICEF is supporting the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA), leading the WASH and education sectors. The PDNA will inform recovery priorities and help accelerate the restoration of essential services.
  • In addition to its US$137.6 million 2026 HAC appeal, UNICEF requires US$65.7 million to sustain critical interventions and support the implementation of the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum.

title: WFP Lesotho Country Brief July 2026 (Reporting Period: June 2026)
content:
• WFP remains a key food security partner to the Government, strengthening national systems and providing technical assistance to improve the Government’s capacity to manage and implement national programmes.
  • The Lesotho Meteorological Services seasonal climate outlook for July to September 2026 indicates an increased likelihood of dry spells over most of the eastern and central parts of the country.
  • WFP is working with the Disaster Management Authority and Lesotho Meteorological Services to strengthen preparedness and early action ahead of the anticipated El Niño, helping improve national readiness for potential climate-related shocks.

title: Rebuilding lives in Assam: Assam flood - Early recovery & rehabilitation appeal
content:
CURRENT SITUATION

  • A week after the floods, thousands of families remain unable to return to normal life. Homes are buried under silt and debris, livelihoods have been destroyed, access to safe water and sanitation remains limited, and many households continue to live in temporary shelters with little means to recover.
  • The disaster has created a prolonged recovery crisis beyond immediate relief. Many affected communities, particularly those NOT traditionally flood-prone, lost homes, agricultural land, livestock, and essential household assets built over years, with local communities estimating that full recovery may take 5-10 years without sustained support.
  • The response is now shifting to early recovery and rehabilitation. Immediate priorities include shelter repair, debris and silt clearance, restoration of livelihoods, WASH and public health support, psychosocial care, and rebuilding community resilience, requiring coordinated support from government, humanitarian organisations, donors, and the private sector.

title: WFP Colombia Country Brief, July 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Despite being an upper-middle-income country, Colombia continues to face a complex humanitarian and food security crisis. WFP’s joint food security assessment in the 15 most vulnerable departments found that 37 percent of households—around 7 million people—experience moderate or severe food insecurity. Nationally, food insecurity remains at approximately 25 percent, with Atlántico, Sucre and La Guajira reporting the highest prevalence of severe food insecurity.

• The humanitarian situation is further compounded by persistent violence, forced displacement, the presence of nonstate armed groups, mixed migration flows, climate-related emergencies and economic shocks. From January to June 2026, an estimated 769,800 people were affected by violence, while more than 583,300 people were impacted by weather-related events across the country.

• According to the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), 6.9 million people require humanitarian assistance in Colombia, including 6.6 million in need of food security and nutrition support. Colombia’s decades-long armed conflict has resulted in 10.3 million registered victims, around 90 percent of whom are internally displaced persons. In 2025 alone, violence affected more than 1.6 million people and added approximately 150,000 new victims to the official registry.

• Colombia hosts one of the largest migrant populations in Latin America, with approximately 2.8 million migrants residing in the country. By the end of June 2026, 51,938 migrants had entered and transited Colombia irregularly, representing a 38 percent decrease compared to the same period in 2025.

• WFP has operated in Colombia since 1969. Its Country Strategic Plan supports national priorities on food security, humanitarian response, early recovery and peacebuilding, contributing to SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals).

title: Pakistan Rain Monitor - Issue Number 7 (04 - 10 August 2026)
content:
Using remote sensing techniques, the seven-day forecast of total rainfall for the country is analyzed against the long-term average rainfall to highlight the areas which are expected to receive above normal, normal and below normal rainfall. The satellite data for a period of thirty years from 1993-2023 is extracted from CHIRPS (Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data) and analyzed to estimate deviation from normal rainfall. For the forecast of total precipitation for next seven days, the data is sourced from global model of ECMWF (European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts).

The satellite-based national rainfall forecasts analysis for 04 - 10 August indicate above normal rainfall across most of the northern, northeastern and central parts of the country, while below normal rainfall is expected in the southern and southwestern parts of the country. Given the ongoing flood conditions in parts of north and central areas, additional rainfall may exacerbate the risk of flooding, GLOF and landslides, particularly in vulnerable locations across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan, Azad Jammu & Kashmir, and northern Punjab.

title: India Floods 2026 Situation Report
content:
ASSAM (19 JULY - PRESENT)

  • A total of 87 deaths have been confirmed, and more than 705,000 people have been affected, with Sivasagar being the worst-hit district. Thousands of people remain displaced, many still living in roadside shelters or unable to return home after losing their houses, livestock, and belongings.
  • A total of 56,606 hectares of agricultural land has been affected, with large areas covered by sand and silt, making cultivation difficult for the coming seasons. Many homes remain filled with debris that families are unable to clear on their own, while limited access to safe drinking water is increasing the risk of disease.
  • Many people remain missing, with concerns some may still be buried under debris and silt. This has increased the need for drone assessments to support search efforts.
  • Response is now shifting from immediate relief to early recovery, focusing on shelter repair, essential household items, debris clearance, livelihood support, WASH, health and psychosocial care. The scale of the crisis continues to stretch existing response capacity.

title: Venezuela Earthquake: Flash Update #4 (31 July 2026)
content:
Context

Five weeks after the June 24 earthquakes in Venezuela, the death toll and affected population continue increasing. OCHA has formalized the national response into a six-month Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum (July–Dec. 2026).

  • Toll: 5,546 dead, 16,740 injured, 6,462 rescued alive. Rescuers describe no longer searching for survivors, and international search and rescue missions are scaling back. There are critical information gaps related to missing persons.
  • Children: CECODAP estimates that over 1,400 children and adolescents remain at significant risk of harm due to the earthquake.
  • Displacement: As of July 26, 107 transitional camps for affected populations are housing 24,477 people (87% capacity). Most displaced people remain concentrated in Caracas and La Guaira.
  • Education: According to civil society organizations, over 900 schools have been affected, including 18 school facilities that have totally collapsed and 40 that have severe structural damage. 120 teachers have been reported dead.
  • Economic effects and reconstruction costs: June inflation hit 13.8%, more than double May's rate. National reconstruction cost estimates now range from USD 12–15 billion. Government and private sector banking institutions are exploring credit programs for housing repair and replacement.
  • Humanitarian funding request: OCHA's Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum requests USD 298 million to reach 1.3 million people over six months (JulyDecember 2026). This is in addition to the USD 930 million humanitarian funding required for 6.2 million people in Venezuela prior to the earthquake.
  • Priority needs as per the OCHA Rapid Needs Assessment: health (53%), safe water (52%), food security (50%), psychosocial support (27%), sanitation/hygiene (22%), protection/safety/dignity (18%), shelter (17%).

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 79, as of 4 August 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Preventive population movement in Bangassou, Mbomou Prefecture
  • More than 3,000 Chadian refugees receive food assistance in Bétoko, Lim-Pendé Prefecture

GENERAL CONTEXT

Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • Between 27 and 29 July, part of the population of Bangassou moved preventively to neighbourhoods perceived as safer. Some people crossed the Mbomou River to seek refuge in the Ndou village in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), following rumours of a possible attack on the town by armed elements. In response to these security concerns, the Central African Armed Forces (FACA) and Internal Security Forces (ISF) conducted night patrols from 28 to 29 July. The situation has gradually returned to normal, and those who had temporarily relocated have returned to their usual places of residence in the town.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Food Security

Lim-Pendé Prefecture – North-West

  • On 29 July, the World Food Programme (WFP), in partnership with World Vision, provided cash-based food assistance to 3,365 Chadian refugees in Bétoko, 15 km from Paoua. The assistance enabled beneficiary households to cover their food needs for 60 days.

Education

Lim-Pendé Prefecture – West

  • Plan International distributed, from 27 to 30 July, school kits to 437 students, including 272 boys and 165 girls, in schools within the Ngaoundaye Mixed Sub-Prefectural Schools A and B formal education network, as well as to teachers and learners enrolled in the Accelerated Education Programme. The kits included school bags, slates, pens, pencils and notebooks. Teaching kits containing chalk, dusters, attendance registers and correction supplies were also provided to six schools (Mixed Sub-Prefectural Schools A and B, Touga, Bolélé, Bang and Ngouboye). The intervention was carried out under an integrated education and child protection response project for conflict-affected children in Lim-Pendé Prefecture, funded by the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (ECHO).

title: Ebola Outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda - External update #4 - 31 July 2026
content:
Highlights

• Uganda has officially declared the end of its 2026 Ebola outbreak, two and a half months after it was first announced. The declaration on 28 July followed completion of the mandatory 42- day monitoring period, which began after the last locally transmitted case of a Ugandan national was discharged on 16 June. A total of 20 confirmed cases were reported during the outbreak, including 18 recoveries and two deaths.

• In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Ebola continues to spread rapidly, with 3,360 confirmed cases and 1,487 deaths reported as of 27 July. Declared on 15 May, the outbreak has reached 48 health zones across five provinces.

• Ituri remains the epicentre, accounting for nearly nine in ten confirmed cases and deaths. Transmission is also affecting North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo, reflecting the growing geographic spread and the need for sustained surveillance, community engagement and cross-border preparedness.

• Forcibly displaced people face heightened risks as the outbreak expands near displacement sites. The affected provinces currently host around 4.4 million forcibly displaced people, including 3.8 million internally displaced people (IDPs), around 274,000 refugees and asylumseekers, and 290,000 returnees. Around 46,800 South Sudanese refugees also live in Ituri, the outbreak epicentre.

• While no cases have been reported among refugees or asylum-seekers, 19 cases have been confirmed among internally displaced people, including five deaths, mainly in Ituri.

title: UNRWA Situation Report #231 on the Humanitarian Crisis in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem) [EN/AR]
content:
All information updated for 15 - 28 July 2026 [1]
Days 1011 - 1024 since the start of the war in the Gaza Strip

Highlights

The Gaza Strip

  • UNRWA summer learning activities started on 18 July, with 39,509 children (21,666 girls, 17,843 boys, including 875 children with disabilities) participating between 20 and 26 July. Summer activities also started at the UNRWA Rehabilitation Centre for the Visually Impaired (RCVI).
  • On 21 July, UNRWA resumed operations at Beach Camp Health Centre in western Gaza City, which had been closed since sustaining damage during the September-October 2025 military escalation. On 29 July, UNRWA also opened the Bahrain Medical Point, in southern Gaza City. Together, the two facilities are expected to serve a large catchment area (almost 100,000 people), expanding access to essential primary healthcare services across densely populated areas of Gaza City.
  • The operating environment in Gaza continues to deteriorate, with a significant escalation in hostilities observed in the humanitarian area – also known as the “green zone” – west of the so-called “yellow line” of control designated by Israeli forces. There have also been additional advances of the yellow line across multiple areas, including in eastern Middle Area, Gaza City and Khan Younis. Multiple evacuation orders and shelter-in place orders were issued over the past week with several humanitarian infrastructure affected (including more than ten UNRWA premises).
  • Restrictions on the entry of lubricant oil and spare parts continue to pose a critical challenge for humanitarian operation, More than half of UNRWA’s fleet is no longer operational due to the shortage of engine oil and spare parts. In addition, 62 water wells have been affected by fuel and lubricant shortages, leading to a reduction of 42 percent in UNRWA’s production and distribution of clean water.

The occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem

  • On 27 July, the UNRWA Kalandia Training Centre in East Jerusalem was subject to an unauthorised entry by Israeli forces and Jerusalem Municipality officials, during which they inspected the premises while educational activities were ongoing. As a United Nations property, the Kalandia Training Centre is protected under international law.

title: UNICEF Europe and Central Asia Region Humanitarian Situation Report No.34 (Ukraine Refugee Response in Neighboring Countries), January - June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • UNICEF’s 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal for the Ukraine Refugee Response enabled the continuation of children’s access to critical services and close coordination among UNICEF, governments and other partners. Flexible and timely donor contributions supported adaptive programming and the gradual transition from emergency assistance toward longer-term, strengthening of national systems.
  • By mid-2026, UNICEF and partners sustained multi-sectoral support for Ukrainian refugee children and families across five refugee-hosting countries in Europe (Belarus, Bulgaria, Moldova, Poland and Romania) with a strong focus on child protection, mental health and psychosocial support and education.
