title: Bangladesh: Population Movement Operation, Cox’s Bazar - Emergency Appeal no. MDRBD018, Operation Update #25
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

Nearly nine years after the large-scale influx of displaced people from Rakhine State in Myanmar into Bangladesh, the situation in Cox’s Bazar remains one of the world’s most protracted and underfunded humanitarian crises. As of 30 June 2026, a total of 1,200,171 displaced people4 live in 33 overcrowded camps in Cox’s Bazar and Bhasan char Island (where 33,819 people live, relocated since 2021), with density reaching 47,000 people/km among the highest globally (Please find Annex 1: PMO 4W map of camp and host). Displaced people continue to remain dependent on humanitarian aid due to restrictions on movement, employment, and the provision of parmanent shelters or community structures. There are currently no durable solutions to the protracted displacement in sight and continued uncertainty surrounding possible repatriation up to the present.

According to the Government of Bangladesh (GoB) - UNHCR Population Dashboard as of June 2026, while 51 per cent of the population is female and 49 per cent male, 44 per cent comprises the largest adult group (18–59). The people living in camp settlements are particularly vulnerable as 78 per cent of them are women and children, and 12 per cent are Persons with Special Needs (EVIs), including persons with disabilities, single parents, children/older persons at risks.

The humanitarian situation has further deteriorated due to renewed violence in Myanmar’s Rakhine State, resulting in a fresh influx of displaced people into Bangladesh. Since 2024, an estimated 220,000 people have entered Bangladesh from Rakhine State, placing additional pressure on the already confined and overcrowded camp.
However, according to the population dashboard, 153,640 new arrivals out of 220,000 have been biometrically registered as of June 2026 and remaining is in process. Many newly arrived families are currently sharing overcrowded shelters with relatives and host households, exposing them to heightened protection, health, and psychosocial risks.

The developments/changes in the situation in Rakhine State, Myanmar could trigger another wave of displacement into Bangladesh, further intensifying security risks, border instability, and pressure on already overstretched humanitarian resources in Cox’s Bazar. This ongoing, complex, and protracted displacement crisis has left the affected population living in camps almost fully reliant on humanitarian assistance to meet their basic needs. The situation is further compounded by frequent cyclones, seasonal rainfall, flash floods, fire incidents, and heightened security concerns within the camps.

The host community people, particularly in the Ukhiya and Teknaf sub-districts of Cox’s Bazar, have been significantly affected by the prolonged displacement crisis. The strain on forest resources, shrinking opportunities in the daily labour market, and rising tensions between the displaced and host communities are ongoing challenges. To continuously support the host population living close to the camps, as in the previous response plans, the UN-led Joint Response Plan (JRP) 2025-265 includes interventions aimed at supporting over 300,000 people in the host

title: Armenia / Population movement: Imminent DREF Final Report (MDRAM016)
content:
Event development

Update regarding the event’s development

The regional escalation of conflict in the Middle East in early 2026 heightened regional tensions and disrupted air travel and regional connectivity. The escalation affected commercial air traffic, and several countries issued advisories recommending alternative evacuation routes for their citizens, indicating potential risks of restricted mobility and increased reliance on land corridors. Armenia was identified as one of the accessible transit routes, particularly through its border with the Islamic Republic of Iran.

The imminent DREF operation in Armenia was therefore triggered by a potential sudden cross-border population movement into Armenia, particularly through the Syunik region and the Nurduz–Agarak border crossing point, linked to the regional escalation and continued disruption of airspace in the region. The projected movement was expected to follow a transit corridor from Meghri to Goris in Syunik region and onward to Yerevan, with Yerevan serving as a logistical hub and onward travel point.

Based on scenario analysis, it was anticipated that Armenia could become one of the viable evacuation routes for Armenians living in Iran (estimated at 60,000–80,000 people), as well as foreign nationals, including students, business travellers, and diplomatic staff. It was estimated that approximately 70–80 per cent of arrivals would travel independently or with embassy support, while 20–30 per cent could require short-term humanitarian assistance, particularly vulnerable individuals such as older persons, families with children, and those lacking sufficient financial means or onward travel arrangements.

The activation timeframe was projected at 0–4 weeks, with the situation remaining dynamic depending on the evolution of regional hostilities and transportation disruptions. Potential humanitarian concerns included congestion at border crossing points and extended travel times; fatigue, dehydration, and psychosocial stress following prolonged journeys; temporary strain on local services and infrastructure, particularly in Meghri; protection risks related to lack of documentation, language barriers, and misinformation; and family separation or communication breakdowns generating Restoring Family Links (RFL) needs.

Overall, the anticipated situation was characterized as a rapid-onset, short-duration, transit-focused population movement that could create localized humanitarian pressure at entry points, even if it did not evolve into large-scale displacement within the country.

During the operational period, some cross-border movements into Armenia were recorded; however, the number of arrivals remained limited and did not reach the predefined trigger thresholds for activating a large-scale humanitarian response.

Available data indicates that between 28 February and 15 April 2026, approximately 18,300 entries into Armenia and 17,500 exits from Armenia of Iranian nationals were recorded through the Agarak border crossing point. These figures reflect continued regular two-way cross-border movements rather than a significant influx associated with the regional escalation.

At the same time, according to official information from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Armenia facilitated the transit of foreign nationals from a significant number of countries, initially reported as 41 and subsequently increasing to up to 60 countries over time. These movements included foreign citizens, diplomats, and other individuals exiting the region through Armenia. Overall, movements remained predominantly transit-oriented, with most individuals continuing onward travel through existing arrangements or embassy-supported evacuation mechanisms, resulting in limited humanitarian needs.

As a result, the anticipated escalation scenario did not materialize. The number of people requiring humanitarian assistance remained limited and did not place additional pressure on national response capacities. Therefore, while preparedness measures were justified and necessary, the predefined trigger thresholds for activating a large-scale response were not reached.

Consequently, the situation remained stable throughout the operational period, and no large-scale humanitarian needs requiring activation of response activities were observed.

title: Jordan: Country Factsheet (June 2026)
content: As of June 2026, Jordan hosts over 393,000 refugees registered with UNHCR, with numbers gradually declining due to voluntary returns to Syria. For over a decade, the Kingdom has generously allowed refugees access to public education, health and other services. UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, continues to ensure refugees are protected through, e.g., registration, legal documentation, legal assistance and community engagement, while also coordinating the overall refugee response with the government. title: UNICEF Mali Humanitarian Situation Report No. 2 (Mid-Year), 30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Mali’s humanitarian crisis significantly deteriorated during the first half of 2026, with the 25 April attacks marking a major escalation in insecurity. Conflict incidents increased by 39 per cent between Q1 and Q2, reaching 987 incidents and causing 283 casualties, including six children.
  • Children and families faced growing risks as insecurity disrupted essential services and livelihoods. Around 415,000 people remained internally displaced (58 per cent children) and nearly 280,000 refugees, while localized displacement after April affected almost 40,000 people, including 21,600 children. title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #19 (31 July to 3 August 2026)
content:
The nineteenth Situation Report provides an update on IOM’s response to the 24 June earthquakes in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, covering the period from 31 July to 3 August 2026.

Highlights

Between 31 July and 3 August, IOM continued its multisectoral response in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities through interventions in shelter and camp coordination and management, health, protection, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), information management, and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA).

During the reporting period, IOM distributed 245 plastic tarpaulins, 234 solar lamps, 234 collapsible water containers, 235 kitchen sets, 227 hygiene kits and 74 mosquito nets to address priority shelter and household needs of earthquake-affected families.

To date, IOM-supported teams have delivered 7,615 medical consultations to 6,733 earthquake-affected people through health, mental health and psychological support services in temporary accommodation sites and affected communities.

IOM initiated the characterization of earthquake-affected community settlements, reaching 20 settlements in La Guaira, one in Miranda and one in Carabobo, expanding needs and displacement monitoring beyond temporary accommodation sites.

IOM Activities

IOM continued co-managing five temporary accommodation sites in La Guaira: Campo de Golf, Mare Abajo II, Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex, Playa Grande and Cesar Nieves, supporting service delivery, population registration, community information services and operational coordination.

At Campo de Golf, the allocation of new family tents, expansion of solar lighting and improvement of community and service spaces continued. At Mare Abajo II, community outreach activities began to promote available services, identify needs and strengthen communication channels with site residents, while household registration and verification activities continued. At Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex, essential services were maintained for 796 people from 221 households, including registration, community orientation, connectivity and restoring family links.

During the reporting period, IOM distributed 245 plastic tarpaulins, 234 solar lamps, 234 collapsible water containers, 235 kitchen sets, 227 hygiene kits and 74 mosquito nets to earthquake-affected families. To date, IOM has delivered 4,987 kitchen sets, 4,580 plastic tarpaulins, 3,441 solar lamps, 3,313 collapsible water containers, 2,527 hygiene kits, 2,384 buckets, 1,066 mosquito nets and 822 emergency shelter kits.

In WASH, IOM continued expanding access to safe water and sanitation services through the activation of a potable water system at Campo de Golf, water quality monitoring, chlorination activities, sanitation infrastructure improvements and waste management support. To date, IOM has provided 3,313 collapsible 10-liter water containers, 285 semi-collapsible 10-liter water containers and 2,527 hygiene kits.

IOM and its implementing partner Ven Da Tu Mano continued delivering health, mental health and psychological support services through mobile teams. During the reporting period, 90 consultations were conducted in Cesar Nieves, while mobile health services at Jose Maria Vargas Sports Complex reached a cumulative total of 2,509 consultations. To date, IOM-supported interventions have provided 7,615 medical consultations to 6,733 earthquake-affected people.

IOM continued registration and information management activities through the unified Information Management System (IMS) across the five temporary accommodation sites. During the reporting period, IOM initiated data collection in earthquake-affected community settlements, characterizing 20 settlements in La Guaira, one in Miranda and one in Carabobo, while Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) teams conducted additional assessments in Carabobo.

In protection, IOM continued providing legal assistance, case management, child protection activities, trafficking in persons prevention, violence against women and girls prevention and community information services. Community outreach activities were launched in Mare Abajo II, and IOM supported the coordination of a documentation campaign that enabled 182 people to access national identification services.

As co-lead of the Infrastructure and Temporary Accommodation Working Group together with UNHCR, IOM continued supporting operational coordination, service mapping, information management and joint planning across temporary accommodation sites.

In PSEA, IOM conducted refresher sessions with 24 humanitarian workers, distributed 1,000 informational leaflets and key messages to NFI teams, and carried out awareness activities with 15 community leaders and 17 humanitarian workers in Playa Grande.

IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue strengthening infrastructure, service delivery, WASH interventions, shelter support and Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) activities in temporary accommodation sites.

IOM will also continue delivering health, mental health, psychological support and protection services while strengthening referral pathways for specialized assistance.

In addition, IOM will maintain mobility monitoring, registration activities, information management, community settlement assessments and coordination with authorities and implementing organizations to support evidence-based response planning.

title: Cameroon Cholera Outbreak: Situation Report #2 (August 4, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • As of August 2, 53 suspected cholera cases had been reported in Minawao Refugee Camp, which hosts 81,022 refugees and is operating at 324% of its intended capacity, creating conditions conducive to rapid disease transmission.
  • Multiple transmission chains are suspected within the camp, increasing the risk of further spread among vulnerable refugee and host populations.
  • As of August 2, the cholera outbreak in the Far North Region had resulted in 990 reported cases and 28 deaths across nine affected health districts.

OUR RESPONSE

  • International Medical Corps is coordinating with health authorities, UN agencies, camp management and humanitarian partners to support a harmonized response.
  • We are implementing cholera prevention and response activities focused on outbreak containment, case management and community protection.
  • Efforts include strengthening treatment capacity through additional staff, essential medicines and cholera supplies, and strengthening surveillance, community alert systems and risk communication to support early detection and treatment.
  • We also are scaling up risk communication, hygiene promotion, infection prevention, disinfection, and emergency activities involving water, sanitation and hygiene.

Following the detection of suspected and RDT-positive cholera cases in Minawao Refugee Camp, International Medical Corps launched an emergency response to support outbreak containment and reduce cholera-related morbidity and mortality among refugee and host communities. Implemented in coordination with national authorities and humanitarian partners, our intervention addresses critical operational gaps and is expected to directly benefit more than 14,500 people through enhanced surveillance, case management, infection prevention and control, risk communication and community engagement, and water, sanitation and hygiene interventions.

Patients suspected to have cholera have received direct clinical care from International Medical Corps teams in the temporary treatment unit that we have set up in the main section of the Minawao Medicalized Health Center, located inside the camp. This care continues while efforts to expand treatment capacity remain underway. We so far have managed 53 patients, including 26 discharged as recovered, with no deaths reported to date, while we have identified and monitored 217 contacts. The Mokolo Health District has led efforts to conduct rapid investigations, contact tracing, active case finding, household disinfection and refer suspected cases for higher care, while International Medical Corps has strengthened response readiness through training on cholera case management and diagnostics. We also have supported treatment and IPC activities by providing contingency stocks and mobilizing additional personnel, medicines, consumables and response supplies.

title: UNHCR Bangladesh - Operational Update June 2026
content:
KEY UPDATES

● WORLD REFUGEE DAY: UNHCR and partners marked World Refugee Day on 20 June with sports, games, cultural activities, and student engagement programmes. In Cox’s Bazar, an interagency Solidarity Football Tournament brought together refugees, humanitarian workers, and government officials. In Dhaka, a student-led art competition on the theme ‘Forced to Flee’ ended with a certificate ceremony at Daffodil International University, and a screening of the first film in the Rohingya-language Lost Land at the Liberation War Museum.

● ONWARDS MOVEMENTS: As of end-May, an estimated 10,700 individuals from Myanmar and the Bangladesh camps undertook onward movements by land or sea in 2026, bringing the total since January 2022 to 380,700, with 2,600 reported dead or missing. In late June, two boats carrying an estimated 500 people, reportedly departed Northern Rakhine and encountered dangerous monsoon weather. Reports that the boats capsized in the Andaman Sea with no survivors are being investigated. Insecurity in Rakhine State, reduced assistance in Cox’s Bazar camps and lack of solutions continue to drive refugees to search for safety and opportunities elsewhere in the region. UNHCR and partners continue to raise awareness of the dangers of undertaking such perilous journeys. Read the Route-based Snapshot. Read the UNHCR-IOM Joint Statement.

● NEW ARRIVALS: Rohingya and other residents fleeing conflict in Myanmar’s Rakhine State continued to seek safety in Bangladesh, despite a closed-border policy that has limited access to asylum. Between 1 January and 30 June 2026, border protection monitoring reported 2,219 individuals denied access to Bangladesh, bringing the total to 14,706 since 2024. However, many incidents are unreported. In June, 1,611 newly arrived individuals were biometrically identified through a joint exercise with the Government of Bangladesh. Since the exercise began in 2025, a total of 153,640 individuals (40,326 families) have received family cards granting access to basic assistance — representing 12.8% of the current population. Unlike regular refugee registration, suspended by the Government since May 2022, individual refugee identity documents are not issued through this process. UNHCR continues to advocate with government counterparts for full registration and access to shelter for new arrivals.

● STRATEGIC TRANSFORMATIONS OF THE ROHINGYA RESPONSE: UNHCR reached key milestones in the transition of WASH, health and nutrition services, including the handover of WASH Area Focal responsibilities to UNICEF in five Ukhiya camps and the Transit Centre, and of Community Health Focal responsibilities to WHO in six Ukhiya camps and Teknaf’s Nayapara Registered Camp. UNHCR will retain its role as Area Focal Agency in Teknaf camps and continue distributing hygiene items in Ukhiya camps through 31 December. Preparations continued for the handover of nutrition centres on Bhasan Char to UNICEF and WFP, now scheduled for 1 August.

● REFGUEE-LED ENTREPRENEURSHIP: Seven refugee-led gas stove repair and pressure cooker maintenance shops were established and became operational from 1 July, creating livelihoods opportunities for graduates of the UNHCR-supported ‘small engine mechanics’ curriculumbased skills training. The shops help ensure continued access to essential stove maintenance services and mark a transition towards community-led ownership of these services, from a vendor-led to a refugee-led approach.

title: Lebanon: Flash Update #48 - Escalation of hostilities in Lebanon (as of 3 August 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • At least 4,333 deaths and 12,250 injuries recorded due to hostilities since 2 March, with 353 people killed and 249 injured since the 19 June ceasefire announcement, according to the Ministry of Public Health.
  • 821,077 people reported returning to their areas of origin, while 360,132 people remain displaced, as of 30 July. As of 3 August, 26,300 Internally Displaced Persons (>53% women and girls) remainin 247 collective shelters.
  • UXO incidents reported on 2 and 3 August, highlighting significant risks to civilians and humanitarian personnel operating in conflict-affected areas.
  • Water access severely affected for 700,000 people due to conflict-related damage to water and electricity infrastructure in South and Nabatieh governorates from 2024-2026.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Lebanon continues to face a severe humanitarian and protection crisis. Confronted with ongoing hostilities, protracted displacement, and attempts to return to homes and villages that have been heavily damaged or destroyed, affected communities across the country face heightened protection risks and sustained humanitarian needs. Reports of daily airstrikes, demolitions, shelling, and other security incidents persisted during the reporting period (31 July-3 August) across Bint Jbeil, Marjaayoun, Nabatieh, and Hasbaya districts in Nabatieh Governorate, as well as Tyre district inSouth Governorate. During the reporting period, two incidents involving unexploded ordnance (UXO) were reported: the first on 2 August in Kafra, Bint Jbeil District (Nabatieh Governorate), where Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) were escorting civilians in the area, and the second on 3 August in Tebna, Saida District (South Governorate). As population returns increase to heavily conflict-affected areas, the risk of exposure to UXO is increased. The destruction of homes, agricultural land, and civilian infrastructure continued in southern Lebanon during the reporting period, undermining the safety, sustainability, and dignity of returns, while increasing humanitarian needs related to access to essential services such as water, healthcare and education, as well as shelter, protection and livelihoods.

The Ministry of Public Health reported 4,333 people killed (including 392 women and 253 children) and 12,250 injured (1,452 women and 1,037 children) as of 2 August. Since the latest ceasefire announcement on 19 June, 353 people have been killed and 249 injured. Since 2 March, 135 health care professionals have been killed while on duty and 410 injured.

Displacement levels remain high nationwide, although the number of internally displaced persons (IDPs) continues to decrease at a slower pace. As of 30 July, 360,132 people remain displaced across Lebanon, according to the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), representing a 4 per cent decrease from 22 July. While the number of IDPs declined in most districts, increases in IDP figures were recorded in several districts from the week before the latest DTM, including in Nabatieh by 3,200, Bint Jbeil by 1,560 (Nabatieh Governorate), Tyre by 1,100 (South Governorate), Baalbek by 1,130, and Hermel by 123 (Baalbek El Hermel Governorate). The increase in IDP caseloads, primarily in South and Nabatieh governorates, highlights the continued movement of displaced people closer to their areas of origin without fully returning. This consistent trend since the ceasefire announcement underscores the persistent access, security, infrastructure, and service-related challenges in and around the IDF-declared military area, where many communities remain unable to return safely and sustainably.

People living in collective shelters face challenging conditions and diminishing coping capacities. Approximately 26,300 people remain accommodated in 247 collective shelters across Lebanon (DRM) as of 3 August. Sustained basic services are required in these shelters, which face challenges due to shortages of fuel to sustain electricity supply and water pumping, heightening risks related to health, hygiene, and safety. Cash assistance remains a priority stated by those in collective shelters to enable them to meet essential food, healthcare, and hygiene needs. As shelter consolidation efforts continue, some IDPs have reported receiving insufficient information about alternative accommodation options or inadequate notice of shelter closures. This contributes to protection risks, including secondary or involuntary displacement, loss of access to assistance and services, and increased psychosocial distress.

Return movements continue, though security, access, and service-related challenges remain barriers for many. 821,077 people had begun the return to their areas of origin as of 30 July, representing a 9 per cent increase in the comparable figure from the previous week (22 July). Despite continued return movements, the number of people present within the IDF-declared military zone remain unchanged according to DRM, as widespread destruction of housing and infrastructure, movement restrictions, ongoing military activities, and strained or non-functional health, water, and electricity hindered returns. Cash, access to health care, restoration of essential services, shelter interventions, and emergency livelihood support remain critical humanitarian priorities for returning communities.

Conflict-related damage to water and electricity infrastructure severely limits water access for more than 700,000 people. A preliminary assessment conducted by the South Lebanon Water Establishment (SLWE) identified widespread damage and destruction to water infrastructure across the South and Nabatieh governorates as of July 2026. Between 2024 and 2026, approximately 175 water reservoirs, 16 pumping stations, 124 boreholes, nine springs, and 85 generators sustained conflict-related damage. The assessment also identified contamination of water sources from explosive remnants, heavy metals, and other hazardous substances as major public health and environmental concerns. As a result of the extensive damage and destruction of water and electricity infrastructure, more than 700,000 people face reduced access to safe drinking water, contamination risks to food and water supplies, heightened health and hygiene concerns, and agricultural losses. Direct and indirect losses were estimated to exceed $550 million. Emergency interventions to restore minimum water services and prevent further deterioration of humanitarian conditions remain critical.

Protection needs remain acute in Lebanon, with ongoing risks affecting communities in prolonged displacement, those returning to conflict-affected areas, and host communities. Protection risks remain high, particularly for conflict-affected women, children, older persons, and persons with disabilities. Among those who remain displaced, especially in collective shelters and vulnerable informal settlements, overcrowding, damaged housing, lack of privacy, gender-based violence risks, restricted access to essential services, documentation challenges, and financial constraints are increasing vulnerability and weakening community coping capacities. In areas of return, insecurity, the presence of unexploded ordnance, limited access to health care, WASH, mental health and psychosocial support, and sexual and reproductive health services, disrupted livelihoods, and housing, land, and property (HLP) issues undermine safe and sustainable return conditions and heighten protection risks.

Funding constraints remain a major challenge to sustained humanitarian assistance. The 2026 Lebanon Flash Appeal, a six-month emergency response entering its final month, has received less than half of the $639.9 million required as of 3 August, or $289.3 million (45.2 per cent).

title: Sudan conflict - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms Area) #42 Reporting period: 01 – 31 July 2026
content:
The WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) was activated as the Emergency Telecommunications Cluster (ETC) on 25 May 2023 in response to the conflict crisis in Sudan. This Situation Report provides a monthly update on LTC telecoms activities1 .

Summary Points

• In July, despite funding shortfalls, LTC Telecoms continued coordination and high-level advocacy with humanitarian partners and national authorities to maintain telecommunications services for emergency responders and support the delivery of lifesaving assistance.

• LTC Sudan Telecoms is prioritizing the renewal and expansion of Security Communications System (SCS) licences, including High Frequency (HF) and Very High Frequency (VHF) radio licences, to enable secure communications in Khartoum and Omdurman. The cluster has applied for new licences and additional frequencies to boost communication for responders.

• On 22 July, UNICEF, the Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) Working Group, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Go Green Initiative, officially launched the Ald-Aim Community Centre in Khartoum, marking a key milestone in efforts to expand community access to information, learning opportunities and essential digital services.

Situation overview

July was characterized by worsening conflict dynamics, growing health emergencies, sustained largescale humanitarian needs, and inadequate funding levels, leaving millions of Sudanese civilians dependent on humanitarian assistance while facing heightened protection, food security, and health risks. Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) intensified in several areas, particularly in North Kordofan, Darfur, and parts of the Kordofan region, resulting in civilian casualties, displacement, and damage to critical infrastructure.

North Kordofan emerged as a major hotspot during the reporting period. The humanitarian situation was further aggravated by a growing cholera outbreak. Humanitarian actors expanded surveillance, treatment, and prevention activities, but response efforts remained constrained by insecurity, limited access, and significant funding shortages

title: Early Action Protocol Activation Report: Kenya Drought, July 2026 (EAP №: EAP2022KE02, Operation №: MDRKE055)
content:
EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL SUMMARY

Back in October 2022, the IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) allocated CHF 365,775 to the Kenya Red Cross Society (KRCS) to implement early actions aimed at reducing and mitigating the impacts of drought in Kenya. These early actions were pre-agreed with the National Society and are outlined in the Early Action Protocol MDRKE055_EAP-6.pdf

Kenya is currently facing a severe and evolving drought crisis driven by the poor performance of consecutive rainfall seasons, with the 2025 October–November–December (OND) short rains performing significantly below average. This exacerbated existing vulnerabilities across the Arid and Semi-Arid Lands (ASALs). Prolonged rainfall deficits, above-average temperatures, and delayed seasonal recovery have resulted in acute water shortages, deteriorating pasture conditions, declining livestock productivity, and increased food and nutrition insecurity among already vulnerable populations. The severity of acute food insecurity situation was confirmed by the NDMA Report on Drought and Food Security Situation and Ongoing Interventions February 2026.docxindicating that approximately 3.69 million people in Kenya are projected to require humanitarian food assistance.

Poor rainfall performance has reduced water and pasture availability across the ASALs, prompting many pastoral households to migrate in search of these resources to sustain their livestock and livelihoods. While mobility remains a traditional coping strategy, it has increased pressure on limited rangelands and water points, sometimes triggering tensions within and between communities competing over scarce resources. These disputes have occasionally disrupted livelihoods, led to loss of life, and threatened community cohesion. Increased inter- and intra-community tensions have been reported, particularly along the Turkana–Ethiopia border and in Marsabit and Lamu counties. Concurrently, livestock movements from Mandera to Wajir are placing additional strain on already scarce grazing and water resources, increasing the likelihood of conflict.

The Kenya Red Cross Society (KRCS) implemented the Drought Early Action Protocol following trigger activation based on the Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) forecast indicating a Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) below -0.98 in Kitui, Kwale, and Kilifi Counties. The activation allowed early actions to be implemented ahead of the projected below-average OND rain season to mitigate the anticipated impacts of drought. The EAP was designed to support 30,000 households (150,000 people) through a combination of early warning dissemination, livelihood protection, and improved water access. Sector-specific interventions targeted 4,500 households under livelihoods and 1,500 households under WASH, while early warning messaging and community engagement reached a broader population.

title: Somalia | Complex Emergency - DREF Final Report (MDRSO025)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met
23-09-2025
What happened, where and when?

Somalia experienced one of its most severe droughts in decades following multiple successive failed rainy seasons, culminating in the near-total failure of the 2025 Deyr (October–December) rains. As the Jilaal (January–March) dry season progressed, drought conditions intensified nationwide, driven by prolonged rainfall deficits, extreme dry conditions, and record-low river levels. According to national authorities, approximately 4.61 million people were affected, including more than 490,730 internally displaced persons (IDPs).

The humanitarian consequences deteriorated rapidly. Between February and March 2026, an estimated 6.5 million people experienced severe acute food insecurity (IPC Acute Food Insecurity Phase 3 or above), nearly double the number recorded in August 2025. Of these, more than 2 million people were classified in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency), requiring urgent humanitarian assistance to address critical food consumption gaps, protect livelihoods, and prevent further loss of life.

The nutrition situation also reached alarming levels an estimated 1.84 million children were projected to suffer acute malnutrition, including approximately 483,000 children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) requiring lifesaving treatment. In January 2026, acute malnutrition was classified as Critical (IPC AMN Phase 4) in 18 of 48 analysed districts and Serious (IPC AMN Phase 3) in another 19 districts. Conditions were expected to deteriorate further between February and June due to worsening food insecurity, a high disease burden, and reduced humanitarian funding that constrained access to health and nutrition services. IDPs remained among the most vulnerable populations, with urgent integrated, multi-sectoral interventions required to prevent further deterioration and reduce mortality among children and pregnant and breastfeeding women.

Disease outbreaks compounded the crisis. By early December 2025, Somalia had recorded 3,375 diphtheria cases with 139 associated deaths, 11,599 measles cases, 11,952 malaria cases, and continued transmission of acute watery diarrhoea (AWD)/cholera. The declaration of a Marburg Virus Disease outbreak in neighbouring Ethiopia further increased cross-border public health risks, while the combination of disease outbreaks, malnutrition, and food insecurity significantly heightened vulnerability among affected communities.

The drought affected large parts of the country. More than 1.1 million people were impacted in Galgaduud and Mudug, over 1 million people were affected across Togdheer, Sanaag, Awdal, Woqooyi Galbeed, Gedo, and Bari, and more than 930,000 people were affected in Bay, Bakool, and Lower Shabelle. Water shortages became increasingly severe as sections of the Shabelle River dried up in Middle Shabelle, leaving more than 65 villages in Jowhar District without reliable water sources and forcing communities to rely on failing shallow wells and overstretched boreholes. Similarly, sharply reduced water levels along the Juba River left an estimated 200,000 people in Gedo Region facing critical water shortages.

According to the World Food Programme (WFP), Somalia was approaching a major humanitarian breakdown. Consecutive rainfall failures, record-low river levels, collapsing livelihoods, and rapidly worsening food security mirrored the warning signs that preceded the 2011 famine and the 2022 near-famine emergency. By the close of the DREF operation, Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) prevalence had exceeded 25 per cent among IDPs and agropastoral livelihood groups, reaching levels comparable to the early stages of previous famine crises. Nearly one million people were projected to enter IPC Phase 4 (Emergency) within weeks, while conflict, climate shocks, displacement, disease outbreaks, and declining humanitarian funding were expected to sustain a protracted Grade-3 health emergency throughout the remainder of 2026. Although humanitarian planning figures for 2026 estimated approximately 4.8 million people in need, this reduction from the estimated 7.5 million affected in 2025 reflected narrower geographic targeting and funding constraints under the humanitarian reset rather than any meaningful improvement in underlying humanitarian conditions.

title: Algeria: Fire 2026, DREF Operation (MDRDZ015)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
18-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 18 July 2026, the wildfire emergency in Algeria reached a significant operational peak, with 154 forest, vegetation and agricultural fires recorded within 24 hours across several wilayas. Of these, 138 fires were extinguished, while 16 remained active at the time of reporting.

The incident formed part of a wider sequence of fires that had affected the country since early July; the General Directorate of Civil Protection reported that 913 fires had been extinguished nationally between 8 and 15 July.

The fires affected northern, north-eastern, central and western Algeria, including Annaba, Souk Ahras, Skikda, Guelma, Bouira, Médéa, Mila, Mascara, El Tarf, Jijel, Sétif, Béjaïa, Tlemcen, Saïda, Tissemsilt, Biskra and Chlef.

The Ministry of the Interior, Local Authorities and Transport subsequently confirmed six fatalities linked to the fires and instructed the affected wilayas to undertake a comprehensive inventory of losses.

In Seraïdi, Annaba, more than 100 patients were evacuated from a rehabilitation hospital, while approximately 150 homes were affected or threatened. Preventive evacuations were also carried out in several localities, including El Tarf, Béjaïa, Guelma and Bouira.

The Government of Algeria has led a strong and coordinated national response, ensuring the rapid mobilization of the competent authorities and emergency services. As fires continued later in July, additional national resources were mobilized, including military personnel, firefighting vehicles, ambulances, aircraft and helicopters in several affected wilayas.

Government efforts have focused on protecting lives, supporting affected communities, securing threatened areas and maintaining close operational coordination across the affected wilayas.

The Algerian Red Crescent mobilized its provinces committees, volunteers and logistical resources from the beginning of the emergency.

Teams provided first aid, drinking water, food assistance, psychosocial support and essential humanitarian assistance to affected communities and emergency responders.

Response and monitoring activities continue, while high temperatures, dry vegetation, difficult terrain and the risk of fire re-ignition remain important operational considerations.

title: SLE: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 08-2026 - SLE: Flash Flood - 08-2026 - Freetown (2026-08-04)
content:
Description

On the early morning of 3 August 2026, Freetown experienced approximately six to seven hours of continuous heavy rainfall, resulting in widespread flash flooding, severe erosion, and slope collapse incidents across several low-lying and hillside communities. The incidents caused significant damage to homes and infrastructure, displaced hundreds of people, resulted in fatalities and missing persons, and contaminated critical water sources.

The National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA), together with SLRCS and other partners, immediately deployed field teams to conduct search and rescue operations and preliminary assessments in the affected communities

The heavy rain fall resulted in significant humanitarian impacts across several communities, particularly in Portor Community, Juba, Metchem Community, and Femi Turner Drive. Preliminary assessments indicate that more than 300 houses were flooded and damaged forcing hundreds of families to leave their homes and resulting in the loss of household belongings and livelihoods.

The incident also resulted in three confirmed fatalities after a compound wall collapsed during the heavy rains, killing a five-year-old girl, her mother, and grandmother. Additionally, two children remain missing, with search and rescue operations continuing, no injuries has been officially confirmed.

Critical infrastructure was also affected. Eight community boreholes, which serve as the main source of drinking water, were contaminated by floodwaters and declared unsafe for consumption, increasing the risk of waterborne disease outbreaks. Further damage was recorded at Femi Turner Drive, where severe erosion caused the collapse of a perimeter wall, resulting in three vehicles being washed away.

title: MNG: Flood - 08-2026 - Urban flood (2026-08-04)
content:
Description

Heavy rainfall on 1 August 2026 caused river and flash flooding in several parts of Ulaanbaatar, particularly in Khan-Uul and Songino-Khairkhan districts. The Tuul River exceeded the dangerous flood level and overflowed near the Biocombinat area, flooding homes, businesses, and public facilities.

More than 190 people required rescue or evacuation assistance across at least three affected areas. Two children were found unconscious after being swept away by floodwater, received emergency first aid, and were transferred to hospital. No deaths or missing persons were reported.

A preliminary assessment in Khan-Uul District identified 22 affected households, of which 20 were low-income or otherwise vulnerable. At least 65 people were evacuated, 38 were initially accommodated in temporary shelter, and 10 people remained displaced as of 4 August because their homes were not yet safe for return.

Immediate humanitarian needs include food, hygiene kits, cleaning and disinfection materials, essential household items, safe water, temporary accommodation and early-recovery support. Continued rainfall and rising river levels remain a concern, and residents are advised to avoid flood-prone areas and follow official warnings.

The Capital City Emergency Management Department, police, Khan-Uul District Governor's Office, and other relevant authorities deployed response teams to the affected areas and carried out rescue, evacuation, and flood-recovery operations. Authorities continue to implement recovery measures and assess when displaced households can safely return to their homes.

title: Lebanon Health Sector Emergency Situation Report Issue #20 - August 03, 2026
content:
Situation Update

Lebanon's health response continues to operate in a fragile environment shaped by insecurity, access constraints, population movements, damaged infrastructure, and limited resources. During the reporting period, newly reported attacks on healthcare and ongoing service delivery challenges continued to affect access to essential health services, particularly in conflict-affected, border, displacement, and return areas.

Since 13 July, two new incidents were reported through the Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care, resulting in four injuries and no deaths. Since the ceasefire announcement on 17 April, 67 attacks on healthcare have been documented, resulting in 39 deaths and 179 injuries. Overall, since 2 March, 213 incidents have been recorded, causing 135 deaths and 410 injuries, underscoring the continued need for monitoring and protection of healthcare.

In parts of South and Nabatieh governorates, including border villages, return areas, and some locations north of the Zahrani River, service delivery remains constrained by movement restrictions, transportation barriers, damaged infrastructure, variable facility functionality, and fragmented referral pathways. Health worker access, particularly for physicians serving PHCCs in Arkoub and Sour, remains affected by movement and transport challenges. Three hospitals remain non-operational, and 27 PHCs remain closed, while some facilities are gradually resuming services through cleaning, rehabilitation, temporary relocation, PSU-based services, or alternative health team arrangements. Health partners continue to provide PHCC- and PSU-level services across multiple governorates, including outreach, consultations, vaccination, chronic disease care, nutrition support, emergency referrals, acute and chronic medications, assistive devices, and hygiene-related items.

On 29 July, the Health Sector convened an After-Action Review with the Ministry of Public Health and partners to reflect on the 2026 emergency response, including the Flash Appeal, Flash Appeal extension, and LRP 2026. Discussions highlighted improved coordination and partner readiness that enabled the immediate response to escalation, while identifying persistent challenges related to sustainable financing, shelter preparedness and lengthy approval processes, information management and timely data sharing, disease surveillance, workforce capacity, referral pathways, and accountability to affected population.

Health partners identified several priority needs to sustain and expand the response, including continued access to essential medicines for acute and chronic conditions; support for secondary healthcare services, particularly emergency, trauma, obstetric, neonatal, and intensive care; expanded mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), especially for children and adolescents affected by conflict and displacement; strengthened emergency medical services (EMS) and ambulance networks; replacement of damaged or depleted medical equipment and supplies; expanded physical rehabilitation services and provision of assistive devices for people with conflict-related injuries and disabilities; and support for follow-up surgical care and specialized treatment for war-wounded patients requiring multiple reconstructive, orthopedic, and rehabilitation related interventions to ensure continuity of care and prevent long-term disability.

Partners emphasized the need to shift from short-term gap-filling toward preparedness, stabilization, recovery, and health system strengthening through updated service mapping, simplified reporting, stronger referral systems, and sustained national and subnational coordination.

title: Attacks on Health Care Bi-Monthly News Brief, 08 - 21 July 2026
content:
Ten years after the adoption of UN Security Council Resolution 2286, health care continues to come under relentless attack in conflicts around the world. Still Under Attack: A Decade of Monitoring Attacks on Health Care after UNSCR 2286 draws on ten years of data collected by Insecurity Insight to reveal the scale, patterns, and human impact of violence against health workers, facilities, patients, and medical transport. The report highlights the growing normalisation of these attacks, examines emerging threats, and sets out urgent recommendations to strengthen the protection of health care and ensure greater accountability for violations.

Over the period 2016-2025, more than 3,600 health workers have been reported killed, 1,558 kidnapped and 2,575 arrested amid armed conflict. In total, more than 14,800 incidents have directly affected health workers in addition to the deaths, arrests, and kidnappings, including a wider range of injuries from assaults, sexual violence, and threats. Health workers are highly vulnerable in situations of armed conflict: they are unarmed and dedicated to humanitarian activities, not military ones. Their safety depends largely on conflict parties’ respect for their medical mission and on health workers’ ability to manage risks associated with their work in areas affected by hostilities.

The largest group of health workers killed during conflict are health workers who come from the communities they serve. Of the 3,618 health workers killed between 2016 and 2025, approximately 68% – over 2,400 people – worked in a local health structure. More than 500 killed health workers were national staff working for INGOs that were running health programmes, accounting for a further 18% of those killed. The 67international health workers killed during conflict over the past decade account for 2% of the total recorded killings.21 These figures indicate not only the enhanced vulnerability of local health workers, but also a clear concentration of lethal risk affecting them.

This pattern reflects the structural features of how health care is delivered in conflict-affected contexts. Local health workers provide the majority of day-to-day care through services embedded within communities. Because of this, they are more likely to be perceived as affiliated with one side involved in the conflict, regardless of their status or impartiality in the provision of care. Ethnicity, language, residence, or prior interactions with armed actors can lead to assumptions about political or military alignment. More broadly, in contexts where health care is criminalised, instrumentalised, or deliberately targeted, providing care to civilians or wounded combatants can be interpreted as a hostile act. These dynamics undermine respect for the medical mission and can increase the risk of attacks.

title: Dengue in the Pacific: Multicountry Situation (As of 3 August 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Since 1 January 2025, twelve dengue outbreaks have been reported across Pacific Island Countries and Areas (PICs).

• During 2025, dengue outbreaks were reported in American Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Nauru, Samoa, Tonga, and Tuvalu. A total of 21,258 confirmed cases and 21 deaths were recorded across the Pacific. Fatalities were reported in Fiji (n=8), Samoa (n=7), Tonga (n=3), Nauru (n=2), and Kiribati (n=1).

• Between 1 January 2026 and 2 July 2026, a total of 4 478 dengue confirmed cases, 173 hospitalisations and 3 deaths have been reported across the Pacific.

• The Pacific Syndromic Surveillance System (PSSS) has reported a total of 8 852 Dengue-like Illness (DLI) cases to date, a lower trend compared to the same period last year.

• In 2026 dengue outbreaks were officially declared in New Caledonia, Tonga and Shefa province Vanuatu.

• The most affected countries and areas in 2026 include: Cook Islands, French Polynesia, Samoa, and New Caledonia. These account for 94% of confirmed cases.

• Dengue serotype-1 (DENV-1) and serotype-2 (DENV-2) are currently in circulation.

title: UNFPA Sudan Situation Report (1 May to 30 June 2026)
content:
Sudan is currently enduring one of the world's most severe humanitarian and displacement crises, characterized by over three years of conflict that has severely damaged infrastructure and isolated communities in regions such as Darfur, Kordofan, and Blue Nile. The collapse of the health system has critically limited access to essential sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services, heightening maternal and newborn health risks, while widespread insecurity and the breakdown of community protection mechanisms have significantly intensified threats for women and girls, particularly regarding gender-based violence (GBV). Despite an estimated 4.6 million people returning to their areas of origin, these populations face substantial challenges due to destroyed infrastructure and severely limited access to essential services. The humanitarian outlook remains precarious, as the upcoming rainy season is expected to further disrupt aid delivery, heighten public health risks through disease outbreaks, and exacerbate existing protection vulnerabilities.

UNFPA is responding to the crisis in Sudan through provision of integrated SRH and GBV services through 14 partners across 86 health facilities. UNFPA reached over 167,000 individuals with essential health services in May and June 2026, including maternal and newborn care, family planning, and immunization services, while utilizing cash and voucher assistance to reduce financial barriers to safe deliveries and obstetric care. Additionally, integrated programming supported survivor-centred care for GBV, encompassing clinical management of rape, psychological support, and referrals to protection services. Further operational support was directed to conflict-affected areas, including the deployment of mobile health teams and community midwives to sustain emergency obstetric and newborn care.

In 2026, UNFPA is appealing for US $129.2 million to respond to critical SRH and GBV needs in Sudan. To date, around 33% of this funding has been received, leaving a significant gap of US $86 million. UNFPA continues to call for urgent financial support to address the growing needs of women and girls across the country.

title: Humanitarian Feedback Bulletin: Accountability to Affected Populations - Renk, South Sudan I June 2026 Issue #3

title: Situation Report 4 - Extreme Weather Events in India - Assam, Odisha, Gujarat, Kerala and Maharashtra (Date: 2nd August 2026)
content:
A. Situation Overview :

India is facing multi-state monsoon emergencies across Assam, Odisha, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Kerala, with Assam and Odisha the worst-affected due to severe flooding, large-scale displacement, and extensive crop and livestock losses.

1. Assam Flood - Severe Flooding Across 5 Districts

Impact on Humans

Heavy monsoon rains and rising river levels have caused widespread flooding across Assam, affecting 7 districts, 20 revenue circles, and 349 villages. As per ASDMA’s DRIMS report, 1,78,837 people have been impacted, and 15,060 hectares of crop area remain submerged. Floodwaters from the Dikhou (Sivasagar) and Dhansiri (South), Numaligarh have inundated major population clusters in Golaghat, Sivasagar, Charaideo, Bajali, Dhemaji, Sonitpur and Jorhat. The affected population comprises 75,388 males, 76,104 females, and 27,345 children, with the highest caseloads in Charaideo (75,199), Sivasagar (58,824), Jorhat (28,846) and Golaghat (14,545). No human deaths or missing persons have been reported as of 1 August 2026.

title: Agrometeorological 10 days Bulletin for 1–10 August 2026 Across the Northern Tonle Sap Basin of the PEARL Project
content:
Flood Early Warning

With floods forecasted during the next 10 days, protect roots from standing water and secure the orchard. On low ground, raise soil mounds around young trees 30-50 cm (about knee height) but do not bury the graft union. Open diversion channels one hand wide and one palm deep to lead water to safe outlets; keep inlets free of trash. Move tools, fertilizers, and crates to higher shelves (about one palm above floor). Mulch 10-15 cm (about a palm to a palm-and-a- half) with dry rice straw or chopped prunings, keeping a hand-width gap at the trunk. Harvestable fruit in very low plots should be picked early and stored above floor level. After floods recede, remove (rogue) trees that do not recover and dispose of plant waste away from the orchard; wash tools with soapy water.

Pest & Disease Early Warning

No elevated pest or disease risk for the next 10 days. Keep the canopy airy by removing crossing branches and lower shoots that touch the ground; avoid wetting leaves late in the day. Collect and destroy fallen fruit daily to reduce fruit-fly breeding; solarize in sealed bags left in the sun for two to three days or deep-bury away from trees. During flowering, avoid overhead irrigation; harvest only when foliage is dry to reduce anthracnose. Keep mulch 10-15 cm (about a palm to a palm-and-a-half) under the canopy, with a hand-width gap at the trunk. Clean pruning tools with soapy water and sun- dry.

title: Yemen: Agrometeorological Early Warning Bulletin (01 - 10 August 2026) [EN/AR]
content:
Overview:

In early August 2026, Yemen will likely experience peak summer rains over the western highlands, while hot conditions continue across the interior desert and coastal areas.

Key Concerns:

Precipitation Conditions: During the first dekad of August 2026, rainfall is expected to concentrate over the Central Highlands and Southern Uplands, with moderate to locally heavy convective showers and thunderstorms. Cumulative totals may locally exceed 200 mm in parts of Ibb, Dhamar, and Sana’a, raising the risk of flash floods across major watersheds. The Siham and Zabid watersheds are at Alert level, while Mour, Sordod, Dnah, Tuban, and Banna remain at Minimal level (Fig. 1). In contrast, the Tihama coastal plain, southern areas, and eastern plateau are likely to see only light, isolated rainfall. The International Research Institute for Climate and Society (IRI) indicates roughly a 50% chance of below-average rainfall over the Tihama Plain, Northern Highlands, and eastern regions.

Temperature Conditions: From 1–10 August 2026, maximum temperatures are expected to exceed 42°C in northern and eastern desert areas, with 35–40°C likely across many western lowlands and central regions, increasing the risk of heat stress and heatwaves (Fig. 2). Highland areas should remain comparatively cooler at 25–35°C, though still slightly above climatological averages.

Implications on Agricultural Livelihoods

  • Positive Impacts
    • Improved soil moisture for rainfed sorghum, millet, maize, sesame, and coffee in the western and central highlands.
    • Better crop establishment, with enhanced germination and vegetative growth of recently planted crops.
    • Improved rangeland conditions and increased pasture availability for livestock.
    • Increased water availability, including recharge of small reservoirs, ponds, and shallow groundwater where rainfall is sufficient.
  • Potential Adverse Impacts
    • Localized flash floods may damage terraces, agricultural infrastructure, and crops, particularly in valleys (wadis) amid ongoing general water stress fir the majoiur agro-ecological areas of the country.
    • Soil erosion and nutrient losses may occur due to heavy runoff on sloping farmland.
    • Increased disease risks due to high humidity and intermittent rainfall, particularly fungal diseases and bacterial infections affecting vegetables, coffee, and fruit trees.
    • Heat stress will persist in coastal and desert regions, affecting crops and livestock while increasing irrigation requirements.

Adaptation and Coping Strategies:

Key measures FAO and partners can take to mitigate the anticipated meteorological impacts during the first dekad of August 2026 include:

  • Crop Production and Field Management
    • Complete planting of rainfed cereals in areas that have received sufficient rainfall.
    • Clear and maintain field drainage channels to reduce flooding and waterlogging.
    • Monitor crops for fungal diseases after extended wet periods and apply appropriate control measures where feasible.
  • Livestock Management
    • Protect livestock from heat stress by providing adequate shade and reliable water supplies, particularly in hot lowland areas.
  • Flood Risk Management
    • Avoid cultivation or grazing in active wadis during periods of intense rainfall due to the risk of flash floods.
    • Maintain and utilize rainwater-harvesting structures to capture runoff for later irrigation and water use.

title: WFP Senegal Country Brief, July 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP and the Ministry of National Education signed a new partnership agreement supporting WFP’s 2025-2029 Country Strategic Plan, laying the foundation for the sustainable scale-up of school meals in Senegal.

• Through its Mastercard Foundation-funded youth employment and food systems project Salouma, WFP enrolled 24,329 young people across eight regions, over 81 percent of them women. Partner organizations began delivering training and agricultural and livestock kits.

• WFP supported the revision of Senegal’s rice fortification roadmap and the introduction of fortified rice in school meals, benefiting 6,188 children and strengthening efforts to improve nutrition and reduce micronutrient deficiencies.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Food security and nutrition remain fragile in Senegal as households enter the June-August lean season. An estimated 836,786 people are projected to face crisis-level food insecurity, representing a 66 percent increase compared to March 2026. According to the latest Fill the Nutrient Gap assessment, 60 percent of the population lacks access to a healthy diet, while 46 percent cannot afford a nutritious diet.

• The onset of the agricultural season coincides with increased pressure on household food stocks and purchasing power, particularly in vulnerable rural areas already affected by climate variability and limited livelihood opportunities.

• Against this backdrop, the Government of Senegal is advancing Sénégal 2050: Agenda National de Transformation (Jubbanti), which provides the national framework for human capital development, food sovereignty, youth employment, and climate resilience.

• WFP aligns its interventions with these priorities through its Country Strategic Plan (CSP) 20252029, built on four pillars: (i) crisis response through food and nutrition assistance; (ii) prevention and treatment of malnutrition and school meals to support human capital; (iii) climate-smart livelihoods and sustainable food systems with a focus on women and youth; and (iv) strengthening national systems through technical assistance and capacity development.

title: Mali | Riverine Floods: Early Action Protocol Annual Report(EAP №: EAP2023ML002, Operation №: MDRML021)
content:
In March 2025, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) Emergency Disaster Relief Fund (DREF) approved the Mali Red Cross (CRM) Early Action Protocol (EAP) to enable the implementation of anticipatory actions aimed at reducing the humanitarian impacts of riverine floods across Mali.
The Early Action Protocol (EAP) targets flood-prone areas and primarily aims to reduce loss of life, mitigate economic damage, and prevent waterborne diseases such as diarrhea and cholera. The protocol is designed to reach up to 4,000 households, approximately 24,000 people, with a total budget of CHF 493,567.
Activation of the EAP is triggered by hydrological and meteorological forecasts produced by the National Directorate of Hydraulics (DNH), indicating that thresholds corresponding to at least a five-year return period have been reached. Once these thresholds are met, the Mali Red Cross (CRM) has a lead time of 4 to 8 days to activate the planned early actions and deploy its teams in the field.

Planned interventions include the activation of regional crisis committees, strengthened inter-agency coordination, community-based vulnerability assessments, door-to-door and radio-based awareness campaigns, distribution of WASH and health items, provision of empty sandbags for dike reinforcement, construction of emergency shelters, protection of critical infrastructure, and continuous monitoring of the evolving situation.
These measures were defined through national dialogue platforms, community consultations, and simulation exercises (“dry tests”) conducted in 2019 and 2020, and were subsequently refined following the real activation of the EAP in September 2022. They were selected based on their effectiveness in reducing priority risks, their operational feasibility within short lead times, and their acceptance by at-risk communities.

The Mali Red Cross has strong institutional and operational capacity to implement the EAP, including a nationwide network of trained volunteers, experienced technical teams across sectors, pre-positioned stocks in multiple regions, framework agreements with local suppliers, and close collaboration with government technical services—particularly the General Directorate of Civil Protection (DGPC). These capacities ensure a timely, efficient, and well-coordinated response, even in hard-to-reach areas.

Beyond immediate response, the EAP contributes to strengthening long-term preparedness and community resilience to flooding, including in situations where anticipated events do not fully materialize. This is achieved through sustained awareness-raising, reinforcement of protective infrastructure, and improvements in early warning systems

title: Cape Verde | Drought - Simplified Early Action Protocol (sEAP2025CV01 | MDRCV006)
content:
RISK ANALYSIS AND EARLY ACTION SELECTION

Priority risks and their historical impact.

Cape Verde is exposed to several natural hazards, including, but not limited to, droughts, floods, landslides, tropical storms, heatwaves, epidemics, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, locust infestations, coastal erosion and sea-level rise (IFRC, 2025; World Bank Group, 2025; World Bank Group and GFDRR, 2020). According to the INFORMRISK database, in 2025, Cape Verde has a risk and exposure index (probability of physical exposure associated with various risks) of 0.8 on a scale of 0 to 10, with a vulnerability index of 3.3 and an adaptation capacity deficit index of 4.1. This suggests that, although the country has an overall low level of exposure to all hazards combined, its low adaptive capacity linked to institutional challenges (disaster risk management and governance) and to those arising from a lack of infrastructure and health services increases the vulnerability of the population to disaster risks. These risks are exacerbated by high rates of rural exodus, soil degradation, poor connectivity between the islands, persistent poverty and high levels of debt (World Bank Group, 2025).
According to the EM-DAT database, which provides information on major disasters, Cape Verde recorded 24 major events between 1900 and 2024, affecting a total of 234,264 people and causing 85,298 deaths (Table 1). These disasters include droughts, which account for 50 per cent of recorded events, epidemics (13 per cent), tropical storms (13 per cent), floods (8 per cent), locust swarms (8 per cent) and volcanic activity (8 per cent).

title: Aceh, North Sumatra and West Sumatra Provinces, Indonesia Flood 2025 - DREF Operational Update (MDRID028), 31/07/2026
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event
26-11-2025
What happened, where and when?

Tropical Cyclone Senyar originated as Tropical Disturbance 95B over the Strait of Malacca on 21 November 2025. The system gradually intensified into a tropical depression by 25 November and was officially upgraded to a tropical cyclone by Indonesia’s Meteorological, Climatological, and Geophysical Agency (BMKG) on 26 November 2025.

Forming near the equator northwest of Aceh Province, the cyclone tracked across Sumatra, affecting Aceh, North Sumatra, and West Sumatra. It made landfall on 26 November 2025, bringing torrential rainfall, destructive winds, and severe storm surges to multiple provinces.

Heavy rainfall had already intensified from 23 November, but the cyclone’s landfall triggered widespread flash floods and landslides. A total of 35 districts and cities across three provinces were directly affected, while many neighbouring areas experienced severe access and logistical disruptions. Emergency response operations were rapidly activated as structural damage and humanitarian needs escalated.

Current Humanitarian Situation and Recovery Needs

As of the reporting date of 15 June 2026, affected communities have not yet fully recovered from the disaster. While humanitarian response activities from agencies have concluded, recovery needs remain significant. Although there are no longer people living in internally displaced person (IDP) centres, many affected families continue to live in temporary houses constructed by the government, stay with relatives, or remain in their own homes despite ongoing challenges related to damaged structures, poor sanitation conditions, and an uncomfortable living environment.

Large areas of agricultural land remain covered by hardened layers of mud and waste, which are costly and difficult for individual households to remove, preventing communities from restarting agricultural activities. Many households also lost their tools and equipment needed for their businesses and livelihoods. Most affected families expressed the need for capital support to restart their businesses and restore their livelihoods.

The current situation is perceived as more challenging by some affected communities, as assistance received during the two to four months of displacement has ceased, while households now need to cover food and other basic needs despite significantly reduced or lost income sources. Many affected people are seeking temporary employment as daily labourers or selling remaining crops from available trees to meet their immediate needs.

Some village public health clinics have also not yet resumed operations, as health equipment and supplies were damaged or swept away during the disaster.

Government Housing Recovery Assistance Specific government stimulus assistance has been provided to households affected by the floods in Sumatra that occurred in late November 2025. Housing assistance is provided based on the level of damage: IDR 15 million for houses with minor damage (0–30 per cent damage), IDR 30 million for houses with moderate damage (30–70 per cent damage), and IDR 60 million for houses with severe damage (more than 70 per cent damage) for reconstruction. Housing damage assessments refer to the regulations of the Minister of Public Works and the BNPB Implementation Guidelines.

For disaster-affected households whose homes are severely damaged and no longer habitable, and who choose not to stay in temporary housing (huntara), the government provides Dana Tunggu Hunian (DTH) or Housing Waiting Funds amounting to IDR 600,000 per family per month.

As of June 2026, according to Indonesia’s Disaster Geoportal Data Bencana Indonesia, government housing recovery support includes:

(1) Aceh: The government has built 18,738 temporary houses and 260 permanent houses, distributed stimulus assistance to 15,192 houses with minor damage and 11,069 houses with moderate damage, and distributed 13,704 DTH assistance.
(2) North Sumatra: The government has built 1,024 temporary houses and 548 permanent houses, distributed stimulus assistance to 2,332 houses with minor damage and 1,228 houses with moderate damage, and distributed 4,288 DTH assistance.
(3) West Sumatra: The government has built 830 temporary houses and 19 permanent houses, distributed stimulus assistance to 811 houses with minor damage and 375 houses with moderate damage, and distributed 2,992 DTH assistance.

title: MAR: Population Movement - 07-2026 - Massive population movement at Bab Sebta (2026-08-01)
content:
Description

1. Executive Summary

An exceptional population movement toward the Bab Sebta (Ceuta) border crossing has generated significant humanitarian needs on the Moroccan side of the border. The situation escalated rapidly between 30 and 31 July 2026, resulting in a major migration, humanitarian, and security crisis affecting both Morocco and the Spanish autonomous city of Ceuta.

According to reports from the Moroccan Red Crescent (MRC) on ground, local information and international media sources, tens of thousands of people have gathered in and around Fnideq and attempted to enter Ceuta by sea and land. Spanish authorities have deployed military reinforcements, while Moroccan security forces have strengthened border controls and crowd management measures. The humanitarian impact includes fatalities, injuries, food and water shortages, psychosocial distress, and protection concerns among vulnerable groups.

The Moroccan Red Crescent, as an auxiliary to the public authorities, is well positioned to support the response through health and first aid services, WASH, food assistance, protection, psychosocial support, restoring family links (RFL), community engagement and accountability (CEA), and logistics.

2. Background

Ceuta is a Spanish autonomous city located on the northern coast of Africa and bordering Morocco. Together with Melilla, it constitutes the European Union's only land border with Africa. The area has historically served as a migration route for individuals seeking entry into Europe.

Since late July 2026, a substantial increase in migration movements originating from northern Morocco, particularly the Fnideq area, has evolved into a major cross-border humanitarian emergency. Large numbers of migrants have attempted to enter Ceuta by swimming around border barriers or by approaching land crossing points.

3. Current Situation

The situation deteriorated significantly on 30 and 31 July 2026.

Spanish authorities deployed additional police and military personnel to Ceuta to restore order and manage the influx. Moroccan authorities simultaneously reinforced security deployments around Fnideq and key border crossing points. Crowd control measures, including water cannons and dispersal operations, have been reported near the border area.

Large crowds continue to gather around the border area, and migration attempts remain ongoing despite heightened security measures.

Several dozen confirmed; assessment ongoing

*International media have reported 41 confirmed fatalities, while field-based operational reporting indicates figures may be higher and remain under verification. Most fatalities are reportedly linked to drowning incidents or crowd-crush events near crossing areas.

Reported Injuries

Field teams report:

  • Open wounds and lacerations;
  • Fractures of upper and lower limbs;
  • Exhaustion and dehydration;
  • Injuries linked to swimming attempts and crowd movement.

The total number of injured persons remains under assessment.

6. Moroccan Red Crescent Field Observations

The Moroccan Red Crescent has reported:

  • Significant numbers of individuals presenting with cuts, fractures, and physical trauma related to attempted sea crossings.
  • Insufficient access to food among newly arrived populations.
  • Limited access to safe drinking water.
  • Continuous arrivals from other parts of Morocco, increasing pressure on local response capacity.
  • Elevated levels of stress and psychosocial distress among migrants and their families.
  • Presence of vulnerable groups including women, children, and unaccompanied minors.

7. Multi-Sectoral Needs Analysis

Sector

Key Findings

Priority

Proposed Actions

Health & First Aid

Very High

Mobile clinics, first aid posts, ambulances, trauma kits

WASH

Food Security

Very High

Shelter

Very High

Protection & PGI

Women, children, vulnerable groups at risk

Very High

MHPSS

Psychological First Aid and psychosocial support

RFL

CEA

Logistics

8. Security and Operational Outlook

The situation remains highly volatile and is characterized by:

  • Continued arrivals and attempted border crossings.
  • Large crowd concentrations around Fnideq and the Ceuta border area.
  • Significant military and police deployments on both sides of the border.
  • Traffic disruptions and localized movement restrictions.
  • Risks of stampedes, crowd incidents, and accidental exposure to security operations.
  • Potential deterioration should migration attempts continue at the current scale.

9. Target Population (Planning Scenario)

For the initial response phase, the Moroccan Red Crescent proposes a planning scenario targeting up to 8,000 people requiring immediate humanitarian assistance.

This figure should be adjusted following rapid assessments and verification of needs on the ground.

10. Proposed Operational Strategy

The proposed response includes:

  • Deployment of first aid and emergency health teams.
  • Establishment of medical and first aid points.
  • Distribution of safe drinking water.
  • Distribution of emergency food assistance.
  • Implementation of Protection, PGI, MHPSS, RFL, and CEA activities.
  • Conducting a Rapid Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA).
  • Strengthening logistics, volunteer management, and coordination mechanisms.
  • Supporting authorities and humanitarian partners through auxiliary action in line with Red Cross Red Crescent principles.

11. Main Operational Risks

  • Continued influx of migrants.
  • Evolving and incomplete population data.
  • Security and access constraints.
  • Limited operational resources.
  • Adverse weather and maritime conditions.
  • Increased pressure on local humanitarian and public services.

12. PMER

The response should include:

  • Daily situation reports.
  • Tracking of beneficiaries reached.
  • Regular review of assumptions and planning figures.
  • Monitoring of sectoral indicators.
  • Ongoing operational assessments and lessons learned documentation.

Request For Assistance
